K0.p: A general category of tales in which someone wins a contest through trickery or deception rather than fair means.

K1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Chincha, Peru): Alexander Lat. Am. 231.
K1.p: A contest is won through the help of magic rather than skill or strength.

K1.1.p: A magical animal helps a man win a contest for him.

K1.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys. H1588. Contest of dogs.
K1.1.1.p: A magic bullock, or young bull, wins a fight on behalf of its master.

K2.r: Type 1081; S. A. Indian (Chincha, Peru): Alexander Lat. Am. 231.
K2.p: Animals assist a man in winning a contest, often by their cleverness or aid.

K2.1.p: A king promises wealth to whoever the cat jumps toward, and a clever woman brings a mouse to lure the cat toward herself.

K3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 234 No. 46.
K3.p: Someone else is put in place of the real contestant so that the substitute wins the contest.

K3.1.p: A relative takes the place of the real contestant and wins the contest in his stead.

K3.2.p: A young knight takes the place of an old man in a tournament and wins in his name.

K3.2.1.p: A supernatural being takes the place of a pious warrior in a tournament and fights for him.

K3.3.p: A woman takes her husband's place and fights in combat in his stead.

K3.4.p: A wise man disguised as a monk wins a debate against a learned heretic by secretly substituting for the real contestant. The victory comes through trickery rather than fair argument.

K5.p: A contest against a magician is won through a trick rather than by skill or magic. The hero outwits the magician.

K10.p: An athletic contest is won by cheating or trickery rather than by fair strength or speed.

K11.r: *Dh IV 46ff.; *BP III 339ff.; *Von den Steinen Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 275; *Fb “væddeløb”; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 93, Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; N. A. Indian (Southern Ute): Lowie JAFL XXXVII 70 No. 40.
K11.p: A running race is won by trickery rather than by speed.

K11.0.1.p: A man challenges the devil to a race, and the race is decided by deception.

K11.1.r: (Told of animals or of men; often of the hare and the turtle.) *Type 1074; *Dh IV48; Chauvin III 32; *Parsons JAFL XXI 221 n. 2; BP III 340ff., *343.—North Carolina: Brown Collection I 703; Finnish-Swedish: Hackman FFC VI No. 275*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 92*; Spanish: Espinosa III 457f.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Basset Contes Berbères 139; Japanese: Ikeda. — Indonesia: *Dixon 192, 334 n. 18, DeVries’s list No. 120; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 445, (Tinguian): Cole 198. — N. A. Indian: *Boas BBAE LIX 307, (Oaxaca, Mexico): Boas JAFL XXV 214; S. A. Indian (Araucanian): Lehman-Nitsche Int. Cong. Americanists XIV 686, (Amazon): Alexander Lat Am. 288.—Africa (Cameroons): Mansfield 224, (Benga): Nassau 95 No. 5, (Kaffir): Kidd 239 No. 8, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 390 No. 15, (Suk): Mervin The Suk 38, (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 274, Thomas 153, (Vai): Ellis 199 No. 16; Bahama: Edwards MAFLS III 69; Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 308 n. 1; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 261 No. 60, Jekyll 39ff.; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 86 No. 18, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 271, (North Carolina): Backus JAFL XI 284, Parsons JAFL XXX 174, (South Carolina): Stewart JAFL XXXII 394, Parsons MAFLS XVI 79, (Florida): Parsons JAFL XXX 225f.
K11.1.p: A trickster wins a race by secretly placing relatives or look-alikes along the course. The opponent keeps thinking the trickster is just ahead of him.

K11.2.r: (Cf. K25.1.) *Types 221, 250, 275; *Dh IV 72ff., 91, 160ff.; Wienert FFC LVI *54 (ET 139), 114 (ST 248); BP III 278, *339.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 102, 121; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 441, (Kalispel): Curtis N. A. Indian VII iii, (Jicarilla Apache): Goddard PaAM VIII 236 No. 45; Africa (Vai): Ellis 189 No. 5, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 155 No. 30; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 261 No. 60; American Negro (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 270f., (Pennsylvania): ibid. XXX 209, (North Carolina): ibid. XXX 189.
K11.2.p: In a race, one contestant wins by riding on the other's back, so the rider reaches the goal first while the runner does the work.

K11.3.r: *Dh IV 66ff.; *BP III 341ff.; Jacobs Aesop 162 No. 68; Haupt Zs. f. deutsches Altertum XII (1865) 527; *Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 22), 135 (ST 412); Halm Aesop No. 420.—Japanese: Ikeda; Ainu: Chamberlain, B. Aino Folktales (London, 1888) No. 14; N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Schoolcraft Algic Researches 181, (Cherokee): Mooney RBAE XIX 290 No. 43; Africa (West Africa): Cronise and Ward Cunnie Rabbit, Mr. Spider and the Other Beef (London, 1903) 155f.; West Indies: Flowers 494; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 102; American Negro (Pennsylvania): Parsons JAFL XXX 214, (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 174, (South Carolina): Parsons MAFLS XVI 79, (Florida): Parsons JAFL XXX 226.
K11.3.p: A fast animal loses a race to a slow one because it stops to sleep on the road and lets the slow animal pass it. This is the hare and tortoise story.

K11.4.p: A rival sabotages a chariot race by replacing the bronze linchpins of the hero's chariot with wax ones, so the chariot falls apart and the hero is dragged to death.

K11.5.p: A trickster pretends to be lame so he is given a handicap in a race. He then returns after the race and eats the prize food.

K11.6.p: A man challenged to a running race by an ogre gets out of it by offering his little son as the racer. He means a rabbit, which the ogre takes to be a child.

K11.7.p: A racer wins by throwing pepper into his opponent's eyes to blind him.

K11.8.p: A contest of speed to reach a goal is won by a man who shoots an arrow to the goal and so touches it first.

K11.9.p: A race between a deer and a hare over an obstacle course ends in dispute, with the hare accused of removing the obstacles from his own course.

K12.r: **Hackman En Finländsk-Svensk Saga av Östeuropeiskt Ursprung (Brages Årsskrift IV, Helsingfors 1910); Icelandic: Boberg; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 137a.
K12.p: A wrestling match is won by trickery rather than by strength.

K12.1.r: The ogre: “Why do you glare so?”—“I am looking to see where to throw you.” The ogre flees (Cf. K18.1.) *Type 1070; Hdwb d. Märchens I 193b. n. 9; *Hackman cf. K12.
K12.1.p: In a wrestling match with an ogre, the man chooses where to throw the ogre, and the ogre is squeezed so hard that his eyes bulge out.

K12.2.r: (Cf. K11.6, K15.1.) *Type 1071; Köhler-Bolte I 477ff.; *Hackman cf. K12.
K12.2.p: A man challenged to wrestle by an ogre sends his old grandfather to wrestle instead. He means a bear.

K12.3.p: A giant is invincible at wrestling because each time he touches the earth his strength is renewed. This is the story of Antaeus.

K12.4.p: A man with a fever wrestles a stone image. He places the image at the wrestling place, and the fever enters the image and shatters it.

K12.5.p: A porcupine and a deer wrestle. The deer loses every time but always claims to be ill.

K13.r: (Argonauts and Amycus.) *Hackman cf. K12; *Frazer Apollodorus I 102 n. 2.
K13.p: In a boxing contest, a fatal boxer kills every challenger until the hero defeats him.

K14.p: A rowing race is won by cheating: the trickster's boat has already been sawed through, so the opponent's boat sinks or falls apart during the contest.

K14.1.p: A rowing contest is won by trickery using a magic boat that gives the trickster an unfair advantage.

K15.r: *Hackman cf. K12; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 135.
K15.p: A climbing contest is won by trickery, with the trickster deceiving the opponent about who or what is competing.

K15.1.p: In a climbing contest, the trickster sends a squirrel in place of a child, and the ogre agrees to compete against the squirrel, thinking it is a young person.

K16.p: A diving contest is won by trickery, with the trickster deceiving the opponent to win the underwater competition.

K16.1.p: In a diving contest, the trickster stays hidden by breathing under floating brush at the surface, so he is not noticed while his rival is submerged.

K16.2.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 101, (Angola): Chatelain 205; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 239; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 373 No. 67, (South Carolina): Stewart JAFL XXXII 394, Parsons MAFLS XVI 40.
K16.2.p: During a diving contest, the trickster eats food while his opponent is under water and cannot see him.

K17.r: Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 51; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 302 n. 104.
K17.p: A jumping contest is won by trickery, with the trickster deceiving the opponent about the jump.

K17.1.p: In a jumping contest, the contestants jump into the ground, but a hole has already been dug and covered with boughs so the trickster falls in farther than expected.

K17.1.1.p: A contest asks who can go deepest into the earth, and the wren wins by going into a mouse hole.

K17.2.p: A jumping contest from a church tower is won by trickery: the devil is told not to look behind him, and the man cheats by running down the stairs instead of jumping.

K17.3.p: A jumping contest is won by tricking the opponent into jumping into a trap.

K17.4.r: Anonymous Historia de Pedro Urdemales (Yungay, Chile, 1885) No. 11. Literary treatment by Mark Twain.
K17.4.p: A jumping frog contest is won by cheating: one frog has been filled with shot so it cannot jump far.

K18.r: *Fb “kaste” II 103a; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; Africa (Bankon): Ittman 88.
K18.p: A throwing contest is won by trickery, with the trickster deceiving the opponent about the throw.

K18.1.p: In a throwing contest, the trickster shouts to warn people beyond the sea, and the ogre is so frightened by the cry that he loses.

K18.1.1.r: Offers him the ogre’s cane. The ogre is intimidated. N. A. Indian (Penobscot): Speck JAFL XXVIII 56.
K18.1.1.p: During a throwing contest, the trickster shouts to the Angel Gabriel.

K18.1.2.p: During a throwing contest, the trickster calls to Angel Gabriel or St. Peter, warning him to step out of the way of the missile he is about to throw.

K18.2.r: K1746.) *Type 1063; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 22.
K18.2.p: In a throwing contest, the trickster shows the ogre a golden club thrown onto the cloud, which is really only a bright spot on the cloud.

K18.3.r: *Type 1062; BP I 148; Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr II 237, 251; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 95; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 51; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 431ff., (Navaho): Matthews MAFLS V 84; Africa: Meinhof Afrikanische Märchen 178, (Jaunde): Nekes 252.
K18.3.p: In a throwing contest, the hero throws a bird in place of a stone, and the bird flies out of sight while the ogre's stone falls.

K22.r: Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 37 No. 5, (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 277, Thomas 145, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 377 No. 2; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 124 No. 26; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 74 No. 34, Edwards MAFLS III 65; South American Negro: C. F. Hartt Amazonian Tortoise Myths (Rio de Janeiro, 1875) 20, Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 83 No. 27; West Indies: Flowers 495ff.
K22.p: A small animal challenges two large animals to a tug-of-war and arranges things so they unknowingly pull against each other, or the rope is tied to a tree, letting the small animal win.

K23.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 141, (California): Gayton and Newman 74.
K23.p: A contest in shinny (a stick-and-ball game like hockey) is won by a trick rather than skill.

K24.p: A swinging contest is won when one contestant tricks the other into losing.

K25.p: A flying contest is won by a trick rather than by flying faster or farther.

K25.1.p: In a flying contest, one contestant wins by secretly riding on the other's back, so the rider arrives first while the carrier does the flying; a wren hides in an eagle's wings.

K25.2.p: In a flying contest with loads, one animal chooses cotton and the other chooses salt; the salt-carrier wins because it foresees rain, which dissolves the salt and makes the load lighter.

K26.p: A blowing contest is won by a trick rather than by strength of breath.

K27.p: A riding contest is won by secretly swapping in a different rider or mount.

K28.p: A tournament is won by deception using a horse that was borrowed.

K30.p: A hunting contest is won by a trick rather than by real hunting skill.

K31.r: Philippine: Fansler MAFLS VII 137; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 142.
K31.p: A shooting contest is won by a trick rather than by true marksmanship.

K31.1.p: In a shooting contest, the contestant wins by producing a bird the opponent has never heard of: a wife sent in tar and feathers, crawling on all fours, is passed off as the strange bird, and the ogre cannot dispute it.

K31.2.r: At the distance no one can see it. He tells them that he will shoot it. He shoots and has his dog bring the hare. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 207 No. 417.
K31.2.p: A shooting test is won by a trick proving good eyesight: a man places a dead hare under a tree, shows it to his dog, and tells others to look at the hare under the tree, so they cannot see it is not there.

K31.3.p: In a shooting contest, the contestant secretly substitutes a bird for the arrows, so the shot appears to succeed.

K32.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 328 n. 187.
K32.p: A trapping contest is won by a trick rather than by skill at catching animals.

K33.p: A harpooning contest is won by a trick rather than by skill with the harpoon.

K40.p: A labor contest, such as a test of work, is won by a trick rather than by effort.

K41.p: A contest in plowing a field, in which the winner is decided by a contest of work.

K41.1.p: In a plowing contest between God and the devil, God wins by secretly taking the devil's horse to plow while the devil sleeps, and then trades the devil his own hare, which the devil thinks has plowed so much that he gladly swaps his horse for it.

K41.2.p: In a plowing contest, a pig does the plowing while a dog sleeps, and the dog then runs back and forth in the furrow to claim the win.

K42.p: A harvesting contest, a competition to see who gathers the crop fastest or best.

K42.0.1.p: A trickster wins a hay-harvesting contest against an ogre by shouting that wolves are coming, which frightens the ogre into fleeing or giving up.

K42.1.r: Type 1089*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1089*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1089.
K42.1.p: A contest in which two contestants race to thresh grain, won by a trick or deception.

K42.2.p: A mowing contest in which the trickster takes the center of the field while the ogre, given a blunt sickle, is left mowing only the outer edges.

K42.2.1.p: God outwits the devil in a mowing contest: God uses a chisel and tricks the devil into swapping his scythe for it.

K44.p: A chopping contest won through deception rather than skill.

K44.1.p: A chopping contest where the hero must cut bundles of bamboo hanging in the air, but the rival has secretly hidden strips of iron inside them so the axe or blade is ruined.

K46.p: A contest of strength in which the contestants try to pull up trees, won by deception.

K47.p: A sewing contest won by a trick rather than by skill with the needle.

K47.1.p: In a sewing contest the ogre uses the entire length of thread for a single stitch, so when he walks back from the first stitch the tailor has already finished.

K48.p: A bridge-building contest won through a trick or deception.

K50.p: A contest of endurance, such as staying awake or going without food, won by a trick rather than by true endurance.

K51.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 25; cf. DeVries FFC LXXIII 400ff.
K51.p: A contest to see who can stay awake longer, won by deception.

K51.1.p: In a staying-awake contest the trickster wins by secretly giving his rival a sleeping drug or sleep-inducing potion.

K52.p: A contest to see who will spot the sunrise first, won by deception.

K52.1.r: (Sometimes told with human actors.) *Type 120; Dh III 147ff., 150ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 269; Irish: Jackson FL XLVII 285; Japanese: Ikeda. Cf. Harris Friends 3 No. 1.
K52.1.p: In a sunrise contest one animal sits on a hill facing east while the other waits lower down facing the trees to the west; the sun lights the treetops first, so the lower animal wins.

K52.2.p: In a sunrise contest one contestant stays awake while the other sleeps; the waker cries out too early that he sees the sun, waking the sleeper, who then wins.

K53.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 34ff.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 133; Africa (Nigeria): Dayrell 153ff.; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 97 No. 51; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 261f. No. 61; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 370 No. 66.
K53.p: A fasting contest in which the winner gains an advantage through deception rather than real endurance.

K60.p: A contest of absurd or impossible tasks, won through a trick.

K61.p: A contest to push a hole into a tree with the head, where the trickster has secretly prepared the hole beforehand so he wins easily.

K62.r: *Types 1060, 1640; *BP I 148; *Fb “sten” III 554a, “øst” II 763a; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 438; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 51; Caucasian: Dirr Kaukasische Märchen 7 No. 2; Malay: Hambruch Malaiische Märchen 109; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IX 289; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 146 No. 30.
K62.p: A contest to squeeze water from a stone, in which the trickster secretly squeezes a cheese or egg instead, while the ogre fails with the stone.

K63.r: *Types 1061, 1640; BP I 68 n. 1, II 528; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 387 No. 13.
K63.p: In a contest of biting, one character bites a stone while the other bites a nut, and the trickster wins by deception. The contest is decided by a trick rather than real strength.

K63.1.p: A hero wins a contest by eating iron grains, having secretly swapped in soft food for them so the opponent cannot match the feat.

K64.p: Two men each hold one end of a steak in their teeth and try to pull it away from the other. The Dutchman answers "Yah!" while the Irishman is still speaking through clenched teeth, so he loses his hold and the steak.

K66.p: A contest held in a dream, where the rival is won over by a deceptive trick rather than real ability.

K69.p: A miscellaneous absurd contest that a character wins by deception, not by real skill.

K69.1.p: In a contest with a magician to get grain out of a closed bamboo, the trickster brings stalk-boring insects that bore holes into the bamboo so the grain can be taken out.

K70.p: A strength contest that one character wins through trickery rather than actual power.

K71.r: *Type 1052; *BP I 149; Africa (Dzalamo): Meinhof ZsES XI 280. Cf. Type 1640.
K71.p: In a contest of carrying a tree, the trickster has his rival carry the branches while he carries the trunk and rides on it, so he seems to carry less.

K72.p: In a contest of carrying a horse, the ogre carries it on his back and soon tires, while the man carries it between his legs by riding it, winning the contest.

K73.p: A contest of hand squeezing is won by cheating, since one contestant secretly wears an iron glove. His opponent cannot match that grip.

K74.p: In a finger-pulling contest, the man wins because one of his fingers is made of iron, so the rival cannot pull it.

K80.p: A contest of some other physical skill that one character wins through deception rather than real ability.

K81.r: Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 128; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 137b; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 313, (Greenland): Rink 108.
K81.p: An eating contest won by deception, where one character appears to eat more than the rival through a trick.

K81.1.r: K82.1.) *Type 1088; Saintyves Perrault 282; Krohn Tutkimuksia Suomalaisten Kansansatujen alalta 220ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 86; *Fb “æde” III 1139b.—Icelandic: Flateyjarbók I 211, MacCulloch Eddic 93, Boberg; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 439; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 330 n. 191b; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IX 368, XII 349.
K81.1.p: In an eating contest, the hero secretly slips his food into a bag so the ogre thinks he is the bigger eater. In many versions the hero cuts the bag open, and the ogre, copying him, bursts and dies.

K81.2.r: (Cf. K82.2.) N. A Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 69; Africa (Congo): Weeks 214 No. 10.
K81.2.p: In an eating contest, the trickster wins with the help of substitutes, such as relatives who eat on his behalf.

K81.3.p: In an eating contest, the hero produces unlimited food, and his opponents must keep eating it until they are defeated.

K81.4.p: A contest to see who can eat least, in which one party is secretly supplied with food, but the plan is discovered and foiled.

K82.p: A drinking contest won by deception rather than real drinking ability.

K82.1.r: (Cf. K81.1.) *Type 1088; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 93; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 49, 94.
K82.1.p: In a drinking contest, the trickster lets the water run out through a hole, so the dupe drinks himself to death trying to keep up.

K82.1.1.p: A wager in which a buffalo and a heron try to drink the sea dry: the buffalo drinks while the tide is coming in, but the heron drinks while it is going out and wins.

K82.1.2.p: A character who is supposed to be made drunk avoids intoxication by boring a hole in the bottom of his cup, so the drink runs away.

K82.2.r: (Cf. K81.2.) Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 66 No. 14; Icelandic: Boberg.
K82.2.p: A drinking contest is won by trickery with the help of relatives who secretly assist the cheater. The cheater appears to outdrink the rival while the helpers cover for him.

K82.3.p: A man wins a drinking contest against the devil by pretending to drink whisky while actually drinking water, and the devil is secretly given vinegar instead.

K82.4.p: In a drinking contest the cheater only pretends to swallow, while a rival drinks until he dies. One animal keeps its mouth in water and so appears to drink as much as the other.

K83.p: A contest of scratching is won by deception, with the cheater using a trick rather than skill to beat his rival.

K83.1.r: *Type 1095; BP III 356, 363; *Penzer III 34; *Bolte Zs. f. vgl. Litgsch. n. F. VII 456; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 454.
K83.1.p: A man sends his wife to meet an ogre he must compete with in scratching. She frightens the ogre by showing him deep scratch wounds that her husband supposedly made on her body, and the ogre flees in terror.

K83.1.1.p: A scratching contest with the devil is won when the man's wife shows the devil scratch marks in her oak table, convincing the devil that the man's scratching is fierce.

K83.2.p: Two rivals try to scratch the skin off each other, and one wins by covering himself with several ox-hides so the other cannot hurt him.

K84.p: A contest of voice or sound is won by deception rather than real ability.

K84.1.p: A contest of shrieking or whistling is won by a trick, not by sheer loudness or skill.

K85.p: A contest of seeing or sharp eyesight is won by a trick or deception.

K86.p: A contest of hearing or keen hearing is won by a trick or deception.

K87.p: A laughing contest is won by deception rather than genuine ability.

K87.1.p: In a laughing contest an ogre tries to laugh as long as a dead horse that seems to grin, and he laughs until he dies, so the dead horse wins.

K90.p: Contests of other kinds won by deception that do not fit the more specific categories.

K91.p: A cursing contest is won by sending a curse, here an arrow that is sent as the curse.

K92.p: A gambling contest is won by deception, with the winner cheating or getting help to make sure he wins.

K92.1.p: In a gambling contest a coin is rubbed on a pear so that it attracts a fly, and the winner's coin is the one the fly lands on first.

K92.2.p: A game is won by using loaded dice that are weighted so they land on the winning numbers.

K92.3.p: A girl distracts her lover's opponent so that her gambling lover wins the game.

K95.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 14; U.S.: Baughman; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 701; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K95.p: Three daughters wet their hands and whoever's hands dry first will marry first. The youngest waves her hands and declares she does not want a man, so her hands dry first and she wins.

K97.p: A duel or fight is won not by strength but by tricking the opponent.

K97.1.p: A boar fights a tiger in a duel and smears mud on its body so the tiger, thinking the boar is harder to hurt or hard to grip, is defeated.

K97.2.r: Zs. f. d. Phil. XXVI 12—13; Icelandic: *Boberg.
K97.2.p: A combat is won by secretly swapping out one fighter's weapons for useless or inferior ones.

K98.p: A beauty contest is won by cheating rather than by real beauty.

K98.1.p: In a beauty contest, the rivals are covered with leaves so the trickster looks more beautiful by comparison and wins.

K100.p: A bargain or trade in which one party is cheated, usually by being sold something worthless or falsely described.

K110.r: French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 23; Missouri French: Carrière.
K110.p: Someone sells a worthless object falsely claimed to have magical powers.

K111.p: A worthless object claimed to produce treasure or wealth is sold to a buyer who is cheated.

K111.1.r: *Type 1539; BP II 10ff.; Penzer V 5—13; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 26 No. 5.
K111.1.p: A seller passes off an ordinary animal as one that drops gold, and the buyer is cheated.

K111.2.r: *Type 1539; BP II 10; *Fb “hat” IV 202b; India: Thompson-Balys; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 196, 443.
K111.2.p: A hat is sold as magic because it pays bills or produces money, but it does not work.

K111.3.p: A bag is sold as magic because it always provides wealth, but the claim is false.

K111.4.p: A fake formula for making gold is sold to a king, and the seller then takes away the gold the king supplied for the process.

K112.p: A worthless object claimed to produce food on its own is sold to a buyer who is cheated.

K112.1.p: A kettle is sold as magic because it cooks food by itself, but it does not work.

K112.2.p: A stone is sold as a magic soup-maker, though it only works once a few vegetables and some meat are added.

K112.2.1.p: A pot is sold as a soup-maker that already holds all the ingredients, so the buyer gets nothing special.

K112.3.p: A tree that bears cakes is sold as magic, though it is a fraud.

K113.r: *Type 1535, 1539; BP II 10; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 275.
K113.p: A worthless object claimed to bring the dead back to life is sold, and the buyer, trying to use it, kills his own wife or mother and cannot revive her.

K113.0.1.p: Seven devils' wives copy a ritual of death and revival performed over the hero; lacking the real water of life and death, the seven enemy devils are killed.

K113.1.p: A bone is sold as magic because it brings the dead back to life, but it does not work.

K113.2.r: (Cf. D1225). *BP II 10; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 99; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 196; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 422ff.
K113.2.p: A trickster sells a whistle falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.3.p: A trickster sells a book falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.4.p: A trickster sells a wand falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.5.p: A trickster sells a fiddle falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.6.p: A trickster sells a knife falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.7.p: A trickster sells a horn falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K113.8.p: A trickster sells a bugle falsely claimed to bring the dead back to life. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K114.p: A trickster sells an object falsely claimed to give prophetic answers like an oracle. The buyer is cheated by a worthless object.

K114.1.p: A trickster sells a cow hide falsely claimed to give oracular answers. The buyer is cheated by a worthless hide.

K114.1.1.p: A trickster sells a horse hide falsely claimed to give oracular answers. The buyer is cheated by a worthless hide.

K114.2.p: A trickster sells a bird skin falsely claimed to give oracular answers. The buyer is cheated by a worthless skin.

K114.3.p: A trickster sells a pill falsely claimed to give oracular answers. The buyer is cheated by a worthless pill.

K114.3.1.r: *Wesselski Gonnella 99ff. Nos. 4, 4a, 105 No. 9; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K114.3.1.p: A dupe swallows a pill sold as oracular, spits it out and says it is dog dung. The trickster insists he told the truth and demands payment.

K114.4.p: A trickster sells a bamboo cup falsely claimed to give oracular answers. The buyer is cheated by a worthless cup.

K115.p: A trickster sells objects falsely claimed to have healing powers. The buyer is cheated by worthless charms.

K115.1.p: A woman sells a letter to be worn around the neck, falsely claimed to prevent eye trouble. It works only as long as the wearer believes in it.

K115.1.1.r: Actually works. When opened it contains nonsense. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K115.1.1.p: A letter charm is falsely sold as an aid in childbirth. The buyer is cheated by a worthless charm.

K115.1.2.p: A letter sold as a magic charm is opened and found to contain insulting remarks. The buyer is cheated by a worthless charm.

K115.1.3.p: A letter charm is falsely sold as protection against plague. The buyer is cheated by a worthless charm.

K115.1.4.p: A letter charm is falsely sold as an aid in conceiving children. The buyer is cheated by a worthless charm.

K115.2.p: A worthless stone claimed to be a healing charm is sold as a cure; in the note, a sailor boy sells seasick passenger a piece of coal as a "Babylon stone" cure.

K115.3.p: A trickster sells a worthless potion, claimed to cause pregnancy, which when opened is found to contain snake's eggs.

K116.p: A trickster sells a supposed rejuvenating object, one that is claimed to restore youth but does not.

K116.1.p: The victim is betrayed by a fake fountain of youth that the swindler has sold to him.

K116.2.p: A trickster sells a stick supposed to restore youth, which is worthless.

K117.p: A trickster sells a supposedly inexhaustible vessel, one claimed to never run out of its contents, though it does not work.

K117.1.p: A trickster sells a supposedly inexhaustible bottle that never runs out, though it is worthless.

K118.p: A trickster sells a tree that is claimed to bear magic fruit, but the tree is worthless.

K118.1.p: A trickster sells a tree supposedly able to produce clothes, which is worthless.

K119.p: A trickster sells some other supposedly magic object that turns out to be worthless.

K119.1.p: A trickster sells an object claimed to work by itself, without a user's effort, but it is worthless.

K119.1.1.p: A fishing rod is sold under the claim that it will bring fish straight to the fisherman's home, but it does not work.

K119.1.2.p: A sickle is sold under the claim that it reaps by itself, but it is worthless.

K119.2.p: A trickster sells acorns claimed to protect the buyer's pigs, but they are worthless.

K120.p: A trickster sells something presented as valuable treasure that turns out to be false.

K121.p: Lime or ashes are sold as if they were gold.

K122.p: Mudcakes covered in gold leaf are sold as valuable gold.

K123.p: Gilded or plated ware is sold as if it were solid gold or silver.

K126.p: A trickster, posing as a night watchman, swaps a worthless bag for a bag of gold at night.

K130.p: A trickster sells animals that turn out to be worthless.

K131.p: A trickster sells an animal as a messenger, though it cannot perform that role.

K131.1.r: *Type 1539; *BP II 10; Köhler-Bolte I 323; *Herbert III 35; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K131.1.p: A rabbit is sold to someone as a swift letter-carrier, though it is worthless for that job. The buyer is cheated by the claimed talent.

K131.1.1.p: A hare that is said to be able to speak is sold as a messenger, though it cannot do the job. The buyer is deceived by the false claim.

K131.2.p: A bird is sold to someone as a messenger, though it is not suited to carrying messages. The buyer is cheated by the false claim.

K132.r: Types 1535, 1539; *BP II 10; Köhler-Bolte I 323; Missouri French: Carrière.
K132.p: A wolf is sold to someone as a goat or sheep. The buyer is deceived about what the animal really is.

K133.p: A wild animal is sold to someone as a watch-dog, though it cannot guard anything. The buyer is cheated by the false claim.

K133.1.p: A wolf is sold to someone as a watch-dog, though it cannot guard the home. The buyer is cheated by the false claim.

K133.2.p: A bear is sold to someone as a watch-dog, though it cannot guard the home. The buyer is cheated by the false claim.

K134.p: A trickster cheats a buyer in the sale of a horse, usually by a false claim or a misleading trade. The buyer ends up with a worthless or faulty animal.

K134.1.r: *Wesselski Bebel I 133 No. 33; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 112; England: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1631.
K134.1.p: A seller says he is parting with a horse because it eats too much and will not climb trees. The buyer later finds the horse bites everyone and refuses to cross a bridge, though the seller's words were literally true.

K134.2.p: A trickster is caught in the rain and keeps his clothes dry by hiding them under his horse, which will not move. He tells the king the horse ran so fast he never got wet, and the king buys it.

K134.3.p: A trickster grooms his master's old mule so that it looks valuable, then sells it back to him unrecognized for a large profit.

K134.4.p: A trickster in disguise wins back his own horse by trading with a man he has cheated before.

K134.5.p: An owner trades away a blind horse while describing it in words that are literally true, so the buyer is misled.

K134.6.p: Someone sells or trades a horse that refuses to move when urged, a balky horse, to an unsuspecting buyer.

K134.7.p: Someone trades a dead horse to an unsuspecting buyer as if it were alive.

K134.8.p: A trickster temporarily lames a valuable horse so its owner will sell it cheaply, then buys it for a trifle.

K135.p: Animals with supposed magical powers are sold to buyers who are deceived about those powers, which do not exist.

K135.1.p: A dog, or in some versions a goat, with supposed magical powers is sold to a buyer who is deceived about its abilities.

K135.1.1.p: A dog, said to be magical, is claimed to swallow up the cold, so that a sleeper near it stays warm in winter. The claim is false.

K135.1.2.p: A dog is claimed to chase a hare and bring it back to the hunter's home by itself. The claim is false.

K135.1.3.p: A dog is sold as a magic animal that excretes sweet dung, but the buyer is cheated. (The note-free headline also notes the variant where a goat stands in for the dog.)

K136.p: A dead buffalo is sold to a buyer after the seller makes it look alive.

K137.p: An animal is sold as able to speak, though it cannot do so.

K137.1.p: Two jars of live black wasps are sold as if they were interpreters of a foreign language.

K137.2.p: A parrot that knows only two words is sold as one that speaks a foreign language.

K139.p: Other worthless animals are sold to unsuspecting buyers.

K139.1.p: Animals created by magic are traded for real animals, and the magic animals vanish afterward.

K140.p: Other worthless objects are sold to buyers who are deceived about their value.

K140.1.p: A magic object is exchanged for one that is useless for magic.

K141.p: A sausage filled with blood is sold as if it were a good sausage.

K142.p: Worthless glass is sold as a diamond.

K143.p: Dung is sold to a buyer as though it were something valuable.

K143.1.p: A pot of cow dung is covered with cheese and sold as cheese.

K144.p: Ghee (clarified butter) is traded for a goat or cow, but the ghee turns out to be worthless or fake.

K144.1.p: Pus from a sore is sold as ghee.

K144.2.p: An earthen pot holding rice water with clarified butter poured over its top is sold as a pot of clarified butter.

K144.3.p: Mud is sold as fresh butter.

K147.p: Worthless fruits or plants are sold to buyers.

K147.1.p: Unripe green plantains are sold as mature plants.

K148.p: Two cheats sell each other worthless goods, each trying to trick the other.

K149.p: A miscellaneous case of a trickster selling worthless objects to a dupe as if they were valuable.

K149.1.p: A swap is rigged: the dupe hands over a basket of stones believing it holds bread, while a few coins showing through a slit in the lid make him think it is full of money.

K150.p: A trickster sells a dupe a service that is useless or never delivered.

K151.p: A beggar gives a bishop, for a gulden, the bogus advice that to stay warm in winter on horseback he should wear all his clothes.

K152.r: Type 1525; Scotch: Campbell-McKay No. 11; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3442, Legends Nos. 859f.
K152.p: A thief disguised as a devil frightens an owner, who then pays the thief to go away.

K153.p: A dupe pays to learn a dance called the backwards and forwards dance, which is really just moving toward and away from a fire.

K154.p: A trickster pretends he can control the sun and sells this service, promising that the sun will shine on the fools' backs on their way to town in the morning and back home in the afternoon.

K157.p: A trickster sells a dupe a permission or license that he has no right to grant.

K157.1.p: A man collects tolls he has no right to take and gives receipts stamped "Brass Gate"; people take this to be some official government phrase.

K158.p: A trickster persuades a gullible person to sacrifice an animal and give it to him as payment for services that are actually worthless.

K170.p: A trickster cheats a dupe through a bargain that looks simple and fair but is rigged.

K170.1.p: A man forms a partnership with an ogre under terms that secretly favor the man at the ogre's expense.

K171.p: A trickster cheats a partner by dividing shared profits or goods unfairly while appearing fair.

K171.0.1.p: A giant is cheated when the spoils of a hunt are divided between him and his partner.

K171.0.2.p: A jackal cheats the other animals out of an elephant that they killed together.

K171.1.r: (Cf. J242.8.) *Type 1030; *BP III 355, 363 n. 1; **J. Hackman “Sagan om skördelningen” Folkloristika och etnografiska studier III 140ff.; *Krohn “Bar (Wolf) und Fuchs” JSFO VI 104ff.; Wünsche Teufel 70ff.; Taylor PMLA XXXVI 58 n. 34; *Köhler-Bolte I 69; **Hdwb. d. Märchens I 193a, 593b; *Fb “rød”.—Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 441, (1928) 271; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 161; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; West Indies: Flowers 497; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 441, 447ff.; American Negro: Parsons JAFL XXX 175.
K171.1.p: A trickster divides a crop unfairly: he takes the part that grows above ground and leaves the root part to the dupe, or the reverse, depending on the crop.

K171.2.r: *Type 9B; *Dh IV 249ff.; *Krohn “Bar (Wolf) und Fuchs” JSFO VI 97ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 193b.
K171.2.p: A trickster divides grain unfairly: the dupe takes the chaff, which looks larger, and the trickster keeps the grain. At the mill the grain makes a different sound from the chaff, revealing the trick.

K171.3.p: A clever man divides nuts and olives unfairly, taking the kernels of the nuts and the outside flesh of the olives, leaving the other parts to his partner.

K171.3.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 456), 103 (ST 164); Halm Aesop No. 315.
K171.3.1.p: A trickster offers a sacrifice of nuts and dates but gives only the shells of the nuts and the insides of the dates, keeping the good parts.

K171.4.p: Pigs are divided unfairly: all those with curly tails go to the trickster and the rest go to the dupe.

K171.5.p: Animals are divided unfairly for shearing: the trickster takes the sheep to shear, leaving the dupe the pig, which has no wool.

K171.6.p: A trickster divides a catch of fish so that the victim receives only the bones, while the trickster keeps the good meat.

K171.7.p: Two partners share a wife, and one cheats the other by dividing her body between them, giving the worse half to the cheated partner. The child of the cheater is not allowed to nurse from the good half.

K171.7.1.p: A shared cow and bull are divided so that one partner gets the front of the cow and the back of the bull, and the other gets the rest.

K171.7.2.p: Two partners divide a flock of sheep, with one taking the lambs and leaving the other only the milk, but the lambs drink up all the milk.

K171.8.p: A barber and a jackal share a garden, and the jackal claims the garden produced no fruit at all so he can keep it for himself.

K171.9.p: A monkey and a fox share bananas, and the monkey cheats the fox by climbing a tree and throwing the peelings down to him.

K172.r: *Types 650A, 1000; *BP II 293; *Fb “næse” II 716a, “vred” III 1195b; Köhler-Bolte I 327; Irish myth: *Cross, Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “domestique”; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 240; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 433f.; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 113.
K172.p: A trickster and his master agree that whoever first gets angry must accept punishment. The trickster then insults the master until the master loses his temper and must be punished.

K172.1.r: The mistress tells them, “You don’t know the coin.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 365, 813.
K172.1.p: A servant and his mistress agree that when angry they will curse each other with a penny, and the servant keeps raising the amount until onlookers are amazed.

K173.p: A baker sets his price for bread at the rate of twenty loaves, but the trickster agrees to pay that rate and then eats thirty loaves.

K174.p: A trickster is promised a sack of corn as his reward and has an enormous sack made so that he receives far more than expected.

K174.1.p: A trickster is promised as much grain as fits in a rope and encloses the whole crop with it.

K175.p: An ogre must grant three wishes to a peasant, who wishes for all the tobacco and brandy in the world plus more brandy, and the devil cannot fulfill them.

K176.p: Two parties agree that whoever first says good morning wins a disputed property. A trickster arrives early, witnesses adultery, and keeps the property without greeting anyone.

K176.1.p: Two rivals settle a beauty contest so that whoever first greets the other in the morning loses.

K177.r: Danish: Kristensen Jyske Folkeminder VII No. 30; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1568A*.
K177.p: Two people agree to fast together, but the servant girl secretly eats while the miser starves.

K178.p: An ogre and a trickster agree to fell a large tree. The trickster dulls his axe on a stone and swaps with the ogre, who must then do all the work with the dull axe.

K181.p: A man is to receive a peck of grain for each stack of the crop, and he makes the stacks very small so he gets more stacks.

K182.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 462; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 188 No. 370; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2449.
K182.p: A woman must sell an ox and give the money to the poor, but she sells it for five pennies only if the buyer also takes a cock for twelve florins, and she keeps the florins.

K182.1.p: A house is sold with a small niche reserved by the seller, and the niche becomes such a nuisance that the buyer pays a large sum to be rid of it.

K183.p: An ogre agrees to a contract to pay in copper coins, and each time a coin is paid out he must make a new one. A man buys a large property, then threatens to buy more, and the ogre tries to back out of the contract.

K185.p: A trickster gets land by a bargain that sounds modest but is secretly a deception. The victim sells land believing the deal is small or fair.

K185.1.r: *Type 2400; *Basset Revue d’ethnographie et des trad. pop. IV 97; Köhler-Bolte II 319ff.; Katanoff “Türkische Sagen über Besitznahme v. Ländern nach Art der Dido” Keleti Szemle III (1902) 173ff.; *Fb “ride” III 52b; Basset RTP VI 335, *VII 549, VIII 409; Rosières RTP VI 52; Sébillot RTP V 186; Cordier RTP II 295, 354.—Icelandic: Gering Islendsk Æventyri (Halle, 1883) II 92ff., Herrmann Saxo II 656, Boberg; French: Sébillot France IV 111, 180, 214; Estonian: Loorits, Some Notes on the Repertoire of the Estonian Folk-Tale, Tartu 1937, 23ff.; Greek: Aly Volksmärchen bei Herodot 114, 117; Egyptian: Legrain Louqsor sans les Pharaons (Paris, 1914) 64; N. A. Indian (Wyandot): Barbeau GSCan XI 271 No. 91.
K185.1.p: A buyer asks for as much land as an ox-hide can enclose, then cuts the hide into very thin strips to surround a large area.

K185.2.p: A deity is granted as much land as he can lie on or cross in three steps, and he takes the whole earth by his size. The note says his worshippers claim he owns the entire world.

K185.3.p: Land is sold as far as a goose can fly without landing, and the buyer carries the goose so its outstretched wings cover a huge territory.

K185.4.r: Harou RTP XXIII 169; Java: Bezemer Fabelen en Legenden 216ff.
K185.4.p: Land is sold as far as a shawl will cover, and the seller makes an enormous shawl so the buyer gets a vast area.

K185.4.1.p: Land is sold as far as a saint's hood can cover, but the seller snatches the hood up at the right moment so it cannot cover the whole territory.

K185.4.2.p: A land grant is made as far as a saint's mantle can cover, with the mantle used to claim a large area.

K185.5.p: Land is sold to whoever wins a race around the bounds, and one contestant has supernatural speed to win.

K185.6.p: Land bounds are fixed by how far a man can throw an axe or spear, and the thrower is extraordinarily strong so he claims a large area.

K185.7.p: Land is sold as far as a person can walk or enclose within a set time, and the buyer covers a huge area in that time.

K185.7.1.r: Fb “ride” III 52b; Harou RTP XIV 90; India: Thompson-Balys.
K185.7.1.p: Land is sold as much as a horse or cow can circle in one day, and the buyer rides or leads the animal around a large area.

K185.7.2.p: A buyer rides around land while the seller is distracted by a sermon, so he encloses a large area that was meant to be small.

K185.7.3.p: A king promises a wounded chieftain as much land as his chariot can drive around, and the charioteer is bribed to turn back whenever the chieftain faints from blood loss, so the land is cut short.

K185.8.r: *Fb “plove” II 850a, “ride” III 52b; cf. Olrik Danske Studier (1910) 4ff.; Icelandic: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 446b nn. 450—454, Mac Culloch Eddic 181, Boberg; Frisian: Lübbing Friesische Sagen 95.
K185.8.p: Land is sold as much as can be plowed or fenced within a set time.

K185.9.p: A buyer is to get fields that crackle when burned, and he secretly puts bamboo on them so that they crackle when set alight.

K185.10.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: L. de Backer L’Archipel Indien (Paris, 1874) 334.
K185.10.p: Land is bought as much as a tree can shade, and the buyer makes the purchase just before sunset so the shadow stretches very far.

K185.11.r: Indonesia: Snouck Hurgronje De Atjèhers (Leiden, 1893) II 84.
K185.11.p: Land is sold as much as is needed to grow a certain plant, and the buyer plants a fast-spreading weed that overruns the whole country.

K185.12.p: A saint's enemy is promised as much land as he can see from a certain point, but the saint causes a cloud to block his view so he gets little.

K185.12.1.p: A land grant is made as far as a person can see on a clear day, with the clear day giving a wide view.

K185.12.2.p: A land grant is made as far as a person can see from a high place, such as a hill or mound.

K185.13.p: Saints agree that whoever can throw a staff far enough to reach a distant island will own the land. One contestant's staff turns into a spear or dart that flies that far, and when the saint touches the weapon it turns back into a staff.

K185.14.p: A land grant is made covering as much ground as an ox's voice can be heard across.

K186.p: A trickster strikes a bargain with an ogre to buy trees on the condition that they are neither straight nor crooked.

K187.r: *Type 1610; **Reinhard JAFL XXXVI 380; *BP I 62; *Basset 1001 Contes I 321; Köhler-Bolte I 495; *Chauvin V 282 No. 166; *Wesselski Märchen 202 No. 13; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 614; Hibbard 80 n. 3; Wesselski Mönchslatein 161 No. 122.—English: Wells 161 (Sir Cleges); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K187.p: A boy promises a soldier whatever the king has promised to give the boy, but the soldier ends up receiving the beating the boy was due.

K188.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 146 No. 1800A; West Indies: Flowers 498.
K188.p: A man confesses that he will steal only a small amount, then steals a rope with a mare tied to the end of it.

K191.r: Ward II 320; *Herbert III 168f. No. 22; *Crane Vitry 152 No. 45; Wienert FFC LVI *50 (ET 96), 97 (ST 108); Halm Aesop No. 268; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 47.
K191.p: Sheep and wolves make peace by exchanging hostages: the dogs go to the wolves and the young wolves go to the sheep. The wolves then attack and kill the sheep.

K192.r: Wienert FFC LVI *71 (ET 356), 108 (ST 208); Halm Aesop No. 175; Herbert III 9; Crane Vitry 182 No. 110; Jacobs Aesop 208 No. 33.
K192.p: A man helps a horse against a stag on condition that the horse lets himself be saddled and bridled, and then the man will not let him go.

K193.p: A bargain is deceptively made by playing on a name that has a second, unexpected meaning.

K193.1.r: Anderson FFC XLII 360; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *925.
K193.1.p: A king unwittingly gives away an estate called Old Saddle, because that is the estate's name.

K194.p: A bargain is struck that the sun will reverse its course. An eclipse is taken as the sun doing so, and Atreus becomes king as a result.

K195.p: A trickster is offered a ribbon long enough to reach from ear to ear. He has already had one ear cut off, and that ear is in a distant city.

K196.p: A seller tricks a buyer by making a literal, technically true bargain that the buyer did not expect.

K196.1.r: Man sells three hundred foxes to buyer who agrees to “take them as they run”: reds, silvers, crosses. He gets a large payment to bind the bargain, waves his hand at the woods: “I sold them as they run; and they’re running.” Canada: Baughman.
K196.1.p: A man is sold foxes "as they run," and he is cheated because the seller means the foxes are running away from him.

K196.2.p: A man boasts of a hog so large that a person cannot reach its back even with a raised hand. A stranger buys it unseen, then finds the hog's back is well below the raised hand when shown.

K196.3.p: A trickster lends bamboo on condition that it is returned exactly as it was lent, so the borrower cannot return it altered.

K197.p: A servant is granted time off for Christmas holidays only until the log burns out, so the master soaks the log so it burns for a week.

K198.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1533*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1529 I*; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 324f. No. 48, FFC CXXVIII 271f. No. 170.
K198.p: A cheater agrees to trade his good horse for a peasant's poor horse on condition that the peasant eats its droppings. The peasant manages it, but when the gentleman wants his horse back and must do the same, he cannot.

K199.p: A miscellaneous deceptive bargain that does not fit the other categories in this group.

K199.1.p: A poet is promised as much gold as would stick to his hair if poured over him, so he smears his hair with tar to catch it.

K200.p: A debtor cheats a creditor in paying back what he owes, using a trick to avoid full payment.

K210.r: Irish: Beal XXI 312f., O’Suilleabhain 34, 36; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3390, Legends Nos. 490f., 749f.; Missouri French: Carrière.
K210.p: A man who has promised his soul to the devil tricks the devil out of collecting it, so the devil loses the bargain.

K211.p: The devil is tricked into losing a soul bargain by being given a task that cannot possibly be finished.

K211.1.p: The devil is set to count every letter in the church Bible, which he cannot do because he cannot read the holy words.

K212.r: *Type 1145—1154; Irish: Beal XXI 311, O’Suilleabhain 33; India: Thompson-Balys.
K212.p: The devil is tricked into giving up a soul bargain by being frightened into fleeing.

K212.1.p: The man whispers to the devil that his wife is coming after him again with her broom, and the frightened devil flees.

K213.p: The devil is beaten in a knapsack until he agrees to release the man from the bargain.

K214.p: The man turns the devil's own magic power against him, forcing the devil to give up the bargain.

K215.p: A man who has promised himself to the devil for money fakes his own hanging by stuffing his clothes with straw and hanging them up. The devil, believing he has hanged himself, considers the bargain fulfilled and leaves him alone.

K216.p: The devil agrees to release the man if he performs a task that seems impossible, which the man accomplishes through trickery.

K216.1.p: The man must sell all his goods before the devil can claim him, so he puts an evil old woman in a glass case; the devil recognizes her and refuses to buy her, freeing the man.

K216.2.r: *Type 1091; *BP I 411, III 358; *Fb “pige” II 816a, “kjende” II 140, “tjære” III 811a; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 755f.
K216.2.p: The man sends his naked wife, tarred and feathered and crawling on all fours, to the devil as an unknown animal the devil has never seen, and so wins his release.

K216.2.1.r: The devil says to the supposed animal, “Get out of my tobacco!” Dh I 194; *BP I 411, III 358.
K216.2.1.p: The tarred and feathered wife overhears the devil reveal the secret name of a plant he has discovered, which is tobacco.

K216.3.r: The sleepy man: “I am just thinking, that on earth there are more crooked trees than straight ones ... more hills than plains ... more water than land ...” The devil goes to ascertain these things, meanwhile the man sleeps. Unsuccessful imitation by another man. Lithuanian: Balys Index. No. 813*.
K216.3.p: The man must stay awake for three nights in a row, and by not sleeping he fulfills the devil's condition and escapes the bargain.

K217.p: The devil loses the man he bargained for, but gains two other souls when two people commit suicide out of envy of the man's escape, and he rejoices.

K218.p: The devil is cheated of a promised soul through a religious or magical means rather than by a clever trick of the man.

K218.1.r: Type 810; Irish: Beal XXI 309, O’Suilleabhain 30; Scotland: Baughman.
K218.1.p: The devil is tricked out of a promised soul when a priest draws a sacred circle around the intended victim. The religious protection keeps the devil from claiming the person.

K218.2.p: The devil is cheated of his victim because a boy carries a Bible under his arm.

K218.3.r: *Type 811*; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 423; Russian: Andrejev No. 811.
K218.3.p: The devil loses his claim on a man because the man becomes a priest.

K218.4.p: The Virgin Mary intervenes, and the devil is cheated of the promised soul.

K218.5.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3268, Legends No. 410ff.
K218.5.p: A picture of the Virgin Mary saves a priest from the devil.

K218.6.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3267, Legends Nos. 405—409.
K218.6.p: A priest who sold his soul to the devil saves himself by penance: he orders his servant to cut him into pieces or crucify him, which saves his soul from the devils.

K218.7.p: The devil cannot take a man bound to him by contract because friends pray over the corpse.

K219.p: A general heading for other tricks used to cheat the devil out of a person's promised soul.

K219.1.p: A man gets the devil to lose his promised soul by getting the intended victim drunk. The devil can punish the drunk man's body but cannot claim his soul.

K219.2.p: A man who has sold his soul to the devil sells it to a comrade, who then gives it to the devil. The devil can take only one soul per person, so the first man is saved.

K219.3.p: The devil is to fill a cask with money to win a soul, but God knocks the bottom out of the cask so it can never be filled.

K219.4.p: The devil is promised a man's soul whether he is buried inside or outside the church and above or below ground. The man arranges to be buried in a church wall, partly in and partly out of the ground, so the devil cannot claim him.

K219.5.p: A man cheats the devil by giving him a sole (the bottom of a shoe) instead of a soul.

K219.6.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3285, Legends Nos. 472, 489.
K219.6.p: The devil is given an animal in place of the human being he was promised.

K219.7.p: The devil is given a flea instead of a man's soul.

K220.p: A general heading for cases where the terms of a bargain make payment impossible, so the debt is never due.

K221.r: *Type 1185; cf. 1184; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 382; German: Schambach und Müller Niedersächsische Sagen und Märchen No. 170.
K221.p: A debt is agreed to be paid at the harvest of the first crop, and the man who owes it plants acorns, so the harvest that would require payment never comes.

K222.r: *Type 1184; *BP III 14, 200; Dh I 179; *Krappe Balor 154ff.; *Fb “djævel” I 189a, “løv” II 518; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 152 No. 79.
K222.p: A debt is to be paid when the last leaf falls, but the last leaf on the oak tree never falls, so payment is never due.

K223.p: A student who has made a bargain with the devil must return a level bushel of gold at the end of a year, or be taken. He returns the level bushel at once and keeps the surplus gold heaped above it.

K224.p: A man buys a horse on condition that he pays ten florins and owes sixteen. In court he insists on the bargain, arguing that if he paid the sixteen florins he owed, he would break the terms, since he would no longer owe anything.

K226.p: A debt to the devil will be returned to him only when pigs walk home instead of running, which is impossible, so the debt is never repaid.

K230.p: Other tricks in paying back debts, where someone cheats a creditor by deceiving them about repayment.

K231.p: A general heading for cases where a debtor simply refuses to pay what he owes.

K231.1.p: A general heading for cases where one party refuses to do his share of a mutual agreement.

K231.1.1.r: Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 109; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa: Meinhof 200, (Ekoi): Talbot 337, (Nigeria): Tremaine FL XXI 492, (Vandau): Curtis Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York, 1920) 44; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 230ff. Nos. 39, 40, 41; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 241 No. 14; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 109 n. 2; West Indies: Flowers 499ff.
K231.1.1.p: Two parties agree to sacrifice family members in a famine, and the trickster then refuses to carry out his side of the bargain.

K231.1.2.r: Christiansen FFC XXIV 46; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 501.
K231.1.2.p: Two parties agree to divide food, and the trickster eats the other's food and then refuses to share his own.

K231.1.3.p: A wolf helps a dog, who in return refuses to help the wolf steal the farmer's sheep. A farmer plans to kill his faithful old dog, but the wolf devises a plan to save the dog. The dog rescues the farmer's child from the wolf, and is rewarded. When the wolf asks for help stealing the sheep, the dog refuses.

K231.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 81, 94 (Herakles); India: Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/420).
K231.2.p: A person who has completed a task is denied the reward they were promised, through deception.

K231.2.1.p: Dancers are given one coin instead of the ten they were promised, and then have even that one taken away. The interpreter explains that they are complaining the coin is bad.

K231.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 78f. (ET 438, 448), 139 (ST 442); Halm Aesop Nos. 49, 58; *Crane Vitry 177 No. 102; Herbert III 8, 36; Scala Celi 56b. No. 316; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 305; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 501.
K231.3.p: Someone in trouble promises a sacrifice to a god or saint for help, then breaks the promise once the danger is over.

K231.3.1.p: A sailor in a storm promises a saint a candle as large as a mast, but privately intends never to buy it once the storm has passed.

K231.3.2.p: A person promises a golden lamb to a goddess, then sacrifices an ordinary lamb instead.

K231.3.3.p: A woman postpones sacrificing her cock to a saint until a hawk carries the bird off, then offers it up to St. Martin as if it were the sacrifice she had long owed.

K231.3.4.p: A man who has promised a horse as a sacrifice to a saint tries to take it back, but the horse will not move from the church until money equal to its value is paid.

K231.3.5.p: A sick man promises a deity one hundred bulls in return for recovery, and when reminded he owns no such herd, he explains that he does not expect the deity to come collect.

K231.4.p: A debtor refuses to pay the devil because he learns that the devil is dead, so the debt cannot be paid.

K231.5.p: A debtor repudiates a debt secured by a bond that turns out to be worthless.

K231.5.1.p: A man pledges his loyalty as security for a debt. When the debt falls due, he offers the creditor his loyalty instead of money.

K231.5.2.p: A man gives hogs as collateral for a loan.

K231.6.p: A debtor falsely offers to return the goods he bought in place of paying for them.

K231.6.1.p: A trickster buys milk on credit from several women, then pours it all into one container and says each may take back her own milk, which is now impossible to separate.

K231.6.1.1.p: Told to put a small vessel of milk into a huge container, each of the shrewd group secretly pours in water instead, believing the others' milk will hide his own water.

K231.6.2.p: A trickster gets strong drink by cheating when he returns goods to a seller.

K231.6.2.1.p: A trickster returns a bottle of water in place of the bottle of rum he has just bought.

K231.6.2.2.r: now half rum and half water. Sometimes trickster repeats operation, getting richer mixture with each transaction. U.S.: *Baughman.
K231.6.2.2.p: A trickster fills his gallon jug half full of water and then has it filled with rum at the store. When the seller refuses to give credit, he pours back half a gallon of the liquid.

K231.7.p: A debtor tells his creditor that he has already received his reward, in the hope that the creditor will not expect payment.

K231.8.p: A toad receives water from a frog but refuses to give earth in return.

K231.9.p: A servant is refused payment because of a single mistake.

K231.10.p: A man refuses to pay a murderer for committing a killing, and then kills the murderer himself.

K231.11.r: Later: “Drink up the river, you shall then have fish. All the fishes there are mine.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1634; Russian: Andrejev No. *2104.
K231.11.p: A debtor cheats a creditor by promising to pay with fish in return for bacon, then does not deliver the fish.

K231.12.p: A debtor keeps putting off repayment by always promising to pay the next day, so the debt is never settled.

K231.12.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1183*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1183*.
K231.12.1.p: The debtor tells the creditor to come back tomorrow; the devil calls daily at the gate, and when the inscription on the gate rots away he claims the debtor.

K231.13.p: A debtor cheats by agreeing to leave money on a dead friend's coffin and then refuses to pay the debt, with one party taking cash left by the other.

K231.14.p: A man who has to pay a beggar for standing in a water tank all night refuses to pay, arguing that the beggar warmed himself by seeing the temple lights.

K231.15.p: A trickster cheats in a bargain by pretending to be deaf whenever he is asked to keep his side, such as throwing down nuts he agreed to share.

K232.r: Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 68, 375, (Hottentot): Bleek 50 No. 24, (Benga): Nassau 198 No. 29; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 349 No. 61.
K232.p: A person who has borrowed something simply refuses to give it back.

K232.1.p: A man uses a verse with a double meaning to justify keeping borrowed goods that he was supposed to return.

K232.2.p: Something is borrowed for one day and one night, and the borrower keeps it permanently.

K232.2.1.p: A fairy or god lends a stronghold for a day and a night and loses it, because the borrower refuses to give it back once the time is up.

K233.p: A trickster leaves without paying for what he has received.

K233.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 37 No. 244; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K233.1.p: A bird has new clothes made and then flies away without paying the tailor.

K233.2.p: Drinkers argue over who must pay; the bartender is blindfolded to catch one of them, and while he is blindfolded the drinkers slip out of the tavern.

K233.3.p: A trickster has one of each pair of boots sent back to be stretched and leaves town wearing a pair made from the leftover boots.

K233.4.p: A man orders a bottle of beer, returns it undrunk, and takes a loaf of bread instead; he refuses to pay for either, reasoning that he returned the beer and never drank it.

K233.5.p: A jackal refuses to pay for being carried across a river.

K233.6.p: A healer agrees to take payment only if the patient recovers, and then claims the cure satisfies the debt without any fee being paid.

K233.7.p: Goods are handed over on partial payment, and the buyer refuses to pay the rest.

K233.8.p: A woman promises to marry a man in return for a pair of earrings, then escapes with the earrings without marrying him.

K234.p: A trickster calls all his creditors together at once, starts a fight among them, and escapes paying any of them.

K234.1.p: A king promises a valuable dog to each of two powerful, hostile tribes; at a feast he prepares for them, they fight and the king escapes.

K235.p: A debtor gets rid of a creditor by killing or chasing him away instead of paying what is owed.

K235.1.p: A fox is promised chickens in payment but is chased off by dogs when he comes to collect them.

K235.1.1.p: A husband promises a cow to a tiger as payment, and his wife scares the tiger away so he never gets it.

K235.2.r: *DeVries Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsche Taal- en Letterkunde XLVII 293ff.; Icelandic: Boberg.
K235.2.p: Thor agrees to give his hammer to a giant in exchange for the goddess Freyja as a wife, then disguises himself as a woman and kills the giant who comes to collect it.

K235.3.p: A man bargains with the devil that the devil may take him if he is caught at first grasp, then holds a cat that flies in the devil's face so the devil cannot take him.

K235.4.p: A defeated warrior, owing tribute to his conqueror, kills the victor rather than paying.

K236.p: A debt is paid in a literal or technical way that is not really payment, so the creditor is cheated.

K236.1.p: A promise to deliver fifty ships is kept by delivering ships that are mostly fake, forty-nine of them molded out of earth.

K236.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 306; Scala Celi 81a No. 463; *Crane Vitry 255 No. 277; Herbert III 24.
K236.2.p: Someone who has sworn never to drink except after a bargain keeps buying and selling the same mule many times a day so that he can keep drinking.

K236.3.p: Tribute is paid in snow that has been enchanted, and after payment the snow turns into its proper form, which is not the valuable thing owed.

K236.3.1.p: A saint ransoms a prince for a large amount of gold and silver, but later the money vanishes, and the saint explains that since it was made from nothing it simply returned to nothing.

K236.4.r: Dies in grave. Irish myth: Cross.
K236.4.p: A marriage contract is fulfilled in a literal way: the man is to be released when earth is put at his head, meaning he is buried.

K237.p: A trickster disguises himself so that his creditors do not recognize him and so he avoids them.

K238.p: A debtor tricks someone into granting a delay in repayment that was not really deserved.

K238.1.p: A creditor agrees to wait until the debtor has been shaved, but the debtor refuses to finish shaving so the wait never ends.

K238.2.p: A man who owes a thousand ducats gets his own creditor arrested for owing him ten, hoping to delay paying his large debt.

K239.p: Someone refuses to reveal where the Rhine treasure is, and the condition for telling is met only when the one person who knows is killed, so the secret is never told.

K241.p: A trickster castrates a dupe and promises to come the next day to be castrated himself, but sends his wife in his place.

K242.r: *Wesselski Arlotto II 225 No. 92; Gonnella 98 No. 2; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525L*; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K242.p: A creditor who demands his money is falsely reported as insane, so his claim is dismissed.

K245.r: Keeps it. Wesselski Theorie 15; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K245.p: A king promises beggars new clothes, then burns their old clothes and collects much gold and silver from them.

K246.p: A person pretends to be dead so that he does not have to pay what he owes. The trick works on the creditor, who gives up the debt.

K247.p: A customer is invited to buy something and takes the invitation to mean he may have the goods for nothing. He then takes them without paying.

K248.p: A debtor avoids paying by setting the creditor impossible tasks to perform first, so the payment never comes due.

K249.p: A general heading for tricks of avoiding or cheating on payment of debts that do not fit the more specific categories.

K249.1.p: The devil is given a grain crop that he can produce by naming it, but he is tricked into forgetting the name and calls out thistles, so his harvest is thistles.

K249.2.r: The interpreter says, “He gave me some of the egg-white but none of the yolk.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 616.
K249.2.p: A man dreams of an egg under his bed, and an interpreter demands half of what he finds as payment. The egg turns out to be a silver cup full of gold coins, and the man gives the interpreter part of the cup but none of the gold.

K249.3.p: A cheat sells a supposedly money-dropping ass, which turns out to produce no money. The buyer beats the ass to death, and the cheat demands that the buyer return the ass so that he will repay the money.

K249.4.p: A person pays with worthless goods, claiming they are valuable goods that have been magically transformed.

K250.p: A general heading for other tricks that cheat someone in a bargain or deal.

K251.p: A general heading for tricks in which someone makes a false claim for compensation for damage or loss.

K251.1.r: *Type 1655; *BP II 201; *DeVries Volksverhalen II 381 No. 145; India: Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 176 No. 24; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII *262 No. 63.
K251.1.p: A trickster who has only one grain of corn is eaten by a cock. He demands the cock as compensation, and receives it. The same pattern follows when a hog eats the cock and an ox eats the hog.

K251.2.p: A trickster demands that a guest return the food the guest has just eaten, and instead of being refused he is paid damages for the loss.

K251.3.p: A trickster claims payment for the loss of a charm after a princess lets his fly escape, the fly being alleged to be a magic charm.

K251.4.p: A man claims damages for a horse that he says is lost, but the owner has hidden the horse in the loft of the inn stable.

K251.5.p: Someone accidentally breaks a water pot and claims that to pay for it, he must be given an elephant.

K251.6.p: A lame man claims that the other man's father lamed him, and so demands payment from the other man.

K252.p: A general heading for tricks in which a person sells himself into slavery and then manages to escape.

K252.1.p: A person sells another person into slavery by deception, then escapes with the payment or without being held.

K253.p: A profitable partnership is made with both sides of a quarrel, so the trickster gains from each of them.

K254.p: Goods are taken or sold improperly, with the trickster misappropriating what belongs to someone else.

K254.1.p: A dog, acting as a wolf's shoemaker, secretly eats the cow, hog, or other materials the wolf gave him to make shoes.

K254.2.p: A trickster secretly eats the offerings that were meant for the gods or spirits as a sacrifice.

K255.p: Someone demands a far-too-high price for a service or goods and gets it paid.

K255.1.p: Someone charges thirty cakes for cooking twenty-five cakes, overcharging for the work.

K255.2.p: A crab demands seven patas of payment for the four patas of paddy that a frog borrowed from him.

K255.3.p: A crow, for helping a swan find food for its young, demands the swan's young one as payment.

K255.4.p: A camel promises a jackal a pound of flesh in return for help, and then the jackal demands the camel's tongue instead.

K256.p: A worker is tricked into accepting wages that seem generous but are actually very small, or are otherwise deceptive.

K256.1.p: A worker is promised as much rice as will fit on a leaf, but the leaf used is a lotus leaf, which is large, so the pay is far greater than it seems.

K256.2.p: A worker is paid two grains of grain and a plot of land to plant them in. The grain multiplies until it covers the employer's entire land.

K258.p: A thief sells stolen goods back to their owner.

K258.1.p: A trickster steals a farmer's cow and then sells the cow back to the farmer.

K258.2.p: A merchant buys the same article several times, from the same seller or from different sellers, and gets paid or profits each time.

K261.p: A trickster asks a goldsmith what he would pay for a lump of gold of a certain size. The goldsmith, believing the man has such gold, pays him a large sum in advance.

K261.1.r: The man says that he had not said that the skin was a mink skin and that, anyway, the cat’s name had been “Mink.” U.S.: Baughman.
K261.1.p: A man asks a peddler what he would pay for mink skins. The peddler offers ten dollars, and the man tosses in a cat skin. The next day the peddler complains he was cheated into buying a cat skin.

K262.r: Priest: “From earth are you come.” Man: “Now the steer is dead.” Priest: “In earth shall you remain.” Man: “Father, do you want the meat?” Priest: “I wish you were in hell!” etc. Danish: Kristensen Vore Fædres Kirketjeneste 139ff.; 152ff.
K262.p: A poor man gets a steer from a rich man in return for permission from a priest to speak three words at the burial of the rich man's enemy, and the priest ends up regretting the bargain.

K262.1.p: A devil helps a shepherd boy become a minister on the condition that the boy names Satan each time he enters the pulpit. The boy does so in such a way that the devil begs to cancel the deal.

K263.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 310 n. 2; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 701; India: Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 214 No. 37, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 218; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 36 No. 29; West Indies: Flowers 502.
K263.p: Two parties agree that one must not scratch, but the trickster scratches secretly while talking, without being detected.

K264.p: A bet or wager is won by a trick, because the terms seem fair but are rigged.

K264.1.p: Two men bet on whose horse will jump highest. The trickster makes his worthless horse jump out of a window, and the duke refuses to risk his own horse.

K264.2.p: A bet is made that a cat will carry a lantern into a room, and the trickster wins by having the cat do it.

K265.p: A man with an unanswered question hires a clever person, who charges a small fee for each easy preliminary question. The fee runs out before the main question is reached, so it goes unanswered.

K266.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 201 No. 393; Chauvin V 64 n. 1.
K266.p: A foolish wife gives away a bag of money or a magic bag, and the husband trades a new bag to get the old one back.

K275.p: A trickster pretends to count out payment, but the money drops through a hole in his hat into a pit hidden beneath it, so he cheats the buyer without paying.

K278.r: Africa (Zezuru): Posselt Fables of the Veld (London, 1929) 110 (Northern Rhodesia): Worthington The Little Wise One (London, 1930) 25ff., (Nyanja): Rattray Some Folk-Lore Stories ... in Chinyanja (London, 1907) 145f. No. 22, (Namwanga): Dewar Chinamwanga Stories (Livingstonia, 1900) 47, (Fang): Anthropos XXVIII 292 No. 7, (Bulu): Krug JAFL XXV 114, (Mossi, Nioniossee, Samo, Yarse, Silmi-Mossi, Fulah): Tauxier Le Noir du Yatenga (Paris, 1917) 458f. No. 59.
K278.p: A dupe is refused food until his hands are clean, but the grass around the food has been burned, so every washing leaves his hands dirty and he never gets to eat.

K282.p: A trickster sells something that does not belong to him.

K282.1.p: A man orders a load of hay from a seller without paying, and has it delivered to an inn. He then sells the hay to the innkeeper and keeps the money, and when the real owner comes to collect, the trickster has disappeared.

K283.p: A trickster gets a girl to reveal where her hidden gold is by promising to turn it into ornaments for her, then takes it.

K285.r: Wealth (or woman) is on platform. First thing touched is ladder leading up. India: *Thompson-Balys.
K285.p: A trick in which a person is made to keep whatever they first touch, so the trickster gets something valuable from them.

K286.p: A seller advertises reduced prices but uses false weights, so the buyer still pays too much.

K287.p: A seller waters down milk and sells it as pure milk.

K300.r: *Bloomfield Am. J. of Philology XLIV 97ff., 193ff., XLVII 205 ff.; *Penzer II 183ff.; *Chauvin VII 134 No. 403 n. 1; Fb “røver”.
K300.p: A general heading for tales of thefts and cheats.

K300.1.p: Cows that are stolen set off a war between the people involved.

K301.r: Succeeds by cleverness. *Type 1525; *BP III 379; *Fb “stjæle” III 575b; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 850; Werner Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIX 71ff.; Wesselski Theorie 17f.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 7; Greek: *Frazer Pausanias IV 192; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries Volksverhalen II 385 No. 157; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 71f.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 349—51, 446f.; Africa: Weeks Jungle 43, (Duala): Lederbogen JAS IV 65, (Cameroon): Lederbogen 129f.
K301.p: A man undertakes to steal various closely guarded things, showing himself to be a master thief.

K301.1.r: *Type 1525; BP III 379ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K301.1.p: A young man learns robbery as a trade and boasts about his thieving.

K301.2.p: A whole family makes its living as thieves.

K302.r: *BP III 36; Chauvin V 245 No. 147; Japanese: Ikeda.
K302.p: A woman who is a master thief.

K302.1.p: A courtesan runs away with men's possessions after they have been with her.

K304.p: Whole nations or peoples are described as thieves.

K305.p: Two thieves compete to see who can steal the most cleverly.

K305.1.p: In a thieving contest, the first thief steals eggs from under a sitting bird, while the second thief meanwhile steals the first thief's breeches.

K305.2.p: Friends compete to see who can steal the most from one another without being caught. Each tries to outdo the other in the theft.
