K305.3.p: Young men carry out a sequence of cleverly planned thefts, showing their skill at stealing.

K306.p: Thieves steal from one another, so that goods pass back and forth between them.

K306.1.r: (Cf. K341.7.1, K362.4.) *Gering Islendzk Æventyri (Halle, 1883) II 210ff.; *DeVries Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsche Taal; en Letterkunde XLV 213ff.
K306.1.p: Two thieves steal a ham from a former companion who has since married. The ham is stolen back from them, and they then steal it again.

K306.2.p: A thief is robbed of the loot he has just taken.

K306.3.p: A man is robbed of his gold chain while he is with a prostitute. In revenge he swallows her string of pearls.

K306.4.p: A blind man steals from his neighbor, and the neighbor in turn steals from him.

K307.p: Thieves betray one another, breaking faith to take the goods for themselves.

K307.1.p: One thief hides inside a money bag, and the other thief carries it off, unaware that his partner is inside.

K307.2.p: A thief who has been trusted with the money of other thieves cheats them and keeps it for himself.

K308.p: The youngest brother proves to be a better thief than his elder brother.

K310.p: Ways a thief can get into a house or treasury.

K311.r: French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 23; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
K311.p: A thief gets past guards or owners by pretending to be someone else or by wearing a disguise.

K311.0.1.p: A thief disguises himself, dressing half in white and half in black, to pass among two groups of guards and steal back his father's corpse. The guards are twenty knights in black and twenty in white.

K311.1.p: A thief disguises himself as a corpse, with another robber hidden inside the dead man's shroud.

K311.1.1.p: A fake dead man is smuggled in a sack by an accomplice, and the intended victim kills him.

K311.2.p: A thief disguises himself as an angel to gain access to his victim.

K311.3.r: Type 123, BP I 37ff.; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 118, (Zulu): Callaway 144, (Basuto): Jacottet 62ff.; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 236ff. Nos. 40, 42, 43; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 116 No. 91.
K311.3.p: A thief disguises his voice so he can be let in to take the goods, here the children of the house.

K311.4.p: A thief becomes a monk so he can rob a monastery.

K311.4.1.p: A thief disguises himself as a yogi, a Hindu ascetic, in order to rob.

K311.5.p: A thief gets into a place by pretending to be a demon. The disguise frightens the owners away or otherwise lets the thief take what he wants.

K311.6.p: A thief gets into a place by taking the form of an animal. The animal disguise lets him move past guards or owners unnoticed.

K311.6.1.p: A robber disguised as a bear is killed. The bear disguise fails and he dies.

K311.6.2.p: A man lets himself be carried off by monkeys, who mistake him for a cow. He steals their magic cups.

K311.6.3.p: A thief disguises himself as a parrot to get in or steal unnoticed.

K311.6.4.p: A magician turns himself into a crocodile in order to steal.

K311.6.5.p: A thief disguises himself as a pig to get in or steal unnoticed.

K311.7.p: Thieves disguise themselves as interior decorators and steal the hangings (wall curtains or tapestries) in a palace.

K311.8.p: A thief gets in by disguising himself as the son of the owner, so he is let into the house and robs it.

K311.8.1.p: A thief disguises himself as the owner's wife to get into the house and steal.

K311.8.2.p: A thief poses as a long-lost son-in-law to gain entry to a house and steal.

K311.8.3.p: A thief pretends to be a girl's bridegroom and calls for her, so that she comes out and he can steal.

K311.8.4.p: A thief wears the owner's clothes so that he passes as the owner and can steal.

K311.8.5.p: A thief disguises himself as the owner's grandmother to gain entry and steal.

K311.9.p: Thieves disguised as fine gentlemen steal the provost's purse. They are admitted to court without question.

K311.10.p: A thief gets in by disguising himself as a palace official and steals.

K311.11.p: Thieves disguise themselves as musicians to get into a place and steal.

K311.12.p: A thief disguises himself as a servant or menial worker to get inside and steal.

K311.12.1.p: A thief disguises himself as the owner's cook to get into the house and steal.

K311.12.2.p: A thief disguises himself as a woman servant to get into the house and steal.

K311.13.p: A thief gets into a house by pretending to be a barber, using the disguise to gain access and steal.

K311.14.p: A thief gets into a house by pretending to be a merchant or peddler, using the disguise to gain access and steal.

K311.15.p: A thief disguises himself as a god in order to carry out a theft.

K311.16.p: A thief disguises himself as a girl or young woman in order to carry out a theft.

K311.16.1.p: A thief disguises himself as an old woman, having first passed as a girl, in order to carry out a theft.

K311.16.2.p: A thief wearing the clothes of a bride he has robbed kills the bridegroom.

K311.17.p: A thief disguises himself as a beggar in order to gain access and steal.

K312.r: *Type 954; *Penzer I 133 n. 1; *Fb “kiste” II 134; Chauvin V 83 n. 3; *Basset 1001 Contes II 302; *Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 432; Missouri French: Carrière; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 391.
K312.p: Thieves hide inside oil casks that are brought into a house, and the girl of the house kills them. One cask holds oil, the others hold the hidden robbers.

K312.1.p: A thief hides in a cage that is carried into a house so he can get inside.

K312.2.p: A master thief gets into a heavily guarded city by hiding in a wood-gatherer's basket.

K314.p: A trickster pretends to be running away from a drunken husband so that he is let into a house.

K315.p: A thief gets into a treasury by way of a secret passage.

K315.0.1.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 2; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K315.0.1.p: An underground passage leads to a closed chamber, giving a thief a way in.

K315.1.r: *Type 950; *BP III 394; Köhler-Bolte I 200; *Chauvin VIII 186; **Huet RTP XXXIII 1, 109, 253; *Frazer Pausanias V 176ff.; Penzer V 245, *X 285; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K315.1.p: A thief enters a treasury through a passage that he himself built as the architect of the building.

K315.2.p: A thief bores a hole in a house wall and pushes in a blackened pot as a feeler to test whether it is safe to enter.

K315.3.p: Thieves enter a palace through a hole in the wall and carry off a newly married bride.

K316.p: A thief gets into a place by way of the chimney.

K316.1.p: A thief steals from a giant by fishing through the giant's chimney.

K317.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 312 No. 68; India: Thompson-Balys.
K317.p: A thief makes a copy of a key by pressing a wax impression of the original lock or key.

K317.1.p: A thief gets in by burning off the locks.

K317.2.p: A thief gets into a wine cellar by taking off its lock while the mother of the house is away. He makes a wax impression of the key so he can copy it.

K318.p: A trickster lures a king's watchdog away by carrying a rabbit under his coat, so that the dog chases him. While the dog is gone, he sneaks in and robs the place.

K321.r: Africa (Benga): Nassau 155, 204 Nos. 19, 32, (Ekoi): Talbot 57, 62, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 51 No. 6, 83 No. 13; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 248 No. 24; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 12ff. No. 2.
K321.p: A thief fills his victim's bag with ashes and cuts a hole in it, so the ashes trail out and show him where the victim's food supply is kept.

K321.1.p: A girl is made to carry a shell with ashes in it, and the ashes fall out as she walks, so that she is followed to where her food is hidden.

K322.p: A thief steals a hoard of gold by spying on the secret place where its owner hides it.

K323.p: A thief who has grass stuck to his clothes pretends to take it back to the ground where it belongs, using this excuse to move about and steal.

K324.p: A thief uses a coat of invisibility to sneak in and steal without being seen.

K325.r: (Cf. K341.2.2.1.) Ransacks it while “recovering.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K325.p: A thief pretends to be sick so that the victim takes him into his house, and then he steals from within.

K330.p: General methods for tricking the guardian or owner of goods so that a thief can take them.

K330.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 332 n. 199 (occurs in most versions).
K330.1.p: A man is tricked into handing over his clothes.

K331.r: Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 350; Cook Islands: Beckwith Myth 270; West Indies: Flowers 503.
K331.p: Goods are stolen while their owner is asleep, the thief having tricked or distracted the guardian.

K331.1.p: A man claims he sleeps with his eyes open, and tricks an ogre into sleeping the same way so that he can rob him.

K331.2.r: Magic or drugs. Dickson 63, 67 n. 13, 68 n. 15; Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 107; Finnish: Kalevala rune 42; India: *Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1142).
K331.2.p: The owner is put to sleep and the goods are stolen.

K331.2.1.p: A master thief puts the people watching over the goods to sleep and then cuts off their hair.

K331.2.1.1.p: A thief puts the owner to sleep by covering her with lice, which keeps her awake and scratching, then steals while she sleeps.

K331.2.1.2.p: A master thief puts the guards to sleep and then steals their meat.

K331.2.2.p: The guards are worn out by the trickster so that they fall asleep, and then the goods are stolen.

K331.3.p: While the owner sleeps, a worthless animal is swapped in place of a valuable object.

K331.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Kordofan): Frobenius Atlantis IV 134ff. No. 13.
K331.4.p: A mouse's tail is put into the mouth of a sleeping owner, making him cough up a magic object he has swallowed.

K331.5.p: A trickster steals a magic doll while its owner is asleep.

K331.6.p: A man hides a bag of money at the top of a high tree, but a servant who sleeps with him steals it.

K331.7.p: A thief lies down between a king and queen while they sleep and steals jewelry from both of them without waking them.

K332.r: *Type 1525A; BP III 379ff.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 850; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 297.
K332.p: A thief gets the owner of the goods drunk so that the owner cannot guard them, and then steals them.

K332.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 225.
K332.1.p: A thief drugs the person guarding the goods with a narcotic so they fall asleep and the goods can be taken.

K333.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Oceanic (New Zealand, Tahiti, Mangaia, Hawaii, Melanesia, Micronesia, Indonesia): Dixon 46, 59, 65; Maori: Clark 160; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 230; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/931).
K333.p: A thief robs a blind person, taking advantage of their inability to see.

K333.1.r: Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 78, 202; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 354 n. 278.
K333.1.p: A blind hunter's arrow is aimed for him by his mother or wife, who tricks him into believing he missed, so she can secretly eat the animal he killed.

K333.2.p: Three old women share only one eye between them, and the hero takes that eye from them.

K333.3.r: N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 36.
K333.3.p: A buzzard steals a coyote's eyes while the coyote is tossing them up in the air.

K333.4.p: A thief overhears a blind beggar say his money is hidden in a stick, then swaps the beggar's stick for another so he can take the money.

K333.5.p: A thief robs a blind person by throwing pepper into their eyes to blind them further, then steals from them.

K334.p: A thief flatters the owner so that the owner willingly hands over the goods.

K334.1.r: *Type 57; *Basset RTP VI 244 n. 4; Crane Vitry 172 No. 91; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 121), 97 (ST 115); Halm Aesop 204; *Chauvin III 76 No. 49; Jacobs Aesop 202 No. 8; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 17 No. 11.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 29 No. 12.
K334.1.p: A raven holding cheese in his beak is flattered by a fox into singing, so he drops the cheese, which the fox then eats.

K334.2.p: A goat gets a camel to talk, and while the camel is distracted, the goat eats all the camel's food.

K335.r: Type 1166**; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 303 n. 109b; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 278, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 52 No. 6, (Wakweli): Bender 63; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 98 No. 20, Nights 61 No. 12.
K335.p: A thief scares the owner away from the goods so the thief can take them.

K335.0.1.p: The owner is frightened away from the goods by a false report that an enemy is approaching.

K335.0.2.p: The owners are frightened away from their goods by a false report of a deadly epidemic. In the tale, a poor parson uses this to rid himself of unwelcome guests, who leave behind the food they brought.

K335.0.2.1.p: Thieves steal a pig and make it pretend to be a person with plague, so the owner and family flee and leave their goods behind.

K335.0.3.p: A trickster quarrels with the owner of the goods, then pretends to die and frightens the owner away.

K335.0.4.p: The owner is frightened away from the goods by a bluff or false threat.

K335.0.4.1.p: The dupe is convinced the trickster turns into a wolf when he yawns three times, so the dupe flees and leaves his clothes behind.

K335.0.4.2.r: Africa (Nuba): McDiarmid Sudan Notes and Records X 229f.
K335.0.4.2.p: A porcupine is convinced that a rabbit's ears are horns, so the porcupine flees and leaves its food behind.

K335.0.5.p: A thief scares the owner away from his goods by making ghosts of the dead appear. The owner flees and the thief takes the property.

K335.0.5.1.p: A thief ties candles to crabs or beetles and lets them loose in a churchyard. The parson and sexton think they are the souls of the dead, while the thief steals from them.

K335.0.5.2.p: A thief frightens a priest as he crosses a cemetery, while an accomplice steals the priest's chickens.

K335.0.6.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 388 No. 14.
K335.0.6.p: A trickster frightens the owner away from his goods with a fierce animal that is pretended to be a dog but is really a lion.

K335.0.7.p: A thief scares away the guards watching his dead father's body by pretending to be demons.

K335.0.8.p: A town crier is frightened away when he hears the voice of a churchman who is robbing a grave.

K335.0.9.p: A delivery boy is frightened into handing over his chickens. The trickster turns up his eyelids and puts on boar's tusks to look monstrous.

K335.0.10.p: A trickster lights torches and bluffs an old woman into giving him money, claiming the torches belong to a man coming to collect damages from her.

K335.0.11.p: Servants are frightened by the fierce behavior of robbers and hand over their masters' food.

K335.0.12.p: A thief disguised as the devil frightens the owner away so he can take the goods.

K335.0.13.p: A trickster frightens the owner away from his goods by calling up a herd of wild buffalo.

K335.1.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 211 No. 428, 215 No. 446; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K335.1.p: Robbers are frightened away from their goods, and a trickster steals the goods they left behind.

K335.1.0.1.r: Chauvin II 83 No. 5; Bødker Exempler 273 No. 6.
K335.1.0.1.p: A frightened robber flees and leaves his coat behind.

K335.1.1.p: An object falls on the robbers from a tree. They flee and leave their money behind.

K335.1.1.1.r: *Types 1650, 1653; *BP I 520; *Köhler-Bolte I 71, 99, 337, 341; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 182 No. 345; *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 194; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 350; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 306; N. A. Indian (Malecite): Speck JAFL XXX 484.
K335.1.1.1.p: A door falls on the robbers from a tree. They flee and leave their money behind.

K335.1.1.2.p: A cow-hide falls on the robbers from a tree. They flee and leave their money behind.

K335.1.1.3.p: A person falls from a tree onto the robbers. They flee and leave their money behind.

K335.1.2.p: Robbers are frightened away from their goods by the dead.

K335.1.2.1.p: A corpse is thrown among the robbers, frightening them away from the treasure.

K335.1.2.2.r: Type 1654**; DeVries Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsche Taal- en Letterkunde XLV 213; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 211 No. 429; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1654*, 1654A; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1654*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1654*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 130 No. 1532, 137 No. 1654*, 142 No. 1716*; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
K335.1.2.2.p: A man pretending to be dead frightens robbers away from their treasure.

K335.1.3.p: A trickster who has stolen or found an ox hits the dead animal and shouts that other people did it, so the thieves who come to take the treasure run off and leave it behind.

K335.1.4.p: Animals climb onto each other's backs and cry out, making a frightening noise that drives robbers away from the goods.

K335.1.4.1.p: Animals simply cry out, and the noise frightens robbers away.

K335.1.5.p: Robbers are scared off from the goods by the sound of a bagpipe being played.

K335.1.6.p: Robbers are frightened away from the goods by a man hidden nearby who makes a threatening presence known.

K335.1.6.1.p: Thieves steal a chest that secretly holds a hidden lover, and they flee when he cries out.

K335.1.6.2.r: They can hear him but cannot see him. India: Thompson-Balys.
K335.1.6.2.p: Robbers are frightened from the goods by Thumbling, a tiny hero hidden among the goods.

K335.1.6.3.p: Thieves come to steal the bees, carry off the heaviest hive to the forest and build a fire under it, but they run away when a man inside the hive starts screaming.

K335.1.7.p: A guardian beast is defeated by a hero's mirrors, which overcome it and let the goods be taken.

K335.1.8.p: Robbers are frightened from the goods by a man covered in tar and feathers, who looks like a fearsome monster.

K335.1.9.p: Robbers who come to steal from a stable are driven off when a bear spends the night there with its keeper.

K335.1.10.p: Tricksters scare robbers away from their goods by threatening to cook one of them. The robbers flee in terror and leave the loot behind.

K335.1.11.p: The sons of a thief are frightened off by a threat to bring three very strong men to punish them.

K335.1.12.p: Thieves are frightened by ghosts who tie fruit to their hair; the thieves think the fruit is missiles being thrown at them.

K336.p: A trickster fills the owner's house with smoke until the owner, unable to bear it, gives him a place to stay for the night.

K336.1.p: A fire is set in a village so that robbers can steal the goods while the people are distracted.

K336.2.p: A trickster fills the house with smoke so that his partner cannot see to eat.

K337.p: A giant's food is oversalted so that he must go outside to fetch water, and while he is gone his goods are stolen.

K337.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 87.
K337.1.p: A thief sends the owner to fetch water in a leaky basket, so the owner is kept away from home while the goods are taken.

K338.p: A thief ties the owner's hair to something so the owner is held in place while the thief escapes with the goods.

K341.r: Type 15*; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos 1525J, 2425, 2436*; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K341.p: The owner's attention is diverted so that goods can be stolen without the owner noticing.

K341.1.r: *Wesselski Arlotto I 203 No. 34; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K341.1.p: A trickster claims to have lost money on the road, and the other guests leave the fire one by one to search for it, leaving him alone with the fire and their belongings.

K341.2.r: Types 1, 1*; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Apapocúva-Guarani); Métraux MAFLS XL 112.
K341.2.p: A thief pretends to be dead so that the owner's attention is diverted, and then steals the goods.

K341.2.1.r: Japanese: Ikeda; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 72 No. 15; (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 172, (Virginia): Bacon and Parsons JAFL XXXV 275f.; Andros Islands, Bahamas: Parsons MAFLS XIII 10 No. 8.
K341.2.1.p: An animal repeatedly pretends to be dead, and when the owner comes close enough to be lured away from the goods, it steals them.

K341.2.2.p: A thief pretends to be sick so that the owner's attention is diverted, and then steals the goods.

K341.2.2.1.p: A man pretends to be sick so that he can go back and secretly steal gold he has hidden.

K341.3.r: *Type 1525D; *BP III 391 n. 1; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 850; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525H*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1525CI*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 129 No. 1525A.
K341.3.p: A thief pretends to hang or stab himself to distract the owner's attention, and steals while the owner is occupied.

K341.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 18ff. No. 2; West Indies: Flowers 504.
K341.4.p: A thief persuades the owner of goods to dive for treasure, and robs him while he is busy diving.

K341.4.1.p: The owner is persuaded to climb a tree, and while he is up there his goods are stolen.

K341.4.1.1.p: The owner of a horse climbs a tree after the thief, who drops down and rides off on the owner's horse.

K341.5.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 8; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K341.5.p: The owner is lured into chasing game while the thief steals his goods.

K341.5.1.p: Horses or cattle are stolen by releasing a rabbit so that the drivers run off to chase it.

K341.5.2.p: A partridge pretends to be wounded to lure a woman away from her food, and a jackal eats the food while she is gone.

K341.6.r: *Type 1525D; *BP III 390 n. 2; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 160 No. 22; Andros Islands, Bahamas: Parsons MAFLS XIII 11 No. 9; Antigua, British West Indies: Johnson JAFL XXXIV 74 No. 33; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 86 No. 28.
K341.6.p: A thief drops shoes in different places to distract the owner, and steals a ram while the shepherd goes after the shoes.

K341.7.p: An animal's cry is imitated to lure the owner's attention away from his goods, and a rascal steals an animal meanwhile.

K341.7.0.1.p: A baby's cry is imitated to lure the owner's attention away from his goods.

K341.7.1.p: Cattle are let loose to draw the owner's attention away from his goods.

K341.7.2.p: A cat is made to mew to draw the owner's attention away from his goods.

K341.7.3.p: A golden deer is sent to lure a girl's guardians away so that she can be abducted.

K341.8.p: A thief pretends to show how a horse can be stolen, and then rides it off.

K341.8.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1532*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1528*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1332*.
K341.8.1.p: A trickster pretends to ride home to fetch tools so he can perform tricks, and rides away on the horse instead.

K341.8.2.r: Dealer allows him to climb on horse to see how he rides; thief runs off with horse. India: Thompson-Balys.
K341.8.2.p: A thief pretends to be a buyer interested in a horse, then demonstrates how a horse could be stolen and rides the animal away while the dealer is distracted.

K341.8.3.p: A thief asks a knife-maker to show how a purse-cutting knife works, then uses the knife to cut the maker's purse and rob him.

K341.8.4.p: A king who wants to learn the art of stealing from a thief loses his signet ring during the lesson.

K341.9.p: A thief tells his pursuer that he has gone up to heaven by a tree; while the man lies on the ground gazing upward, the thief steals his horse.

K341.9.1.p: A thief persuades the owner to take his place so he can go and catch the thief, and then the thief steals the owner's horse.

K341.10.p: A trickster pays guards to start a fight so that the master leaves to investigate, and then the trickster goes to bed with the master's wife.

K341.11.p: A thief keeps the owner's attention on a man fishing in the street while the thief's confederates rob the owner.

K341.11.1.p: The owner is sent off to see a cat that fishes for its master, and goods are stolen while she is away.

K341.12.p: A trickster falsely announces a wedding celebration to draw the owner's attention away, so that goods can be taken.

K341.13.p: A tailor working for a stingy woman tosses a scrap of cloth out the window as the devil's share; while she runs to fetch it, he cuts a piece of cloth for himself.

K341.13.1.p: A master thief pretends to angrily throw needle and thread at his son, but the bundle he throws contains stolen cloth.

K341.14.p: While a woman's lover is visiting her, a thief steals the lover's belongings.

K341.15.p: One thief occupies the owner's attention while an accomplice steals the goods.

K341.15.1.p: While an accomplice makes a purchase from the shopkeeper, a thief steals pastries.

K341.16.p: A man throws a stone to draw away the guardian sharks, then slips into a cave and steals lobsters.

K341.17.p: A trickster gets children to dance and, while they are busy, steals their food.

K341.17.1.p: Thieves get a nursemaid to dance while they steal the prince she is looking after.

K341.18.r: Africa (Nubia): Basset Contes populaires d’Afrique 133ff. No. 52, (Swahili): Steere 13ff.
K341.18.p: A helpful animal amuses a princess with tricks and gets the key to the treasury from her.

K341.19.p: A trickster poses as an entertainer and steals meat while the host is busy gathering friends.

K341.20.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525J*; Russian: Andrejev 1525II*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K341.20.p: One thief steals while the other keeps the robbed gentleman busy by telling him a tale about what is happening.

K341.21.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1629*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1525 II*.
K341.21.p: While singing and dancing in a farmer's house, a thief signals to his friend in the loft how to steal the bacon.

K341.22.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1629*; Italian Novella: Rotunda (K341.16); India: Thompson-Balys.
K341.22.p: A thief tells the farmer to climb into a tub and sit quietly without looking around, claiming he is working a magic spell. While the farmer is distracted in the tub, the thief steals all his property.

K341.23.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen JAS IV 65.
K341.23.p: A thief sets a fire to draw the owner's attention away so that goods can be stolen.

K341.24.p: A man stands in the pillory to draw a crowd's attention, while an accomplice picks the pockets of the people who come to jeer at him.

K341.25.p: A fox drops a goldsmith's child so that the goldsmith leaves his gold bench to rescue it, and the fox steals the gold while he is away.

K341.26.p: A partridge plays hide-and-seek with some girls so they stop watching their basket of curds, and meanwhile a fox eats the curds they are carrying to market.

K341.27.p: A trickster starts a quarrel between people and, while they are arguing, steals from them.

K341.28.p: A miser is lured away from his money by a false report of a money tree, and the thief takes his hoard while he is gone.

K341.29.p: A man uses a cock as a decoy to lure a girl's fox-husband away, then runs off with the girl himself.

K342.r: Chauvin V 91 No. 196, 212 No. 121; India: Thompson-Balys.
K342.p: A thief acts as umpire in a contest between three men who are quarreling over a rescued girl. He says she will go to whoever returns first with the arrow he shoots, and while they all run to fetch it, he takes the girl.

K343.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 69 No. 10.
K343.p: A thief persuades the owner to go away, and while the owner is gone, the thief steals the goods.

K343.0.1.p: A innkeeper is tricked into going under the floor of the granary, and while he is hidden there, he is robbed.

K343.1.r: Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 110; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 77 No. 17; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 77 No. 1, Nights 241 No. 41; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 251 No. 29, 255 No. 36; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 97; West Indies: Flowers 505.
K343.1.p: The owner is sent on an errand, and while he is gone, his goods are stolen.

K343.1.1.p: A youth pretending to be a rich man's servant gets a sack of bread from a baker. He drops two loaves in the mud and sends the baker's boy back for fresh ones, and while the boy is gone, he runs off with the rest of the bread.

K343.1.2.p: A woman is falsely told that her father is wounded, so she leaves her water pot behind, and a jackal takes it.

K343.2.r: Africa (Zulu): Callaway 6; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 123 No. 23.
K343.2.p: A thief advises the owner to hang up freshly slaughtered meat overnight, and then steals the meat while the owner is away or asleep.

K343.2.1.r: *Type 1792; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 790; Lee Decameron 257f.; Taylor MPh XV 226.
K343.2.1.p: A stingy parson does not want to share his freshly slaughtered pig, so the sexton advises him to hang it in the garden overnight so that everyone will think it was stolen. The sexton then steals it himself.

K343.2.2.p: A thief advises the owner to hang up new cloth outdoors overnight, and steals it while the owner sleeps.

K343.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Cameroon): Gantenbein 70; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 128 No. 24, 230 No. 39, 280 No. 47, Work JAFL XXXII 403, (Virginia): Smiley JAFL XXXII 368, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXIV 8, MAFLS XVI 31f.; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 109 No. 38.
K343.3.p: A rascal sends his companion away so that he can steal the shared food supply by himself.

K343.4.p: Monkeys lure a tortoise up into a tree and then carry off his load of salt.

K343.5.p: A cheat tells his dupe that food has been found somewhere, sending him off to get it, and then steals the dupe's clothes as soon as he leaves them behind.

K344.r: (Cf. K355.) Bødker Exempler 292 No. 50; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 123 No. 23.
K344.p: A trickster convinces the owner of some goods that they have gone bad or been spoiled, so the owner gives them up cheaply or hands them over.

K344.1.p: A trickster asks a woman for a knife to cut him a slice of white bread, then says he has just cut a dog with that knife, so she gives him the whole loaf to avoid the bread being polluted.

K344.1.1.p: A servant puts his single fish in with a Brahmin's whole catch, and the Brahmin, deeming all of them polluted, gives the servant the entire catch.

K344.1.2.p: A servant eats all of his master's anchovies, then serves the master a covered dish and claims the fish smell so bad they must be thrown out, and the master tells him to throw them away.

K344.1.3.p: A trickster tells his companions he is an executioner who cuts up partridges, and they hand over all of their partridges to him.

K344.1.4.p: A trickster puts filth into someone's food, and the victim may then give up all of it.

K344.2.p: A trickster convinces a farmer that dung has ruined his rice field, and the farmer gives the field to the trickster.

K344.3.p: A son-in-law steals his father-in-law's pants by making him believe he has soiled them, so the father-in-law hands them over.

K345.p: A thief robs someone who has come to help or show sympathy, taking advantage of the helper's kindness.

K345.1.r: Africa (Benga): Nassau 86 No. 4, (Thonga): Junod 221, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 386 No. 12.
K345.1.p: A helper is sent off to fetch a remedy, and while he is gone the trickster robs him.

K345.2.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 346a n. 126; BP III 392f.; Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 502), 106 (ST 183); India: *Thompson-Balys.
K345.2.p: A weeping boy tells a passing thief that he has lost a silver cup in a well; the thief strips off his clothes and dives in, finds nothing, and comes up to find his clothes have been stolen.

K345.3.p: A dupe is left to look after a child while the trickster steals his goods.

K345.4.r: Africa (Kiyansi): Van Whig Biblioteca Africana IV 52.
K345.4.p: An antelope sends a leopard off to get fire, then eats the game the two of them had caught while the leopard is away.

K346.r: Bødker Exempler 279 No. 21; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Wute): Sieber 191; West Indies: Flowers 505.
K346.p: A thief is trusted to guard someone's goods and then steals them.

K346.1.r: Steals the horse. *Type 1540; **Aarne FFC XXII 3-109; *BP II 440; Berber: Basset Contes Berbères (Paris, 1887) I 114; India: Thompson-Balys.
K346.1.p: A thief guards his pursuer's horse while the pursuer follows a false trail, and then the thief rides off on the horse.

K346.1.1.p: A thief disguised as an old woman persuades a king to swap clothes with him, and then rides off on the king's horse.

K346.2.p: A herdsman slaughters the animals that were entrusted to his care.

K346.3.p: A woman is persuaded to go back for a comb she supposedly forgot, and the guard steals her goods while she is gone.

K346.4.p: A thief is trusted to watch over shawls while people pray, and he runs off with them.

K346.5.p: A man leaves his cloak with someone as a pledge that he will come back, and the holder runs away with the cloak.

K346.6.p: A thief is entrusted with his victim's jewelry or valuables for safekeeping while she crosses a river, then takes the goods and abandons her.

K347.r: Goods stolen. Type 314*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K347.p: A trickster gets an owner to lower his guard by claiming a family relationship to him, and then steals the goods.

K347.1.p: A prostitute tricks her intended victim by claiming to be his daughter, so he drops his guard and she can rob him.

K348.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 71), 119 (ST 293); Halm Aesop No. 247; Panchatantra III 10 (tr. Ryder 343); West Indies: Flowers 505.
K348.p: A trickster stirs up a quarrel between the owner of some goods and another person, and while they fight he steals the goods.

K351.p: A trickster is allowed to try on clothes and then runs off wearing them.

K351.1.r: (Or tries on boots and makes away with them.) Nouvelles Récréations No. 23; Pierre Faifeu No. 21; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K351.1.p: A trickster convinces a tailor to leave his goods with him by claiming he will receive an order to clothe fifty poor people, and then makes off with the goods.

K351.2.p: A thief borrows a cloak supposedly to carry food, then disappears with the cloak.

K351.3.p: A trickster is allowed to try on ornaments and then leaves with them.

K352.p: A trickster poses as a doctor and gets a wife to kill a pig for him to eat, so that he consumes the whole animal.

K353.p: A trickster poses as a magician, claims to cast a spell over some food, and then eats it himself.

K354.p: A trickster asks for hospitality, then drives out the owner and takes over the house.

K354.1.r: (Often told of camel and tent.) India: Thompson-Balys.
K354.1.p: A crow asks a sparrow for shelter, gradually takes over the nest, and finally kills the young birds.

K355.r: K344.) American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 26 No. 6; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 84, Edwards MAFLS III 74; West Indies: Flowers 504.
K355.p: A trickster fouls the house so badly that the owners are forced out and he is left in possession. In one version he stays in an upper room and throws filth down on those below.

K355.1.p: A trickster pretends he accidentally spat in the wine, and so is allowed to drink it himself.

K356.p: Two tricksters pretend their father has died so they can collect his rent, then flee with the money.

K357.p: Pickpockets hit a man on the leg so that he lifts his hand off his purse, letting them steal it.

K358.p: Thieves signal to each other to commit a theft using a foreign language so the victim cannot understand them.

K359.p: Miscellaneous tricks for getting past a guardian or owner of goods that do not fit the other categories in this group.

K359.1.p: A thief uses magic to become invisible so he can steal goods unseen.

K359.2.p: A thief fools the guardian of goods by giving a false name that has a double meaning.

K359.2.1.r: “Never mind the fly, guard against the cow.” India: Thompson-Balys.
K359.2.1.p: A thief who has been caught eating sweets gives his name as "Fly," so that when the owner complains, the fly is blamed. A child's shout that "Fly is eating" makes the owner think a fly is responsible.

K359.3.p: A trickster tricks a woman into putting him inside a basket, so that he can find out where the household keeps its food and then steal it.

K359.4.p: A crow befriends a pigeon in order to gain access to the pigeon's household, so that he can steal food there.

K359.5.p: Goods are stolen by a thief who uses magical disguise or impersonation to fool the owner or guardian.

K360.p: A general heading for thefts carried out by means not covered by the other theft categories.

K361.p: A thief takes goods for himself after being ordered to deliver or use them for someone else, betraying the order he was given.

K361.1.p: A jackal is ordered to carry meat to a lion's family but instead brings it to his own home.

K361.1.1.p: A man who falsely claims to be a child's mother's husband takes the child away with him.

K361.2.p: Tricksters are given food meant for a bear and eat it all themselves.

K361.3.p: A man is given food by a tiger to use as bait for a deer, but he eats the food himself.

K361.4.p: A monk entrusted with finding a husband for a girl instead keeps the dowry for himself.

K361.5.p: An uncle entrusted with his niece's inheritance slanders her so that her marriage will be broken off and he will not have to hand over her money.

K361.6.p: A greedy husband who wants his wife's jewels tells her he has vowed to give them to a god, so that she will hand them over.

K362.r: *Wesselski Mönchslatein 126 No. 109; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 274; West Indies: Flowers 506-8.
K362.p: A general heading for thefts in which the thief gets goods by presenting a false order to the person guarding them.

K362.0.1.p: A thief obtains a unique weapon from its keeper by lying about what it is needed for.

K362.1.r: *Type 1541; *Fb “tosse” III 832a, “pølse” II 907b; BP I 521, 526; Christensen DF L 46; *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 194 n. 3; Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 1541.
K362.1.p: A numskull is told to keep a sausage "for the long winter." A trickster claims to be Long Winter and so receives the sausage.

K362.2.r: *Type 1525A; BP III 379; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman.
K362.2.p: A thief holds up a corpse at a lord's window so the lord shoots it and goes off to bury it. The thief then gets a shroud and a ring from the lady to bury the corpse with, and keeps the ring for himself.

K362.3.r: *Wesselski Mönchslatein 126 No. 109; Scala Celi 101a No. 543; Mensa Philosophica No. 56; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K362.3.p: A thief pretends to be a messenger from a husband, asking his wife to send a certain silver cup away for repairs, and then takes the cup.

K362.3.1.p: A thief asks for a silver platter, claiming it is needed to hold sweets for a planned gift. The servant carrying it is told to wait while it is filled, and the thief vanishes with the platter.

K362.4.p: A thief pretends to be the master of the house, so that the wife tells him where the valuables are hidden. The wife is deceived because it is dark.

K362.5.p: A hare disguised in a lion's skin tricks a lioness into handing over meat, as if sent by her mate to collect it. The hare thus steals food by posing as an authorized messenger.

K362.5.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 180.
K362.5.1.p: A fox steals milk from a tiger's mate by delivering a message that deceives her. The fox gets the milk through a misleading message rather than by force.

K362.6.r: Jewish: Bin Gorion Born Judas II 245.
K362.6.p: A person gets back money left on deposit with a banker by presenting false tokens to the banker's wife, who hands it over when the banker refuses to return it.

K362.7.p: Someone forges another person's signature on a document to get money. It is theft carried out by faking authorization.

K362.8.p: A clerk mistranslates a master's order to a maid so that the pie meant for the master is instead given to the clerks.

K362.9.p: A thief steals a lawyer's scarlet robe, then returns and tells the lawyer's wife that her husband sent him for the hood to go with it. She gives him the hood, and he escapes with it.

K362.10.r: (Cf. K437.5, K1354.1.) Thief sent to man’s house for water, demands money. Man’s wife refuses and thief shouts to the husband who replies, “Give him what he wants.” India: *Thompson-Balys.
K362.10.p: A trickster gets what he wants by telling the victim to give him whatever he asks for, as if it were a legitimate request. The motif is a false claim of authority to obtain goods.

K362.11.p: A hero tells the king that his ancestors in heaven want him rewarded with gold. The claim is false, and the king hands over the gold on that pretext.

K364.r: Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Africa (Luba): DeClerq Zs. f. Kolonialsprachen IV 221; Philippine (Tinguian) Cole 195.
K364.p: A partner secretly takes more than his share of goods the two held in common. It is theft by someone who shares the property.

K365.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 130 No. 1525G*; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Benga): Nassau 160 No. 20; West Indies: Flowers 508.
K365.p: A thief carries out a theft with the help of an accomplice who plays a part in the scheme.

K365.1.p: An accomplice lets himself be sold as a slave so that the thief can take the payment, after which the accomplice escapes or returns.

K365.2.p: Guests rent a room at an inn, then empty the mattresses of their feathers, take firewood, and so on, throwing the goods out of the window to a confederate who collects them.

K365.3.p: A wife's lover steals money, having learned from the wife where the money is buried.

K366.p: A trickster uses a trained animal to carry out a theft for him.

K366.0.1.p: A thief hides stolen money in flour and feeds it to an animal, then later asks for a donkey, as the animal is supposed to produce the money in return.

K366.1.p: A trickster has a cow that steals other cows, so that the cows are taken to him.

K366.1.1.r: He thus tests the parson’s text, “He who gives in God’s name shall have it back a hundred-fold.” *Type 1735; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 324; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 25; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 167 No. 129.
K366.1.1.p: The trickster's cow leads the parson's cows to him, so that the trickster gains a hundredfold return on his cow.

K366.1.2.p: Two brothers are offered a choice between a cow and a calf. One takes the cow, but the cow longs for the calf and returns to it, so the brother who took the cow loses it.

K366.1.3.p: A cow allows itself to be sold and then returns to its original master, so the seller gets the price and keeps the cow.

K366.1.3.1.p: An animal pretends to be dead, is sold, and then escapes and returns to its owner.

K366.1.4.p: A trickster has a cow that he trains to steal; the cow is turned into a rice field, and later the cow is forced to give back the rice it stole.

K366.2.p: A trickster trains a bird to steal things for him.

K366.3.p: A trickster trains an ant to steal things for him.

K366.4.p: A trickster trains a dog to steal things for him.

K366.5.p: A talking goat is trained to swallow gold coins from a temple and then bring them back out for its master, who gets the money.

K366.6.p: A trickster trains a turtle to steal things for him.

K366.7.p: A trickster has butterflies trained to steal things for him.

K366.8.p: A trickster trains an octopus to steal things for him.

K371.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 57, Coster-Wijsman 35 No. 16; Africa (Thonga): Junod 209.
K371.p: A trickster hides inside a pile of food and eats it from within without being seen.

K371.1.r: *Type 1; BP II 116; Dh IV 225, 304; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 46ff.—Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr II 3, III 3; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 115; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 438; Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 16 No. 8; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 17 No. 4, 306 No. 52, (South Carolina): Parsons MAFLS XVI 39, Stewart JAFL XXXII 395, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 276; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 10.
K371.1.p: A fox pretends to be dead and is thrown onto a wagon of fish, then throws the fish off and carries them away.

K372.r: *Type 15; BP I 9; Dh IV 241; *Krohn Bar (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 74ff.; *Fb “ræv” III 113b, “bjørn” IV 43b; *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 238.—Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr III No. 3; French: Sébillot France III 63f.; Missouri French: Carrière; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 19; New Mexican Spanish: Rael Hispania XX 231—4; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 437; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis III 13, (Fjort): Dennett 90 No. 23; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 80 No. 17, Jones Negro Myths from the Georgia Coast (Cambridge, Mass., 1888) No. 24, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 253—55, (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 192f., (South Carolina): Parsons MAFLS XVI 7—12, JAFL XXXII 394, XXXIV 3; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 1; Bermuda: Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 240.
K372.p: A trickster pretends to have been invited to be a child's godfather so he can steal the food the two of them stored for winter, and gives the child silly names on each visit, such as "Just Begun" and "Half Done."

K372.1.p: A trickster eats the bait or food that his trapping partner, a tiger, left at the snare, and the tiger is blamed for the theft.

K373.r: “But the owner has refused to accept it.” “Then you may keep it.” Danish: Kristensen Kirketjeneste 126.
K373.p: A rascal steals a priest's watch and offers it back to him as payment for a favor; the priest refuses to accept stolen goods and tells the thief to return the watch to its owner.

K374.p: A trickster pretends to teach someone to dance, then runs off with their valuables.

K375.p: Thieves steal chickens and then hold a fake funeral to hide the theft.

K378.p: A trickster kisses a pile of money and steals some of it with every kiss by taking coins into his mouth.

K382.p: A thief steals fire by swallowing it and then escaping with it.

K400.p: A thief manages to get away with a theft without being caught or blamed.

K401.r: *Penzer IV 191f. n. 1; Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 6 (Lee 257); Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 129.
K401.p: The thief shifts the blame for a theft onto an innocent person, who is punished for it.

K401.0.1.p: A thief accuses his partner in crime of having stolen the gold that both of them actually took. The accuser tries to shift the blame onto the partner.

K401.1.r: *Type 15; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 21; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 173, 177, 179, (Zulu): Callaway 164, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 366 No. 17, (Hottentot): Bleek 18 No. 9, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 48 No. 5, (Basuto): Jacottet 10 No. 1, (Benga): Nassau 93 No. 4, (Kaffir): Theal 95, 96, 114, Kidd The Essential Kaffir (London, 1904) 384, (Fang): Tessman 57; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 80 No. 17, Friends 147 No. 20, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 222; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 238. See all references to K372.
K401.1.p: A trickster eats the group's shared food and then pins the blame on a sleeping companion. He smears the companion's mouth with the food so the companion looks guilty.

K401.1.1.r: *Penzer V 61 n. 3; Bødker Exempler 287 No. 37; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K401.1.1.p: The real thief leaves a trail of stolen goods that leads to the innocent dupe's home, so that the dupe appears guilty. In the example, a crane scatters fish from one animal's home to another's, and the mongoose follows the trail and kills the snake.

K401.2.r: Icelandic: Boberg; Bødker Exempler 303 No. 74; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 178 n. 1 (Palamedes); Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 100.
K401.2.p: Stolen goods are secretly placed in an innocent person's house so that he is accused of the theft.

K401.2.1.r: Chauvin II 87 No. 23; Penzer V 47 n. 3, 214, 226f.
K401.2.1.p: A crow makes a snake appear to be a thief by getting it to try to swallow a stolen collar, so the snake is blamed for the theft.

K401.2.2.r: Bødker Exempler 281 No. 25; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K401.2.2.p: A crow drops a stolen necklace into a snake's hole. Men find it and kill the snake, which had eaten the crow's young birds.

K401.2.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 349, 892.
K401.2.3.p: A stolen object is secretly passed into an innocent person's possession, and that person is then condemned for it.

K401.3.p: Stolen goods are put in the room of a suitor, who is then falsely accused of the theft. The accusers want to be rid of him, and he is poor.

K401.4.p: A thief pretends that money entrusted to him has been stolen from him, so he keeps it.

K401.5.p: A thief successfully accuses the owner of stealing property the thief wants for himself, so the owner loses it.

K402.r: *Type 785; *BP II 149, 153; Wienert FFC LVI 40, 107; Oesterley No. 83; Herbert III 205; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 57; Penzer V 130 n. 1; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K402.p: Accused of eating a lamb's heart, the thief insists the lamb never had a heart. This is a clever tall-tale defense.

K402.1.r: (Usually the master confounds the rascal by frightening the geese so that they use both legs) *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 229 No. 75; Boccaccio Decameron VI No. 4 (*Lee 177); Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2424*; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 191; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 508.
K402.1.p: Accused of eating a goose's leg, the thief claims the goose never had a leg. He backs up his claim by showing geese standing on one leg.

K402.2.p: The thief claims that the bird he is accused of stealing or eating had no tail.

K402.3.r: **Keidel “Die Eselherz Fabel” Zs. f. vgl. Litgsch. n. ser. VII No. 58; Gaster Exempla 229 No. 244; Penzer V 130 n. 1; *Chauvin II 99 No. 58; Bødker Exempler 299 No. 63; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K402.3.p: A donkey who collects tolls is killed by a lion for demanding payment. The fox eats the donkey's heart, and when the lion asks for it, the fox says the donkey could not have had a heart since he was foolish enough to ask the lion for toll.

K403.r: *Type 1529; *BP III 9, 391 n. 3; Chauvin VII 137; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 229 No. 487; *Basset 1001 Contes I 492; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 150 No. 1852*; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 437.
K403.p: While the owner sleeps, the thief steals his horse and harnesses himself to the wagon. When caught, he claims he is the horse transformed into a man.

K404.p: The thief escapes by leaving the severed tail of a stolen animal behind and claiming the animal escaped and left its tail.

K404.1.r: *Type 1004; BP III 392 n. 1; *Fb “hale” I 537, “svin” III 676a; Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 1004; Missouri French: Carrière; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 110 No. 2; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 241; Africa (Vai): Ellis 249 No. 41; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 98 No. 20, Nights 230 No. 39, 241 No. 41, (Virginia): Smiley JAFL XXXII 368, (South Carolina): Parsons MAFLS XVI 31f., JAFL XXXIV 8; Bahama: Cleare JAFL XXX 228; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 252 No. 29; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 109 n. 2, 113.
K404.1.p: The thief steals animals, sticks their severed tails in the ground, and claims the animals escaped underground.

K404.2.r: The thief kills one ox and puts the tail in another ox’s mouth: the owner thinks one ox has eaten the other. Type 1004; *BP III 392 n. 2; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525G*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1525G*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1525G*.
K404.2.p: A thief leaves an ox's tail in another person's mouth, so that the stolen ox appears to have escaped and left its tail behind.

K404.3.p: The thief cuts off the tails of stolen sheep and hangs them in a tree, making the owner believe the sheep escaped through the air.

K405.p: A thief successfully claims that goods he has stolen belong to him, and is believed.

K405.1.p: A thief carts off grain, and when his wagon falls into a ditch, the owner he has robbed helps him out. The thief has persuaded the owner that the grain is really his own.

K405.2.p: A thief pawns a stolen pot with its real owner, who gives him a receipt. When accused of theft, the thief shows the receipt to prove the pot was legitimately his.

K405.3.p: A thief is caught with a stolen religious image but claims that the saint gave it to him personally, and this claim succeeds.

K406.p: A thief disguises a stolen animal as a person so that no one will recognize it as stolen livestock.

K406.1.p: A thief dresses a stolen sheep as a person sitting at the helm of a boat, so the animal passes as a passenger.

K406.2.r: (Mak.) Whiting Speculum VII 552; Fb “lam” II 370a, “hundehvalp” IV 228b; *Baugh MPh XV 729; *Smyser JAFL XLVII 378; *Stroup JAFL XLVII 380, Southern Folklore Q. III 5f.; *Cosbey Speculum X 310ff.; Middle English: Second Shepherd’s Play; Irish myth: Cross (K521.1.3); Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 144 No. 1735B*.
K406.2.p: A thief dresses a stolen sheep as a baby lying in a cradle, so that it looks like a human child.

K406.3.p: A thief uses magic to transform a stolen animal into something else so that it cannot be identified as the stolen creature.

K407.p: A thief escapes being identified by cutting off a body part, which removes the evidence that would reveal him.

K407.1.r: *Type 950; BP III 395ff.; *Krappe “Trophonios and Agamedes” Archiv für Religionswissenschaft XXX 228-241; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Grote I 122; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K407.1.p: A thief has his companion cut off his head so that the body cannot be identified and he escapes detection.

K407.2.r: *DeVries Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsche Taal- en Letterkunde XLV 213ff.
K407.2.p: A thief has his arm cut off as he enters a hole in a wall, and then lets his companion also enter and have his arm severed, so that the two arms cannot be told apart and neither is identified.

K407.2.1.r: (Previously he had severed father’s or brother’s head to escape detection.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K407.2.1.p: A thief's confederate cuts off his own arm to give the family a believable alibi, so their grief over the loss seems genuine and they are not suspected.

K407.3.p: An elephant cuts a piece from its own leg and places it on a shelf, so that it will not be accused of stealing meat.

K408.p: In a single night a thief pawns the same stolen cow four times, stealing it back each time, and finally returns it to its owner.

K411.p: A thief gives himself an alibi by playing music and dancing all night, while a confederate carries out the actual theft.

K411.1.r: Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 271 No. 6, (Nago): Basset Contes populaires d’Afrique 217ff. No. 90.
K411.1.p: A thief pretends to be sick to create an alibi for the time of a theft.

K412.p: A thief avoids detection of a stolen bull by putting boots on its feet, so that its tracks look like a person's.

K413.p: Thieves stretch a chain across the road so that their pursuers are blocked and they get away.

K414.p: After a thief is quartered, his pieces are sewn back together so that the body appears whole and he escapes detection.

K415.r: *Type 950; BP III 395ff.; *Schoepperle I 214 n. 3; Boccaccio Decameron III No. 2 (Lee 62); *Penzer V 274f., 284, VII 36, 217ff.; *Chauvin V 83 No. 24 n. 2; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2440*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 435; Africa: Werner African 223.
K415.p: The guilty person marks everyone else in the group in the same way as himself, so that no one can be singled out and he escapes detection.

K415.1.p: Many people all confess to the theft, so it becomes impossible to tell who the real thief is.

K416.r: *Wesselski Mönchslatein 119 No. C; Mensa Philosophica No. 52.
K416.p: A thief who has been caught with stolen property pretends to be sorry and claims he has found the stolen cow, then returns it to the owner. The owner is scolded for not guarding her property well.

K416.1.p: A thief claims he has recovered a stolen horse, and returns it to its owner after using it as much as he likes.

K417.p: A thief swallows the stolen goods so that he cannot be searched and caught with them.

K417.1.p: A thief who has stolen flowers eats them to hide the evidence.

K418.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1635*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1545*.
K418.p: A thief tricks the owner into trying to solve a riddle about the theft that has just taken place, so the owner wastes time while the thief gets away.

K419.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a thief avoids being caught by means not covered elsewhere in this group.

K419.1.p: A thief who has eaten the food he was trusted to deliver claims he delivered it, but he cannot remember who answered the door to receive it.

K419.2.p: A thief avoids detection by dressing up as a woman.

K419.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525K*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1525 I*.
K419.3.p: An umpire or judge awards a coat, which the thief has stolen from the umpire himself, to the thief.

K419.4.r: Boldly says: “Master, the devil from hell sends you bacon.” The farmer: “Take yourself off to hell with the bacon.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1627B*.
K419.4.p: A thief carrying off stolen bacon accidentally walks into the farmer's living room and offers him the bacon.

K419.5.p: A thief paints one side of a stolen horse black and leaves the other side white, so that the guards give conflicting descriptions of it.

K419.6.p: A thief who steals grain from a granary replaces the emptied sacks with husks, so the theft is not noticed.

K419.7.p: A goldsmith who is working in the king's treasury steals gold by making a golden human figure and claiming it is a corpse.

K419.8.p: Thieves carry off a woman on a bier, pretending she is dead, and drown out her cries for help with loud wailing so no one hears.

K419.9.p: The blame for a theft is pinned on inanimate objects, such as things that cannot be held responsible.

K419.10.p: The blame for a theft is placed on fairies rather than on the real thief.

K420.p: A thief either loses the goods he has stolen or is discovered and caught.

K421.p: A robber by mistake takes worthless goods and leaves behind the valuable ones.

K421.1.p: A thief who hopes to take a bigger prize ends up losing the smaller one he already had.

K421.2.p: Thieves are told to look for money hidden in a hornet's nest, and they are stung instead of finding any money.

K421.3.p: Two swindlers each try to pass off worthless goods as genuine on the other, and both end up cheated. Each walks away with something useless, so the trickery backfires on both.

K422.r: *Type 952; *BP III 453; *Fb “stjæle” III 575a; *Kittredge Witchcraft 200f. nn. 95—101; Alphabet No. 669; England, U.S.: Baughman; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 300 No. 10.
K422.p: A thief is left unable to move or act because of magic. His theft is stopped in its tracks by a supernatural force.

K423.r: Irish myth: *Cross. See all references to D1602 and its subdivisions.
K423.p: A stolen object finds its way back to its owner by magical means, without anyone recovering it in the ordinary way.

K423.0.1.p: A stolen animal magically goes back to its owner. It returns home by supernatural means after being taken.

K424.p: A thief is convicted because people who saw the theft are able to locate the stolen goods on him or where he hid them.

K425.p: A king places his own daughter in a brothel as a trap to catch a thief. The scheme is a disguised bait to expose the criminal.

K426.r: Type 990; **Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 353; XXX—XXXII 127; *Hertel ibid. XXI 282.
K426.p: A thief breaks into a grave to rob a corpse, but the woman he is robbing, who only seemed dead, wakes up and he is caught or frightened off.

K427.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 48; West Indies: Flowers 509.
K427.p: A clever animal gives away a thief by its behavior, revealing where he is or what he has done.

K427.1.p: A horse catches a thief by the arm with its teeth and holds on until help arrives. The animal keeps the thief pinned until people come to take him.

K428.r: The statue says, “Whoever would tell the truth now is likely to have his head smashed.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 8.
K428.p: A thief has threatened to smash a magic statue's head if it betrays him, yet the statue reveals his crime anyway by a roundabout hint.

K431.p: A thief sleeps with a magic ring hidden in his mouth. A mouse tickles him by pulling its tail through his mouth, making him cough up the ring.

K432.p: A robbery victim tricks the robbers into thinking all is well while secretly calling for help. The deception lets rescuers arrive.

K432.1.p: A clever woman who is being robbed invents an excuse for screaming, so that neighbors come and the robbers are stopped.

K432.1.1.p: A clever husband who is being robbed sends his wife to shout and call for help. Her outcry brings others to the house.

K432.2.p: A householder pretends to help burglars divide their loot, but he handles the weights so noisily that the police are alerted and come.

K433.r: Thief is caught. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K433.p: A thief hides a small stolen pig inside a larger pig to dodge a tax, but a child's curiosity reveals the trick. The child notices an extra pair of hind legs.

K434.p: A clever girl discovers a robber hiding in the house and outwits him. She turns the situation to her advantage through her cleverness.

K434.1.r: I need a finer one.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 959A*.
K434.1.p: A girl finds a robber hiding under the bed and grabs him by the beard. Her mocking remark calls his beard a coarse bundle of flax, catching him out.

K434.2.p: A robber disguised as a guest tries to haul up his accomplice with a rope, but a princess notices him and catches him instead.

K434.3.p: A girl tells a thief that the money is in a chest. When he leans in to look, she slams the lid down on him, trapping him.

K435.r: U.S.: Baughman; West Indies: Flowers 509f.; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 235 No. 4, 239 No. 10.
K435.p: A thief is caught because a child, singing or chanting a song, unknowingly reveals what he has done or where the stolen goods are hidden.

K435.1.p: A husband makes up rhymes about cakes that his wife has secretly stolen, and the rhymes give her away.

K436.p: A blind thief tries to steal dates from a withered palm tree, but the rope slips and he is killed.

K437.p: A robber is defeated or overpowered by his intended victim.

K437.1.r: Spending the night in company with a suspicious-looking stranger, the man does not go to sleep, but leaves his clothes in bed and waits to see what will happen. When the stranger wakes up in the night, he stabs at his sleeping companion, who shoots him down. (Cf. K525.1.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 965*.
K437.1.p: A robber is tricked when his loot is secretly swapped for something worthless.

K437.2.r: Using a candle made of human fat or hand of a corpse, he tries to charm the household into a deep sleep (D1162.2.1). One man who is suspicious and has not gone to sleep sees this and kills the robber. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 963*.
K437.2.p: A robber who is disguised as a beggar and asks for a night's lodging at a farmhouse is killed, apparently by a hand of glory, a magic severed hand used by thieves.

K437.3.p: A man scares off a robber with a sausage pretending it is a gun. The robber overhears him boasting about it at an inn, and the innkeeper secretly lends the man a real revolver. When the robber returns to attack again, he is shot dead.

K437.4.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 962*; Russian: Andrejev No. 961 I*.
K437.4.p: A man believes he has killed a robber and takes the robber's stick or knife with a large handle. The robber, now disguised as a beggar, recovers and asks to look at the stick, and the man becomes suspicious and finds money hidden inside it.

K437.5.p: Two robbers send a youth to sell bracelets, but he instead offers to sell the robbers themselves as slaves, and he is paid for them while they are enslaved.

K439.p: Miscellaneous tricks in which a thief loses his goods or is found out.

K439.1.p: A thief is betrayed when the stolen goods are exchanged, revealing his guilt.

K439.2.p: A thief claims the stolen goods are his own, and the master recognizes the claim as false and so detects him.

K439.3.r: Chauvin II 83 No. 7; Bødker Exempler 273 No. 5; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K439.3.p: A thief is tricked into robbing himself: he has put a coat on the goods he plans to steal, and his partner moves the coat, so the thief takes his own things.

K439.4.r: (Playing poison.) American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 54 No. 7, Nights 297 No. 50; Bahama: *Parsons MAFLS XIII 122; West Indies: Flowers 511.
K439.4.p: A thief refuses to eat food that the owner pretends has poisoned him, and so is revealed or fails to be deceived.

K439.5.p: A sheep thief pretends to buy wethers from the ram and names the price himself, but the owner overhears and takes the ram to the thief to collect payment.

K439.6.p: Robbers are poisoned by food that has been prepared for them.

K439.7.p: A robber is persuaded to give himself time and to come to the man's office to collect a promised larger sum, so that he can be caught there.

K439.7.1.p: A tortoise asks a greedy man to give it the first ruby so it can be sure the second will match. It then dives into the water with the first ruby and disappears.

K439.8.p: The owner pretends to believe the thief is a family god, and binds him in order to hold him.

K439.9.p: The owner feigns madness so as to raise an alarm, and the thieves are captured.

K439.10.p: A person hiding nearby sees thieves burying or concealing treasure, then secretly takes it for himself.

K439.11.p: A thief hides inside a large bottle to get into a room, but the bottle is put into water to boil and he is caught.

K440.p: A miscellaneous category of tricks and cheats that do not fit the other headings of the thefts and cheats section.

K441.p: Someone gets a reward or payment twice over for the same thing, and succeeds in collecting both.

K441.1.r: Chauvin V 274 No. 155 n. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
K441.1.p: A married couple both receive a pension from the king. Each falsely reports the other dead and collects the whole pension.

K441.2.r: *Herbert III 375 No. 23; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 125; Scala Celi 20a No. 122; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K441.2.p: A lawyer is paid with a car by a widow and with an ox by her opponent. He argues for the opponent that the ox pulls the car, so he should be paid for it too.

K441.2.1.p: A dishonest notary makes up a debt and collects payment from both parties to it.

K441.3.p: A man is paid by two different people for the same exclusive right to supply goods to one customer, as he promises to deal with both.

K441.4.p: A trickster is paid by both a husband and wife, who have separated, each hiring him to reconcile them.

K442.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 159 No. 31, (Ekoi): Talbot 387.
K442.p: Someone falsely claims a reward for returning or finding something they did not actually recover.

K442.1.p: A reward is offered for the return of a stolen princess, and the abductor himself returns and demands the reward.

K443.r: U.S.: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 512.
K443.p: Someone obtains money or other goods by threatening to reveal a secret or wrongdoing.

K443.1.p: A hidden lover pays the person who discovered him to keep quiet and buy his freedom.

K443.2.r: *Type 890; Cosquin Études 457ff.; Norwegian: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 113 No. 890; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K443.2.p: A clever wife collects money from men who try to seduce her, in return for keeping their attempts secret.

K443.2.1.p: A clever wife gets her husband appointed to the job held by a man who tried to seduce her.

K443.3.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 196 No. 95.
K443.3.p: Guards or watchers are paid money to keep quiet after letting goods be stolen, under threat of exposure.

K443.3.1.p: Watchers are forced to pay money after letting a chest be stolen. The chest is falsely said to hold money, and they are threatened with severe punishment.

K443.4.p: A watcher pays money after allowing a wooden cow, which people think is real, to be stolen.

K443.5.p: A trickster lures wolves out of a stable with music, then makes their keeper pay him for his carelessness.

K443.6.p: After seeing a princess naked, a trickster makes her promise to marry him in exchange for keeping silent.

K443.6.1.p: A trickster forces a man to hand over his beautiful wife by threatening to reveal that he saw a princess naked. The people who looked into the carriage find his dead wife inside, not a princess.

K443.6.2.p: A trickster demands money as the price of keeping quiet after he has slept with a princess or queen.

K443.7.p: A fox eats his fellow lodger's food, then blames another animal and demands a larger animal in compensation at each inn he visits.

K443.8.p: A trickster tricks a priest into revealing confessional secrets, then extorts money from him to stay silent. He first confesses an affair with the priest's maid, then overhears the priest scolding her.

K443.9.p: Women lure a man into a compromising situation, then shout for help so he is caught and must pay to avoid trouble.

K443.10.p: A rascal extorts money from someone in exchange for keeping quiet about his companion's poverty.

K443.11.r: Shrewd suitor persuades usurer to charge him 100 per cent interest, then has him arrested. Thus gets daughter for wife. India: Thompson-Balys.
K443.11.p: A moneylender is blackmailed, with someone threatening to expose him in exchange for payment.

K443.12.p: A clever fox persuades a king that his newly married daughter's feet have brought bad luck to the groom, and the king pays half his kingdom to compensate. The palace had vanished after the wedding, leaving only a hut.

K443.13.p: A rascal extorts money in exchange for keeping quiet about someone breaking a food taboo.

K444.r: *Type 1626; **Baum JAFL XXX 378; *BP IV 139; *Dunlop-Wilson II 201; Basset 1001 Contes I 516; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 95; Barbeau JAFL XXXII 178; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 243 No. 540; *Oesterley No. 106; Scala Celi 73a No. 415; Ward II 240; Herbert III 246; Alphabet No. 238; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 22 No. 98; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs. f. Vksk. 1954, 135.—Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 1626*; Russian: Andrejev No. 2100*; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K444.p: Three pilgrims agree that whoever has the most wonderful dream gets the last loaf. One eats it, claiming he dreamed the others were dead so they would not need it.

K444.1.r: First brother (knocking egg against wall): “Casca cascorum.” Second (breaking shell and sprinkling dirt over it): “Sar, sale, sapiensa”. Third (eating egg): “Consumatus es.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 153 No. 1942; Japanese: Ikeda.
K444.1.p: A man wins an egg as a reward for speaking a suitable saying.

K444.2.p: A boy eats a bag of cakes and claims it was full of cobras, so he never needed to share.

K444.3.p: A boy eats the rice he was carrying for the road and throws the empty bag away.

K445.r: The emperor and courtiers are all afraid to admit that they cannot see the clothes. Finally a child seeing the naked emperor reveals the imposture. *Type 1620; **Taylor MPh XXV 17; *Chauvin II 156 No. 32, VIII 130 No. 120; *Wesselski Gonnella 133 No. 33; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K445.p: An impostor pretends to make fine clothes for the emperor, claiming they can be seen only by people of legitimate birth. Nobody dares admit seeing nothing, so the emperor goes out naked.

K445.1.p: God will reveal himself only to those of legitimate birth, and everyone is too afraid to admit they cannot see him.

K445.2.p: Whoever hears a singing snake must die. A deaf man kills it, since he cannot hear it sing.

K446.r: *Type 1615; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 197 No. 387; Chauvin V 254 No. 151 n. 2, VII 153; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 566.
K446.p: A rascal sees robbers dividing their loot, slips a coin with a red string through it into their pile, and then claims the money as his own because it is marked. The robbers divide the money anyway.

K446.1.p: A trickster drops half a grain into a grain cellar, then demands half of all the grain there.

K447.p: Hidden gold is found when a king offers a high price for gold.

K448.p: A cheat marks an object he covets with his own name, then later claims it as his property.

K451.p: A corrupt judge or referee who is secretly in league with a trickster and rules in the trickster's favor. Used as a general heading for the trick.

K451.1.r: *Type 613; *BP II 468ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 489; **Christiansen FFC XXIV 46ff.; Jewish: Gaster Exempla 191 No. 29, Neuman; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 395.
K451.1.p: A dishonest umpire is asked to settle a religious argument, and his accomplice wins a ridiculous bet as a result.

K451.2.r: *Type 1551; *Clouston Tales II 27; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 632; *Penzer V 104; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 213 No. 437; Chauvin II 96 No. 51, VII 150 No. 430; *Oesterley No. 132; Crane Vitry 141 No. 20; Alphabet No. 766; Hazlitt Shakespeare Jest-Books II 176; Bødker Exempler 295 No. 56; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K451.2.p: A trickster bets a shepherd that the sheep he is herding are pigs, with the next passerby as judge. The trickster's accomplice arrives and declares them to be pigs, so the trickster wins.

K451.3.r: Chauvin II 91 No. 34; Bødker Exempler 287 No. 36; Penzer V 59 n. 2; Edgerton JAPS XL 271; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K451.3.p: A rascal and a simple man secretly find treasure together, and the rascal hides it and then tries to have his partner convicted by a false witness, a tree in which the rascal's father is hidden.

K451.4.p: A trickster's accomplice falsely values a worthless piece of glass at a huge price, and a priest is tricked into buying it as a diamond.

K451.5.p: A man pretending to be the returned heir of a dead man has an accomplice who answers for the corpse. He pretends to speak to the body for identification, and the accomplice replies in its voice.

K452.p: A dishonest umpire keeps for himself the goods that are being disputed between two parties.

K452.1.p: Two people dispute a found oyster and the umpire eats the oyster as his fee, giving each of them half of the shell.

K452.2.p: When a contest cannot be decided, the dishonest umpire simply keeps the stakes for himself.

K453.p: A trickster cheats by using his knowledge of the law, exploiting legal rules or loopholes to win.

K455.p: A trickster tricks someone into giving him credit or favors that he does not deserve, such as food or drink on account.

K455.1.p: A parasite gets a free supper by convincing the host that he is a friend of a certain guest, and convincing the guest that he is a friend of the host.

K455.2.p: A trickster gets a free supper by pretending to be an invited guest.

K455.3.p: An old beggar dressed up as a gentleman borrows large sums of money on his supposed credit.

K455.4.r: *Bédier Fabliaux 447; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 150 No. 1848. Cf. Wesselski Bebel II 136 No. 111.
K455.4.p: Three men eat at an inn, and each leads the host to believe another will pay. None has money, so the host is cheated.

K455.4.1.r: Then he flees. (Cf. K242.1.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K455.4.1.p: A trickster buys chickens on credit by telling the owner that a priest will pay. When the owner comes to collect, the trickster says a heretic has come to confession with the priest.

K455.5.p: Feasters who cannot pay are jailed, then get out by naming a priest as their guarantor. The priest, told that the host is possessed, agrees to come heal him in two weeks, and the host loses his money.

K455.6.p: While the servant fetches a glass, the trickster drinks the wine, then complains the bottle is empty, so the servant has to bring another.

K455.7.r: Wager. Each lie is corroborated by a confederate, who poses as a newly arrived stranger. *BP II 509; Japanese: Ikeda.
K455.7.p: The greatest liar gets his supper for free, because the host cannot out-lie him.

K455.8.p: A person gets credit, favors, or goods based on a forged document.

K455.8.1.p: A forged letter is used to obtain credit, special treatment, and entertainment from others.

K455.8.2.p: A trickster uses a forged will or testament to deceive his host and win credit or goods from him.

K455.9.p: A trickster offers worthless chests as security so that people will extend him credit.

K455.10.p: A trickster borrows a small sum, uses it to pay in advance for a bigger loan, and repeats this chain until he gets a huge amount of credit for almost nothing.

K461.p: A trickster takes goods that were given in charity meant for someone else's family.

K461.1.p: A bear helps the fox's mother gather berries, but the fox secretly eats them.

K461.2.p: A monkey pretends to cry as if hungry so that a girl gives it her food, and then the monkey eats the food.

K464.p: A trickster overhears the sexton (church official) and tricks him into giving money by praying to the Virgin for a sum and promising to repay double at month's end; the sexton throws him the money but never gets it back.

K465.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 204 No. 405; Chauvin VIII 107 No. 83.
K465.p: An owner secretly bids on his own goods at an auction, driving up the price until a rival buyer pays an outrageous amount.

K471.r: *Type 9 C; Dh IV 249ff.; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 97ff.
K471.p: A fox swaps the bear's dark porridge for his own lighter porridge by stealing a spoonful and letting the bear taste it, so the bear believes the fox's porridge is just as bad as his own.

K473.r: Frightens bear. *Type 3; Dh IV 243; Krohn Bar (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 59ff.; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 287; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 21 No. 5, 377 No. 68.
K473.p: A fox smears milk over his head and claims his brains have been knocked out, faking a wound to deceive others.

K474.p: A trickster tricks rescuers into digging out his well: after his own well collapses, he throws his clothes into the hole and hides, so passers-by think he has drowned and dig it out.

K475.r: Köhler-Bolte I 513; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “équivoque”; India: Thompson-Balys.
K475.p: A cheat succeeds by using words with double meanings so that his victim agrees to something without realizing the trick.

K475.1.r: He says, “I haven’t it.” The confederate says, “I didn’t steal it.” Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 505), 103 (ST 162); Halm Aesop 301.
K475.1.p: A thief hands the stolen meat to his accomplice, passing it along so it cannot be traced to him.

K475.2.r: Before horse race starts they ask: “Do we have your leave to go?” They go home. India: Thompson-Balys.
K475.2.p: Two prisoners are made stable boys after promising not to escape secretly, and they exploit the wording of their promise by asking whether they have leave to go.

K475.3.p: A man robbed of his plate of cakes on the way to a fair warns another vendor, with a joke, that robbers wait halfway there; the second vendor goes on and suffers the same fate.

K476.p: A cheat succeeds by swapping valuable goods for worthless substitutes.
