K476.1.p: A divider of a slain ox arranges the bones and entrails so they look like the choicest meat, as Prometheus does in the story of his division.

K476.1.1.p: A trickster substitutes a rock for a ham, passing off a worthless stone as valuable meat.

K476.1.2.p: A tortoise cheats a leopard by substituting a bundle of resin for a bundle of meat.

K476.2.p: A cheat uses worthless articles passed off as valuable ones to obtain credit or goods on trust.

K476.2.1.p: A cheat gives a lump of lead, passed off as gold, to help pay for a church, and then borrows money against it.

K476.2.2.p: A man wraps lead in a bag and pretends to have found it. A merchant, believing the bag holds gold, claims it and pays the man a large reward.

K476.3.r: Wine-casks partitioned: one half wine, other half water. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K476.3.p: A seller passes off plain water as wine.

K476.3.1.p: An innkeeper serves sweetened water in place of wine, a cat in place of rabbit, and a mule in place of beef.

K476.4.p: A cheat swaps a genuine set of rings for a set of fake ones; in the note, the jewels are bought with counterfeit money.

K476.4.1.p: Priests replace solid gold calf images with gilded ones made of cheaper metal and keep the gold for themselves.

K476.5.p: A toad, while swimming with a lizard, swaps her own ugly daughter for the lizard's pretty daughter.

K476.6.p: A trickster replaces fat geese with lean ones.

K476.7.p: A woman gives a friend a dried comb while she herself keeps and eats the honey.

K476.8.p: A cheat swaps a magic cow for an ordinary cow.

K477.p: A trickster gains someone's attention or access through deception.

K477.1.p: A woman bribes a man to get her an audience with the pope. He turns his back on the sacrament and claims she told him to, so she is summoned into the pope's presence.

K477.2.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 74 No. 64; Wienert FFC LVI 38; Halm Aesop Nos 177, 339.
K477.2.p: A speaker first hooks the audience by starting a story, and only then gets into his real speech.

K477.3.p: A person gets into an enemy's presence by pretending to bring a message from a relative of the enemy.

K478.p: A peasant sells butter to a baker and has it weighed together with the bread he is buying, so the weights cheat the baker.

K481.p: A trickster called Demi-coq uses magic animals and magic water to collect money.

K481.1.p: A blackbird, seeking revenge for the capture of his wife, carries a rope, a club, a cat, ants, and a river in his ears.

K482.p: A cheat collects money for burying a person who is only pretending to be dead.

K482.1.p: A husband and wife each take money from different people to bury the other, who is supposedly dead.

K482.2.p: A trickster tells the children of a treasure's owner that the owner is dead, and receives the treasure from them.

K483.r: Dh I 188; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 134.
K483.p: The devil secretly changes the color of his cows while he sleeps, so that their owner cannot recognize them. Only cows that have not been changed, such as all-black or all-red ones, are truly the devil's.

K484.p: A trickster cheats someone by falsely crying out an alarm to get something from them.

K484.1.p: A trickster raises a false alarm at a bank and demands that the bank pay him what it supposedly owes him, and so gets money.

K484.2.p: A host who has too much sour wine spreads a rumor that a dragon is at his house. A crowd gathers, and he sells all his wine to them.

K484.3.r: Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 4; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Persian: Lorimer Persian Tales (London, 1919) 321 No. 52.
K484.3.p: A man is falsely accused after a false alarm of robbery is raised, and the man who was cheated ends up imprisoned.

K485.r: *Type 825; *Dh I 258; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3100, Legends Nos. 192—195.
K485.p: The devil sneaks into Noah's ark. He wants to know what Noah is doing, and he forbids Noah's wife to enter the ark until Noah has also invited him.

K486.p: A miller cheats twice: he admits he uses an oversized measure, agrees to switch to a smaller one, and then measures the grain back to customers using that smaller measure, still cheating them.

K487.p: A counselor falsely accuses conspirators of plotting so that he can seize their estates and property for himself.

K488.p: A lawyer's dog steals meat from a butcher. The lawyer tells the butcher that he, as the dog's owner, is liable for damages, and then charges double the damages as his fee.

K491.r: *Type 1675; *BP I 59; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VII 93; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 247f. No. 552; India: Thompson-Balys.
K491.p: A trickster is paid in advance to educate a donkey, and then gradually starves the donkey so it dies instead of being taught.

K491.1.p: A trickster is paid to teach a monkey to talk, and cheats the person who hired him.

K491.2.p: A horse is to be taught to speak, and the trickster who is paid to do this cheats the one who pays.

K492.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 125 No. 1374B; India: Thompson-Balys.
K492.p: A girl serves her father a piece of her own flesh, disguised as chicken.

K492.1.p: A woman serves a beggar burning coals instead of food.

K493.p: A dupe is tricked by being asked ambiguous questions, which he understands differently from how they were meant, so that he betrays himself.

K494.r: Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 6 n. 1.
K494.p: A wolf announces dawn too early to collect a debt, since the debt is due at daybreak. He imitates a rooster's crow, but he is caught.

K495.p: A trickster pretends to be sick so that his partner has to do all the work.

K496.p: Foxes persuade a man to plant cooked food, and then they eat the plants at night.

K498.p: People are tricked into eating meat during Lent, because the meat is disguised as butter.

K499.p: A collection of other cheating tricks that do not fit the more specific categories listed above.

K499.1.p: A trickster sells his mother's wine to a merchant without asking her. She secretly keeps back part of it, because the buyer is slow to come and take the casks away.

K499.2.p: A trick in which a hollow object is used to secretly add or take something from food or drink.

K499.2.1.p: A saint asks for broth without butter, but the cook secretly pours butter into it through a hollow mixing stick.

K499.2.2.p: A saint asks for nettle pottage without milk, but the cook secretly pours milk into it through a pipe. The secret comes out, and the saint blesses the cook's successors.

K499.3.p: An old man tricks a crocodile by taking advantage of its lack of knowledge about farming.

K499.4.p: A trickster ruins a cat's liking for milk by heating its milk until it is scalding.

K499.5.p: A trickster, unwilling to pay the burial fee for an old cow, gives the cow as a gift to an unsuspecting Brahmin. The cow dies soon after, and the Brahmin has to pay the fee.

K499.6.p: God tricks the birds by describing the tamarind fruit falsely to them.

K499.7.p: A gullible king gives a minister large sums of money to build an imaginary weapon, and then gives him more to have it destroyed.

K499.8.p: A trickster outwits a rival by swapping beds with him, so that the maiden brings the trickster his food instead of the rival.

K499.9.p: A treacherous friend drinks from another's flask so that he can save the water in his own.

K499.10.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 175.
K499.10.p: A fox pretends to go off to work but actually goes out to sleep.

K500.r: *Chauvin VIII 136 No. 132; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 113—118); Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 1—8.
K500.p: A character gets away from death or danger by using a trick or deception.

K510.p: A death order is avoided by deception.

K511.r: *Types 428, 930; *Aarne FFC XXIII 69ff., 91; *BP I 282; *Fb “brev” IV 61ab; *Chauvin VIII 143ff. Nos. 145ABC; *Cosquin Études 143ff.; Gunkel Märchen im alten Testament (Tübingen, 1921) 132; *Boje 79; *Penzer I 52, II 113f., III 277ff.; Alphabet No. 593; *Dickson 235 n. 33; Tupper and Ogle Walter Map 271.—Icelandic: Hdwb. d. I, *Boberg; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 151 n. 2; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 828; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IV 290.
K511.p: A messenger carries a letter ordering his own death, but the letter is secretly changed on the way so that he is honored instead.

K511.1.r: Hare persuades the boy that the father said, “Kill the rooster for the hare.”) Africa (Nyika): Bachmann ZsKS VI 84f., Meinhof Afrikanische Märchen 95ff. No. 18, (Namwanga): Dewar Chinamwanga Stories (Livingstonia, 1900) 57ff., (Kaffir): Alexander und Mohl Mitt. d. Sem. f. Orient. Sprachen VIII 15ff. No. 5.
K511.1.p: A victim escapes death by persuading the executioner that a different victim has been ordered killed. The note's example involves a boy who was told to kill a hare.

K511.2.p: An ogam inscription on a shield orders that the bearer, who cannot read it, be killed. A poet who can read it tells the king that it actually requests honorable treatment for the bearer.

K512.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Wells 96 (Chevalere Assigne); Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 74; Italian: Boccaccio Decameron II No. 9 (Lee 56), Basile Pentamerone II No. 6, III No. 2; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 95 No. 53.
K512.p: An executioner who has been ordered to kill the hero or heroine secretly arranges for them to escape.

K512.0.1.p: Slaves ordered to drown a newborn heroine are moved by her smile and instead place her in a calfshed or hollow tree, where cowherds find her and raise her.

K512.0.2.p: An executioner is persuaded to let the hero go by being told that the prince will soon want the hero back.

K512.1.p: A servant ordered to kill the hero smears the hero's coat with an animal's blood to fake proof of the killing, and lets the hero escape.

K512.1.1.p: A servant ordered to kill the hero shows a bloody knife or sword from a slain animal stand-in as proof of the execution, and the hero escapes.

K512.2.r: *Types 671, 709; *Böklen Sneewittchenstudien 79ff.; *BP I 450ff., 463; *Aarne FFC XXIII 57, MSFO XXV 181; *Prato RTP IV 178; Chauvin V 208 No. 120; *Cox 474; *Saintyves Perrault 68; Fb “hjaerte” I 631a, “lever” II 404b, “tunge” III 894a.—Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC No. 706C*; Missouri French: Carrière; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman (S350); Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Shuswap): Teit JE II 730 No. 50; S. A. Indian (Quiche): Alexander Lat. Am. 172.
K512.2.p: A servant ordered to kill the hero (or heroine) secretly substitutes an animal and brings its heart to the master as proof of the killing.

K512.2.0.1.p: A servant sparing the victim substitutes the brains of another animal, not the helpful animal, as the proof of death.

K512.2.0.2.p: A servant sparing the children brings the eyes of an animal instead of the children's eyes that were demanded as proof.

K512.2.0.3.p: A servant brings the eyes, ears, or fingers of a corpse in place of those demanded from the living victim as proof.

K512.2.1.r: BP III 137 (Grimm No. 141); English: Wells 96 (Chevalere Assigne), Alphabet No. 593; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 5; S. A. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.
K512.2.1.p: An animal is substituted for a child and served to the master at a meal, so the child is spared.

K512.2.2.p: A servant ordered to take the hero to executioners sends his own child in the hero's place.

K512.2.2.1.p: When the victim escapes, the executioner makes the substitution, putting another person in the victim's place.

K512.2.3.p: A servant sparing the victim drowns a substitute puppet or dummy in place of the real person.

K512.2.3.1.p: A servant sparing the victim brings a clay head as proof that the execution was carried out.

K512.2.4.p: Instead of killing the victim, the executioner cuts off a body part as proof of death, and spares the victim.

K512.2.4.1.p: A compassionate executioner cuts off a boy's sixth toe as proof that he has been killed, and spares the boy.

K512.3.p: A compassionate executioner pretends to torture the victim while actually sparing them.

K512.4.p: A servant ordered to give the hero poison instead gives a sleeping potion, so the hero survives.

K513.p: An executioner is bribed to let a condemned criminal go free.

K514.r: *Oesterley No. 156; *Herbert III 133 No. 117; Icelandic: Anssaga Bogsveigis (FAS II) 359; Greek: Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Achilleus”; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 313 n. 128; Africa (Ba Ronga): Einstein 260, (Zulu): Callaway 40.
K514.p: A person escapes execution by disguising themselves as a girl.

K514.1.p: A girl is substituted for a boy so that the boy is spared when the father would otherwise slaughter him.

K515.p: A person escapes death by hiding.

K515.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Hrólfssaga Kraka 3, 22, Hálfdanarsaga Brönufóstra (FAS III) 565; Greek: Fox 155 (Zeus and Kronus), Grote I 6; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 189, (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 28; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 355, (Pangwe): Tessman 366, (Fang): Tessman 108; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 275 No. 88.
K515.1.p: Children are hidden so they will not be executed or killed.

K515.2.p: A girl saves herself from being killed by hiding inside a very large harp.

K515.3.p: Sleeping people are covered with an ox hide so that their pursuers or killers do not find them and they survive.

K515.4.p: A character escapes death by hiding inside a kettle.

K515.5.p: A character escapes death by hiding inside a bin of rice.

K515.6.p: A character escapes death by hiding underground in the earth.

K520.p: A character avoids death by using a disguise, pretending to be dead or ill, or putting a substitute in their place.

K521.p: A character avoids death by disguising their appearance or clothing so that they are not recognized.

K521.1.r: *Types 311, 510B, 1137; *BP I 399ff., III 375 (incident B2); *Hackman Polyphemsage 160ff.; *Fb “hest” I 599b; English: Wells 20 (William of Palerne); Africa (Fang): Einstein 76, Trilles Proverbs 203.
K521.1.p: A character escapes by putting on the skin of an animal or of a human being, so as to pass unrecognized.

K521.1.1.r: Penzer I 141 n. 2; Frobenius Das Zeitalter des Sonnengottes (Berlin, 1904) I 199ff; Jewish: Grünbaum Neue Beiträge zur semitischen Sagenkunde (Leyden, 1893) 234f.
K521.1.1.p: A man is sewn up inside an animal's hide and is carried away by birds, escaping in that disguise.

K521.1.2.r: Þiðriks saga I 261—72 (cf. 339—40); Asbjørnsen and Moe No. 58 (type 590); Gonzenbach No. 68 and Köhler’s notes.
K521.1.2.p: A character escapes by dressing in the skin of a bear.

K521.1.3.p: A character escapes by dressing in the skin of a monkey.

K521.1.4.p: A character escapes by putting on the skin of an old woman.

K521.2.p: A character escapes death by altering their bodily appearance so they are not recognized.

K521.2.1.p: A character escapes by shaving off their beard so as not to be recognized.

K521.2.2.p: A character escapes by mutilating their own body, such as cutting off the ears or putting out the eyes, so as not to be recognized.

K521.2.3.p: A warrior whose face has been ruined and beard torn off hides from an enemy by disguising himself as a king wearing a mask.

K521.2.4.p: A character escapes by disguising themselves as a farmer.

K521.2.5.p: A character escapes by disguising themselves as a carpenter.

K521.3.p: A character escapes by disguising themselves by painting or smearing their body, for example with soot.

K521.3.1.p: A character escapes by covering their body with clay so as not to be recognized.

K521.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 8.
K521.4.p: A character escapes danger by changing into different clothes so that others do not recognize them.

K521.4.1.p: A character escapes danger by dressing in clothes of the opposite sex.

K521.4.1.1.r: *Chauvin V 96 No. 31 n. 1; Boccaccio Decameron II No. 9 (Lee 54); Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K521.4.1.1.p: A girl escapes danger by disguising herself as a man.

K521.4.1.2.p: A man in danger is dressed by his hostess as a woman and made to bake, so he escapes being killed.

K521.4.1.3.p: A man in danger is dressed by his hostess as a woman and set to grind corn, so he escapes being killed.

K521.4.1.4.p: A man in danger takes his wife's place in bed, wearing her night-cap, so that his attacker mistakes him for her.

K521.4.2.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 396 No. 18.
K521.4.2.p: A character escapes danger by disguising themselves as a musician.

K521.4.2.1.p: A musician in danger puts on his musician's clothes as if he were about to play, and so escapes.

K521.4.3.r: (Cap o’ Rushes.) *Type 510B; *Cox Cinderella; *BP II 45; *Saintyves Contes de Perrault 187, 196ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 385ff., (Ojibwa): Laidlaw Ontario Arch. Rep. (1918 reprint) 36.
K521.4.3.p: A character escapes danger by disguising themselves as a person of low social standing.

K521.4.3.1.p: A character escapes danger by disguising themselves as a washerman, a laundry worker.

K521.4.4.p: A character escapes danger by disguising themselves as a waiter at an inn.

K521.4.5.p: An adulteress escapes from prison by disguising herself as an old woman.

K521.4.6.p: A hero escapes by making bark sheaths for his fingers, so he can leave without waking his nymph wives, who had made him sleep with his fingers in his mouth.

K521.5.p: A character escapes by hiding inside a huge pumpkin shell.

K521.6.p: An abbot escapes from his lover's husband by disguising himself as a priest.

K521.7.p: One animal escapes danger by pretending to be another animal, a jackal pretending to be a goat.

K521.8.p: A goat escapes a jackal by covering itself with flowers, so it is not recognized or caught.

K521.9.p: Women escape from an enemy camp by disguising themselves as ascetics or holy mendicants.

K521.10.p: A hare escapes a lion by being tied up in a bundle of brushwood.

K521.11.p: A hare and a bride travel hidden in a pot to escape a tiger; when challenged they answer that the pot is ruined, and so are not caught.

K522.p: A character escapes danger by pretending to be dead.

K522.0.1.p: A character fakes death to get out of a marriage they do not want.

K522.1.r: *Type 3; Dh IV 243; Krohn JSFO VI 55ff.; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 329 n 191a; Africa (Kaffir): Kidd 242 No. 9.

K522.1.1.p: A woman smears a fleeing man with goat afterbirth and blood so that his pursuers think she has just given birth, and they stop chasing him.

K522.2.r: “He smells already.” Type 1139; cf. Indonesian: Coster-Wijsman 52 Nos. 77, 78.
K522.2.p: An ogre carries away a man who is pretending to be dead.

K522.3.p: A woman feigns death to escape a plot by her husband to kill her.

K522.4.p: Parrots caught in a net play dead, and the captor throws them out, so they escape.

K522.4.1.r: Bødker Exempler 283 No. 28; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K522.4.1.p: A trout pretends to be dead, and the fisherman ignores it and leaves it, so it escapes.

K522.5.p: A character escapes by pretending to be buried.

K522.6.p: A character escapes by pretending to have drowned, and a wrecked boat or coffin washes ashore carrying them to safety.

K522.7.p: A trickster is attacked by an angry mother, who stabs ox guts and believes she has killed him, so he gets away.

K522.8.p: A character escapes by pretending to have been hanged.

K523.r: Maori: Clark 167; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 78, (Angola): Chatelain 99 No. 6.
K523.p: A character escapes by pretending to be ill.

K523.0.2.p: A character feigns illness to avoid a meeting they do not want to attend.

K525.1.2.p: A bride leaves a wooden figure in the bed in her place and slips away while her sleeping groom is left with the wooden picture.

K525.1.3.p: To save a child from death, a maid puts a block of wood dressed to look like the child in its bed. The enemy strikes the block instead of the child.

K525.2.p: A man steps aside at the last moment so that the blow or capture falls only on his shadow.

K525.5.p: A man escapes a blow by leaving his mantle (cloak) behind, so that only the cloak is struck.

K525.6.p: A person escapes by leaving a dog behind in their place.

K525.7.p: A girl escapes from an ogress by putting a pig in her own place.

K525.8.p: A magic object that destroys or harms is first tested on something lifeless before it is used on a living person.

K525.8.1.p: A magic belt that destroys is tried on a tree to see what it will do.

K525.9.p: Rather than human blood, a cock's blood is given to spirits in place of a person's blood, so that the person is spared.

K525.10.p: A person escapes by leaving false images made of spittle behind, which are taken for the real person.

K527.p: A person escapes death by having another person put in place of the intended victim.

K527.5.p: A man tricks his captor or sacrificer by calling an animal by his son's name, so the animal is killed in the son's place. The son is saved from being sacrificed.

K528.p: A person escapes a dangerous ordeal by secretly sending a stand-in to face it in their place.

K528.1.p: The hero is forced to smoke a deadly pipe, but a helpful insect riding on his head smokes it for him and takes the danger.

K528.2.p: A holy man offers himself in place of a deacon who has been condemned to die by heathen captors, so the deacon is freed.

K528.3.p: Two wicked men facing a fiery test ask that a third, pious man be tested alongside them, so the trial is shared or passed onto him.

K531.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 66, *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Fox 127 (Paris).
K531.p: A hero escapes from a battle by using magic to make himself invisible.

K532.p: A character escapes by hiding under a magic cloak or mantle that makes him invisible.

K532.1.p: A character escapes by vanishing into a magic mist that hides him from pursuers.

K532.2.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 61; India: Thompson-Balys.
K532.2.p: A thief creates a magic storm to cover his escape.

K533.p: A fugitive escapes by changing shape or appearance several times in succession, so the pursuer cannot keep track of him.

K533.1.p: A fugitive keeps changing into different forms until the pursuer is tricked into injuring himself.

K534.p: A person escapes by reversing their shoes, or in the case of a boat, by using it in a reversed way, so pursuers follow the wrong trail.

K534.1.r: *Fb “sko” III 288b, “gå” IV 194b, “hestesko” IV 214a; Laport FFC LXXXIV 49; Köhler-Bolte II 381; *Child III 476n., 479f., 487, 489; *Babler Sudetendeutsche Zs. f. Vksk. VII (1934) 77; England: Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 8 n. 1; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 155; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes II 407; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis VII 6.
K534.1.p: A rider escapes by turning a horse's or ox's shoes around backward, so the tracks point the wrong way.

K534.2.p: A person escapes by wearing snowshoes reversed, so the tracks in the snow point the wrong way.

K534.3.p: The hero walks backward so that the footprints he leaves seem to lead in the opposite direction.

K534.4.p: A person escapes by rowing a boat stern first, facing away from the direction they are going.

K536.p: A captive's captors are fooled into thinking he intends to stay with them, so they relax their guard and he can get away. In the note, a captured general has heavy boxes carried into the temple, which the captors take to be gold and conclude he will not try to leave.

K536.1.p: A girl escapes from a male captor by making him believe that she is preparing for a wedding, so he lets down his guard.

K538.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 871*; Russian: Andrejev No. 871*.
K538.p: A princess escapes from a captor who sleeps with her holding a lock of her hair by cutting off her hair and leaving the captured part behind.

K540.p: A captive escapes by frightening or overpowering the captor through an intimidating display or show of power.

K541.r: *Chauvin VIII 136 No. 132; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 513f.; Philippine (Tinguian): *Cole 195.
K541.p: A captive escapes by claiming to be invulnerable, so that the captor is awed and lets him go.

K542.p: A captive escapes by falsely claiming he can get away at any time. When the captors run to the rear to guard an escape route, he slips away.

K543.r: Fox to bear, who is biting his foot: “You are biting the tree root.” Bear lets loose. *Type 5; *BP II 117 n. 2; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 62ff.; *Fb “bjørn” IV 43b; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia, Malay Peninsula: *Dixon 190 n. 11, *DeVries’s list No. 1; S. A. Indian (Brazil): Hartt Amazonian Tortoise Myths (Rio de Janeiro, 1875) 29; Africa: Werner African 296, 299, (Kaffir): Theal 187, (Mpongwe): Nassau 17 No. 1, 45 No. 6, (Zulu): Callaway 6, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 395 No. 18, (Nakami): FL X 386; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 58 No. 12; West Indies: Flowers 514; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 103.
K543.p: A captive escapes by biting the foot of the captor who holds him.

K543.1.p: A fox, caught by the tongue by a crocodile, says the crocodile has caught the clothes she has been washing. The crocodile lets go, and the fox escapes.

K544.r: *Dh IV 1ff.; *Chauvin II 99 No. 57; *Penzer V 127 n. 1; Bødker Exempler 298 No. 62; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 852; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 3, Dixon 193; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 374 No. 56; Africa (Zanzibar): Bateman 17 No. 1.
K544.p: A captive escapes by claiming that his external soul or heart is not with him. The captor then believes he has left it at home, so he is of no use as a remedy and is let go.

K545.p: A captive escapes by falsely telling his captor that rescuers are coming, so the captor flees.

K546.p: A pope escapes captivity and death by dressing in full papal regalia and overawing his captor.

K547.p: A captive escapes by frightening would-be captors so that they give up or run away.

K547.1.p: A small cock, lost in the woods, orders a fox, a bear and a wolf to get into his belly. The beasts, frightened, apologize and promise never to bother him again, and the bear even carries him home.

K547.2.p: A man removes his wig, false teeth and wooden leg, and this startles Indians who had threatened him, so they are overawed and he escapes.

K547.3.p: A man hides in a hollow log and fires his rifle up through it while Indians sit on the log, scaring them away.

K547.4.p: A jackal escapes a farmer by claiming to be king of the jackals and saying he will call upon his subjects.

K547.5.p: A ferocious animal, usually an ogre, misunderstands a remark made by its victim and flees in fright.

K547.6.p: An ogre is frightened away when the victim beats a tom-tom.

K547.7.p: A goat trembles so hard from fear of a tiger that the shaking of his beard frightens the tiger away.

K547.8.p: A shepherd threatened by a tiger says he will report the matter to an ass, and the tiger, fearing this, flees.

K547.9.p: A threatening tiger is challenged to a strength contest. He is tricked into holding wood for a plow and is injured.

K547.10.p: A queen hides her king, who is disguised as a child, and tells an ogress that she has borne a child with a moustache. The ogress is frightened away.

K547.11.p: A hero threatens a tiger with a plowshare and leads him into the village.

K547.12.p: A captive escapes by frightening a tiger into believing that a goat in a cave is the ghost of his father.

K547.13.p: A witch is so frightened by seeing her intended victim split a boulder with a single sword blow that she lets him escape.

K547.14.p: A trickster escapes by pretending he is holding up the sky, and the leopard holding him captive lets him go out of fear that the sky will fall.

K548.p: A captive or threatened person escapes by making the attacker think many defenders are present.

K548.1.p: A woman alone in a house calls out the names of men who supposedly live there, then rolls cheeses down the stairs, so the attackers think the men are rushing down at them.

K548.2.p: A man makes robbers believe his house is full of people by beating drums all over the house, and the robbers flee.

K548.3.p: A person pretends to call out to helpers, and the robbers, believing others are coming, run away.

K550.r: *Type 122A; *BP II 207; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 246; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 306 n. 109cc; West Indies: Flowers 515.
K550.p: A captive escapes by making a request or proposing an action that lets him get away later on.

K550.1.p: A person escapes punishment by swearing an oath whose wording is technically true but misleading.

K551.p: A condemned person is granted a postponement of death on condition that he first performs some particular act.

K551.1.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death until he finishes praying, and the delay lasts until rescue arrives.

K551.1.1.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death until he has confessed his sins.

K551.1.2.r: Herbert III 84, 508; Chauvin II 191; Icelandic: Boberg.
K551.1.2.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death until a mass has been said.

K551.2.p: A condemned prisoner is granted a reprieve until he has finished drinking his glass, and he leaves it half finished so the delay continues.

K551.2.1.p: An iguana persuades a jackal to let him go so that he can finish his drink.

K551.3.r: Rescuers come. *Types 592, 920; *BP II 501; *Wesselski Märchen 199; DeVries FFC LXXIII 41ff., 324; *Thien Motive 36f.; *Child V 483 s.v. “horn”; India: Thompson-Balys.
K551.3.p: A condemned victim is granted a reprieve from death until he has blown a horn three times.

K551.3.1.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death for as long as someone plays the fiddle.

K551.3.2.r: Rescue arrives. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 173; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 113), 99 (ST 127); Halm Aesop No. 134.
K551.3.2.p: A captive is granted a reprieve from death for as long as he plays music by whistling.

K551.3.2.1.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death for as long as he sings a song.

K551.3.3.p: A maiden about to be murdered is allowed three cries before her death.

K551.3.4.r: Rescue arrives. *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. IX 87; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 173; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 91; India: Thompson-Balys.
K551.3.4.p: A wild boar is allowed to squeal before a wolf eats him.

K551.3.5.p: A condemned person is granted a reprieve from death for as long as someone plays the bagpipe.

K551.3.6.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ndau): Curtis Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (Boston, 1920) 45ff.
K551.3.6.p: A condemned victim is granted a reprieve from death on condition that he first blows a horn three times.

K551.3.6.1.p: A girl about to be killed by robbers is allowed to dance first, and she asks to bring her party of strong men, who are actually disguised, and they overcome the robbers.

K551.3.6.2.p: A mare is allowed to dance before being killed, then gallops off into the jungle carrying a persecuted boy hidden in her belly.

K551.3.6.3.p: Captured men are ordered to dance before they are killed, and they arrange their dance steps so as to defeat their captors.

K551.3.7.p: A small bird called a titmouse is granted permission to sit on a branch and sing before it is sacrificed.

K551.4.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 410; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “toilette”; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 116 No. 970; India: Thompson-Balys.
K551.4.p: A condemned person is granted a delay from death until a toilet or personal task is done, and this delay allows an escape.

K551.4.1.p: A condemned person is granted a delay from death until they change their clothes, and this lets them escape.

K551.4.2.p: The devil must wait while a man ties his stocking, and the stocking is never tied, so the man keeps his freedom and is not taken.

K551.4.3.p: A robber insists on stripping a woman before throwing her off a cliff, and she asks him to turn his face while she undresses, then pushes him off instead.

K551.4.4.p: A condemned hero is granted a delay from death until he has bathed and had a drink, and this lets him escape.

K551.4.5.p: A captive escapes by pretending to go to the river to wash clothes and then running away.

K551.4.6.p: A condemned victim is granted a delay until his mouth is washed, and a crow is shot with an arrow as it goes off to wash its mouth.

K551.4.7.p: A captive escapes by pretending to go off for a bath.

K551.4.8.p: A captive escapes by pretending to go back for a hair ribbon.

K551.5.r: When she sees robber under her bed she pretends not to see him and combs her hair at the window. She says, “When I am married my husband will come home from the tavern and seize me by the hair and I shall cry: “Help!” Rescue comes. Type 959*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 959B*; Russian: Andrejev No. 959*; Chinese: Graham.
K551.5.p: A girl about to be killed is allowed to make her toilet, and she calls for help so that rescuers come.

K551.6.p: A condemned person escapes by asking to die while riding on a horse.

K551.6.1.p: A condemned person escapes by asking to ride on a sacred buffalo before dying.

K551.7.p: A captured animal asks for a delay so that it can give a war alarm, and its captors allow it.

K551.8.p: A wolf is kept waiting outside the door until the children have been christened, and so he loses his feast.

K551.9.r: (Cf. G303.12.5.4.) Type 1184*; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 36, Beal XXI 313.
K551.9.p: A man who has sold his soul to the devil asks to live as long as a candle lasts, and so he escapes death.

K551.10.p: A captive escapes death by asking to give a last kiss, and uses that closeness to attack the captor.

K551.11.p: A captive wins a delay of ten years (or five, or with an ass, a donkey) by promising to teach an elephant (or an ass) to speak, reasoning that someone will likely die or the task will become impossible before then.

K551.12.p: A captive is granted a reprieve from death until he has dried himself in the sun after being covered in mud.

K551.13.p: A condemned person is granted a delay so that he can pay one last visit before being put to death.

K551.13.1.p: The condemned person's delay lasts only until the last visit is over, and he uses the time to escape.

K551.14.p: A captive is granted a reprieve until he has taken six steps toward God; he takes unusually long strides and so escapes.

K551.15.p: A captive is granted a delay from death until a magic object heals him, and he uses the time to escape.

K551.16.p: A woman escapes by pretending she must go to defecate, and so is allowed to leave and then runs off.

K551.17.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 174 No. 75.
K551.17.p: A condemned or captured person is granted a reprieve in exchange for being allowed a drink of water.

K551.17.1.p: A kidnapped woman escapes by asking her captor for a drink of water.

K551.17.2.p: A jackal, tied up, persuades a woman to untie its legs so it can get a drink, and then escapes.

K551.18.p: A wolf is granted a delay from death until it reads a horse's passport; the wolf is kicked to death.

K551.19.p: A wolf is granted a delay from death while it counts the hairs in a horse's tail; the wolf is kicked to death.

K551.20.p: A tailor asks a wolf to stand still to be measured for a suit of clothes, and the wolf is beaten instead.

K551.21.p: A condemned man is granted a delay until a minister shows the king how to harvest pearls.

K551.22.p: A captive is granted a set, definite period of life before being put to death.

K551.22.1.p: A condemned man is given one year to settle his affairs before he is put to death.

K551.22.2.p: God grants a man twenty more years of life on condition that he plays no tricks.

K551.22.3.p: A crocodile grants a boy a five-day reprieve from death.

K551.23.p: A jackal about to be killed by a crocodile asks to be allowed to clasp a tree first, and escapes by this plea.

K551.24.p: A condemned person is granted a delay before death on condition they perform some task, and they use the delay to escape. In this motif, the escape is by flying away in a machine kept there.

K551.25.p: A person threatened with being taken captive escapes by pretending to go and fetch something the captor wants, then never returns.

K551.26.p: A turtle about to be killed asks to go to a pool first to pick flowers, and uses the chance to escape.

K551.27.p: A person about to be killed is allowed to delay death until they fall asleep, and uses the time to escape.

K551.28.p: Captors delay a captive's death so they can see a supposed wonder, and the captive uses that delay to escape.

K553.r: Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 117), 105 (ST 179); Halm Aesop No. 231; Spanish: Espinosa III 446; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 164; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 366ff. No. 65 (variant); West Indies: Flowers 516.
K553.p: A captured creature persuades its captor to wait and fatten it before eating it, and so gains time to escape.

K553.0.1.p: A hero who is to be eaten by cannibals asks to be fattened enough to beat them in a race, then runs away.

K553.0.2.p: A calf, about to be eaten, asks to be allowed to grow up first.

K553.1.r: Escapes. Chauvin II 116 No. 94; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 188, (Basuto): Jacottet 40; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 286 No. 48.
K553.1.p: A captured animal offers to help its captor catch a better, more desirable victim, and so is spared.

K553.1.1.p: A trapped animal tells its captor to wait until men come to free it from the trap, so it can then eat them.

K553.2.p: A troll lets the smaller goats cross the bridge so that he can eat the biggest one, and ends up thrown into the water.

K553.2.1.r: Lamb and ewe escape. Ram butts dwarf into river. India: Thompson-Balys.
K553.2.1.p: A dwarf is persuaded to wait for a ram to come along before it is eaten.

K553.3.p: A ram promises to jump into a wolf's belly, then gives the wolf a hard knock on the head, leaving the stunned wolf thinking it has swallowed the ram.

K553.4.p: A wolf is told by a horse to start eating from the rear, and is kicked to death.

K553.5.p: A captured animal asks to be soaked in a pond first so that it will be juicy and tender to eat.

K553.6.p: A trickster cornered by a leopard jumps into a swamp, then claims he is too dirty to eat, and the leopard, after smelling him, agrees.

K555.p: An executioner is kept busy or interested until rescue arrives, sometimes until the executioner changes his mind.

K555.1.p: A condemned person gains a respite from death by making a very long speech that holds the executioner's attention.

K555.1.1.r: *BP I 222; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 365A*, Legends Nos. 349, 360.
K555.1.1.p: A condemned person delays death by telling a long tale about how flax is prepared.

K555.1.2.r: *BP I 222; 331; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1199 I*.
K555.1.2.p: A condemned person delays death by telling a long tale about how bread is made.

K555.2.p: A condemned person delays execution by singing or telling a very long song, keeping the executioner occupied until rescue arrives.

K555.2.1.r: Unsuccessful imitation. (Cf. Z20.) Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 364.
K555.2.1.p: A tale in which a formula-tale, a long repetitive story with an endless chain of incidents, saves a girl from the devil by keeping him listening until she is rescued.

K555.2.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1084A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1084 I*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1615*.
K555.2.2.p: A soldier escapes death by singing an endless song, as he has bargained with Death to do.

K555.3.p: Jackals persuade a tiger to settle an argument, keeping him busy so that the intended victim escapes.

K557.r: *Type 332; *BP I 377ff.; Wesselski Märchen 214 No. 17; **Christiansen Danske Studier (1915) 72ff.; Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 332; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K557.p: Death is cheated when a man who has chosen Death as his godfather turns his bed around after seeing Death at its foot, so Death cannot take him.

K558.r: *Crane Vitry 161 No. 62; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 283; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 25; U.S., England: Baughman; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 161; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K558.p: A condemned man is allowed to choose the tree he will be hanged from, but he cannot find one suitable.

K558.1.p: A man who is allowed to choose his tree asks to die by falling from it, and so escapes hanging.

K558.2.p: A man asks to be beheaded while standing in a tank of water; he ducks, and the executioners end up killing each other.

K561.p: A captive escapes by persuading the captor to talk, so that the captor's attention is diverted from the captive.

K561.0.1.p: A captive tries to escape by persuading the captor to talk, but the attempt fails.

K561.1.r: *Type 6; *BP II 207; *Chauvin II 200 No. 39; *Fb “ræv” III 113b; **Dargan MPh IV 39; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 743; *Graf FFC XXXVIII 39f.; *F. N. Robinson Works of Chaucer 858 (Nun’s Priest’s tale).—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 239*; Russian: Andrejev No. 241 I*; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “coq”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 23 No. 12; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 146 No. 27; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 326 No. 110; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 239f. No. 12.
K561.1.p: A captured animal gets its captor to open his mouth and talk, then escapes when the captor's mouth releases it.

K561.1.1.r: The cat answers at last, “Even so, I eat you up.” Type 111.
K561.1.1.p: A cat is not tricked into releasing a mouse it holds in its mouth, though the mouse tells it a story to try.

K561.1.2.p: A frog escapes a crow by telling it to sharpen its bill before eating him, so the crow stops to do so and the frog gets away.

K561.2.r: Dogs are summoned. *Type 122C; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. IX 87; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K561.2.p: Sheep persuade a wolf to sing, and so the wolf lets go of its captive or prey.

K561.3.p: A crocodile is persuaded to open its mouth, and when it does, it shuts its eyes automatically, letting a monkey escape.

K562.p: A rat persuades a cat to wash its face before eating it, and the rat escapes while the cat is busy.

K562.1.r: Escapes. Africa (Nama): Bleek 23, No. 12, (Hottentot): Meinhof Lehrbücher d. Sem. f. orient. Spr. XXIII 165.
K562.1.p: A captive trickster persuades the captor to pray before eating him, and escapes during the delay.

K562.2.p: A hare persuades a cat to perform two gallops before eating him, and escapes during the delay.

K563.p: A captive escapes by making a plea that leaves an opening through which he can get away.

K563.1.p: A jackal in a tiger's house is allowed to sit with its tail hanging down between bamboo stems; it enlarges the gap this makes and escapes.

K563.2.p: A tortoise persuades its tiger captor to put it in a pocket that has a hole in it, and so escapes.

K565.p: A tiny character swallowed by an animal talks it into going to his father's house to plunder, and so gets out.

K565.1.p: A boy swallowed by a fish, which is thrown up on the shore, gets a tiger to cut the fish open by ordering it not to look at him.

K565.2.p: A jackal trapped inside a dead elephant asks a passing god to show his power by making it rain; the hide swells with the rain and the jackal escapes.

K566.r: Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 115), 114 (ST 244); Halm Aesop No. 334; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 30, 31; Japanese: Ikeda.
K566.p: A donkey gets a wolf to pull a thorn out of its foot before being eaten, then kicks the wolf in the mouth.

K567.r: Africa (Thonga): Junod 212, (Kaffir): Theal 188, (Ekoi): Talbot 233; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 60 No. 8, Nights 366 No. 65.
K567.p: A captive escapes by pretending to carry out a task or chore for the captor.

K567.1.p: A prince begs a giant not to eat him, promising to prepare the giant a good dinner.

K567.2.p: A man persuades robbers to put off killing him until he has shown them his treasure, then leads them into a marsh and escapes.

K571.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 44; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 12 No. 3.
K571.p: A captive gets untied by pretending he will dance for his captors.

K571.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 180*; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; India: Thompson-Balys.
K571.1.p: A hare promises to dance if the doorway is left free, and then escapes when it is.

K572.p: A captive escapes from his captor by flattering him.

K573.p: A captive escapes by claiming that the captor will have bad luck if he kills him.

K573.1.p: A man about to be killed by a girl asks her whether she will have to take all the guilt, and so escapes.

K575.p: A condemned man claims that if corpses are buried in the city it will become a ruin, and the king sets him free.

K576.p: A man held by thieves escapes by claiming prices are high in another town, tricking them into leaving him.

K579.p: Escapes by false pleas that do not fit any of the more specific headings under this section.

K579.1.p: A wife accused of planning to run away weeps and threatens suicide to dispel suspicion and get away.

K579.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 317, Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 7, Dixon 190 n. 10.
K579.2.p: A monkey trapped on a bridge over crocodiles saves itself by telling the crocodiles that the king has ordered them to be counted, so they line up to be counted and it crosses over their backs to escape.

K579.3.p: A traveler escapes robbers by pretending to be going their way, then separating from them at the first chance.

K579.3.1.p: A fugitive escapes his pursuers by pretending to be one of them.

K579.4.r: Chinese: Graham; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 6.
K579.4.p: A monkey escapes a trap by pretending to be getting married.

K579.5.p: Captives get a pause from harm while the captor acts as judge between them.

K579.5.1.r: *Wesselski Märchen 251 No. 58; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 30, 31.
K579.5.1.p: A wolf is asked to judge a contest between captives and rules on who should run first; while he sits as referee, the captives get time to plan. They run at him and kill him, so the captives escape.

K579.5.2.p: A tiger is persuaded to help foxes divide their young, which gives the foxes time to slip away into their hole.

K579.6.p: A knight who is refused leave to go out of a city fakes having just killed a public enemy, and the guards help him escape in the rush.

K579.7.p: A thief jailed for stealing a quarter of veal sends a man named Calf to his captor, joking that he is sending a whole calf. The joke gets him released.

K579.8.p: A fox asks a rooster to come down from a tree and sing for him, but the rooster asks the fox to first wake his companion, a dog. The dog kills the fox.

K580.p: The captor is talked into a punishment that does not actually harm the captive, so the captive escapes.

K581.p: A captive is supposedly punished by being placed in the very place he likes best, so the punishment is no punishment at all.

A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 302 n. 108; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 153 No. 17, (Jaunde): Heepe 107; (Benga): Nassau 124 No. 12, (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 88, (Yoruba): Ellis 266 No. 3, (Zanzibar): Bateman 40 No. 2; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 58 No. 12, 115 No. 24, Friends 167 No. 23, cf. K581.1.p: A turtle, eel, or crab begs not to be drowned, so his captor throws him into the water, where he lives and escapes.

K581.2.r: **Ruth I. Cline American Literature II 72ff.; **Espinosa JAFL XLIII 129 ff.; *Dh IV 26; Köhler-Bolte I 266; *Parsons Folklore XXX 227. Missouri French: Carrière, Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 108; Indonesia: *DeVries Volksverhalen II 381f. No. 147 (duck); Oceanic: Meyer Mythen und Erzählungen der Küstbewohner der Gezellehalbinsel 49, 187, Fox and Drew JAI XLV 204; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 446, Speck UPa I 141 n. 8; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 395, (Zanzibar): Bateman 38 No. 2; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 16 No. 4; Barbadoes: Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 270; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 244; West Indies: Flowers 516.
K581.2.p: A rabbit begs not to be thrown into the briar patch, so his captor throws him in there, and he runs off to safety.

K581.2.1.p: Men fold a hare's legs back and throw him on the ground as a punishment, which is what the hare wanted.

K581.3.p: A mole is punished by being buried, which is the very environment it wants, so the punishment does not hurt it.

K581.4.p: A bird is punished by being thrown into the air, which is where it wants to be, so it flies away.

K581.4.1.p: Birds trapped in a net escape by flying off with the net, after the captor pretends to punish them by throwing them into the air, their favorite element.

K581.5.p: A jackal expresses horror at being burned, and his captors burn him instead; he sets fire to a village with his burning tail. This tale also explains why the jackal's tail tip is burnt.

K581.6.p: A thieving insect in a tightly woven basket asks to be put in a loosely woven one, where he cannot see, and so escapes.

K582.p: A captive persuades his captor into a punishment that kills the captor instead of the captive.

K582.1.p: A turtle persuades an animal to swallow him; the turtle then kills the animal from inside and escapes.

K583.r: Wesselski Bebel II 103 No. 15; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 35 No. 165*.
K583.p: A captured wolf escapes punishment when a debate concludes that marriage is the worst punishment. The captor is persuaded into an illusory penalty and lets the wolf go.

K583.1.p: A thief, asked to choose his punishment, begs not to be given the luxury of two wives, which is the one thing he would dislike.

K584.r: Thief, surprised at theft says: “Do your worst, only don’t throw me over the fence.” When thrown over, he escapes. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1627A*.
K584.p: A thief escapes punishment when he is thrown over a fence, which is what he wanted.

K600.p: A murderer or captor is tricked or fooled in some other way so that the captive escapes.

K601.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 130, (Basuto): Jacottet 2 No. 1, (Fjort): Dennett 106 No. 30.
K601.p: A captive escapes by pretending to be a member of the murderer's own family or tribe, so he is spared.

K601.1.p: A captive escapes by pretending to be the tiger's dead father's teacher or spiritual guide, so the tiger lets him go.

K601.2.p: A captive escapes by persuading a giant or ogre not to eat its young, pretending to be a relative who cares for them.

K602.r: (Sometimes “myself.”) *Hackman Polyphemsage 179, 203, 219; *Fb “selv”; Clouston Noodles 194 n.; BP III 378; *Oertel Studien zur vgl. Literaturgeschichte VIII 117f.; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XV 70.—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 56 No. 480; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 262; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 36.
K602.p: A hero escapes a monster by giving a false name that is a word with a double meaning, such as "Noman", so the monster cannot identify who harmed it.

K602.1.r: Child tells mother, “Self did it.” England, Scotland: *Baughman.
K602.1.p: A fairy's child is hurt by a man who tells it his name is "Self", so the fairy cannot name him as the attacker.

K602.2.p: A man who has eaten the sweets gives his name as B, so that when asked who is eating the sweets he answers that Bee is eating them.

K603.r: *Type 1137; **Hackman Polyphemsage 160ff.; *BP III 375; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—7; Icelandic: Boberg.
K603.p: A hero escapes a blind ogre by hiding under the belly of a ram, slipping out between the ogre's legs as the animal walks out.

K604.r: (See for these counsels: J21.12, J21.13, J21.14.) *Type 150; *BP III 230, IV 149 n. 2; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 380; *Wesselski Arlotto II 261 No. 1191; *Chauvin III 103, 110ff., IX 30; *Crane Vitry 144 No. 28; *Gaster Exempla 256 No. 390; *Basset 1001 Contes II 276f.; Jacobs Aesop 213 No. 58; Wienert FFC LVI 35; Halm Aesop No. 271; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 95a; Alphabet No. 191; Oesterley No. 167.—Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 29, 279; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 231.
K604.p: A man frees a bird or fox from captivity, and in return the animal gives him three lessons, which usually mock him for being foolish to let it go.

K605.r: Indonesia: Dixon 224, 225 n. 31, Beckwith Myth 194; Tahiti: Dixon 63, Beckwith Myth 197 n. 21, ch. 13 passim; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 194.
K605.p: A cannibal is sent for water in a vessel full of holes, and while he fails, the intended victim escapes.

K605.1.r: New Zealand: Dixon 85, Beckwith Myth 196 n. 19.
K605.1.p: A cannibal is sent for water, but the water magically moves away from him, so he cannot fetch it and the victim escapes.

K606.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 109; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 137 n. 1.
K606.p: A captive escapes by singing a song that gradually lulls the murderer or captor until they are charmed and let them go.

K606.0.1.p: A captive gets his pursuer to sing while he is held, and the captive escapes while the pursuer is distracted.

K606.0.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 277.
K606.0.2.p: A captive escapes by teaching a song to the watchman who guards him.

K606.0.3.p: A trickster pretends not to see an enemy attacking him and instead sings a song of friendship, disarming the enemy.

K606.1.p: A captive escapes by playing music that distracts or pacifies his captors.

K606.1.1.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 100 No. 18.
K606.1.1.p: A captive escapes by playing magic music that forces the captor to dance, while the victims get away.

K606.1.2.p: A captive escapes by playing music that brings sleep to his captors.

K606.1.2.1.p: A captive escapes by singing the watchmen to sleep.

K606.1.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3276, Legends Nos. 467—471.
K606.1.3.p: A musician in hell plays for the devils and deliberately breaks his fiddle strings, so he must return to earth to repair them and thus escapes.

K606.1.4.p: A witch is distracted and put off guard by a man playing a jew's harp, letting the captive escape.

K606.2.p: A captive escapes by persuading his captors to dance, and while they dance he gets away.

K607.p: An enemy lying in ambush or in disguise is tricked into revealing himself.

K607.1.r: **M. Bloomfield JAOS XXXVI 58; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 110; Mexican Spanish: Espinosa JAFL XXIV 419ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys, Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) III 15, 361; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 853; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 31; N. A. Indian (Oaxaca, Mexico): Boas JAFL XXV 208; Africa (Zanzibar): Bateman 41; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 142 No. 19; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 247 No. 23; West Indies: Flowers 517.
K607.1.p: A hiding animal is fooled into revealing itself: when an enemy calls out at its cave, the animal stays silent until the caller claims they had agreed to call and answer each other, and the hidden one answers and gives itself away, so the other flees.

K607.2.p: A crocodile disguised as a floating log is tricked into giving itself away when told to move upstream, since obeying the suggestion betrays it.

K607.2.1.p: A crocodile lying in ambush disguised as a log gives itself away by speaking.

K607.3.r: U.S.: Baughman; India: *Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 53 No. 11; West Indies: Flowers 517—9.
K607.3.p: A man pretending to be dead is tricked into betraying himself by making a movement, because he obeys a suggestion about how a dead man should act.

K607.3.1.p: A tiger pretending to be dead gives itself away when its penis, still alive, betrays it by moving or reacting.

K607.3.2.p: A man pretending to be dead is tricked into moving by being made to perform an absurd action, which reveals that he is alive.

K607.3.3.p: A leopard hidden inside a bundle gives itself away when it is threatened that a spear will be run through the bundle, and it jerks or reacts.

K608.p: A captured bird escapes by crying and laughing at once: she weeps about her little ones and laughs at the hunter for wasting time, claiming her treasure is in her house, so the hunter lets her go.

K611.p: A captive escapes by lulling the captor into carelessness through some pretended harmless activity.

K611.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 326 n. 174; S. A. Indian (Yuracare): Alexander Lat. Am. 314, Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 502.
K611.1.p: A captive pretends to pick lice from his captor's hair but secretly cracks berries between his teeth, making a noise that deceives the captor.

K611.2.r: Girl pretends to be cooking meal for animal husband: escapes. India: Thompson-Balys.
K611.2.p: A captive escapes by pretending to cook food, keeping the captor busy or unaware while he gets away.

K611.2.1.p: A captive escapes from a madman by sending him off to fetch water for cooking.

K611.3.p: A captive escapes on a ship that runs on wheels, after tricking the captor into putting down his sword and helmet to receive a pretended gift.

K611.4.r: Deceives them. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3303, Legends Nos. 578ff.
K611.4.p: A man held by devils convinces them that he will come back, and they let him leave.

K612.p: A prisoner is released after promising to marry the guard or captor.

K613.p: A prisoner is released after promising lifelong loyalty to the captor.

K614.r: Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 9 No. 5, 35 No. 27.
K614.p: An animal captor is pacified by being fed the captive's family, so it spares the captive.

K615.p: A boy trapped in a hole escapes a descending log by digging a hole to get away from it.

K619.p: Miscellaneous tricks in which a murderer or captor is deceived into letting the victim escape.

K619.1.p: Cannibals are told to go away while the hero is cooked, because he will not taste right if they watch.

K619.1.1.p: A clever girl about to be eaten by an ogress tricks her by shaking sesame seeds into a fire so it sounds like lice burning, persuading the ogress to leave the cooking to her or step away, so the girl can escape.

K619.2.p: A pursuer is tricked into smearing oil on a tree so that he cannot climb it to chase the fugitives who are escaping up it.

K619.3.p: A trickster gets his pursuers to take part in a game that is secretly deadly for them, so they are destroyed while he gets away.

K620.p: A captive or fugitive gets away by tricking the person guarding him.

K621.r: *Type 73; *Thompson CColl II 440f.; Dh IV 184; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 2, 124; Louisiana Creole: Fortier MAFLS II 115; Alu: Wheeler 42, 48; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 95; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 45f. No. 6, (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 174, (Cameroon): Meinhof 89; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 30 No. 7, 47 No. 10, Nights 95 No. 18, 280 No. 47, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 262, (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 178, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 219; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 240 No. 13, 247 No. 23.
K621.p: A captive escapes by blinding the guard, typically by throwing pepper or tobacco into his eyes.

K621.1.p: Escapees break open a nest of red ants and throw it onto the ogre's head, so the ants blind or distract him and they get away.

K621.2.p: Fugitives escape from animals that are chasing them by blowing ashes into the animals' faces.

K622.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 33, (Basuto): Jacottet 102 No. 15; West Indies: Flowers 519.
K622.p: A captive keeps asking to play or go farther and farther away from the watchman until he is out of reach and escapes.

K622.1.p: A captive escapes by pretending that he and his captor must have a debate about which of them should be judged first, so the captor waits while the captive slips away.

K622.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 172.
K622.2.p: A captive escapes by throwing objects far away so that the captor goes to fetch them, leaving the captive free to run.

K623.p: Fugitives escape while their watchman is outwitted by a rope stretched across the road so that he trips or is blocked.

K624.p: Abductors are tricked into running a race, and while they are busy the captive escapes.

K625.r: Boje 112ff.; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K625.p: A captive escapes by giving a sleeping drug to the guards so they fall asleep.

K625.1.r: Type 306; Africa (Ronga): Junod Les Chants et les Contes des Ba Ronga (Lausanne, 1897) 317ff. No. 30.
K625.1.p: A girl's escape plan fails because the hero refuses to take the narcotic offered to him, so he stays alert.

K625.2.r: Irish myth: Cross (K649.1); U.S.: Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
K625.2.p: A captive escapes by getting the watchmen drunk so they cannot stop him.

K626.p: A captive escapes by paying off the guard with a bribe.

K626.1.p: A captive escapes by throwing money or treasure among the guards so that they fight over it while he runs off.

K629.p: A miscellaneous escape in which the captive tricks the guard in some way not covered by the more specific motifs.

K629.1.p: A captive escapes by pretending to bathe the guard, using boiling water in the process.

K629.1.1.p: A man and a woman escape when the woman sends a she-bear back to fetch her supposedly forgotten comb, which gives them time to get away.

K629.2.p: A guard or keeper is lured away from his post so that a prisoner can get free.

K629.2.1.p: A tiger is enticed away by a promise of berries, and the people it was guarding escape.

K629.2.2.p: A tiger is lured away by a dead pig, and the people it was guarding escape.

K630.p: A captive gets free by disabling or weakening his pursuers so they cannot chase him.

K631.p: A captive tricks his captor into giving up his own weapons, so the captor cannot follow.

K631.1.r: *BP III 454; Wesselski Märchen 222 No. 36; Scala Celi No. 537.
K631.1.p: The captive dodges a blow aimed at his hand, and the captor's hatchet lodges in a log, leaving him unarmed.

K631.2.r: Type 1528*; BP III 455; U.S., Scotland: Baughman.
K631.2.p: The captor is tricked into a shooting contest that uses up all his shots, leaving him without ammunition.

K631.3.p: The captive holds a hat just outside his shelter so that the enemies shoot at it, revealing their position or wasting shots and leaving them slow to reload.

K632.r: *Fb “bue” IV 76b; Jewish: *Neuman; N. A. Indian (Hupa): Goddard U Cal I 154ff.
K632.p: Mice gnaw through the enemies' bowstrings so they cannot pursue.

K632.1.p: An army of mice saves a kingdom from invaders by chewing their food, ammunition and other supplies to shreds.

K633.p: The captor's gunpowder is secretly replaced with ashes, so his gun will not fire and the captive can escape.

K634.p: A captive delays pursuit by arranging or destroying the captor's clothes so the captor cannot quickly follow.

K634.1.p: The captive escapes by throwing the captor's clothes on the fire, so the captor cannot follow.

K634.2.p: A master thief persuades his captors to dive into the water, then steals their clothes while they are swimming.

K635.r: Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Hupa): Goddard U Cal I 154ff.
K635.p: A captive ties the hair of sleeping enemies to an object so they cannot get up and pursue him.

K635.1.p: A sleeping maiden's hair is tied to a tree, so she cannot rise and follow.

K636.r: *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 552a n. 285; Herrmann Saxo 125; Kersbergen Literaire Motieven in de Njala (Rotterdam, 1927) 83; Panzer Hilde-Gudrun; Icelandic: *Boberg; Indonesia: Van Baarde Bijdragen voor Taal-, Landen Volkenkunde van Ned.-Indie VII (2) 464; N. A. Indian: Krickeberg Indianermärchen aus Nord-Amerika (Jena, 1924) 209, (Hupa): Goddard U Cal I 154ff., (Montagnais): Speck JAFL XXXVIII 7.
K636.p: Holes are bored in the enemies' boats so that they cannot pursue by water.

K636.1.p: The paddles of the enemies' boat are broken so that they cannot pursue.

K637.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 131, 448, 469, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 634, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 167.
K637.p: The thongs tying the sleds are cut, so pursuers cannot follow.

K638.p: A captive tied to his captor escapes by tying the end of the rope to a post, leaving the captor stuck.

K640.p: A character escapes capture or punishment with the secret help of an accomplice who arranges the getaway.

K641.p: One animal rescues another by scaring off the enemy that is threatening it.

K642.p: An animal that is still free rescues a companion that has been caught.

K642.1.p: A crow and a rat together free a deer that has been caught in a snare.

K643.p: A helper sings or otherwise keeps the pursuers busy and delayed so that the fugitive can get away.

K644.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 82.
K644.p: A monkey distracts the mowers or harvesters so that young birds have time to fly away from the field.

K645.p: A monkey saves birds that are condemned to death by pretending to have a dream that changes the outcome.

K646.r: Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 15; Korean: Zong in-Sob 22, 212; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 31.
K646.p: A fugitive's helper sends a pursuer off in the wrong direction.

K647.p: A helper cuts a prisoner's rope nearly through so that the prisoner can break it and run away.

K648.p: A bird's call draws the pursuer's attention away so that the trickster can get away.

K649.p: Miscellaneous escapes in which a helper aids the escape in ways not covered by the more specific categories.

K649.1.p: A helper hides the fugitive from the pursuers.

K649.1.1.p: One animal swallows another to hide it from a pursuer and so save its life.

K649.1.2.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 162, (Yuracare): ibid 144.
K649.1.2.p: A tiger-mother hides her guests, who are concealed in a jar.

K649.1.3.p: A helper sits on the hero to conceal him and so save him.

K649.2.p: A rescuer disguised as an officer gets custody of a prisoner so that he can free him.

K649.3.r: Icelandic: Hrólfs saga Kraka 10 ch. 3, Boberg.
K649.3.p: Boys are scolded on purpose so that no one notices who they really are.

K649.4.p: A son is called a daughter so that an enemy pursuing him will not recognize him and he is saved.

K649.5.p: Boys are warned to escape by means of the names of dogs, which convey the danger.

K649.6.p: Sons are warned through talk about oaks to hide themselves.

K649.7.p: A helper in disguise assists a man in escaping from captivity.

K649.7.1.p: A helper disguised as a beggar assists someone in escaping.

K649.7.2.r: Krappe Scandinavian Studies XVIII (1945) 275—283; Icelandic: Þiðriks saga I 261-72 (cf. 339—40), Asbjørnsen og Moe No. 58 (type 590), Boberg.
K649.7.2.p: A helper wearing a bear's skin assists someone in escaping.

K649.7.3.p: A helper disguised as a troll scares off the king's men, while the king's daughter helps the prisoner get away.

K649.8.p: An accomplice saves a fugitive by pretending to chase him in the wrong direction.

K649.9.p: An accomplice creates confusion so that a prisoner can slip away.

K649.10.p: A prisoner escapes by luring a wolf close to him by smearing honey on its feet, then using the wolf to get away.

K649.11.p: A prisoner escapes by cutting his fetters on stones.

K649.12.p: An accomplice convinces the captor to throw away a disguised trickster, who is thereby freed.

K650.p: Other ways of escaping by trickery that do not involve a helper.

K651.r: *Type 32; BP IV 320; Chauvin III 78 No. 57; Fb “ræv” III 113b; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 43; English: Wells 184 (The Fox and the Wolf); Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 75 No. 16, (Pennsylvania): Parsons JAFL XXX 214, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXIV 16, Stewart JAFL XXXII 394.
K651.p: A wolf goes down into a well in one bucket and comes up in the other, rescuing a fox who was trapped below.

K652.r: *Type 31; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 119), 97 (ST 117); Halm Aesop No. 45; Jacobs Aesop 220 No. 82; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia, Indo-China: *Dixon 189 n. 9, cf. DeVries’s list No. 4.
K652.p: A fox trapped in a pit climbs out by standing on a wolf's back.

K655.p: A prisoner kills the guards who come in to torture him.

K656.p: Captors are tricked into drowning themselves.

K657.p: Tales that exaggerate how someone escaped.

K661.p: A person escapes being suspected of a crime by trickery.

K661.1.r: *Type 1600; *Chauvin VI 126 No. 280; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 183 No. 347; India: *Thompson-Balys; cf. Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 308, Coster-Wijsman 53 No. 78.
K661.1.p: A fool's brothers replace the body of the man he has killed with a goat, so that the fool is spared suspicion.

K661.2.p: A statue is mourned and buried in place of a murdered person, so that the death is explained.

K661.3.r: Africa (Larusa): Fokken ZsKS VII 82ff. No. 1, (Masai): Hollis The Masai (Oxford, 1905) 212ff.
K661.3.p: An insect in the nose of a murdered person makes it seem as if the person is snoring, which allays suspicion that the person is dead.

K661.4.p: A waxen statue is left in place of an abducted queen, so that her disappearance goes unnoticed.

K671.p: A captive escapes by throwing his hat to lions, which fight over it while he gets away.

K672.p: A captive escapes by throwing his shoe at a serpent, which chokes on it while he gets away.

K675.r: (Sometimes magic pillow or magic sleeping card.) *Schoepperle I 257 n. 1; *Wesselski Märchen 254 No. 61; Child I 393, III 506b, IV 459b; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 54 No. 400B*; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
K675.p: A man who is supposed to spend the night with a girl is given a sleeping potion so he cannot stay awake to be with her.

K675.1.r: Chest is stolen. When he escapes he is accused of being a robber. He is saved by his mistress’s maid who explains all, transferring the role played by her mistress to herself. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K675.1.p: The girl's lover, who was meant to be drugged, unknowingly drinks the sleeping potion himself. He falls into a deep sleep and is thought dead, so he is placed in a chest.

K676.p: A trickster gets pursuers to ride in his basket, then leaves the basket hanging from a tree limb and escapes while they are stuck.

K677.r: *Type 301; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 165 (Gonzenbach No. 64).
K677.p: A hero tests the rope he is to be hauled up on and discovers that his companions plan to cut it. He does this by placing stones on the rope.

K677.1.p: A hero hides inside a treasure box, so that when his companions pull the box up they cannot leave him behind as they planned.

K678.r: Indonesia: Dixon 227; Marquesas: Handy 41; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 97ff. No. 18.
K678.p: A hero cuts a rope while an ogre is climbing it toward his intended victim, sending the ogre to his death.

K683.p: A small animal in the mouth of a larger one makes the captor spit it out, freeing the small animal.

K685.p: A captive escapes by grabbing hold of the branches of a tree as he passes under it.

K686.p: A captive escapes by announcing a great catastrophe, such as the end of the world, so that his captors flee or let him go.

K687.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1065.
K687.p: Birds escape being caught in a net by flying away with it.

K700.p: A person is captured through a trick or deception.

K710.p: A victim is lured into willingly entering captivity or a helpless state.

K711.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 163—167; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 522.
K711.p: A victim is tricked into getting inside a bag.

K711.0.1.p: Birds are lured into a bag by a trick.

K711.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 94.
K711.1.p: A victim is tricked into entering a magic bag, which then closes on him and traps him.

K711.2.p: A leopard is persuaded to get into a bag so that he can see the trickster perform a marvel, and is trapped.

K711.2.1.p: A miser is persuaded to thrust his head into a bag, and a thief then pulls a noose tight around his neck.

K711.3.r: Africa (Nubian): Rochemonteix Quelques Contes Nubiens (Cairo, 1888) 55ff. No. 5, (Swahili): Steere 13ff.
K711.3.p: An ogre is tricked into rolling himself in a mat and is burned.

K711.4.p: A witch asks a boy to pass down fruit from a tree; when he bends down to hand it over, she grabs him and stuffs him into her sack.

K713.p: A victim is tricked into letting himself be placed in chains or shackles.

K713.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—67; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 20; West Indies: Flowers 522f.
K713.1.p: A victim is tricked into letting himself be tied up.

K713.1.1.r: Africa (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 215; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 12ff. No. 2, Harris Nights 325ff. No. 56; West Indies: Flowers 523f.; Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 324 n. 2; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 233 No. 1.
K713.1.1.p: An animal lets itself be tied up to keep from being swept away by a storm.

K713.1.2.r: Carried to his death. (Cf. J2132.6.) *BP III 75 n. 2; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 28; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 87.
K713.1.2.p: An animal lets itself be tied to another animal for safety.

K713.1.3.p: An animal is persuaded to be tied up by the promise of food.

K713.1.4.p: An animal is persuaded to be tied up out of curiosity to learn secret names.

K713.1.5.p: An ogre lets himself be tied up so that he can learn magic.

K713.1.6.p: An animal lets itself be tied up so that it can learn music.

K713.1.7.p: An unfaithful wife ties her sleeping husband's hair to the bed so that her lover can kill him.

K713.1.8.p: Women tie a sleeping warrior's hair to the wall of a hostel while he sleeps.

K713.2.p: A victim is tricked into putting a collar around his neck.

K713.3.p: A hare persuades a wolf and a fox to put their heads through loops in a rope, and then strangles them.

K714.p: A victim is tricked into entering a box or prison.

K714.1.r: *Wesselski Arlotto I 209 No. 50; Irish myth: Cross; Africa (Thonga): Junod 216.
K714.1.p: A victim is tricked into a prison and kept there.

K714.1.1.p: A trickster persuades a policeman to take his place in the stocks. Then the trickster tricks the policeman's wife into giving him jewels.

K714.2.r: M. Bloomfield in Penzer VII xvii; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 294, Dixon 197; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 62 No. 13, (Virginia): Bacon and Parsons JAFL XXXV 267, (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 175, Brown Collection I 704.
K714.2.p: A victim is tricked into entering a box.

K714.2.1.p: A victim is tricked into jumping into a box by being made to believe he is going to heaven.

K714.2.2.p: A tiger is enticed into a coffin.

K714.3.r: India: Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 74 No. 14; West Indies: Flowers 524.
K714.3.p: A dupe is tricked into entering a hollow tree.

K714.4.p: A trickster gets a victim to climb into a basket, and the victim is then caught.

K714.5.p: A woman is talked into putting her head into a jug, and she is then caught while she cannot pull free.

K714.6.p: An animal is enticed into a lion's den.

K714.7.p: A victim is led into a cave by following a deer that a demon has sent to lure them there.

K714.8.p: A fish is tempted into a trap with the promise of new skins.

K714.9.p: A lion is tricked into getting stuck in a cave entrance, and a hare then eats it.

K714.9.1.p: A fox tricks a lion into falling into a pit.

K715.r: M. Bloomfield in Penzer VII xiii; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K715.p: A victim is tricked into letting himself be hanged: he asks the executioner to show him how the gallows works, and then the hero hangs the executioner instead.

K717.r: *Type 331; *BP II 414ff. (spirit); Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 29 No. 1 (bees).
K717.p: Insects or a spirit that have escaped from a bottle are tricked into going back in, by being told they cannot return.

K721.r: Seized. *Type 61; *Graf FFC XXXVIII 26ff.; BP II 207; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 122), 98 (ST 124); **Dargan MPh IV 39; *Chaucer’s Nun’s Priest’s Tale; Spanish: Espinosa III 225, 258; Japanese: Ikeda.
K721.p: A rooster is persuaded to crow with its eyes closed.

K721.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 70.
K721.1.p: A victim is tricked into shutting his eyes and opening his mouth, and then hot stones are thrown down his throat.

K722.r: *Types 545AB; BP I 325ff., III 487; Missouri French: Carrière, India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K722.p: A giant is tricked into turning himself into a mouse, and a cat then eats him.

K722.1.p: A dragon in the form of a child is lured into a pot and boiled, on the claim that it will get to see "courage."

K724.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1525M*; Flemish: Meyer FFC XXXVII No. 1528*.
K724.p: A victim is persuaded to waste all his bullets, and then he is seized.

K725.p: A victim is lured away from the protection of his friends and then captured.

K726.p: A victim is persuaded to ride on the trickster's back, and is then captured.

K728.r: Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 319; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 216; N. A. Indian: Boas RBAE XXXI 324.
K728.p: Foxes crawl into a whale's house and are killed there.

K730.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 47.
K730.p: A victim is caught in a trap.

K730.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 59), 66 (ET 307), 90 (ST 23), 94 (ST 73), 97 (*ST 111, 114); Halm Aesop Nos. 44, 340.
K730.1.p: An animal is caught because it is curious about what the trap is.

K730.1.1.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 19; Africa (Jaunde): Heepe 249.
K730.1.1.p: The trapper claims the trap is a prayer house, and the animal goes in out of curiosity and is caught.

K730.2.p: A frog tricks a herd of deer into dancing their way into a hunter's snare. The deer are lured into the trap by the frog's deception.

K730.3.p: A leopard traps a lion using a cave with two entrances, one large and one small. The lion goes in through the big entrance, the leopard slips out the small one, and attacks the lion from behind.

K730.4.p: A tortoise misleads an elephant onto the wrong path so that it walks into a trap. The tortoise's false directions cause the elephant's capture.

K730.5.p: Birds are lured into a trap by the promise of a feast. They fall for the bait of free food and are caught.

K731.p: A wild boar is caught after being tricked into entering a church. The animal is captured inside the building.

K732.r: Burned. *Type 124; *BP I 40; U.S. (Maine and New Hampshire): Ford JAFL XV 63; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 11; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Flathead): McDermott JAFL XIV 250; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 38 No. 8, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXIV 17, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 267.
K732.p: An intruder is caught by being trapped in a chimney. The thief or intruder becomes stuck or cornered there.

K735.r: (Cf. B361.) *Type 160; Chauvin II 106 No. 71; England: Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1323, 1/89); Mono-Alu: Wheeler Nos. 2, 6, 18, 48ff.; Africa (Benga): Nassau 86, 191 Nos. 4, 25, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 386 No. 11, (Fang): Trilles 267.
K735.p: A victim is caught by falling into a concealed pit set as a trap. The general category covers all such pitfall captures.
