K735.1.p: Mats are laid over holes so that the victim steps onto them and falls into the pit below. The covering hides the danger.

K735.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 80.
K735.2.p: A victim is caught when he sits on a seat that is a trap. The seat gives way and drops him into a pit.

K735.3.p: A knight falls into a pitfall and is captured, while his horse gets away. The horse escapes but the rider is trapped.

K735.4.p: A victim is caught when a trap bed drops him into a dungeon below. He lies down and the bed collapses into a pit.

K735.4.1.r: Alu: Wheeler No. 2; Telei: ibid. No. 18.
K735.4.1.p: A pit is hidden under a bed to catch whoever lies on it. The bed becomes the trap.

K735.5.p: A dupe is tricked into going down a well and is then left there to die or be stuck. He is abandoned in the well after being deceived.

K735.6.p: A tiger is lured into a pit by being tempted to leap after a boar leader. The tiger jumps after the boar and falls into the hole.

K736.r: Traps victims. N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 307 n. 113.
K736.p: A door snaps shut on the victim, trapping him. The trap is a spring-loaded or sudden closing door.

K737.r: Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 258 No. 38, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 366 No. 17.
K737.p: A victim is captured by having the entrance to his own home closed off. He is shut in or kept from getting out.

K737.1.p: A dupe is lured into a hole and then the entrance is closed on him. He is trapped underground with no way out.

K737.2.p: A tiger is persuaded to walk into a house and is then locked in. The door is closed behind it, capturing the animal.

K741.p: A figure covered with tar or another sticky substance captures an intruder. The intruder talks to it, then strikes it and gets stuck to it.

K741.1.p: A horse's back is tarred so that a thief or intruder who touches it gets stuck. The tar on the horse captures whoever tries to take it.

K742.p: A small animal lures a larger one into a tree, where the big animal gets its body caught between branches and cannot pull free.

K743.p: A victim is tricked or lured into a noose and caught in it.

K745.r: Mono: Wheeler No. 34; Alu: ibid. 17, 35; Papua: Ker 7, 17, 36, 73; Aurora: Codrington No. III 12; Lepers Island: ibid. No. III 17.
K745.p: A victim is lured into a building which is then set on fire, burning him inside.

K750.p: A captor catches someone by using a decoy or lure that draws the victim into the trap.

K751.r: (Cf. K757.) *Types 47A, 56A; Chauvin III 76; Crane Vitry 127 No. 304; Herbert III 461; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 29, Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 242, 1131; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 27; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 176, 332; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 298 n. 88; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 14 No. 1, (Fjort): Dennett 79 No. 17; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 310 n. 1, 312, 315, 324; West Indies: Flowers 525ff.
K751.p: A captor catches someone by pretending to be dead, so the intended victim comes close and is seized.

K751.1.p: A hunter hides inside an animal carcass and catches the animal that comes to feed on it.

K751.2.p: A man pretends to be dead and hides in a money chest, and so catches a thief who comes to steal.

K752.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 30 No. 1, (Basuto): Jacottet 100 No. 15, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 384 No. 2; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 79 No. 15, 95 No. 18 (hollow tree).
K752.p: A captor hides under cover such as grass or leaves and seizes the victim who comes near.

K753.r: Egypt: Maspero Contes populaires de l’Ancienne Egypt (Paris, 1882) 85f.; Arabian: Basset 1001 Contes II 301; Indonesia: Overbeck Insulinde I 148.
K753.p: A captor hides inside an object made to look like something harmless, and so seizes the victim.

K753.1.p: Captors hide inside a ship disguised as something else, and so take the people who approach it.

K754.p: A captor hides inside a hollow figure shaped like an animal, and so is carried in and seizes the victim.

K754.1.r: *Fb “stud” III 619b; *Penzer II 133 n. 1; Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 431; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 229 n. 1, 231 n. 1.
K754.1.p: The Greeks hide soldiers inside a huge wooden horse left before a city, and the soldiers open the gates to take the city.

K754.2.r: *Penzer I 133 n. 1; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 859.
K754.2.p: A captor hides inside a hollow artificial elephant, and so gets close enough to seize the victim.

K754.3.p: A captor hides inside an artificial bird, and so gets close enough to seize the victim.

K755.p: A captor catches a victim by disguising himself as someone else, such as a trusted person.

K755.1.p: A woman is abducted after someone falsely signals that her husband is returning, so she goes out and is taken.

K756.r: Africa (Kaffir): Theal 119, (Fjort): Dennett 85 No. 10; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 242 No. 17; Antigua, British West Indies: Johnson JAFL XXXIV 68.
K756.p: A captor catches animals or people by imitating the voice of an animal, so the victim comes to the sound.

K756.1.p: A hunter catches birds by imitating their song, so the birds come close and can be taken.

K756.2.p: A would-be thief tries to catch someone by making an animal make noise, so the owner comes out and the attempt fails.

K756.2.1.p: A thief tries to lure the owner out at night by making the owner's pig squeal, so the owner comes out to check and the theft fails.

K756.2.2.p: A trickster captures an animal by ringing a cowbell so the animal thinks a cow has wandered far off, drawing it away from its safety to be caught.

K756.3.p: A bird catches fishes by imitating the voice of a friend, so the fishes come close enough to be caught.

K757.p: A trickster pretends to be sick, so that the victim comes near to help or see, and is then captured.

K758.p: A captor hides inside baskets of food, so that the victim who carries or takes them is caught.

K761.p: A captor disguises himself by putting on the clothes of a slain enemy, so he can get close and capture the enemy's people.

K762.p: A stranger asks a woman for fire, and then carries her off.

K763.p: A captor hides in a hollow tree so that the intended victim, passing by, is caught.

K764.p: A witch disguises herself as a starving beggar woman to win a child's trust and then captures the child.

K767.p: A hare carries a lion disguised and covered with honey, so that other animals approach it and are caught in a trap.

K770.p: A general heading for other tricks by which a victim is captured through deception that does not fit the more specific categories.

K771.p: A unicorn is tricked into driving its horn into a tree, where it becomes stuck and can be captured.

K771.1.p: A lioness is lured into pushing her head into a wall while chasing a hare, and the hare escapes through a hole while she is stuck.

K772.p: A victim is enticed into dancing and is captured while dancing.

K772.1.p: Crabs are persuaded to take moonlight walks and are then eaten by their captor.

K773.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 7 n. 1, 15, 60.
K773.p: A trickster tricks the victim into picking out the trickster's teeth, a deception that leads to the victim's capture or harm.

K774.1.p: The sight of women's bare breasts is used to pacify enemies and calm their hostility.

K774.2.p: The sight of unclothed women calms the anger of a young hero who is raging.

K775.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 214 No. 73.
K775.p: A merchant is lured into looking at a supposed bargain and is captured while he does so.

K775.1.p: A merchant is captured when he is taken aboard a ship to inspect the wares being offered, and the crew then seizes him.

K776.r: Dickson 67 n. 13, 122 n. 71; Malone PMLA XLIII 415; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 5, Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 169; West Indies: Flowers 527.
K776.p: A person is captured or overpowered after being made drunk or drugged.

K776.1.p: A captor lulls defenders to sleep with enchanting music, then takes them.

K776.1.1.p: A harper sings the garrison of a fortress to sleep while the attackers stop their own ears with their fingers, so the fortress falls.

K776.2.p: A man is made drunk and left alone in a temple, where he is at the mercy of demons.

K777.p: A castle is taken by pretending to surrender, then the attackers enter once the gates are opened.

K778.p: A woman uses her charms or trickery to help capture a person or place.

K778.1.p: A disguised female warrior, an Amazon, invites enemies into the forest one at a time and overpowers each.

K778.2.p: An Amazon disguised as a leper seduces enemies and ties them up one by one.

K778.3.p: A captor is lured to a courtesan's house and seized there.

K778.4.p: A bridegroom is invited to the women's quarters to eat with his bride and is then attacked there.

K778.5.p: An adulterous wife lures her husband into a trap so that he will be killed.

K781.r: (Cf. K811.1.1, K2340.) Dickson 240, 241 n. 44; Krappe “Die Sage von der Tarpeja” Rheinisches Museum für Philologie LXXVIII (1929) 248—67; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 31.

K782.p: A captor hides and waits in an enemy's usual place, then seizes them there.

K783.p: A person is captured after being blinded.

K783.1.p: An enemy is blinded by being thrown chili powder in the eyes and is then overpowered.

K785.r: Type 1083; Magyar: Honti FFC LXXXI 35 No. 1083.
K785.p: In a duel fought with long poles, an ogre is driven backward until he is forced into a pigsty.

K786.p: A fairy wins a kiss in a game, then embraces a woman and flies away with her through the smoke hole in the roof.

K787.p: A maiden is sent to a meeting with her lover, but the lover is captured there instead.

K788.p: A woman is lured into the forest and captured there.

K788.1.p: A princess is lured into the forest and captured by a boy or thief who is playing a harp.

K800.p: A general category: a character is killed or crippled by being tricked into it.

K810.p: A trickster deceives a victim into his power, where the victim is killed or maimed.

K811.r: *Type 56B; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 32; West Indies: Flowers 528.
K811.p: A victim is coaxed into a house or dwelling by a trickster and then killed there.

K811.0.1.p: An animal that has long been fed by hand is tempted into a palace, where the trickster kills it.

K811.1.r: (Cf. K871.2.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 661, 662; *BP II 85, III 106; Gaster Thespis 211, 328; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Grote I 150; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Yanagita Folklore Studies XI 2 No. 2; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/555).
K811.1.p: Enemies are invited to a banquet and then killed.

K811.1.1.r: (cf. K781.) English: Wells 85 (The Sowdone of Babylone).
K811.1.1.p: Prisoners, with the help of their captor's daughter, kill many of his soldiers during a banquet.

K811.1.2.p: Enemies are invited to a feast and then poisoned.

K811.2.p: Jackals are persuaded to go into a pit to escape an approaching storm, and they die there.

K811.3.r: He comes to see a girl die and is killed himself. Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K811.3.p: A cruel king is lured into his enemy's power by an invitation to what he is told is a false execution.

K811.4.p: Hostile visitors are lured into a house of iron that is hidden behind wooden walls; the hosts then set the house on fire.

K811.5.p: A false friend places food on the far side of a hidden ditch, so the victim falls in and is killed.

K812.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys, Panchatantra III 16 (tr. Ryder) 364; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 32, 75.
K812.p: A victim is burned to death in his own house or hiding place.

K812.1.p: The dupe's house is set on fire, and he is burned while trying to put the fire out.

K812.1.1.p: A boy teaches giants to spread dried grass and naphtha over the hard floor of their cave, then sets it alight and suffocates them.

K812.2.p: Men are lured to their deaths when their fields are set on fire.

K812.3.p: A monkey lures a tiger up into a treetop and then sets the tree on fire.

K812.4.p: An owner burns an intruder to death inside his house.

K813.r: Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 85), 97 (ST 106, 192); Halm Aesop No. 243; India: Thompson-Balys.
K813.p: A stag is killed by a lion after the fox leads the stag into the lion's den.

K813.1.p: A whimbrel sends his unfaithful mate to meet him in a cave, having arranged with a lion to be there to eat her.

K813.2.p: A hare tricks a civet cat into being eaten by a lion.

K814.p: An overly curious dupe climbs into the trickster's basket and is killed.

K815.r: *Type 242; Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 101), 97 (ST 112); Halm Aesop No. 263; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 33 No *127A; India: *Thompson-Balys, Panchatantra III 13 (tr. Ryder) 368; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 276 No. 41, (Kaffir): Theal 177; West Indies: Flowers 528.
K815.p: A victim is coaxed by flattering or friendly words into approaching a trickster, who then kills them.

K815.1.r: Kills him. Chauvin II 94 No. 44; Bødker Exempler 291 No. 48; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K815.1.p: A fox coaxes a rooster to climb down from his perch so they can talk, intending to catch and kill him.

K815.1.1.p: The fox tries to talk a rooster down from his perch, but the rooster calls a dog and the fox runs away.

K815.2.r: Eats her. Herbert III 40ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K815.2.p: A spider politely invites a wasp or fly to rest on her fine web, which is really a trap meant to catch and kill it.

K815.3.r: Are killed. Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 90), 97 (ST 109); Halm Aesop No. 266.
K815.3.p: Dogs are fooled by the smooth, insincere words of wolves and trust them, to their harm.

K815.4.p: A cat invites hens to a feast and then kills them.

K815.5.p: An owl kindly invites a cricket to share his nectar, and the cricket is then killed by the owl.

K815.6.r: Kills him. Panchatantra III 13, (tr. Ryder) 368; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 127.
K815.6.p: A snake promises a frog that he will do it no harm, and then harms the frog anyway.

K815.7.r: *Penzer V 102 n. 2; Chauvin II 96 No. 50; Bødker Exempler 294 No. 55; Panchatantra III 2, (tr. Ryder) 315 (partridge and rabbit); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K815.7.p: A cat is asked to judge a dispute between a sparrow and a hare, then eats both of them.

K815.8.p: A hawk talks doves into electing him as their king, and then he preys on them.

K815.9.p: A tiger flatters a cow into opening her mouth to show that she has few teeth, so he can attack her.

K815.10.p: A weasel gets a cuckoo to admit that it cries at night while asleep, which gives the weasel a way to kill cuckoos.

K815.11.p: A wounded wolf asks a lamb to fetch him a drink, promising he will get his own food afterwards, meaning to eat the lamb.

K815.12.p: A boat is lured to shore by kind words and wrecked, so that its crew is punished.

K815.13.r: Bødker Exempler 306 No. 81; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K815.13.p: A cat makes a truce with mice, and once they have grown friendly with him he eats them.

K815.14.r: (Cf. K713.1.2.) Bødker Exempler 281 No. 26; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 260.
K815.14.p: A crane tricks fish into letting him carry them from one pond to another, and then eats them once he has them in his power.

K815.14.1.p: Fish are lured by kind words and killed by an old man.

K815.15.r: Kills them. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 133*; Russian: Andrejev No. 61 II*; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX No. 133*.
K815.15.p: A cat lures young foxes out of their den by playing music.

K815.16.p: A jackal pretends to be holy and then seizes rats who have come to worship him.

K815.17.p: A king of fishes eats his own subjects as they come to pay him respect day and night.

K815.18.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 71.
K815.18.p: A serpent asks his victim to feed him honey, then grabs him and swallows him whole.

K815.19.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 75.
K815.19.p: A trickster tells a victim to stand ready under a tree to catch a falling bee nest, then throws a club at him instead. The victim, lured in by friendly words, walks up to the trickster and is killed.

K816.p: A dupe is tricked into going to a dance that does not exist, and is killed when he arrives.

K818.p: A victim is talked into giving up his weapons, leaving him defenseless against the trickster.

K818.1.p: A man is tricked into handing his own sword to a captured enemy, who then uses it to kill him.

K818.2.p: A giantess is killed with the spear she herself gave to the hero.

K818.3.p: A victim's arrows are made harmless, so they can no longer hurt the one who is attacking him.

K818.4.p: A victim is deceived by having his weapons hidden away, leaving him unable to fight.

K821.p: Fairies in animal form are persuaded that they will hear music better if they take their own shapes again, and are thereby caught or killed.

K822.p: Women lure a warrior aside so that a confederate can kill him.

K824.r: Bødker Exempler 289 No. 42; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 220 No. 98; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 271a; Africa (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 171f.; West Indies: Flowers 529; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 256 No. 38.
K824.p: A sham doctor kills his patients instead of curing them.

K824.1.r: *BP III 375; **Hackman Polyphemsage; Icelandic: *Boberg; Melanesia, Indonesia: Dixon 188f. nn. 6—8; S. A. Indian (Quiche): Alexander Lat. Am. 169.
K824.1.p: A sham doctor kills an ogre or giant by pretending to treat him.

K825.r: Type 1653; *Cosquin I 244f.; Norwegian: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 141 No. 1654; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 147, 181—8; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K825.p: A victim is persuaded to stick out his tongue, and the trickster cuts it off. The robbers in this group use excuses such as learning to sing, learning a foreign language, or having a hair removed from the tongue.

K825.1.r: Dh III 28; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 306 n. 109aa.
K825.1.p: A cormorant's tongue is pulled out after a louse is put on it, so that the bird pulls its own tongue out trying to get the louse off.

K825.1.1.p: A victim is persuaded to stick out his tongue, and the trickster bites it off.

K825.2.p: An elephant is killed when its trunk is cut off and poked into a cave after the victims hiding there, who are then killed as well.

K825.3.p: A man tricks a victim into biting off his own tongue.

K825.4.p: A man is persuaded to hold out his hand to receive a supposed letter from the king, and is harmed when he does so.

K826.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 295 n. 82, (California): Gayton and Newman 83, 85.
K826.p: A trickster induces ducks to dance with their eyes closed, then kills them.

K827.p: A dupe is persuaded to lower his guard and is then seized by the trickster.

K827.1.r: (Bird has advised other bird how to avoid the fox; he is revenged.) *Type 56A; Dh IV 279; Chauvin II 112 No. 81; Bødker Exempler 306 No. 82; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 258f.; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 36 No. 5, (Hottentot): Bleek 21 No. 11; West Indies: Flowers 529.
K827.1.p: A fox persuades a bird to show him how she acts in a storm, and when she does so he devours her.

K827.2.p: Cannibals are tricked into taking snuff, and while they are off guard and their vigilance is relaxed, the trickster seizes and kills them.

K827.3.r: American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 92 No. 19; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 109 No. 63.
K827.3.p: The victim is persuaded to sing or dance on the trickster's body, and when he comes near the trickster's mouth, he is killed.

K827.4.p: A fox pretends to be dead and kills the crows that come to peck at his body by seizing them.

K827.5.p: A crab smeared with cheese lures a giant by his sense of smell, and the crab then pinches the giant's neck and kills him.

K828.p: A bloodthirsty animal gets itself admitted into a fold or pen by a trick, then kills the peaceful animals inside.

K828.1.r: *Herbert III 36ff.; Hervieux IV 222 No. 51; Jacobs Aesop 209 No. 39; Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 35), 68 (ET 325), 96 (ST 100); Halm Aesop No. 376; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K828.1.p: A fox disguises himself in sheepskin, gets admitted to the sheepfold, and kills the sheep.

K828.2.r: Herbert III 36; Hervieux IV 221 No. 50; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K828.2.p: A fox pretends to be ill, is admitted to the hen-roost, and kills the hens.

K828.3.p: A wolf tries to cheat a ewe by pretending to be a ram.

K831.p: The victim is killed while being bathed, through the bather's treachery.

K831.1.p: A slave washing her mistress's back in a stream pushes her into a crocodile's hole, where she is killed.

K831.1.1.p: The trickster sends the victim to a well to fetch water, then pushes him in.

K831.2.p: Girls pretend to wash a monkey's buttocks, and in doing so they kill it.

K832.p: The victim is tricked into looking around, and while his attention is elsewhere he is seized and killed.

K832.1.p: A jealous wife tells her sister to look down, then pushes her over a cliff.

K832.1.1.p: The victim is persuaded to look into a well or pond, and is pushed in.

K832.2.p: A fencer draws his opponent's attention to something behind him, and when the opponent looks around, the fencer cuts off his head.

K832.3.p: A female accomplice undresses in front of the hero, and while he looks away from her he is attacked.

K832.4.p: A man gets a bear to look away by telling her to listen for hunters, then kills her.

K832.5.p: The victim is persuaded to look for a certain tree, and is pushed over a cliff while looking.

K832.6.p: A man is asked to look at birds and is pulled into a pool while doing so.

K833.r: Is killed. Italian Novella: Rotunda; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G 3/59); S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 74.
K833.p: A trickster pretends to be injured or in need of help, and lures a man into coming to his aid, only to be killed or harmed by him.

K834.p: A victim is killed while sleeping in the house of the killer, after being tricked into staying there.

K834.1.p: The victim is tricked into going to sleep so that he can be killed.

K835.p: A dragon is tricked into listening to a story until it is distracted, and the hero then cuts off its head.

K836.p: A fierce wild boar is fed and then lulled to sleep by having its body rubbed, so that it can be overpowered.

K837.p: A victim is killed while a load is being lifted off his back, leaving him unable to defend himself.

K838.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Hausa): Frobenius Atlantis IX 277ff., 287ff., Nos. 74, 75.
K838.p: A victim is lured into a feeding trough and pounded to death with poisoned fish.

K839.p: Miscellaneous tricks by which a victim is lured into the trickster's power and killed.

K839.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 87.
K839.1.p: The victim is coaxed into eating, and is killed when he is off his guard.

K839.2.p: The victim is lured to come near by a false sign or token that seems to come from a trusted person.

K839.3.p: The victim is tricked into drinking by having his food oversalted, and is killed when he is off guard.

K839.4.p: A king demands milk from all hornless cows, but is tricked into accepting milk from wooden cows, and dies.

K839.5.r: Crushes wolf. India: Thompson-Balys; Maori: Clark 112.
K839.5.p: A camel tricks a wolf into looking at the writing on his breast, leading to the wolf's destruction.

K839.6.p: Supernatural beings are tricked into exposure to daylight, which kills them.

K840.p: A person is deceived into taking the place of another, so that the substitute is killed.

K841.r: *Type 1538; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 172—4, 193, 196; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Wachaga): Gutmann 191.
K841.p: A person is spared execution by trickery, usually by having someone else take his place.

K841.1.p: The condemned man avoids execution by persuading others that the man being executed at that moment will become king in heaven.

K842.r: (Cf. K714.2.1.) *Types 1525A, 1535, 1737; *BP II 10ff., III 188, 192, 393; *Fb “sæk” III 720b; *Cosquin Études 392; *Chauvin V 247 No. 147 n. 1.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1535A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1535B*; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 23; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163-7, 172-4; New Mexican Spanish: Espinosa JAFL XXIV 419ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 104 No. 56; Indonesia: Dixon 191 n. 14, De Vries’s list No. 276, Coster-Wijsman 26 No. 5; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 196, 438, 444; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 419ff.; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis II 220ff., VIII 54f., 61f., 175ff.; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 111 No. 23, 140 No. 29, Nights 177 No. 31, 185, No. 32, (Alabama): Work JAFL XXXII 400; Bahama: Parsons MAFLS XIII 82 No. 39, Edwards MAFLS III 63, Finlay JAFL XXXVIII 293; Antigua, British West Indies: Johnson JAFL XXXIV 54.
K842.p: A prisoner tricks a dupe into climbing into a sack in his place, and the dupe is thrown into the sea and killed. The trickster keeps saying he does not want to go to heaven or marry the princess, so the dupe eagerly volunteers.

K842.1.p: A dupe is persuaded to take the prisoner's place while suspended in the air, and is killed.

K842.2.p: A dupe is persuaded to take the prisoner's place in a pit, where he is killed.

K842.3.p: A tied-up animal talks another animal into taking its place in the sack or bag, so the other animal is the one who gets killed.

K842.4.p: A raja (ruler) takes the place of a man who is condemned to death, having been convinced that the death will send him straight to heaven.

K843.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 276, Dixon 201 n. 38*.
K843.p: A gullible person is tricked into allowing himself to be killed, on the belief that dying will take him to heaven.

K843.1.p: Gullible people are persuaded to be burned to death, on the promise that they will be sent back to life with gifts.

K844.r: Mexico: Boas JAFL XXV 207, 238, Mechling JAFL XXV 202; New Mexico: Espinosa JAFL XXIV 419. Cf. American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 90 No. 17.
K844.p: A dupe is persuaded to take the trickster's place as a musician at a wedding party, and the trickster sets fire to the dupe so that he burns to death.

K845.r: Hanged. (Cf. K852.) Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 71, Voorhoeve 79.
K845.p: A pursuer is persuaded to take the fugitive's place in what he is told is a swing, and is then killed.

K846.p: A trickster who is about to be attacked by a fierce animal gets a dupe to take his place, and the dupe is killed instead.

K850.p: A general heading for tales in which a trickster kills or harms a victim through a game that is really a deception.

K851.r: Indonesia: Dixon 197; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 340 n. 226; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 98, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 378 No. 3, (Basuto): Jacottet 14 No. 1, 18 No. 12, (Thonga): Junod 215, (Zulu): Callaway 6; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 242 No. 16; West Indies: Flowers 530.
K851.p: A trick game in which the players burn each other, and the dupe is burned or boiled to death.

K852.r: *Penzer I 157; *Köhler-Bolte I 210, 585; Icelandic: Boberg; Danish: Christensen DF XLVII 200 No. 36; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 122 Nos. 40-42; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 326 No. 19; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 30 No. 3.
K852.p: A deceptive game in which the victim is tricked into hanging the other players, and the dupe is actually hanged.

K853.p: A trick game in which the victim is drowned.

K854.r: N. A. Indian (Pueblo): Parsons JAFL XXXI 227f.
K854.p: A trick game in which the victim is thrown from a cliff; a spider throws its young down and another animal copies it, with fatal results.

K855.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 350 n. 262. Cf. Indonesia: DeVries Volksverhalen I 374 No. 44.
K855.p: A deadly swinging game in which an old woman makes the swing break while her rival is on it.

K855.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 95.
K855.1.p: A trick game in which bear cubs sway in a tree, and the others fall and are killed.

K856.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/116); S. A. Indian (Quiche): Alexander Lat. Am. 175.
K856.p: A deadly game in which players pretend to die and revive; the hero has the power to bring people back to life but does not revive his enemy.

K857.r: (Not fatal.) Africa (Fang): Tessman 40; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 239 No. 11.
K857.p: A trick game in which the players throw away their knives, and the dupe is then harmed or killed.

K858.r: Africa (Benga): Nassau 144 No. 16; West Indies: Flowers 531.
K858.p: A deadly game in which a dupe has his head cut off while the trickster pretends to shave his neck.

K861.p: A deadly game of sewing each other up; a hare sews an antelope up completely so that the antelope dies.

K863.p: A shooting game in which a blind man shoots an arrow at a target, and it kills his friend.

K863.1.p: A jealous husband tricks a blind poet into killing his wife's lover with an infallible spear.

K864.p: A deadly game in which players throw apples at each other, and the dupe is killed.

K865.p: A deadly game in which a person is tricked into putting their head into the notches of a device, and is then killed when the notches close or the device is triggered.

K866.p: A deadly game in which a victim is persuaded to roll down a hill inside a barrel, and is killed in the fall.

K867.p: A deadly duel or game in which one brother kills another while they pretend to play or fight.

K867.1.p: A pretended sword game in which a brother is deceptively killed.

K868.p: A deceptive game in which two people butt heads against each other like rams, and both are killed. In the note, robbers kill themselves this way.

K869.p: Miscellaneous deadly games in which a victim is tricked into a game that leads to death.

K869.1.p: A fox asks to be frightened, and a titmouse whistles as if calling dogs, so the fox is nearly caught in this deceptive game.

K869.2.p: A deceptive hide-and-seek game, proposed by seven demons so as to kill the hero.

K869.3.p: A deceptive game in which a camel invites a lion to eat it, and the camel is killed by the lion.

K869.4.p: A deadly swimming race proposed by the hero to trick spirits; as each spirit arrives, the hero drowns it.

K870.p: Killing by deception using a narcotic or intoxicating substance that makes the victim helpless.

K871.r: Korean: Zong in-Sob 168 No. 72; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 441; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 397; West Indies: Flowers 531.
K871.p: Enemies are made drunk or intoxicated and then killed while helpless.

K871.1.r: Köhler-Bolte I 512; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
K871.1.p: An army becomes intoxicated and is overcome by the enemy.

K871.2.p: Drunken enemies are slaughtered in their banquet hall.

K872.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Gaster Exempla 230 No. 251, *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 362f., *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
K872.p: A girl from the enemy camp is sent to sleep with an intoxicated general, and she kills him in his bed, as Judith killed Holofernes.

K872.1.p: A girl kills a man who is sleeping with her.

K873.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV 5; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Fang): Einstein 66, (Basuto): Jacottet 16 No. 2.
K873.p: Someone is killed by being secretly given a narcotic or sleeping drug.

K873.1.p: A king is given a sleeping potion and then beheaded in his bed by his wife.

K873.2.p: A groom is murdered while the watchmen and the bride are lulled to sleep by music.

K873.3.p: A boy makes an adversary unconscious by secretly putting opium in half the tobacco in his pipe.

K873.4.p: A poisonous drug is secretly placed into half of a fruit, which is then given to an enemy; the drug is hidden under the fingernail until it is slipped into the fruit.

K874.r: Irish myth: Cross: India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 12; S. A. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 502, RMLP XXXIII 144.
K874.p: A killer pretends to pick lice from someone's head, as a friendly act, in order to deceive the victim into a deadly situation.

K874.1.p: An ape pretends to pick lice from a heron, but instead pulls out its feathers.

K875.p: A killer pretends to comb a victim's hair, as a friendly gesture, and uses this pretense to bring about the victim's death.

K890.p: A trickster tricks a victim into killing himself by his own action.

K890.1.p: A poor man outwits a rich man with a series of pranks, and the rich man dies as a result of them.

K891.p: A victim is tricked into leaping to his death.

K891.1.p: A wolf that has come into a house is tricked into jumping down the chimney, where he kills himself.

K891.2.r: Indonesia, Japan, Melanesia: Dixon 194 nn. 26-28, Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 68, 92.
K891.2.p: An ape is tricked into jumping onto stakes, and is killed by them.

K891.3.p: A monkey is tricked into jumping into water, where it drowns. In this motif a jackal hides in reeds that screen the water, so the monkey cannot see the danger.

K891.4.p: A victim is tricked into jumping onto a funeral pyre that he believes holds his beloved, and so dies.

K891.5.p: A victim is induced to jump over a cliff edge and fall to his death.

K891.5.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 299 n. 91; Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 37 No. 18.
K891.5.1.p: Animals, or giants in some tales, are lured over a precipice to their deaths.

K891.5.2.r: Type 10***; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 41.
K891.5.2.p: A victim is crowded or pushed by others until he goes over a precipice.

K891.5.3.p: Several people are persuaded to let themselves be thrown over a precipice, and so die.

K891.5.4.r: U.S.: Baughman (K894.4, K894.5); India: Thompson-Balys (K894.4); Tonga: Gifford 101.
K891.5.4.p: Several victims are deceived into falling over a precipice.

K892.r: Type 10**; S. A. Indian (Tembé): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 140.
K892.p: A victim is crowded or pushed into the water, and drowns.

K893.p: A victim is forced onto thin ice, which breaks, and he drowns himself.

K893.1.p: A man leads pursuers to the edge of thin ice, then suddenly swerves away, so that they fall through the ice.

K895.r: Sulka of New Britain: Dixon 131, *132 n. 2.
K895.p: Cannibals are enticed to climb a slippery barricade and fall to their deaths.

K896.p: An animal is tricked out of its natural surroundings, where it either dies or manages to escape.

K896.1.p: A beaver and a porcupine each play a trick on the other: the beaver strands the porcupine in the middle of a lake, the porcupine freezes the lake and escapes, then strands the beaver high in a tree.

K897.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 36 No. 3.
K897.p: A victim is tricked into travelling a slippery road lined with knives, and he kills himself by falling onto them.

K897.1.p: A snake is killed when knives are hidden in the animal it is trying to swallow, so it cuts itself open.

K897.2.p: An animal is killed by axes or knives left in a tree, which it runs into or falls onto.

K897.2.1.p: A giant impales himself on a javelin that a fugitive holds behind himself, so the giant runs onto it.

K897.3.p: Robbers make a bathing prince's staircase slippery so that he falls and is killed.

K898.p: A victim is tricked into measuring a wild boar whose bristles are poisoned, and is killed by touching it.

K910.r: Types 10**, 221, 228; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda.
K910.p: A killing carried out through a clever plan or stratagem rather than open fighting.

K911.r: *Type 56B; Wienert FFC LVI *59 (ET 207), 98 (ST 125); Halm Aesop No. 225; Chauvin III 76 No. 50; Herbert III 36ff.; Hervieux IV 220 No. 49.—Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1131; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 35; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 17 No. 1.
K911.p: A person pretends to be dead in order to get close to an enemy and then kills him.

K911.1.r: *Type 1539; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 198 No. 391; Chauvin VII 151ff. No. 430.
K911.1.p: A trickster has himself buried alive, then stabs enemies from the grave when they come to desecrate his body.

K911.2.p: A man feigns death and stabs his brother when the brother comes to mourn him.

K911.3.p: A person pretends to be asleep in order to lure in and kill an enemy.

K911.4.p: A king pretends to be dead, then jumps up and kills the slave nearest to him.

K911.5.p: A person pretends to be deaf so that an enemy comes close enough to be killed.

K912.r: *Types 304, 956AB; *BP I 373; *Fb “hoved” I 654b, “røver” III 132a; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K912.p: Robbers or giants entering a house have their heads cut off one at a time as each one comes in.

K912.0.1.p: Robbers or giants entering a house have their noses cut off one at a time as they come in.

K912.0.2.p: Robbers or giants entering a house have their hands cut off one at a time as they come in.

K912.1.p: A giant or giantess has her or his head cut off as he or she looks out of a window or door.

K912.2.p: Men are lured one by one into a serpent pit and killed.

K912.3.p: An ogre who wants to marry a woman is tricked into helping bury her murdered lover, and she then cuts off his head while he is digging.

K913.p: A hero in disguise attacks an enemy during a feast, killing him among the guests.

K913.1.r: Icelandic: Hálfdanar saga Eysteinssonar ch. 7—8 (cf. introd. 23—24), *Boberg.
K913.1.p: Shipwrecked men in disguise are taken in at a king's house, and at the Yule feast they kill him to avenge a murder.

K914.p: A victim is murdered by an attacker lying in wait for him.

K914.1.p: A bear is shot or killed by an ambusher as it comes out of its cave.

K914.2.p: An enemy passing below a hill is killed when a rock is rolled down onto him.

K914.3.p: Someone is killed in secret under cover of darkness.

K916.r: *Chauvin V 84 No. 24 n. 1; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Blackfoot): Wissler and Duvall PaAM II 57.
K916.p: A dancer uses a move of the dance as a trick to stab a person watching.

K916.1.p: A helper in the form of a peacock dances before the hero's enemy army, and fire from her tail burns the whole army to ashes.

K917.p: A person is treacherously murdered while out hunting.

K918.p: A man is murdered while he is praying.

K921.r: Type 63*; *Fb “ræv” III 114a; Russian: Andrejev No. 63; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K921.p: A fox gets rid of his fleas by sinking into water with a bundle of hay, so the fleas gather on the hay and he dives under to escape them.

K922.p: A false whale is built as a trick, and the enemies who are surprised by it are killed.

K923.p: A victim is murdered by bleeding, with the killer taking more blood than the victim realizes.

K924.p: Someone cuts a drawbridge partway through so that a giant falls into the moat when he crosses it.

K925.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 60 No. 435*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K925.p: A victim is pushed into a fire and killed.

K925.1.p: A hero lures enemies into a building and sets fire to it, burning them inside.

K926.p: A victim is pushed into water and killed.

K927.p: Many animals are slaughtered when they are driven into a stampede.

K928.p: A murder is carried out through a transformation, such as a shapeshifter changing form to kill.

K928.1.p: A serpent disguises itself as a stick lying on the ground. An enemy picks it up, and the serpent bites him, killing or harming him.

K929.p: A general category of murder carried out through a clever scheme or trick rather than open violence.

K929.1.p: Someone is killed by being given poisoned wine to drink.

K929.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 287), 140 (ST 463); Halm Aesop No. 126; Jacobs Aesop 216 No. 66.
K929.2.p: A one-eyed doe is tricked into falling to her death by being approached from the side where she cannot see, since she usually feeds on a cliff keeping her good eye toward the land.

K929.3.r: Dispels his suspicions. Has him killed at night. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K929.3.p: A ruler promises his minister that he will not kill him on any day of his life, then finds a way around the promise to have him killed.

K929.4.p: Enemies are lured into an ambush or danger by a pretended retreat, as the victims are drawn out by a fake flight.

K929.5.p: Someone is killed by hiding gold coins inside meat that an enemy is customarily required to accept, so the enemy is harmed when he eats or handles it.

K929.6.p: Someone is killed through a staged quarrel that is faked to get close to the victim and then kill him.

K929.7.r: Irish myth: Cross; Africa (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 60ff.
K929.7.p: Men are tricked into fighting and killing one another, each unknowingly acting against the other.

K929.8.p: A hero who has run off with a king's promised bride is lured back to court and treacherously killed while his guarantors are away at drinking bouts and cannot protect him.

K929.9.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 356; Chinese: Graham; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 331; Africa (Wachaga): Gutmann 188.
K929.9.p: Someone is killed by being pushed off a cliff.

K929.10.p: An old wife tricks a sparrow into speaking so that he opens his beak and drops the new wife he is carrying in it.

K929.11.p: A king sends a food basket with weapons hidden inside, and the servant who opens it is killed.

K929.12.p: A man is tricked by a false message supposedly from the other world into climbing onto a funeral pyre and dying.

K929.13.p: A hare makes a pursuing she-bear get stuck between trees, and then kills her.

K930.p: A general category of treacherously killing an enemy's children or those in one's care.

K931.r: *Type 37; *Dh IV 247; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 93ff.; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 1144; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 19ff.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 23; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 300 n. 97; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 179; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 44 No. 5, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 388 No. 14, (Zulu): Callaway 24, (Kaffir): Theal 111, (Benga): Nassau 125 No. 12; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 344 No. 60.
K931.p: A pretended nurse secretly kills the enemy's children who have been entrusted to her care.

K931.1.p: A trickster is hired to teach baby crocodiles, but instead of teaching them he eats them.

K932.p: A trickster fouls a bird's nest and its young.

K933.p: A trickster eats all of a tiger's cubs except one, and deceives the tiger about how many there were.

K934.p: A woman looking for a shepherd tests the voices of applicants; the wolf and bear are turned down and the fox is hired, setting up the fox to harm the flock. The fox is chosen as a treacherous shepherd who will kill or harm the enemy's children.

K940.p: A trickster deceives someone into killing their own family members or their own animals, without the victim realizing what he is doing.

K940.1.p: A man is tricked into eating his own children, unaware of what he is served.

K940.1.1.r: (Cf. K941.2, K944.) Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 56.
K940.1.1.p: A man is tricked into eating his own children, and then he sets the village on fire.

K940.2.p: A man is tricked into killing his wife or his grandmother.

K941.p: A trickster falsely reports that a certain thing is very valuable, so the dupe destroys his own property to sell it.

K941.1.r: *Type 1535; *BP II 1ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 27 No. 5.
K941.1.p: A trickster claims that cow hides fetch a large price, so the dupe kills his cows to sell their hides.

K941.1.1.p: A trickster claims that a large price is being paid for his mother's or wife's corpse, so the dupe kills his wives to sell their bodies.

K941.2.r: Spanish: Espinosa III No. 193; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 274.
K941.2.p: A trickster claims a high price is paid for ashes, so the dupe burns his own house to get the ashes to sell.

K941.3.p: Rival enemies each burn their own houses, each hoping to sell the ashes at a high price.

K942.p: An angry man kills his own horse by mistake, because the trickster has switched the places of his horse and the dupe's horse.

K943.r: Herbert III 5; Crane Vitry 168 No. 76; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K943.p: A hermit, deceived by the devil, kills his own father, believing him to be the devil.

K944.r: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 241; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa: Weeks Jungle 384, (Thonga): Junod 217, (Fang): Einstein 155, (Cameroon): Meinhof 70, 73, Lederbogen 77, (Fjort): Dennett 85 No. 20, (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 56, (Jaunde): Heepe 105, (Wachaga): Gutmann 186f.
K944.p: Two people make a deceptive agreement to kill wives or children; the trickster only pretends to carry out the murder, while the dupe actually kills his own.

K945.p: A woman is tricked into giving poison to her husband, believing it is a love potion.

K946.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 279, Thomas 159.
K946.p: A bird flies onto the head of a dupe's child; the dupe strikes at the bird and kills the child instead.

K947.p: A king causes his own men to be burned and killed, either by mistake or through an illusion.

K948.p: A king is lured into sending his sons on deadly quests and into killing his nephews.

K950.p: A general heading for various kinds of treacherous murder carried out by deception.

K951.p: A treacherous murder carried out by choking the victim.

K951.0.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 242ff., 376, 384, Neuman.
K951.0.1.p: A deserted wife chokes her departing husband, after first asking him for one last kiss.

K951.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 38 No. 285A*; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 33; Papua: Ker 103; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 324 n. 167; Africa (Wachaga): Gutmann 188.
K951.1.p: A treacherous murder carried out by forcing hot stones into the victim's mouth.

K951.1.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 199; Africa (Boloki): Einstein 114, (Upoto): Einstein 141.
K951.1.1.p: A murderer kills a victim by throwing hot stones into the victim's mouth, so the victim chokes or burns to death.

K951.1.1.1.p: A tiger is killed by someone who throws a red-hot hatchet into its mouth.

K951.1.2.p: A victim is murdered by having a spear or tongs thrust into the mouth.

K951.1.3.p: A murderer kills a victim by throwing hot fruit into the victim's mouth.

K951.2.p: A victim is murdered by being fed bread that has pins hidden inside it.

K951.3.p: A victim is murdered by having poisoned bread thrown into the mouth.

K951.4.p: A victim is murdered by having a clod of earth pushed into the windpipe so they choke.

K951.5.r: Greek: *Robinson Works of Chaucer 966; India: Thompson-Balys.
K951.5.p: An animal is killed by having a ball of hide, wax, or similar material forced down its throat.

K951.6.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 71.
K951.6.p: A victim is murdered by being fed honey-covered sharpened pieces of wood that injure the throat or stomach.

K952.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Cook Islands: Beckwith Myth 267; Tonga: Gifford 79, 83; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 438, (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 538; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 321 n. 159; Africa (Benga): Nassau 206 No. 32. See also all references to F912.
K952.p: An animal or monster is killed by someone who gets inside its body and kills it from within.

K952.1.r: (Porcupine and buffalo.) India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 302 n. 104.
K952.1.p: A passenger who has been carried across a river by an animal turns on the carrier and kills it by crawling inside its body during the crossing.

K952.1.1.p: A jackal swallowed by an elephant so it can drink water from inside its belly eats the elephant's liver and kills it.

K952.1.2.p: An ungrateful rat defecates on the head of an octopus that rescued it from the sea, or otherwise kills it.

K952.2.r: S. A. Indian (Tehuelche): Alexander Lat. Am. 336.
K952.2.p: A man changes himself into a gadfly so he can enter a giant's stomach and kill him from inside.

K952.2.1.p: A man kills a giant bear by crawling inside it and cutting his way out.

K952.3.p: An animal is tricked into grabbing a hollow log, and a man reaches through the log and pulls out the animal's heart.

K953.p: A victim is murdered by being squeezed to death.

K953.1.p: A victim is murdered by having a corset laced so tightly that it kills them.

K953.2.p: A man is murdered by a snake that is wrapped around him and squeezes him to death.

K953.3.p: A crab is carried by a crane, clings to the crane's neck, and cuts off its head with its pincers.

K953.4.p: A killer pretends to embrace the victim affectionately but actually crushes them to death by squeezing.

K955.r: Type 930; Aarne FFC XXIII 85, 92; Jewish: Neuman.
K955.p: A killer deceptively murders the victim by setting them on fire.

K955.1.p: A killer deceptively murders the victim by scalding them with boiling water or steam.

K955.2.p: A killer deceptively murders the victim by pouring or immersing them in boiling oil.

K955.3.p: A killer murders the victim by shooting them with an arrow that has been set on fire.

K956.p: A killer murders the victim by destroying a soul or life-force that the victim has kept outside their body.

K956.1.p: A victim is killed gradually as their separate soul is destroyed piece by piece.

K957.p: A killer deceptively murders the victim by blinding them.

K957.1.p: A killer murders the victim by throwing hot salt into their eyes.

K958.r: (Cf. K926.) Greek: Grote I 269; Papua: Ker 30, 52, 147; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 163, (Tupinamba): ibid. 135.
K958.p: A killer deceptively murders the victim by drowning them.

K959.p: Murders by treacherous methods not covered by the other headings in this group.

K959.1.p: A killer murders the victim by placing a pot's mouth over the victim's head.

K959.2.p: A killer murders the victim while the victim is asleep.

K959.2.1.p: A woman's father and brothers kill her husband while he sleeps, because he married her against their wishes.

K959.2.2.p: Heroes refuse to kill people who are sleeping, considering it dishonorable.

K959.2.3.p: A man is murdered while lying beside his wife.

K959.2.4.p: A woman marries a king by pretending she can heal him, then murders him in his sleep; afterward she takes the kingdom together with his counsellor.

K959.2.5.p: A hero attacks and kills at night another hero who wanted to sleep before they fought.

K959.3.p: A tent is pulled down over a man, and he is then killed.

K959.3.1.p: A giant's house has a supporting rafter cut halfway through, so it can be pulled down from outside and the giant killed in the collapse.

K959.4.p: A person is killed by being attacked or struck from behind, treacherously.

K959.5.p: Thorns are secretly planted in a field so that birds who land there are killed.

K959.6.p: People lure a boy into a post-hole, then try to crush him by dropping a log on him.

K960.p: Other murders carried out through lies or trickery that cause a victim's death.

K961.r: (The sick lion.) *Type 50; *Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 21ff.; **Graf FFC XXXVIII 20; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 494; Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 55), 50 (ET 102), 99 (ST 129), 100 (ST *133); Halm Aesop No. 255; Herbert IV 431f.; Chauvin III 78; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 19 No. 10.
K961.p: Someone claims that a certain animal's flesh is the only cure for an illness, so that the animal is killed to obtain it.

K961.0.1.r: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 57 No. 20; American Negro: Harris Friends 45ff. No. 6.
K961.0.1.p: Someone claims that the blood of a certain animal is sweet, so the animal is killed to get it, its death brought about by this lie.

K961.1.r: (Cf. K544.) *Penzer V 128f., 128 n. 1; Bødker Exempler 298 No. 62; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda. Also references to K544.
K961.1.p: A disease is said to be curable only by the heart of a monkey, so monkeys are hunted for it.

K961.1.1.r: Wolf is killed. Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K961.1.1.p: A wolf unknowingly insults a sick lion, a fox overhears, and later tells the lion that his only cure is to wrap himself in the wolf's skin, so the wolf is killed for it as tit for tat.

K961.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 882; Africa (Temne): Schlenker Collection of Temne Traditions (London, 1861) 87ff. No. 7, (Hausa): Tremearne FL XXII 464ff. No. 50.
K961.2.p: Someone claims that the flesh or vital organs of a certain person are the only cure for an illness, so that person is killed.

K961.2.1.r: Bødker Exempler 305 No. 79; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K961.2.1.p: A snake is said to be the only cure for a monkey's disease, using its brain, so the snake plans to kill the monkey when he goes to its hole.

K961.2.2.p: An ogress wife says she will die unless she gets the eyes of the raja's six other wives.

K962.r: Penzer V 53 n. 1; Chauvin II 89 No. 29; Bødker Exempler 284 No. 31; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K962.p: A camel is persuaded to offer himself as a sacrifice; other animals pretend to offer themselves to the lion, and the lion eats the camel.

K963.r: *Type 301; *BP II 300ff.; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 115 No. 960; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 78; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 242 No. 17; West Indies: Flowers 532.
K963.p: A man being hauled up on a rope is dropped when someone cuts the rope.

K963.1.p: A mountain climber's rope is cut so that he falls and dies.

K964.p: A hero tells a king that the king's ancestors need the barber's services in heaven, so the king has the barber killed.

K974.p: A man with a deformed head kills the barbers who try to shave him.

K975.r: *Type 590; BP I 551, III 2 n. 1; *Frazer Old Testament II 480; Huet Contes Populaires 134; MacCulloch Childhood 58; Krappe Revue Archéologique (1933) 195—211.—Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 392, (Pawnee): Dorsey CI LIX 104 No. 25, (Arikara): Dorsey CI XVII 84ff. Nos. 25, 26, (Crow): Simms FM II 309 No. 20.
K975.p: A hero's secret source of strength is discovered by treachery and used to kill him.

K975.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson PMLA XXXVII 133.
K975.1.p: Two people pretend to exchange secrets, and one reveals the single thing that can kill him, which the other then uses against him.

K975.1.1.p: A hero tells his enemies how he can be killed, betraying his own weakness.

K975.2.r: *Type 302; Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 1; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 65—67; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K975.2.p: A person learns the secret of another's external soul through deception, and so can destroy that soul's hiding place and kill them.

K976.p: A daughter tricks her father into letting her pull out a magic hair that holds his life, and as soon as it is removed he dies.

K978.r: *Types 428, 930; *Aarne FFC XXIII 64ff., 91; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 38, Beal XXI 314; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 262ff., Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 828, II 267; Japanese: Ikeda. See also all references to K511.
K978.p: A man is made to carry a written order for his own execution, usually unaware of what the letter says.

K978.1.p: A man unknowingly carries a spoken order for his own execution and delivers it himself.

K978.1.1.p: Two animals, a leopard and a crocodile, who have never seen a dog or each other, are sent by a man to the same place to fight over a dog, and they kill each other.

K978.2.p: A message ordering a man's death is lost, so the intended victim is not killed.

K981.p: An oracle's message is altered on its way to someone, so that it brings about a fatal outcome for the person it concerns.

K982.p: A victim is tricked into standing under a tree that then falls on him and kills him.

K983.p: A victim is persuaded to climb a tree and is then killed when the tree is felled.

K983.1.r: Alu: Wheeler No. 54; Mono: ibid. No. 21; Buin: ibid. No. 4; Papua: Ker 86.
K983.1.p: The tree is cut down to get at the victim who has been tricked into staying in its top.

K983.2.r: S. A. Indian (Kaigang): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 148.
K983.2.p: Victims are lured onto a bridge made from a tree-trunk, and they fall to their deaths.

K984.p: A man is tricked into sitting in a mechanical chair that then kills him.

K985.p: A fairy in disguise lends a mortal a magic horse, and the horse leads to the mortal's death.

K986.p: Someone is persuaded to commit murder by being offered land, riches, or wives as payment.

K988.p: A person is thrown out of a magic flying ship and dies in the fall.

K991.p: A dupe is persuaded to go to a dangerous place where he is killed.

K991.1.p: A brother gets his own brother killed by sending him to robbers and giving him false advice on the way.

K1000.r: Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 9—20.
K1000.p: A victim is tricked into injuring himself.

K1010.p: A victim is harmed through false doctoring, where a fake healer pretends to treat him but actually injures him.

K1010.1.p: A fake remedy of covering the victim with dry leaves is applied, and the victim is burned to death.

K1011.r: (Often with a glowing mass thrust into the eye.) *Type 1135; *BP III 375; **Hackman Polyphemsage; *Herbert III 40ff.; Hervieux IV 204 No. 29; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 140.
K1011.p: A trickster pretends to cure someone's eyesight but actually blinds the dupe.

K1011.1.p: A foolish dupe is tricked into thinking that removing his own eyes will cure his headache.

K1011.2.p: A trickster convinces a person with sore eyes that rubbing ashes on them is the cure.

K1012.p: A trickster deceives a dupe into being injured, claiming the injury will make him stronger, while posing as a doctor.

K1012.1.p: A false doctor persuades the dupe that castration will make him strong.

K1012.2.p: A false doctor persuades the dupe that being scalded with hot water will make him strong.

K1013.r: Injures him. *Cosquin Études 385ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 73, 74; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 467; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 271, (California): Gayton and Newman 83; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 387, (Kaffir): Theal 99, (Wute): Sieber ZsES XII 69f., 172.
K1013.p: A trickster poses as a beauty doctor and pretends to make the dupe beautiful, but actually harms him.

K1013.1.r: The ogre with his tar-kettle wanders about and asks everyone, “Have you seen such a one?” *Type 1138.
K1013.1.p: A man called "Such a one" persuades an ogre to have his beard gilded, then covers it with tar so the ogre is caught in the tar-kettle.

K1013.2.r: *Type 8; *Dh IV 239; *Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 67ff.; American Negro: Harris Friends 60 ff. No. 8.
K1013.2.p: A fox persuades a wolf to lie on hay so he can be painted, then sets the hay on fire.

K1013.2.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 175; Africa (Cameroon): Rosenhuber 79.
K1013.2.1.p: A man is told that burning his wife will make her beautiful, and he burns her.

K1013.2.2.p: Someone is tricked into burning children with the promise that they will get the fawn's beautiful spots.

K1013.3.p: A false beauty doctor claims to paint the dupe with a red-hot iron, injuring him.

K1013.4.p: A trickster promises to give a tiger wings, a fake beauty-type treatment that harms the animal.

K1013.5.p: A false hair-restorer applies a treatment that injures the patient instead of helping him.

K1013.6.p: A trickster claims breaking a person's legs will make him a better dancer or faster runner.

K1014.r: (Cf. K1045.) Japanese: Ikeda; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 69ff. No. 9.
K1014.p: A trickster gives pepper as a salve for burns, which makes the wound burn worse.

K1014.1.p: Someone is told to put pepper up his nose as a cure, a painful trick.

K1014.2.p: Someone is told to rub pepper on an injured skin as a remedy, which hurts the wound.

K1015.p: A trickster offers a false cure for toothache that makes the pain worse or damages the teeth.

K1015.1.p: Someone is told to bite on a stone as a cure for toothache.

K1015.2.p: A leopard wants its teeth filed, but a large stone dropped from a tree knocks all its teeth out.

K1016.p: A trickster pretends to treat a wound with remedies such as beetles and barley, but the stuff he pushes into it hurts or harms the victim instead of healing them.

K1017.p: A fake doctor, pretending to check the patient's pulse, cuts through the arteries instead, so the victim is harmed by the one who claims to help.

K1018.p: A hare flatters other animals into holding still so it can bite off their ears.

K1020.p: A dupe is tricked into a foolish attempt to get food that ends in disaster for himself.

K1021.r: *Type 2; *BP II 111; *Dh IV 219; Krohn Bar (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 26ff.; *Fb “ræv” III 113b, “bjørn” IV 43a, “ulv” III 971a.—Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr II 3, III 3; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 159 No. 69; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 44; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 438; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 120 No. 25, Nights 113 No. 21, (Pennsylvania): Parsons JAFL XXX 214, (Virginia): Smiley JAFL XXXII 361, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXIV 12.
K1021.p: A bear is persuaded to fish by dangling his tail through a hole in the ice; when attacked and trying to escape, he loses his tail.

K1021.1.r: Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 199—201, 204; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 35, 88; N. A. Indian (Hupa): Goddard U Cal I 154ff., Kroeber JAFL XXI 224; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 6, 358, (Kaffir): Theal 110, 183, (Basuto): Jacottet 20 No. 2, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 385f., (Hottentot): Bleek I No. 1, (Thonga): Junod 217; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 339 No. 59; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII *241 No. 14, 233f.; West Indies: Flowers 533.
K1021.1.p: The dupe's tail is buried in the ice or his hair is tied fast, leaving him bound and then attacked.

K1021.1.1.p: The dupe's hair is tied to a basket, so when she throws the basket down she kills herself.

K1021.2.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 28 No. 2, Espinosa III Nos. 199—204, 209, 211, 223, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 3. 4.
K1021.2.p: A basket is tied to a wolf's tail and filled with stones, and the wolf is tricked into believing it holds fish.

K1021.3.r: Wears off tail. American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 113 No. 21.
K1021.3.p: A bear is persuaded to slide down a rock, and this leads to his harm.

K1022.p: A dupe is persuaded to steal food and then cannot escape from the place where he stole it.

K1022.1.r: *Type 41; *BP II 109, IV 318; *Dh IV 232; *Chauvin III 45; Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 226); Halm Aesop No. 31; *Graf FFC XXXVIII 71ff.; Herbert III 374 No. 11; Fb “ulv” III 971a.—Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 21; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 438; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis XII 291, 327, (Wachaga): Gutmann 188.
K1022.1.p: A wolf overeats in a cellar or smokehouse and cannot get out through the entrance hole because he is too full.

K1022.1.1.p: A jackal eating into an elephant's dead body is trapped as the body dries up, and is freed when a storm moistens the hide.

K1022.2.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 29 No. 47C*, Espinosa III No. 208.
K1022.2.p: A fox ties a rope from a wolf's neck to a cow the two intend to eat; the cow drags the wolf to a house where he is skinned.

K1022.2.1.p: A water-monster trying to pull a horse into the water is dragged to a house, where he begs for his life and is spared.

K1022.3.p: A bear throws hens down to a fox, falls from the roof-beam himself, and is beaten.

K1022.4.p: A wolf takes cake from a window-sill by imitating a fox, but a bell rings and he is beaten.

K1022.5.p: A turtle is induced to rob a man's garden.

K1022.5.1.p: An otter is persuaded to rob a garden in the same way and is beaten.

K1022.6.p: A fox eats cake and gets a brass pot caught on his neck, so he cannot escape.

K1022.7.p: A thieving wolf is persuaded to stick his head through the handle of a jar of wine so he can carry it off and sing.

K1023.r: Type 49; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1637*; Mexican: Espinosa JAFL XXIV 419ff.; Chinese: Graham; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 38 No. 26; N. A. Indian (Menomini): Skinner JAFL XXVI 75; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 44ff.; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 51 No. 10, 83 No. 16, Remus 135 No. 28, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 274.
K1023.p: A trickster tells a dupe that a wasp nest is a source of honey, so the dupe tries to get it and is stung.

K1023.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Java: Dixon 188 n. 5; cf. DeVries’s list No. 12.
K1023.1.p: A dupe is told to guard a king's drum, which is really a wasp nest, and is stung when he touches it.

K1023.1.1.p: A dupe is told to guard a king's girdle, which is actually a snake, and the snake bites him.

K1023.2.p: A dupe is persuaded to pick up biting ants.

K1023.3.p: A dupe is persuaded to sit on an ant hole.

K1023.4.p: An animal is made to believe the buzzing of a swarm of bees is her children singing in school; she rushes to water to ease the stings and drowns.

K1023.5.p: A dupe is tricked into striking a bee's nest and is badly bitten or stung.

K1024.p: Animals agree to eat one another to avoid starving, and the fox persuades them to begin with the smallest.

K1025.r: *Type 21; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 85; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1025.p: A trickster persuades the wolf to eat his own entrails, which harms him.

K1025.1.p: The fox suggests the wolf eat his own brains; the wolf, wanting brains, bangs his head against a tree.

K1025.2.p: A tiger is persuaded to eat his own eyes.

K1026.r: *Types 1 (and notes to K371.1.), 66**; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 274.
K1026.p: A dupe copies a trickster's thefts and is caught and punished.

K1032.p: A dupe is made to sit on a hot stone, in the hope of getting food, and is burned.

K1032.1.p: A jackal is persuaded to come to the fireplace for food and is burned.

K1033.p: An ogre is tricked into swallowing hot porridge and burning his throat.

K1218.4.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 220; Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 1 (Lee 271); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1218.4.p: Suitors are tricked into playing a corpse, an angel, and a devil. The one posing as the corpse mistakes the others for angel and devil, and they all come to blows.

K1218.4.1.p: Three women humiliate a pestering lover: the first makes him hide on thorns, the second makes him fall into a hole, and the third makes him fall asleep in the street. In revenge he shows them to his friends, naked except for their faces.

K1218.5.p: A girl asks a pestering lover for a weapon to use against her father, but instead she uses it to defend herself against the suitor.

K1218.6.p: A pestering suitor is beaten and then paraded through the streets wearing a humiliating sign.

K1218.7.p: A pestering suitor is tied to a tree as a trick that humiliates him.

K1218.8.p: A pestering suitor is beaten with canes stuffed with straw, and he believes he is seriously wounded.

K1218.9.p: An unattractive fool who wants to marry is subjected to obscene tricks played on him.

K1218.9.1.p: The pestering suitor is tricked into believing he has been granted a secret meeting, and obscene tricks are then played on him.

K1218.10.p: A wife has her lover meet her under a tree where she has hidden her husband; when the husband calls out for his share of the kisses, the embarrassed lover runs off.

K1222.p: A woman tricks a pestering lover by giving him a pike's head in place of herself, leaving him humiliated; afterward he imagines the vagina has teeth.

K1223.r: Type 1441*; Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 47; Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 4 (Lee 254); Icelandic: Boberg; Russian: Andrejev No. 1441*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1223.p: A woman secretly sends someone else in her place to a lover, so he is deceived.

K1223.1.p: A bride escapes a foolish husband by leaving a goat in her place in the bed.

K1223.2.p: A mistress secretly sends a man's own wife to him in her place, without his knowing.

K1223.2.1.p: A virtuous woman sends another man's wife in her place, without his knowledge; the first woman's husband is then substituted for the pursuing lover, who ends up seducing his own wife.

K1223.3.p: A woman who has been asked for a secret meeting tells the suitor's wife, and the two women exchange places.

K1223.4.p: A virtuous woman puts a corpse in her own place in bed to escape a persistent suitor.

K1223.5.p: A king's daughter deceives her father the king by sending her maid in her place.

K1225.r: (Chaucer’s Miller’s Tale). *Type 1361; *F. N. Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Boston, 1933) 786b; *Bolte Frey 251 No. 89; *Barnouw “The Millers Tale van Chaucer” Handlingen van het 6. nederlandsche Philologencongres, 1910; *Thompson The Miller’s Tale (Bryan and Dempster 106ff.); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1225.p: A lover is tricked into kissing someone's buttocks instead of the expected lips; sometimes a rival lover plays the trick.

K1227.p: A lover is put off with a false promise of a later time, so he keeps waiting.

K1227.1.r: She escapes. Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 257.
K1227.1.p: A lover is put off until the girl has finished bathing and dressing, which she never does in time.

K1227.2.r: (Penelope.) *W. Crooke FL IX 97; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 299 n. 2.
K1227.2.p: Suitors are put off until a web is woven, but the weaver unweaves it each night so it is never finished.

K1227.3.r: BP I 221; *Roberts 175; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 120 No. 31; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 345f., 363, 398.
K1227.3.p: A girl delays a wooer by asking him to fetch clothes all night, and she wastes the time trying them on.

K1227.3.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3251, Legends No. 353f., 356—362.
K1227.3.1.p: A girl refuses to dance with a devil until she is well dressed; he keeps bringing finery until the cock crows. Another girl asks for everything at once and is forced to dance until she dies.

K1227.4.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 24; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1227.4.p: A woman asks a lover she does not want to take off his boots before they can be intimate. While he struggles with them she slips away.

K1227.4.1.p: A girl tells a physician who is trying to seduce her that she cannot give in until he has bathed. She prepares the bath herself and pours acid into it.

K1227.5.p: A woman makes an importunate lover wait in her room while she pretends to be ill, then escapes.

K1227.5.1.p: A girl delays consummating a marriage to a suitor she does not want by claiming her stomach is sick.

K1227.6.p: A girl asks an unwanted lover to follow her but not to step on her shadow, which stalls him.

K1227.7.p: A girl says she has vowed not to marry until she has made a pilgrimage, which delays her unwanted suitor.

K1227.8.p: A girl serves as umpire in a contest where suitors shoot arrows, and so escapes being won by one of them.

K1227.9.p: An importunate lover is kept at supper so long that he has to leave, and so is put off.

K1227.10.p: A woman escapes an undesired lover by claiming she is having her menstrual period.

K1227.10.1.p: An abducted princess tells her abductor to wait until her menstrual period ends, which she says will take twelve years.

K1228.r: Knowing that he has deceived another by paying her with gilded coin she answers: “You will have to pay in better coin than is your wont!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1228.p: A woman humiliates a man who tries to become her lover, leaving him embarrassed or foolish.

K1231.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 749; Heptameron No. 27; Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1231.p: A chaste woman sends her would-be lover to her husband to ask permission, which turns him away.

K1231.1.p: A chaste woman sends her lover to his own wife instead, so that he is shamed.

K1232.p: A woman gets her lover to agree to jump off a cliff with her, promising to follow him. She does not jump, leaving him deceived and foolish.

K1232.1.p: A lover's anger is calmed by a sham suicide attempt, and he is later scorned.

K1233.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 28; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1233.p: A lover is humiliated when he proves impotent at the moment of intimacy.

K1235.p: A king is tricked into sleeping with an old hag.

K1236.p: A woman disguises herself as a man to escape an importunate lover.

K1237.p: A girl plays dice with her suitors and locks up any who lose.

K1240.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a lover is deceived into a humiliating position and no more specific motif applies.

K1241.r: *Types 4, 72; *BP II 117; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 59ff.; *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 66; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IX 115, (Nigeria): Tramearne 322, (Yoruba): Ellis 265, (Angola): Chatelain 203 No. 28; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 24 No. 6, Jones Negro Tales from the Georgia Coast Nos 7, 13, (Virginia): Bacon and Parsons JAFL XXXV 265 266, Speers JAFL XXV 285f., (North Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXX 173, (South Carolina): Parsons JAFL XXXIV 5, MAFLS XVI 54, (Louisiana): Johnston JAFL IX 195; American Negro and American Indian: *Thompson CColl II 440, 447; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 235; West Indies: Van Cappelle Mythen en Sagen van West-Indie Nos. 12, 16.
K1241.p: A trickster pretends to be sick so that his victim will carry him on his back, then boasts that the victim acts as his horse.

K1241.1.r: Type 72; Africa (Nupe): Frobenius Atlantis IX 115 No. 3, (Yoruba): Frobenius ibid. X 280ff. No. 40, (Nyanja): Possett Fables of the Veld (London, 1929) 111ff., (Mbundu): Chatelain MAFLS I 203 No. 28, (Xosa): Waters Cameos from the Kraal (Lovedale, n. d.) 24f.
K1241.1.p: A trickster pretends to be sick and gets his victim to carry him, and in this way wins a girl.

K1243.p: A priest gets stuck in a window and is humiliated.

K1251.r: (Sometimes steals the dupe’s goods.) *Type 1530; *Parsons JAFL XXX 237, XXXI 227 n. 2, MAFLS XV (1) 59; N. A. Indian (Mexico): Boas JAFL XXV 206, 237; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 113, 189, (Hottentot, South of Zambezi): Theal 91, (Basuto): Jacottet 44 n. 1; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 314 No. 54.
K1251.p: A trickster convinces his victim that he is holding up a huge rock, and gets the victim to hold it for a while in his place.

K1251.1.r: *Type 9A; Dh IV 249ff.; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 97ff.; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1251.1.p: A fox pretends to be holding up the roof, so he cannot help the bear, who must do the threshing alone.

K1251.1.1.p: A fox pretends to be guarding the sky and watching the earth, so he does not have to work.

K1252.r: (Dupe’s goods are sometimes stolen.) *Type 1528; *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 54; Java: Dixon 186 n. 2; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 420, 426. Cf. Indonesia: DeVries Volksverhalen II 396 No. 185B.
K1252.p: A victim is persuaded to guard a hat that is supposed to cover something valuable, but it covers only a pile of dung.

K1252.1.p: A victim is persuaded to fight a supposedly gold-dropping bear while the trickster steals his clothes.

K1253.p: A page tricks a general into taking his place sitting on eggs, and then calls the king to look at him.

K1262.p: A person is hypnotized into believing he has been transformed into something else.

K1265.r: *Wesselski Arlotto II 225 No. 92, Morlini 275; Alphabet No. 770; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. Malvolio in Shakespeare’s “Twelfth Night”.
K1265.p: A man is falsely reported to be insane, and no one will believe him when he tries to say otherwise.

K1268.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 582; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 340 n. 227.
K1268.p: A man is carried out and dropped in the middle of a stream.

K1271.p: A love affair is secretly watched and then exposed to others.

K1271.1.p: Someone threatens to tell of a secret love affair in order to extort money or favors.

K1271.1.1.r: *Type 570; *BP III 273; Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 570; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2904*; Russian: cf. Andrejev No. 1630*; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 5—8.
K1271.1.1.p: A boy who is to tell a bag of lies about the queen's adultery is stopped, and his wishes are granted.

K1271.1.2.r: *Type 852; *BP II 506; Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII No. 852.
K1271.1.2.p: A princess is made to say the desired words when the hero threatens to falsely report her affair.

K1271.1.3.r: *Type 1750; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 843; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1676*.
K1271.1.3.p: A trickster teaches a woman's chickens to talk, then reports that they say she slept with the priest, and she pays him to keep quiet.

K1271.1.4.r: *Types 1360, 1776; Wesselski Morlini 303 No. 54; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 890; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1271.1.4.p: A man hiding in the roof sees a girl with her lover and falls through; the couple flee and leave him in possession of the place.

K1271.1.4.1.r: *Type 1360B; Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr III No. 84.
K1271.1.4.1.p: A man hiding on the roof sees a woman with her lover and threatens to tell, and is paid to keep silent.

K1271.1.4.2.p: A man hiding in the roof or elsewhere sees a girl with her lover and blows a horn; the couple flee and leave him in possession.

K1271.1.4.3.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 46; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1271.1.4.3.p: A hidden onlooker who has seen a secret affair demands a share of it, or else takes the woman for himself after frightening off the man. In the setting of a man hidden in a roof who sees a girl with her lover and falls, the lovers flee and leave him in possession.

K1271.2.r: (Afraid of ghosts, have chill, etc.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1271.2.p: Lovers caught secretly together in an affair offer ridiculous excuses to explain away what was seen.

K1271.3.p: A secret affair is exposed, and the unfaithful husband is shamed in front of others.

K1271.3.1.p: A wife catches her husband in adultery and, by shaming him, forces him to give her whatever she wants.

K1271.4.r: Hidden shepherd asks “Can you see my lost calves (ass)?” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2905*; Italian Novella: Rotunda (K1532.3); Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 12; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1271.4.p: An adulteress, caught or nearly caught, tells her lover that she can see the whole world, meaning she is watching for the husband or others and keeping them away.

K1271.5.r: A youth and maid come under tree. “Who shall provide for our child?” “He above (God) will take care of it.” The man in the tree: “I will do nothing of the kind!” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2912*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1654*.
K1271.5.p: A person caught in an affair or secret situation claims that God will provide for them, a pious-sounding excuse used to talk their way out.

K1272.p: A man in bed with his wife is scared off by an intruder, who then steals his clothes while he flees.

K1273.r: Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 2 (Lee 274); Mensa Philosophica No. 200; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1273.p: An abbess, caught in bed with a priest, hastily puts his trousers on her head, thinking of her headdress. She is then humiliated by the nuns she had earlier accused of immorality.

K1274.r: Boccaccio Decameron I No. 4 (Lee 14); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1274.p: After a head of a monastery or convent is caught in sexual misconduct, the monks or nuns are granted permission to do the same.
