K1275.r: *Type 886; *von der Hagen II v, vi, 3, 19 Nos. 21, 22; *Bolte Montanus’s Wegkürzer 558 No. 1; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1275.p: A girl who cannot keep a secret reveals something that provokes her rival into confessing her own unchastity.

K1275.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 8; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V 4.
K1275.1.p: A girl refuses her lover a final kiss, which provokes her rival into admitting she has sold kisses.

K1281.p: A wife asks her husband for a hair that will magically draw him to her, but he secretly gives her a hair from an animal pelt instead.

K1281.1.p: A priest asks a woman for a pubic hair to draw her to him, but gets sow's bristles instead, and the sow rushes into church after him.

K1285.r: Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 5; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1285.p: Tricksters pull a judge's breeches off and leave him standing exposed.

K1286.p: A dupe is put through a fake initiation ceremony as a joke at his expense.

K1288.r: *Type 570; *BP III 267ff.; Fb “røv” III 130a, “kysse” II 350; Russian: Andrejev No. 1630*; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 1—8, Espinosa Jr. No. 130.
K1288.p: A trickster persuades a king to kiss a horse's rump, then threatens to make the act public unless he is paid or favored.

K1291.p: The pockets of opposing witnesses are secretly filled with dung, discrediting them.

K1292.p: A hostile brother-in-law is tricked into holding the king's sword, leaving him in a lowly servant's position while the king adjusts his breeches belt.

K1300.p: A man or god persuades a woman to give up her virtue, usually by deception or pressure.

K1301.r: (Cf. K1315.1.) See references to D658.2. Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 62, 80, *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 165f.; Africa (Fang): Einstein 94, Trilles 137.
K1301.p: A god seduces a mortal woman, who is deceived or persuaded into a sexual relationship with him.

K1302.p: A woman is won over or lost through a trick or clever deception. The deception itself leads to her seduction or to a deceptive marriage.

K1310.p: A person seduces a woman by disguising himself or by swapping himself in for someone else, so that she does not realize who she is with.

K1311.r: *Penzer II 45 n. 4, III 126f.; Boccaccio Decameron III No. 6 (Lee 79); Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 30; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas I 364; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 33 No. 11; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 31.
K1311.p: A man pretends to be a woman's husband so that he can seduce her, and she believes it is really him.

K1311.0.1.p: A man poses as the woman's husband and seduces her. When the real husband returns, the wife acts surprised and says the husband has only just left, pretending nothing happened.

K1311.0.2.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 151.
K1311.0.2.p: A trickster kills the husband and wears his skin in order to go to the wife and seduce her.

K1311.1.r: *Type 303; *BP I 528ff.; Icelandic: Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I Nos. 7, 9, Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1311.1.p: A woman mistakes the husband's twin brother for her own husband and sleeps with him.

K1314.p: A man seduces a woman while wearing a coat that makes him invisible, so she cannot see who he is.

K1315.p: A person seduces a woman by pretending to be someone else, such as a holy or professional figure, whom she trusts.

K1315.1.r: (Cf. K1301.) Jones PMLA XXIII 577; Penzer I 145; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas I 365; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1315.1.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to be a god.

K1315.1.1.r: Boccaccio Decameron IV No. 2 (Lee 123); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1315.1.1.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to be the angel Gabriel.

K1315.1.2.p: A man seduces a woman with the promise that the child will be the fifth Evangelist.

K1315.1.2.1.r: Girl born. Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 14; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1315.1.2.1.p: A man seduces a woman by falsely claiming that angelic orders command her to bear a child who will become a pope.

K1315.2.r: Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 239, Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 305 n. 109r.
K1315.2.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to be a doctor.

K1315.2.1.p: A sham doctor persuades a girl to sit on a certain plant as a cure, and she is seduced. He tells her this will heal her burnt groins.

K1315.2.2.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 3; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1315.2.2.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to retrieve a lost gem from her body in a sham procedure.

K1315.2.3.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to repair her vagina in a sham medical process.

K1315.2.4.p: A man poses as a doctor, telling a childless man's wife she must take medicine with him. When the husband arrives at cockcrow as instructed, the trickster claims he came too late and they must do it again.

K1315.3.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to be a magician.

K1315.3.1.p: A man seduces a woman by pretending to be under a spell or enchanted.

K1315.3.2.r: Finishing the tail. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1315.3.2.p: A man tries to seduce a woman by promising to magically turn her into a mare.

K1315.4.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by pretending to be a close relative of hers, so the intimacy seems permissible.

K1315.5.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by falsely presenting himself as a nobleman.

K1315.5.1.p: A prostitute dresses up and pretends to be a noblewoman in order to deceive someone.

K1315.6.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by pretending to be a religious figure, such as a priest or monk.

K1315.6.1.p: Tricksters convince women that, as part of holy duty, they must share the intimacies of marriage with the men posing as holy men.

K1315.6.2.p: A would-be seducer tries to win a woman by threatening that he will perform a miracle if she refuses.

K1315.6.3.p: A girl dresses as a friar and slips into a priest's bed.

K1315.6.4.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by pretending to be a saint.

K1315.7.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by pretending to be a teacher or instructor.

K1315.7.1.p: A seducer pretends to teach a woman about her marital duties, or pretends that he himself needs such instruction, in order to gain intimacy.

K1315.7.2.p: A seducer gets a woman into intimacy by claiming he is teaching her a game.

K1315.8.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by promising to marry her, a promise he never intends to keep.

K1315.9.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by offering to protect her from a danger that does not actually exist.

K1315.10.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by disguising himself as a beggar.

K1315.11.r: Icelandic: Sturlaugs saga St. 641-45 ch. 25, Boberg.
K1315.11.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by disguising himself as a leper.

K1315.12.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by disguising himself as a merchant.

K1315.13.p: A seducer gains a woman's favors by disguising himself as a soldier.

K1315.14.p: A weaver seduces a woman by pretending to be a king.

K1317.r: *Child I 137-41; Nouvelles Récréations No. 54; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1317.p: Another person takes the place of a lover in bed, so the woman is unknowingly intimate with the substitute.

K1317.1.r: Chauvin II 92 No. 38; Bødker Exempler 289 No. 41; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1317.1.p: A servant takes his master's place in bed with the master's lover, so she is intimate with the servant instead.

K1317.1.1.p: A master sneaks into his woman's bed while a servant is there, and the servant takes the master's place in her bed. Thompson's headline phrasing is terse; this is a deception where a servant stands in for the lover in a bedroom.

K1317.2.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 237 No. 79.
K1317.2.p: A leper intercepts a letter meant for a lover and takes that lover's place in bed with a princess.

K1317.2.1.p: An old woman intercepts a letter and takes the girl's place in a man's bed, so that the man sleeps with her instead of the girl.

K1317.2.2.p: A letter intended for one man is delivered to another man, who then stands in for the lover. The note adds that he substitutes for the lover.

K1317.3.p: Spurned lovers, out for revenge, send a man with syphilis to take a woman's place in bed, so that she is infected.

K1317.4.p: A man running is caught by guards, who make him say where he is going. One of the guards then goes in his place to meet his sweetheart.

K1317.5.p: A woman takes her daughter's place in the dark, so that a man sleeps with the mother instead of the daughter.

K1317.6.p: Drugs are used to make someone unable to notice, so that another person can take a lover's place in bed.

K1317.6.1.p: A woman drugs her sister and then takes her sister's place in bed with the sister's lover.

K1317.7.r: Substitution in the dark. Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1317.7.p: A woman mistakes a passing stranger for her lover and takes him to bed.

K1317.8.p: A dark-skinned servant girl is substituted for her mistress in bed, in the dark, so that the man sleeps with the servant instead.

K1317.9.p: A man intercepts a love letter and takes the lover's place in an elopement, so that the woman runs off with him instead.

K1317.10.p: The devil comes to a secret meeting in place of a woman's lover.

K1318.r: *BP III 394 (3); Anderson FFC XLII 364; Köhler-Bolte II 305ff.
K1318.p: A trickster swaps married couples in bed, so that an old man ends up with a young wife and a young man with an old wife. The note says the young couple find the swap satisfactory.

K1321.r: Nouvelles de Sens No. 8; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1321.p: A man seduces a woman by disguising himself as a woman.

K1321.1.r: *Types 516, 1542; Rösch FFC LXXVII 109; *Fischer-Bolte 215; *Krappe Balor 12 n. 42; Penzer I 47n., 48n.; Herrmann Saxo II 239, 493, 641; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 73 n. 2 (Achilles); India: *Thompson-Balys, Ruben FFC CXXXIII 41.
K1321.1.p: A man disguised as a woman gets into the women's quarters and seduces the women there.

K1321.1.1.p: A man disguises himself as a pregnant woman to be admitted to a girl's bed.

K1321.1.2.r: Finally exposed. Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 45; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1321.1.2.p: A seducer stays hidden as a washerwoman for fifteen years without being discovered.

K1321.1.3.p: A man who wants to learn gets into the presence of a learned girl by disguising himself as a woman.

K1321.2.p: A man disguised as a woman carries off a princess.

K1321.3.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 104 No. 857; India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 248; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 304 n. 109n.
K1321.3.p: A man disguises himself as a woman and is courted or married by another man, who is deceived about his true sex.

K1321.3.1.r: *Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 430; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 88; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 303f.
K1321.3.1.p: A man disguised as a woman wins over a hostile chief by charming him, then kills him while he is drunk and asleep.

K1321.4.p: Men disguised as women enter a convent and seduce the nuns, who are impious.

K1322.r: Type 514; BP II 87, III 84; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 155; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 6; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1322.p: A girl disguised as a man wins the love of a princess.

K1322.1.p: A lovely ascetic, who is really a girl in men's clothes, wins the love of a rich woman.

K1323.r: (Cf. K1321.4.) Boccaccio Decameron III No. 1 (Lee 59); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1323.p: A man disguised as a gardener enters a convent and seduces the nuns.

K1323.1.p: A messenger from a lover to a girl held captive in a harem poses as a singer who entertains the harem ladies in their apartments, so he can reach her.

K1325.p: A man seduces a girl by pretending to be dead; she comes to his wake or funeral and he takes advantage of her.

K1325.0.1.p: A hero pretends to be dead and divine maidens have sex with him.

K1325.1.p: A guest in the marriage bed pretends to be asleep while he seduces the wife.

K1326.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 147; West Indies: Flowers 536f.
K1326.p: A person seduces another by pretending to be ill.

K1326.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 95; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1326.1.p: A person seduces another by asking for a sham cure for a sham illness.

K1327.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2907*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1544*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1544A*.
K1327.p: A trickster seduces a farmer's wife and daughter by feigning stupidity to get hired as a laborer; he first gives a silly explanation of animal mating to get taken on.

K1328.p: A man disguises himself as an animal in order to seduce a woman.

K1330.p: A girl is tricked into a man's room or into his power so he can seduce or take her.

K1331.r: *Types 851, 853; BP I 192; **Kristoffer Nyrop Nej: et motivs historie (København, 1891); Dania V 1ff., 164ff., 166; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XV 69 n. 2.
K1331.p: A princess must answer every question with "No"; the hero cleverly frames his question so that her forced "No" wins her to his desires.

K1332.r: *Type 516; **Rosch FFC LXXVII 103; Köhler-Bolte I 464; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 551a nn. 221—295; Panzer Hilde-Gudrun 268ff.; *Schoepperle I 193 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 9; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. bin Gorion Born Judas I 187.
K1332.p: A woman is seduced by being taken aboard a ship on the pretext of inspecting merchandise.

K1332.1.p: A woman is seduced by scattering jewels; she is seized when she stoops to pick them up.

K1332.2.p: A woman is seduced when enticed into a tent to inspect wares.

K1332.3.p: A woman is seduced by the promise of jewels.

K1333.r: *Hertel Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 83ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1333.p: A man seduces a maiden by placing her in a floating chest that carries her to him. The trick gets her into his power.

K1334.p: A man seduces or woos a woman while the two are travelling together through the air.

K1335.r: *Types 313, 400; Penzer VIII 58 n. 2, 213ff., IX 20 n. 1; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 433b. nn. 92—105; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 22 No. 11; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 109. See all notes to D361.1.
K1335.p: A man seduces a bathing girl by stealing her clothes, which leaves her unable to leave the water unless she submits. This is the swan maiden type of tale.

K1336.p: A helpful magical being secretly brings a girl to the hero's bed.

K1339.p: A miscellaneous category of tricks by which a girl is lured into a man's room or into his power.

K1339.1.p: Freshly stripped hides are spread on the grass so that a girl slips on them and is deflowered.

K1339.2.p: A woman is lured up to the upper world by a tree that stretches up to carry her there, where a man can seduce her.

K1339.2.1.p: A man lures a woman onto a platform by pretending to look for a distant ship, then seduces her there.

K1339.3.p: A man lures a woman into his room by pretending to be ill.

K1339.4.p: A trickster seduces two girls by pretending to hold a beauty test that they must submit to.

K1339.5.p: A girl is drugged and seduced. A later pregnancy is then used to force her to marry the seducer.

K1339.6.p: A priest seduces a woman by insisting that she make her confession in his own house.

K1339.7.p: A trickster offers to carry an old woman and a girl across a stream. He carries the girl across, rides off with her, and leaves the old woman on the far bank.

K1339.8.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 305 n. 109s; S. A. Indian (Tenibé): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 140.
K1339.8.p: A woman is told that if it rains she must sleep in a bed where a leak in the roof falls. The trickster then uses the rain to get her into his bed.

K1340.p: A man or woman gains entry into a lover's room or bed by a trick.

K1341.p: A man gets into a woman's room by hiding inside a hollow artificial animal.

K1341.1.r: *Types 854, 900; *BP I 443ff., 446 n. 2; *Krappe Balor 12 n. 41; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 166 (to Gonzenbach No. 68, cf. No. 23); Rösch FFC LXXVII 109; Philippson FFC L 30. -Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 860*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 428.
K1341.1.p: A youth hides inside a golden ram that is carried into the princess's room. Her curiosity about the ram is what gets it there.

K1342.r: *Type 882; Köhler-Bolte I 211f.; Fb “kiste” II 134; Boccaccio Decameron II No. 9 (Lee 57); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. Shakespeare’s Cymbeline.
K1342.p: A man or woman gains entry to another's bedroom by hiding inside a chest, in order to seduce or meet the person secretly.

K1342.0.1.r: (Cf. K1343.1.) *Spargo Virgil the Necromancer 139, 370 n. 7; English: Wells 140 (Floris and Blauncheflur); Icelandic: Boberg.
K1342.0.1.p: A man is hidden in a basket and carried into a woman's room.

K1342.0.2.p: A man hides inside a lamp stand to get into a woman's room.

K1342.1.p: A heroine hides in a box that is bought by a prince, who thereby gets her into his household.

K1342.1.1.p: A man hides in a chest or box, which is then bought by a girl's father, so he gets into the household and reaches the girl. In this tale the heroine is the one hidden in a box that a prince buys.

K1343.r: *Spargo Virgil the Necromancer 139, 369 n. 6; Penzer V 24.
K1343.p: A man is hauled up to a woman's upper room on a rope so he can reach her secretly.

K1343.1.r: (Cf. K1342.0.1.) *Spargo Virgil the Necromancer 136ff., 368ff.; Penzer V 147 n. 1; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; all references to K1211.
K1343.1.p: A man is drawn up to a woman's apartments in a basket on a rope.

K1343.2.p: A man disguised as a woman is carried into a princess's room, and he ends up marrying her.

K1344.r: Icelandic: Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 2; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 142, MAFLS XL 159.
K1344.p: A secret tunnel leads underground into the room of a maiden who is guarded.

K1344.1.r: S. A. Indian (Uru-Chipaya): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 109.
K1344.1.p: A girl is seduced by a lover who comes to her from beneath the ground, through a tunnel.

K1345.r: Type 1363; *Robinson Complete Works of Chaucer 790a (Reeves Tale); *Varnhagen “Die Erzählung von der Wiege” Englische Studien IX 240; Bédier Fabliaux 463; von der Hagen III *xix, 37ff.; Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 6 (Lee 281); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1345.p: Two young men spend the night in a family's shared room, where a cradle is moved in the dark. The moving cradle confuses the men walking about, so the strangers end up sleeping with the wife and daughter.

K1346.r: *Type 575; BP II 134 n. 1; *Krappe Balor 11 n. 40; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1346.p: A hero reaches a maiden's room by flying, using artificial wings or a flying horse to enter her tower.

K1346.1.p: A hero flies on a magic carpet to reach a maiden's room.

K1347.p: A maidservant lets a man into her mistress's room, and he takes the place of the maidservant in the mistress's bed.

K1348.p: A lover gets into a maiden's room by climbing a ladder.

K1349.p: Other ways of getting into a girl's or man's room or bed for seduction, not covered by the more specific headings.

K1349.1.p: A person gets into another's room for seduction by using a disguise.

K1349.1.1.p: A lover disguised as a porter gets into a princess's room.

K1349.1.2.p: A man pretends to be mad so that he can get into a girl's room.

K1349.1.3.p: A trickster disguised as a peddler gets into a woman's room.

K1349.1.4.p: A man disguised as a bridegroom enters his mistress's room.

K1349.1.5.p: A man pretends to be sick so he can enter the room of a princess skilled at healing, and while there he woos her on behalf of his friend.

K1349.2.p: A trickster gets into a woman's room by claiming he has news of her absent lover.

K1349.3.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 31; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1349.3.p: A man gains access to a secret meeting with his friend's mistress by riding his friend's mule. He had tried in vain to learn who the mistress was, and the mule carries him to the secret rendezvous.

K1349.4.p: A lover gets into a guarded young woman's room while a harper lulls her mother to sleep with music, so the mother cannot raise the alarm.

K1349.5.p: A seducer gets access to a woman's room by taking off or picking the locks on her doors.

K1349.6.p: A lover deliberately falls into mud, then has himself carried into his beloved's house to wait there while his clothes are cleaned, so he gets inside.

K1349.7.p: A man sets fire to his own neighboring house so that he has an excuse to get into the bedroom of the woman he wants.

K1349.8.p: A man enters a woman's room through a hidden or secret door.

K1349.9.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 81.
K1349.9.p: A trickster pretends he is searching for a lost ball beside a woman's bed, and while there he seduces her.

K1349.10.p: A man uses a cap of invisibility to slip unseen into a woman's room.

K1350.p: A woman is persuaded, or courted, into sex or marriage by means of a trick.

K1351.r: *Type 1515; *Chauvin VIII 45 No. 13; *Oesterley No. 28; *Crane Vitry 239 No. 251; Elsner Untersuchungen zu den mittelenglischen Fabliau “Dame Siriz”; Fb “hund” IV 227b; *von der Hagen I cxii; Scala Celi 87a No. 510; *Penzer I 169; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 873; Alphabet No. 537; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 95a; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 38; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1351.p: A procuress throws pepper into a dog's eyes so it weeps, then tells a virtuous woman that the dog is a woman turned into a beast for rejecting her lover, and so persuades her.

K1352.r: **N. Soumtzov Piesni i skazki o jivom mertvetzie (Kievskaia Starina, March 1894, reviewed in RTP IX 356).
K1352.p: A man fakes his own death to win a maiden's love, and she shows remorse when she hears he has died.

K1353.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XII 65; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 107, 366, Neuman.
K1353.p: A woman is tricked into giving up her honor: a ruler promises to free her brother or husband in return, then breaks the promise.

K1353.1.p: A trickster offers a woman food in exchange for her favors, saying it will fully satisfy him, and then refuses payment because he claims he is not satisfied.

K1354.p: A man seduces a woman by claiming to bring a false order from her husband or father.

K1354.1.r: *Type 1563; Chauvin VI 180 No. 342; Bolte Montanus Gartengesellschaft 611 No. 73; Köhler-Bolte I 150, 291; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 420ff.; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 115.
K1354.1.p: A youth is sent to fetch two items and, meeting two daughters, asks the master whether he means both; the master says yes, and the youth gets his way with both daughters.

K1354.1.1.p: A trickster pretends to be the girl's father and advises her to have intercourse with him.

K1354.2.p: A man seduces a woman by bringing her a false order supposedly from her husband.

K1354.2.1.r: The husband’s order: “Let him have what he wants.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1354.2.1.p: A trickster asks the husband for one thing and the wife for another, using the husband's supposed request to win the wife.

K1354.2.2.r: When the woman objects, the husband who thinks the friar is engaging in a legitimate process, orders: “Bear the ordeal in peace.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1354.2.2.p: A trickster friar seduces a woman by pretending he must give her a sacrament he forgot earlier.

K1354.2.3.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 180.
K1354.2.3.p: A fox sleeps with a tiger's wife by delivering a false message to her from her mate, the tiger.

K1354.3.p: A man seduces a woman by bringing a false order supposedly from her mother.

K1354.3.1.p: A friar seduces a woman by claiming to carry out her mother's order, but he interprets the order in his own way to suit his purpose.

K1354.3.2.p: A trickster disguised as the bridegroom visits the bride and tells her that he has come at her mother's request.

K1354.4.p: A seducer wins a woman by bringing a false order supposedly from her lover, not from her husband or father.

K1355.r: *Type 930; **Aarne FFC XXIII; *BP I 276ff.; *Chauvin VIII 145 No. 145ABC; Alphabet No. 593; Herrmann Saxo II 287; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 116.
K1355.p: Robbers steal a letter ordering the hero's execution and alter it so that he is instead married to the princess.

K1357.r: *Type 1731; **Spargo FFC XCI 50ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2913*.
K1357.p: A lover gets back a gift he gave a woman, because her husband appears just before the payment for it is made.

K1358.r: *Type 850; *BP II 528; Köhler-Bolte I 428f., 464; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos 5—8, Espinosa Jr. No. 131.
K1358.p: A girl agrees to show herself naked in exchange for a youth's performance of dancing hogs.

K1361.p: A beggar buys the right to sleep first before the girl's door, then at the foot of her bed, and finally in her bed itself, usually paying with a jewel.

K1361.1.p: A transformed person is allowed to sleep before the girl's door, at the foot of her bed, and in her bed, and is freed from the enchantment once admitted to the bed.

K1361.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2916*; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1361.2.p: A man gains a woman's favors piece by piece, with each payment buying a further step, progressing from one part of the body to the next.

K1361.3.p: A man gets into a woman's room by begging to be let in to get warm, and then seduces her.

K1362.r: (Sequel: K1275.) Type 886; *von der Hagen II v, vi, 3, 19 Nos. 21, 22; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1362.p: An innocent girl sells her virginity, then later demands that the knight give it back after her mother beats her for what happened.

K1363.p: A person who does not know what sexual intercourse is is tricked into it and seduced.

K1363.1.p: A man seduces a woman who does not know about sex by means of an obscene trick, which is the joke's point.

K1363.1.1.p: A trickster persuades a naive person that the Devil is being put into Hell, which is a cover for sexual intercourse.

K1363.2.r: Nouvelles Récréations No. 9; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; West Indies: Flowers 538.
K1363.2.p: A friar tells a pregnant woman that her unborn child is imperfect, lacks a nose or fingers, and offers to supply the missing part himself while her husband is away; he is then praised by her when the husband returns.

K1364.p: A woman is abducted after being given medicine that makes her appear dead.

K1366.p: A suitor wins the second daughter by telling her father that the first daughter is dead.

K1367.p: A monk persuades a father to put his daughter adrift in a box, and then seduces her.

K1368.p: A seducer wins a woman by making her jealous of a co-wife, so she turns to him.

K1371.r: *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 549a nn. 175-204; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1371.p: A man abducts a woman who is to marry someone else, taking her away as his bride.

K1371.1.r: *Type 885; Child IV 218, 230, V 260f.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 549b nn. 205-215; *Boje 110ff.; literary treatment: Scott “Lochinvar”, Ibsen “Peer Gynt”; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1371.1.p: A lover snatches a bride away from a wedding to an unwelcome suitor.

K1371.1.1.r: Danish: Grundtvig MS No. 162 in Dansk Folkemindesamling.
K1371.1.1.p: A priest is tricked into performing what he thinks is a mock wedding, but it is a real one: he marries the bride to her true lover instead of the unwanted suitor.

K1371.1.2.p: At a wedding to an unwanted suitor, the lover's foster brother or close friend carries off the bride.

K1371.2.p: A father is deceived into handing over his own daughter in marriage, not realizing she is in disguise and is the one being wed to a lover.

K1371.3.p: A rat takes a new name and wins a bride who was meant for a leopard.

K1371.4.p: A lover in disguise carries off his beloved by force or trickery.

K1371.4.1.p: The lover disguises himself as a king or a knight in order to abduct his beloved.

K1371.4.2.p: The lover disguises himself as a minstrel or wandering musician in order to abduct his beloved.

K1371.5.p: A man gets the bridegroom drunk so that he can sleep with the bride himself.

K1371.6.p: While the chief is busy performing the task a suitor must complete to win her, a rival steals the bride away.

K1372.p: A woman is tricked into becoming engaged to a man she did not choose.

K1372.1.p: A princess is tricked into engaging herself to a suitor whom her father has already rejected.

K1372.2.p: A matchmaker presents a fool to a family as a highly eligible young man, and the fool is accepted as a suitor.

K1375.p: A man seduces a woman by claiming that a vision or dream has promised her to him.

K1375.1.p: A man seduces another man's wife by claiming that her husband's vision orders him to leave home, leaving her open to him.

K1377.r: India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: **Schmerler JAFL XLIV 196-207.
K1377.p: A marriage between close relatives is arranged through trickery.

K1380.p: Miscellaneous tales of seduction carried out by deception, not classed under the more specific headings.

K1382.r: Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 47 No. 58; N. A. Indian: **Schmerler JAFL XLIV 200; Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 270 No. 5.
K1382.p: A trickster pretends to be lame, asks a woman to carry him on her back, and then takes advantage of her.

K1383.r: *Type 1655; *BP II 201; Norwegian: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 141 No. 1655.
K1383.p: A trickster throws a corpse into a river and then accuses a princess of murdering the man, so that she must marry him to avoid scandal.

K1384.r: *Type 36; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 89ff.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 45.
K1384.p: A woman is overpowered and taken advantage of after being caught in a hole or cleft in a tree, or a gap in a hedge.

K1386.p: A man is won over by a woman's indecent trick.

K1387.p: A lecherous trickster seduces women who come down from a tree, and then loses them.

K1388.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 150 No. 1850, Keller.
K1388.p: A trickster forges a letter telling the husband to stay away, so he is held elsewhere while the trickster seduces the husband's wife.

K1388.1.p: The husband is tricked into digging for buried treasure in an ant hill; a snake poisons him and the wife is taken.

K1391.p: A trickster has sexual intercourse with a woman across a stream, using magic to do so from a distance.

K1392.p: A trickster and some girls play obscene tricks on one another, each trying to embarrass or fool the other sexually.

K1393.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 887.
K1393.p: A woman pretends to be sick, with a chill or similar complaint, to get a young boy to come close and so seduce him.

K1394.p: A man who covets his friend's wife manages to make her leave her husband. The two friends agree to beat their wives, but the trickster only pretends to beat his, while the other really beats his, which angers his wife and drives her away.

K1395.p: A woman is tricked into standing naked in a stream while medicine is put into the water, so that she becomes sexually aroused and can be seduced.

K1396.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 7; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1396.p: A guest at an inn is told there is only one bed free, and it is the innkeeper's wife's bed, so he ends up sleeping with her.

K1397.p: Sextus threatens Lucretia that he will kill her and place a naked slave in her bed, shaming her household, and so forces her to submit to him.

K1398.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2914*; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI No. 1547*.
K1398.p: A trickster paints his private parts, and the father wants his daughter's child to be a bishop, which the trick plays on.

K1399.p: Further tales of seduction that do not fit the other categories under this heading.

K1399.1.p: A little prince is lost in the woods and grows up among wild animals, refusing anyone's approach; only a servant girl is able to tame him.

K1399.2.r: *Type 1732*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2908; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC No. 1940B*.
K1399.2.p: A servant takes on false names and deceives the girl, her mother, and her father to win her.

K1399.3.p: A trickster shows a girl how to store up warmth for the winter, which becomes a pretext for seducing her.

K1399.4.p: A woman gets hold of a man's spear or arrow and uses it to lure him into her hut.

K1399.5.p: A teacher seduces a pupil who has been left in his care.

K1400.p: A dupe's property is destroyed as a result of a trick played on him.

K1410.p: A dupe's goods are destroyed through a trick.

K1411.r: *Types 650, 1003; BP II 285ff.; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—7; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1411.p: A youth is told to come home from plowing when the dog does; he beats the dog so it runs home early, then destroys his own horse and harness and goes home.

K1412.p: A trickster sets the house on fire, supposedly to light the road or paint the house red, so the dupe's home is burned.

K1413.r: *Types 1009, 1653A; Penzer V 117 n.; Clouston Noodles 97; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1014A*.
K1413.p: The trickster is told to guard a door, and he lifts the door off its hinges and carries it away.

K1414.p: The trickster is told to watch the bung of a barrel, and he pockets the stopper so that the whole cask of liquid (tar or beer) drains out.

K1415.p: The trickster is told to repair a house, and he tears it down or destroys the house or its furniture instead.

K1416.p: The trickster is told to cut wood and instead tears up the orchard or vineyard.

K1417.p: The trickster is told to close a door tightly, and he fastens it with iron nails so it can never be opened again.

K1418.p: The trickster is told to whet a knife, and he grinds the whole blade away until nothing is left.

K1421.p: The trickster is told to clear land, and he breaks the axe in the process.

K1422.r: *Types 650, 1031; BP II 285ff., *293; Fb “tærske” III 927b; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 436.
K1422.p: The trickster is told to thresh grain, and he uses the granary roof as the threshing flail, wrecking it.

K1423.p: The trickster is told to mow grass, and he tears up the whole meadow instead.

K1424.p: The trickster is told to clear out manure, and he digs a hole instead of removing it.

K1424.1.p: The trickster is told to clean out manure, and he piles it up high instead of removing it.

K1425.p: The trickster is told to tar a wagon, and he covers the entire wagon with tar.

K1427.p: The trickster is told to fill a locked pen, and he chops up the wagon and mules and throws them in to fill it.

K1428.p: The trickster is told to sow grain, and he sows it in a field that has not been plowed.

K1431.p: The trickster saws through the legs of a table so that it collapses under its load.

K1432.p: The trickster is told to fix fences, and he cuts the fence down instead.

K1433.p: The trickster is told to twist twine, and he cuts it instead.

K1440.p: The trickster destroys or maims the dupe's animals.

K1441.p: The trickster is ordered to build a bridge out of something other than wood, stone, iron, or earth, and he uses the carcasses of cattle to build it.

K1442.r: *Type 1006; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 181-8; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. Type 1685.
K1442.p: The trickster is ordered to cast eyes on a certain object, and he kills animals and throws their eyes at it.

K1443.p: A trickster pretends to clean a horse but actually ruins it, for example by scalding it in boiling water or scraping it with a razor. The dupe loses the animal.

K1444.p: A trickster makes a horse pull its own intestines out of its body and then fastens them to a stone. The horse is destroyed.

K1445.p: The trickster is told to bring in the sheep laughing and dancing, and he makes this happen by cutting off their upper lips and breaking their legs, so the sheep are destroyed.

K1446.p: A trickster, hired to drive cattle to the jungle, kills a bull every day and so ruins the owner's animals.

K1447.p: A trickster ties the cattle so tightly that they are strangled. The dupe's animals die through the trickster's overzealous obedience.

K1451.p: A trickster is told to watch the goats and hit any that wander off, and he takes this literally by killing them. The dupe loses his goats.

K1456.p: A trickster swaps his master's gentle tame horse for a vicious bullock, leaving the master with a dangerous animal and a loss.

K1460.p: A trickster causes the death of one or more members of the dupe's family.

K1461.r: Finnish: Kalevala rune 31; S. A. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 133.
K1461.p: A trickster is put in charge of caring for a child and the child ends up dead through his handling of it.

K1461.1.p: The trickster takes out the child's intestines and cleans them, which kills the child.

K1461.2.p: The trickster takes the child to defecate over an ant hole, and the ants kill the child.

K1461.3.r: Impales them. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1013A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1012 I.
K1461.3.p: The trickster cleans several children in a way that kills them.

K1462.r: *Type 1013; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 181—8; India: *Thompson-Balys; New Britain: Dixon 122.
K1462.p: A trickster washes the dupe's grandmother in boiling water, killing her.

K1462.1.p: The trickster is told to heat water for the master's bath and pours boiling water on him, killing him.

K1462.2.p: The trickster is told to cover the house with straw and instead smothers the dupe's mother under the straw.

K1464.p: A trickster tricks the dupe into killing his own children.

K1465.r: Wesselski Theorie 16; *Krappe Archiv f. d. Studium d. neueren Sprachen CLX 162ff.
K1465.p: A slave whose lord has blinded him threatens to leap from a tower with the lord's children unless the lord also blinds himself. The lord blinds himself, but the slave jumps with the children anyway, so all die.

K1466.p: A trickster kills the master's mother by having wood heaved onto her head.

K1500.p: A general heading for tricks that involve adultery, where a deceiver uses or exposes an unfaithful relationship to fool someone.

K1501.p: A husband is deceived by his adulterous wife, who makes a fool of him while carrying on with another man.

K1501.1.p: King Solomon is the cuckolded husband, deceived by his adulterous wife.

K1501.2.p: A cuckolded husband pretends to be asleep when his wife's lover calls, so the lover thinks it is safe to come in and the husband can watch what happens.

K1510.r: *Penzer V 106 n. 1; *Bolte Frey 223f. No. 21; *Hollander MLN XXVII 71; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1510.p: An unfaithful wife tricks or gets the better of her husband.

K1510.1.p: An unfaithful wife kills her husband when he comes home.

K1510.2.p: A man's wife takes revenge on his philandering by having an affair of her own.

K1511.r: *Type 1377; *Basset 1001 Contes II 128; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 185 No. 350; *Campbell Sages xc (Puteus); Chauvin VIII 184 No. 224, IX 23; Alphabet No. 538; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 95b; Dunlop-Wilson II 111f.; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 4; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1511.p: An adulteress comes home late and her husband refuses to let her in. She threatens to drown herself in the well, the husband runs to stop her, and she slips inside and bars the door against him.

K1511.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 678; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 1.
K1511.1.p: An adulteress refuses to let her husband in by pretending not to know him and claiming he is a stranger.

K1512.r: *Type 1417; Bédier Fabliaux 228ff.; Chauvin VI 100 No. 267; *Penzer V 47 n. 3, 223ff., VI 271; Mensa Philosophica No. 40; Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 8 (Lee 222); Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 38; Bødker Exempler 280 No. 24; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1512.p: A wife slips out of bed and puts another woman in her place. The husband, getting no answer, cuts off the sleeping woman's nose or hair. In the morning the wife still has her nose or hair, and the husband is persuaded he was dreaming or that it grew back by a miracle.

K1512.1.r: Cf. Type 882; Köhler-Bolte I 375; Child V 497 s.v. “Substitution”; Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 19; Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 110.
K1512.1.p: A wife who is in fact chaste puts a maidservant in her place with the seducer, and to prove her faithfulness a finger and ring are cut off as evidence. The husband rejects this proof because he knows the finger is not his wife's.

K1513.r: *Type 1418; *Basset 1001 Contes II 4; **J. J. Meyer Isoldes Gottesurteil in seiner erotischen Beziehung (Berlin, 1914); *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 206; Rohde Der griechische Roman 484; BP IV 154, 387f.; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 669; *Schoepperle I 225f.; Hertel Zs. f. Vksk. XVIII 385.—Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 387 No. 116.
K1513.p: A husband makes his wife swear she has slept with no one but him. The lover disguises himself as a donkey driver, and she hires his donkey, falls, and lets him pick her up. She then swears, truthfully in a technical sense, that only her husband and the donkey driver have touched her.

K1514.p: An adulteress gets rid of her husband so she can entertain her lover.

K1514.1.r: (Cf. K1514.9.) *Type 1419A; **Schofield Sources and History of the 7th Novel of the 7th Day in the Decameron (Harvard Studies and Notes II); Bédier Fabliaux 450; Boccaccio Decameron III No. 4 (Lee 213); Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 88; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1514.1.p: A wife hides her unexpectedly returned husband in a chicken house after persuading him that he is being pursued, so she can continue meeting her lover.

K1514.2.r: Boccaccio Decameron III No. 4 (Lee 75); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1514.2.p: The husband is tricked into doing penance while a rascal sleeps with his wife.

K1514.3.r: Boccaccio Decameron III No. 4 (Lee 91); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1514.3.p: The husband is tricked into believing he is in purgatory while his wife entertains her lover.

K1514.4.r: Von der Hagen II xiii No. 27.
K1514.4.p: A returning husband is beaten by servants who mistake him for the lover, whom he had ordered them to beat.

K1514.4.1.p: A husband dressed in his wife's clothing is beaten by the paramour, who was warned in advance, and who claims he was only testing the wife's fidelity.

K1514.4.2.p: A husband hides behind a curtain to catch the lover, who on entering threatens to kill him if he appears.

K1514.4.2.1.p: A cuckolded husband hides under the bed to catch his wife's lover.

K1514.5.r: (Cf. K1566.) Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 27; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1514.5.p: A husband hides in a chest to catch the lover.

K1514.6.p: An adulteress locks her hidden husband up and then meets her lovers.

K1514.7.p: A wife has thieves carry off her hiding husband in a basket, so she is free to be with her lover.

K1514.8.p: A wife throws her husband down a precipice so she can be with her lover.

K1514.9.p: An adulteress gets her lover to unload a cart of wood on her doorstep, so that her husband cannot get in while the lover is inside. The wood blocks the door and keeps the husband out.

K1514.10.p: An adulteress has her husband stand guard for an intruder while she spends time with her lover. He is kept busy watching and is fooled into thinking he is protecting the house.

K1514.11.p: An adulteress pretends to be ill so that she can summon her lover, posing as a physician, to visit her. The husband is not suspicious of the doctor's visit.

K1514.12.p: An adulteress claims she is going off to say her prayers, but actually goes to meet her lover. Her religious excuse hides the tryst.

K1514.13.p: An adulteress arranges to meet her lover in a brothel or disreputable house. The husband arrives there and leaves in shame after finding her.

K1514.14.p: The lover unties the husband's mare, so the horse runs off and the husband chases it. While he is gone, the wife entertains the lover.

K1514.15.p: An adulteress throws a small chest out of the window, so the husband goes to fetch it. While he is outside, the lover moves to a new hiding place.

K1514.16.p: A lover disguises himself as a pregnant woman, and the adulteress is sent by her husband to help as a midwife. She thus meets her lover while doing what seems a proper errand.

K1514.17.p: An adulteress is together with her lover while her husband is asleep beside her. The husband is unaware of what is happening.

K1514.17.1.p: A wife gives her husband a drug so he sleeps deeply, then goes to visit her lover.

K1514.17.2.p: A wife frightens her husband so that he is afraid to share her bed and sleeps alone. She has her servants pretend to be demons to do this.

K1514.18.p: An adulteress makes an excuse to leave the room, supposedly to attend to a bodily need, and instead meets her lover.

K1515.r: (Cf. K1542, K1555, K1566, K1574.) *Type 1419B; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 187 No. 363; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 61; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1515.p: A wife hides her lover in a chest when her husband returns with witnesses; she then swaps the lover for an animal, so the husband is shown to be foolish when he opens it.

K1516.r: The wife holds a cloth in front of his one good eye, so that he cannot see the paramour. *Type 1419C; *Bédier Fabliaux 119, 466; *Chauvin IX 20 Nos. 7, 8; *Wesselski Märchen 187 No. 2; *Jellinek Euphorion IX 162f.; Alphabet No. 536; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 94b; Scala Celi 86b No. 505; Oesterley No. 123; von der Hagen II xxixff.; Dunlop-Wilson II 13; Heptameron No. 6; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 16; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 27; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1516.p: A wife tricks her husband by covering his one good eye, so that he cannot see what she is doing with her lover.

K1516.1.r: The wife pretends to treat his one good eye, so that he cannot see the paramour. *Chauvin IX 20 Nos. 7, 8; Alphabet No. 535; Scala Celi 86b No. 504; Oesterley No. 122; Hitopadesa (ed. Morley) 66; Mensa Philosophica No. 49; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 27; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1516.1.p: The husband's one good eye is treated by a physician, and the treatment is used to cover that eye so he cannot see.

K1516.1.1.r: Entertains his patient’s mistress. Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 87; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1516.1.1.p: A physician treating a man's eye covers his one good eye, leaving him unable to see.

K1516.2.p: A girl covers the good eye of a nurse so that the nurse cannot see her lover coming and going.

K1516.3.p: An adulteress puts out the light so that no one can see her hidden lover.

K1516.4.p: An adulteress covers her husband's eyes while she performs an incantation, and in the meantime the lover escapes.

K1516.5.p: An adulteress persuades her husband to milk a cow while blindfolded, and while he is busy she meets her lover.

K1516.6.p: A faithless wife asks her gullible husband how he would act if he were blind. He closes his eyes to show her, and while his eyes are shut the lover escapes.

K1516.7.p: A wife washes her husband's hair while covering his eyes, so he cannot see her lover slip away.

K1516.8.p: A wife sends her husband to look for a hole in a pot she has bought, which keeps him occupied while her lover escapes unseen.

K1516.9.p: A wife shows her husband her milk-filled breasts and squirts milk into his eyes, blinding him long enough for her lover to escape unseen.

K1517.p: A wife's lover gets away by disguising himself as someone else so the husband does not recognize him.

K1517.1.r: *Type 1419D; *Bédier Fabliaux 229ff.; *Basset 1001 Contes II 143; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 186 No. 351; *Chauvin VIII 39 No. 7, IX 21 No. 8; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 6 (Lee 203); von der Hagen II xxxii ff; Dunlop-Wilson II 114ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 99b.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1517.1.p: Two lovers are at the house; one goes out with a drawn sword to face the husband while the other hides inside, and the wife persuades the husband that she has been sheltering a fugitive.

K1517.1.1.p: One lover is disguised as a robe and carried out of the house by the other, with the wife claiming a tradesman will come back for it.

K1517.2.r: Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 3 (Lee 189); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1517.2.p: A lover escapes by pretending to be a doctor.

K1517.3.r: Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 2 (Lee 186); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1517.3.p: A lover hides in a vat and escapes by pretending to be a buyer who has come to test the vat.

K1517.4.r: (Cf. K1218.1.) J. Prinz “A Tale of a Prioress and her Three Wooers” Literar.-Hist. Forschungen XLVII (Berlin, 1912) 65ff., 113ff.; Hilka Compilatio Singularis Exemplorum No. 14.
K1517.4.p: A lover is hidden in a chest of feathers, and the husband thinks he is a devil.

K1517.4.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 72; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1517.4.1.p: While hidden in the chest of feathers, the lover falls into a cesspool, and the husband takes him for a demon.

K1517.5.p: Caught with the wife, a lover claims he has been trying to force himself on her and failed, and the wife backs up his story.

K1517.6.p: A lover escapes by disguising himself as a monk.

K1517.7.p: A lover escapes by disguising himself as a pregnant woman.

K1517.8.p: A lover escapes by pretending to be a robber.

K1517.9.p: A lover disguised as a cloth merchant is caught by the husband, and he asks the wife to pay him for a pretended sale.

K1517.10.r: Pretends he had come to see him on business. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1517.10.p: A lover leaving the tryst runs into the husband.

K1517.11.p: A lover escapes by pretending he is returning a borrowed basket.

K1517.12.p: An escaping lover is said to be a god or deity, so the husband is deceived into thinking he saw something divine.

K1518.r: *Type 1423; *F. N. Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Boston, 1933) 817 (Merchant’s Tale); *Basset 1001 Contes II 150ff.; Chauvin VIII 98 No. 69, IX 39 No. 34; *Bédier Fabliaux 468; *Stiefel Zs. f. Vksk. VIII 79; *Wesselski Märchen 214f. No. 23; Crane Vitry 240 No. 251; Herbert III 21; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 121 No. 103; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 95b; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 9 (Lee 231); Dunlop-Wilson II 120f.; Mensa Philosophica No. 76.—Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1518.p: The husband sees his wife with her lover from up a pear tree, and the wife convinces him that the tree is magic or that he only imagined it.

K1518.1.p: A husband who has caught his wife with her lover is persuaded that he only had an illusion.

K1521.r: *Type 1364; *Wesselski Märchen 187 No. 2; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1521.p: A wife manages to keep her lover hidden from her husband, so the affair is never discovered. The motif covers the various ways she conceals him.

K1521.1.p: A wife hides her lover in the chimney or fireplace, and the husband never finds him.

K1521.2.p: A wife hides her lover so well in a chest that her husband never finds him.

K1521.2.1.p: A wife hides her lover inside a chest and covers him with clothes so the husband does not find him.

K1521.3.p: A wife hides her lover under a pile of laundry (the wash) so her husband does not see him.

K1521.4.p: A wife hides her lover in the bed, so the husband does not discover him.

K1521.4.1.p: A wife hides her lover under the bed. When her husband comes in, she drops a candle and sends him to fetch another, so the lover can slip away unseen.

K1521.5.p: A wife hides her lover behind a screen so the husband does not see him.

K1521.5.1.p: The lover escapes by hiding behind a sheet that the wife holds up to show her husband, blocking his view.

K1521.6.p: The wife keeps her husband busy with some task while the lover slips away.

K1521.7.p: A wife hides her lover by rolling him up inside a carpet.

K1522.r: *Type 1361; *F. N. Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Boston 1933) 786b (Miller’s Tale); *Hammond Chaucer: a Bibliographical Manual 275; *Barnouw “The Miller’s Tale van Chaucer” Handlingen van het 6. nederlandsche Philologencongres (1910), Mod. Lang. Rev. VII 145; *Thompson in Bryan and Dempster 106ff.
K1522.p: A husband is tricked into hanging in a tub above his house to escape a supposed coming flood, leaving the wife free to be with her lover. The priest who has duped the husband then enjoys the wife.

K1523.r: *Fischer-Bolte 219; Wesselski Märchen 188 No. 2; *Chauvin V 213 No. 121, VIII 96 No. 67; *Köhler-Bolte I 393; Campbell Sages cx; *Krappe Archivum Romanicum XIX (1935) 213—226; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 1; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1523.p: A secret underground passage connects the wife's house to her lover's house, letting her go between them. Her husband is made to believe the woman next door is her sister.

K1524.r: *Crane Vitry 226f. No. 230; Herbert III 18; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 25 No. 19; Mensa Philosophica No. 70; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1524.p: An adulteress falls into mud at her lover's door and claims she must go in to clean her dress, using this as an excuse to visit him.

K1525.r: The numskull: “Commend her rather to the lord below!” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 271 n. 1, Bebel II 99 No. 2, Morlini 286 No. 30; *Bédier Fabliaux 453; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1380 II*; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 34; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1525.p: A husband returns and surprises his wife with her lover and a foolish man who has also blundered in. The wife hides the fool in the bed and the lover under it. The husband, about to leave on a journey, commends them to the Lord above, and a play on words follows about the Lord below.

K1526.p: A friar's trousers are left on the adulteress's bed and presented as a relic that cures sickness. The husband is fooled into thinking the friar came to visit the sick.

K1527.p: The husband comes home unexpectedly to find his wife feasting with her lover, and she convinces him the feast is a celebration for newlyweds.

K1528.p: A wife, suspecting her husband is in disguise and testing her, tells him she knew all along and was only testing him. He then begs her forgiveness.

K1531.r: The devil has let him see his wife’s unfaithfulness in this way. Type 824*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 824*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 824*; Russian: Andrejev No. 824*.
K1531.p: A husband is transformed into a goat and must watch his wife commit adultery.

K1532.p: A husband, gullible and hidden under the bed, spies on his wife and her lover while they believe he is not there.

K1532.1.r: Penzer V 108 n. 2; Bødker Exempler 269 No. 59; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1532.1.p: While the husband lies hidden under the bed, the adulteress tells her lover how much she loves her husband, deceiving the spying husband.

K1532.2.r: Benfey Panchatantra II 258ff., Panchatantra III 12 (tr. Ryder 348).
K1532.2.p: An adulteress, caught with her lover while her husband is hidden under the bed, tells the lover that the husband will die unless she sleeps with a stranger to avert it. The gullible husband accepts this and lets it happen.

K1533.r: Husband is appeased. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1533.p: A husband hides behind a tree to spy on his wife's secret meeting with her lover, but she realizes he is there and tells her lover they should avoid anything that could cause gossip, so the husband is fooled into thinking nothing improper is going on.

K1535.r: (The Tsar’s Dog.) Type 449*; Malone PMLA XLIII 418, 421, 441; Chauvin V 3, 5f., 198, *VI 198, VII 129f.; Penzer III 194; Kittredge Arthur 246ff.; Anderson Roman apuleja i narodnaja skazka I 376-487, 612-633; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3655; Russian: Andrejev No. 499A*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1535.p: An adulterous wife turns her husband into an animal to get rid of him.

K1535.1.p: An adulteress turns her husband into an animal so she can get rid of him and be free to be with her lover.

K1536.r: Scala Celi 87a No. 506; Crane Vitry No. 231; Liebrecht 124; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 38; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1536.p: A woman gets her husband, who is drunk, made into a monk so that she can be rid of him.

K1538.r: *Wesselski Märchen 197; *Child V 3f., 6, 280; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 876; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 305 n. 109t.
K1538.p: A person pretends to be dead in order to secretly meet a lover, often by hiding in a grave or tomb where the meetings take place.

K1538.1.p: A wife pretends to be dead, then slips out of her coffin or grave to go to her lover.

K1538.2.p: A man fakes his own death so that he can live with his mistress.

K1541.p: A priest gives the sexton the offerings of women he has slept with, and says "Take!" when they bring them; when the sexton's own wife comes to make an offering, the priest also calls out "Take!", revealing that he has been her lover too.

K1542.r: (Cf. K1515, K1555, K1566, K1574.) Wesselski Bebel I 206 No. 92; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 193.
K1542.p: A husband, seeing his wife's lover hiding in the hog pen, is frightened when the lover claims to be a miserable hog, and the husband believes his hogs are possessed.

K1543.r: *Bédier Fabliaux 443; **Eberling Auberée, altfranzösische fabel etc. (Berlin, 1891); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1543.p: A procuress leaves a marked coat in a woman's room to get her to a client; later she tells the husband she lost a marked coat, and he is fooled into taking his wife back after he had driven her away.

K1544.r: (Usually shares his bedmate with others, not knowing that she is his wife.) Heptameron No. 8; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 9; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1544.p: A husband unknowingly helps his wife commit adultery by bringing her lover home or otherwise arranging the affair for them.

K1544.1.p: A husband, not knowing who a stranger is, brings him home and entrusts him to his wife's care before leaving on a trip, so the stranger becomes her lover.

K1545.r: *Type 1406; *Liebrecht 124; Bédier Fabliaux 265ff.; *Crane Vitry 227 No. 231, cf. 238 No. 248; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 9 (Lee 231); Christensen DF XLVII 229; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1545.p: Wives bet with each other about who can best fool her husband.

K1546.r: (Cf. K1961.1.2.1, V66.1, X441.) Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 1 (Lee 185); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1546.p: A woman warns her lover that her husband is coming by singing or chanting a parody of a magic spell or incantation.

K1546.1.p: A woman warns her lover that her husband is near by singing a song.

K1546.2.p: A woman encourages her lover by singing a song to him.

K1548.p: A wife pretends her suspicious husband is insane, so that he is taken away and she is free to see her lover.

K1549.p: Miscellaneous tricks by which an adulteress outwits her husband and keeps her affair hidden.

K1549.1.p: A woman has her lover steal her husband's clothes, then the lover comes to the house disguised as the husband, and the real husband, left without clothes, is driven from his home.

K1549.2.p: A wife caught in adultery pretends to be dead, and she comes back to life when she hears her husband say he has seen nothing.

K1549.3.p: A lover is carried away on the mistress's shoulders so that his footprints do not show in the snow and reveal his visit.

K1549.4.r: India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. English, Scottish: *Child No. 274.
K1549.4.p: When the husband arrives and finds the lover's horse outside, the wife claims their cow has given birth to a horse, so the husband thinks he is mistaken.

K1549.5.p: An unfaithful wife sends secret messages to her lover by pouring milk into a stream for him to notice.

K1549.6.p: While travelling, the wife's attendants chase the wrong man, thinking he is her lover, and so the real lover escapes.

K1549.7.p: The husband is fooled about the source of a noise, not realising that a lover is hidden nearby.

K1549.8.p: A woman cooks food for her lover.

K1550.p: A husband gets the better of his unfaithful wife and her lover.

K1550.1.p: The husband finds out that his wife is being unfaithful.

K1550.1.1.p: The husband secretly puts dye on the wife's dress so that he can tell who she has been with.

K1550.1.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 341.
K1550.1.2.p: The husband learns of the wife's affair from the food she prepares for her lover.

K1550.3.p: The husband learns of the wife's affair from the food she prepares for her lover.

K1551.p: The husband comes home quietly and watches his wife and her lovers from hiding.

K1551.1.p: The husband returns secretly and kills a suitor who is not welcome in his house.

K1553.r: *Type 1380; *BP III 124; *Taylor MPh XV 227 n. 1; Stiefel Zs. f. Vksk. VIII 74; Russian: Andrejev No. 1380; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1553.p: The husband pretends to be blind and then takes revenge on his wife and her lover.

K1553.1.p: The husband pretends to be ill so that he can surprise his wife with her lover.

K1554.r: Type 1406*; von der Hagen II *xxxvi No. 41.
K1554.p: The husband sets fire to the house and forces out the lover who was hiding there.

K1554.1.p: A trickster sets fire to a barrel of tow in which the lover is hidden; the naked lover runs out with burning wisps, and the trickster tells the husband he has raised the devil.

K1555.r: *Type 1535; **A. Stepphun Das Fabel vom Prestre comporté und seine Versionen (Königsberg, 1913); *BP II 18; *Basset 1001 Contes II 45; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 412, 420; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 10 No. 5; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 73; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1555.p: The husband carries off a box in which the lover is hidden, and the lover is exposed or otherwise humiliated.

K1555.0.1.p: A dying woman tricks her lover into getting into a chest, asking her husband to bury the chest with her.

K1555.0.2.p: The husband unknowingly carries away the chest with the lover hidden inside.

K1555.1.r: Boccaccio Decameron V No. 10 (Lee 173); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1555.1.p: A lover hides in a hen-coop to escape, but the husband finds him there. The husband then carries off the box or coop with the hidden man inside.

K1555.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2900*; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
K1555.2.p: A naked lover hides in a sooty barrel, and the husband makes money by showing the 'devil' inside to a curious gentleman who pays for a look.

K1556.r: *Type 1360C; **Anderson Der Schwank vom alten Hildebrand (Dorpat, 1931); *BP II 373; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 188a nn. 164—5; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 93, III No. 193.
K1556.p: A cuckolded husband hides nearby and reveals that he knows of the affair by answering, in rhyme, the rhymes his wife and her lover make about their night together.

K1556.1.p: The adulteress blindfolds her husband and makes him chant magic words about the affair, so he unknowingly sings out what she has been doing.

K1557.p: The husband learns of his wife's adultery through a conversation full of riddles and hints, and in this indirect way she confesses and promises to change her ways.

K1557.1.p: After making his wife drunk, the husband finds a love letter from her lover in her purse, proving the affair.

K1558.r: *Köhler-Bolte II 469; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 42; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1558.p: Caught with his wife, the lover pretends to be a crucifix statue. When the husband prepares to castrate the 'crucifix,' the lover runs away naked.

K1558.1.p: The husband actually castrates the wife's lover.

K1561.r: *Wesselski Bebel II 149 No. 161; Nouvelles Récréations No. 60; N. A. Indian (Malecite): Mechling GSCan VI 83 No. 21, (Fox): Jones PAES I 145.
K1561.p: The husband finds the lover in his wife's place, for instance in bed, and beats him or cuts off his private parts.

K1561.1.p: The husband hides in his wife's room and kills the lover when he comes to visit.

K1562.r: The husband calls the neighborhood to see them. *Wesselski Mönchslatein 9 No. 4; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 56; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1562.p: The husband sets a pitfall for the lover. The wife sends her maid to check the way, the maid falls in, and finally the wife falls in herself.

K1563.p: A husband who is a god traps his wife and her lover with magic armor that holds them fast.

K1564.p: The husband secretly blackens the lover's mouth, so when he returns home his wife's face is black, proving she met the lover.

K1565.r: (Often on window.) Type 432; *Krappe Balor 35ff.; *Schoepperle I 218ff.; Irish myth: Cross.
K1565.p: The husband sets blades, such as broken glass, where the lover will go, so that the lover is wounded and the wife's lover is revealed.

K1566.r: Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 8 (Lee 261); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1566.p: The cuckolded man shuts the wife's lover in a chest, then lies down on the chest with the lover's own wife.

K1566.1.p: The cuckold unknowingly lies with his own wife on the chest that holds her hidden lover.

K1567.r: Wife drowns. (Sometimes also paramour.) Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 47; Nouvelles Récréations No. 90; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1567.p: The husband tricks his wife into riding a mule that has been kept from water, and on crossing a stream the mule plunges into the water.

K1568.p: The husband, in disguise, begs food from his wife's suitors, so he can see who they are and how they treat him.

K1569.p: A miscellaneous group of tales in which the husband outwits his wife and her lover in ways not covered by other headings.

K1569.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 43; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1569.1.p: The husband collects a fee from the lover, who is surprised and pays up.

K1569.2.r: Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 71.
K1569.2.p: A husband catches his wife and her lover together and surprises them, then rebukes them for not having shut the door. The husband turns the situation to his advantage by mocking their carelessness.

K1569.3.p: A man fakes an illness so he can leave his bed at night and go to his mistress. The feigned sickness is a pretext for slipping away to a serving maid.

K1569.4.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 65; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1569.4.p: A husband takes the place of his wife's lover without her realizing it, and then beats or otherwise humiliates her. He turns the tables by playing the lover himself.

K1569.5.p: A husband catches his wife's lover by using a signal she had arranged with the lover. He uses the signal himself to lure the lover into being caught.

K1569.6.p: A husband tells his wife to light wicks and hold a knife in her hand before she commits adultery. The lovers are frightened away by the lights and the knife.

K1569.7.p: A husband pretends that his wife's private parts can speak and tell him she has been unfaithful. He uses this false claim to expose her.

K1569.8.p: A husband makes a clever remark that shows he knows all about the affair, which embarrasses both wife and lover. His words leave them with no way to deny it.

K1569.9.p: A husband kills his wife's lover, whom he surprised with her. The wife convinces him that he has killed a thief instead of a lover.

K1570.p: A trickster outwits an adulterous wife and her lover. The trickster exposes or humiliates them through a clever ruse.

K1571.r: *Types 1535, 1725; *BP II 18; von der Hagen III *xxix; Wesselski Märchen 216 No. 27; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1360A*, 2901*, 2902*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1380 VIII*; Russian: Andrejev 1360A*, 1730 IV; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1571.p: A trickster discovers an adulterous affair when food meant for the lover is instead served to the husband. The mix-up reveals the affair.

K1571.0.1.p: A trickster discovers an adulterous affair by getting food that had been prepared for the lover. The food is the clue that exposes the affair.

K1571.1.r: *Type 1535; BP II 18; Scala Celi 37a No. 206; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1571.1.p: A trickster posing as a magician makes an adulteress produce food she has hidden for her lover, so that her husband gets it instead. The hidden food exposes the affair.

K1572.r: She confesses. *Type 1725; BP II 131; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 136.
K1572.p: A trickster convinces an adulterous wife that her husband is about to come home and punish her, so she is frightened into being caught or giving herself away.

K1573.p: A trickster sends his master running after the lover, frightening the lover badly. The master does not know about the adultery, but the lover is terrified anyway.

K1574.r: (Cf. K1515, K1542, K1555, K1556.) *Types 1535, 1725; *BP II 18; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1574.p: A trickster posing as a magician buys a chest that secretly contains a hidden lover. The trickster uses the chest to expose the affair.

K1574.1.p: A sham magician causes the hidden lover to fall into a trap. The lover had been trained by the magician to cling to him, which makes the trap work.

K1574.2.p: A trickster finds a woman's lover and hides him in an outhouse. The husband rewards the trickster for the discovery.

K1577.r: *Type 1361; Chaucer’s Miller’s Tale; *Thompson The Miller’s Tale (Bryan and Dempster 106ff.); Italian Novella: Rotunda. See references for K1225.
K1577.p: A second lover burns the first lover at a window with a hot iron. The burning punishes the lover who is caught outside.

K1578.p: The Hindu god Vishnu takes the form of his aunt's nephew and frightens and torments the aunt's lover. The god's trick punishes the lover.

K1580.p: Other tricks connected with adultery that do not fit the more specific headings above.

K1581.r: **J. W. Spargo FFC XCI; *F. N. Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer 838a. (Shipman’s Tale).
K1581.p: A person gets back a gift that was given to a lover. The gift is recovered through a clever scheme.

K1581.1.p: A lover breaks or removes a household item and convinces the husband that the wife took back the gift he had given her, so the lover keeps the gift.

K1581.2.p: A lover gets back a horse and wagon he had given the wife by telling the husband she took them away because the lover delivered wood of uneven quality.

K1581.3.r: **Spargo FFC XCI; Boccaccio Decameron VIII Nos. 1, 2 (*Lee 247ff.); F. N. Robinson Works of Chaucer 838a (Shipman’s Tale); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1581.3.p: A lover borrows money from the husband to use on the wife, then tells the husband the money was returned to the wife while the husband was away.

K1581.4.r: *Spargo FFC XCI; *Euling Studien über Heinrich Kaufringer (Breslau, 1900) 65ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1581.4.p: Not knowing who the husband is, the lover tells him about his affair with the wife; the husband makes the lover lead him to the scene, where the wife is forced to give back nearly all the money.

K1581.5.p: A lover recovers by trickery and theft a piece of cloth he had lent and given to his mistress.

K1581.5.1.p: The woman returns the cloth but hides a live coal in it, so that the lover, who claims payment for the cloth in front of the husband, has his whole supply of cloth destroyed.

K1581.5.2.p: The lover demands the return of the cloth, threatening to wait for the husband to come home and expose the affair.

K1581.6.r: **Spargo FFC XCI; *Wesselski Bebel II 115f. No. 49; *Bolte Frey 242 No. 76.
K1581.6.p: A lover gets back a valuable piece of jewelry he gave the wife by telling the husband he left it behind as a pledge.

K1581.7.r: **Spargo FFC XCI; *Semerau Die Schwäke und Schnurren des Poggio (Leipzig, 1905) No. 69; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1581.7.p: A lover regains a goose he gave as a gift by a bawdy trick.

K1581.7.1.r: Finally has to flee. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1581.7.1.p: The lover delays handing over the goose, hoping to win greater sexual favors first.

K1581.8.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 178; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1581.8.p: A lover refuses to leave the bed until the woman, fearing exposure, gives back the money.

K1581.9.p: A lover recovers his gift by having the woman spend money to buy his own worthless goods.

K1581.10.p: A lover bargains with the husband and pays him with worthless money.

K1581.11.p: A prostitute is paid with counterfeit money.

K1581.12.p: The husband obtains the gift that the lover had given to his wife.

K1582.p: A lover blackmails an adulterous woman, forcing her to pay to keep the affair secret.

K1582.1.p: After sleeping with a priest's wife, a peasant demands her earrings as the price of his silence, taking revenge on the priest who had cheated him of his wife's earrings.

K1583.p: A lover tricks the husband into taking his own wife to the lover.

K1584.r: Boccaccio Decameron III No. 3 (Lee 71); *Borgeld Vrouwenlist: verbreiding en oorsprong van een novelle uit den Decamerone (Neuphilologische Bibliotheek No. 7, Den Haag, 1926); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1584.p: An innocent confessor is tricked into acting as go-between for an adulteress and her lover, by following her false accusations that lead him to her lover's side.

K1585.p: A husband pretends he is going into meditation with a cloth over his face, secretly sends a servant in his place, and visits his mistress. The wife takes the servant's place, discovers the affair, and on his return the husband confides his adultery to the supposed servant, who is really his wife.

K1586.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 13; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1586.p: A lover pretends to have lost his genitals so that the husband will trust him and not suspect the affair.

K1587.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 66; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1587.p: An adulterous wife uses the public baths as a secret meeting place with her lover, but her child's innocent remark gives the affair away to the husband.

K1588.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 23; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1588.p: A woman tempts a peasant secretary, who draws a line on the floor and dares her to step over it; when she does, adultery takes place.

K1591.r: *Schmidt Cukasaptati (Kiel, 1894, Stuttgart, 1896); Köhler-Bolte I 47, 336, 513; Clouston Tales II 196ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 59 No. *435.
K1591.p: A wife is kept from adultery when a parrot tells her seventy tales, stalling her until her husband comes home.

K1591.0.1.p: An unfaithful wife kills a magic parrot because it has exposed her betrayal of her husband.

K1591.1.p: A peacock is left behind to watch over an adulterous wife and report on her.

K1591.2.p: A dog guards the chastity of its master's wife while the master is away.

K1592.p: A lover disguises prostitutes as nuns and sends them to fetch the mistress to a convent, and the husband is fooled by the ruse.

K1593.p: An adulteress dresses as a boy and runs away with her lover.

K1594.p: A student prolongs his studies with a professor so that he can keep sleeping with the professor's wife.

K1595.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 48; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1595.p: An adulteress claims to be faithful, explaining that her mouth alone has promised fidelity to her husband, so she is willing to do everything except kiss.

K1596.p: A faithful wife, disguised, saves her husband from punishment for adultery.

K1600.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 59-79; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 264f.
K1600.p: A deceiver is caught in his own trick and suffers the harm he meant for someone else.

K1601.r: Type 1117; Africa: Werner African 214, (Hottentot): Bleek 78; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 254 No. 33; West Indies: Flowers 539.
K1601.p: A man who sets a trap or pitfall for someone is himself caught in it.

K1601.1.p: A pitfall is set for someone, but the intended victim escapes it.

K1603.p: A rich man orders poor people to dig a grave to bury them as a sacrifice to end a famine, but a Christian frees them, and the rich man himself falls into the grave and dies.

K1605.p: A thief catcher is struck by his own magic club, which he had used against thieves.

K1610.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a deceiver is caught in his own trap.

K1611.r: *Types 327, 1119; *BP I 124 n. 1; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 22; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 358ff.; (Northern Paiute [Paviotso]): Lowie JAFL XXXVII 226 No. 10; Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 73 n. 3; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 267 No. 77.
K1611.p: The hero and heroine swap places with the ogre's children in bed and switch their caps, so the ogre unknowingly kills his own children.

K1611.1.p: A cannibal's intended victim is marked with a thread around the ankle, but at night the mark is moved to the host, so the cannibal kills the host instead.

K1611.2.p: A guest who plans to kill his host is tricked into sleeping in his own intended victim's bed, so the plotter is killed instead. In the note, the brothers who return home end up killing their own father.

K1611.3.p: A girl takes the place of an impostor on the wedding night. The impostor's mother then beats her, believing she is the heroine who has been wronged.

K1611.4.p: A noose is secretly changed so that the ogre's daughter, not the intended victim, is dragged to her death.

K1611.5.p: A young kid hides one of the tigress's cubs in its own place, and the tigress unknowingly eats her own cub.

K1612.r: *Type 930; **J. Schick Das Glückskind mit dem Todesbrief (1932); *Aarne FFC XXIII 73ff.; *Penzer II 113; **Cosquin Études 73ff., 129ff.; *Chauvin VIII 145; *Fb “teglovn”; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 40 No. 34; *Oesterley No. 283; Scala Celi 130b No. 713; *Herbert III 198, 589; *Gaster Exempla 239f., 246f. Nos. 320, 345; *Hilka Neue Beiträge zur Erzählungsliteratur des Mittelalters No. 6; *bin Gorion Born Judas V 226f.; Verdam Handelingen en Mededeelingen der Maatschappij der Nederlandsche Letterkunde (1898—99; bijlage) 1ff.; *Taylor MPh XV 177; BP IV 352; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 509; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 17 No. 8.—Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII xxiv, Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 229, Voorhoeve No. 151, 142.
K1612.p: A message ordering the death of whoever arrives first is turned against its sender: the person meant to die escapes, and someone else, often the sender's own family, is killed in his place.

K1612.1.p: In revenge, a villain orders that whoever first enters a temple be killed. He himself accidentally enters first and is slain by his own order.

K1612.2.p: Someone orders guards to shoot any thief who approaches, and the king is accidentally shot by his own guards.

K1613.p: A person who plots to poison someone is killed by the very poison he prepared.

K1613.0.1.p: A would-be poisoner is forced to drink from the cup he had poisoned for someone else.

K1613.1.r: Chauvin II 87 No. 22; Zs. d. dt. Morgenl. Ges. XLII 115ff.; B[ö]dker Exempler 280 No. 23; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1613.1.p: A person tries to blow poison onto another, but the poison blows back and poisons him instead.

K1613.2.p: A wife poisons her husband, and before he dies he forces her to drink from the same cup, so she dies too.

K1613.2.1.p: A man gives his wife a poisoned drink, but she pours the two drinks together, and both of them die.

K1613.3.p: A poisoner's own son unknowingly drinks the poisoned beverage meant for his stepbrother.

K1613.4.p: A son who plans to poison his father accidentally drinks the poison himself.

K1613.5.p: A snake is killed by a magic spell that the snake itself taught to a clever woman.

K1614.p: A father who has agreed to hand his daughter over to a cannibal is himself eaten by the cannibal.
