K1615.p: An ogre plans to burn the hero's moccasins while they are camping together, but the hero swaps them, so the ogre's own moccasins are burned.

K1616.p: A man left stranded on an island or remote place gets home anyway and outwits the person who abandoned him.

K1616.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 326 n. 175. Cf. Spanish: Espinosa II No. 49.
K1616.1.p: A young man is sent by his father-in-law to hunt eggs on an island and is deserted there, but he outwits the old man and gets home.

K1616.2.p: A marooned man hides himself in an ogre's clothing and so tricks the ogre, escaping him.

K1617.p: A hero is given arrows with blunted, soft tips and sent against dangerous enemies. The trick is eventually discovered and the enemy is humiliated or defeated.

K1618.p: A deceiver plans to kill the hero during a swinging game by cutting the rope, but the hero cuts the rope first and the deceiver is killed by his own trap.

K1621.r: Comparetti PFLS IX 144; *Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 236 No. 5.
K1621.p: A sheep-thief disguises a tiger as a sheep, but the tiger he has stolen turns out to be the one who harms him.

K1622.p: A thief who has climbed a rope to reach a food store is discovered, and the rope is cut so he falls. He had earlier tricked the guard of the store into lowering the rope, by copying the owner's voice or by learning the password.

K1623.p: A lawyer agrees to pay a debt if he wins his first case, so he refuses to plead. The debtor sues him for double the debt, so whether he wins or loses he must pay, and he settles the debt.

K1624.p: A woman who hires a false suitor for her daughter finds that her scheme goes wrong and the plan does not work out as she intended.

K1625.p: A hermit persuades a foolish father to put his daughter in a floating basket. A prince takes the girl and leaves a monkey in the basket in her place, so the hermit is made to look ridiculous.

K1626.p: People who plan to kill someone are themselves killed, usually by the same trap or plot they prepared.

K1626.1.p: An earl who has agreed to kill a man is killed in combat by that same man.

K1626.2.p: A treacherous counselor who has arranged a ballgame in order to kill someone is himself killed in that same treacherous game.

K1626.3.r: S. Am. Indian (Amuesha): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 150.
K1626.3.p: Boiling water prepared to scald the hero is instead used on the man who prepared it.

K1628.p: Sons have a servant pose as their dead father and falsify his will. The servant cheats them by making the will favor himself.

K1631.r: England, U.S.: Baughman; Danish: Kristensen Vore Fædres Kirketjeneste 88ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 144 No. 1735A*; West Indies: Flowers 541f.
K1631.p: A sexton steals the priest's cow and then teaches his son a false song. The boy is paid by the priest to sing a song in church, but instead sings a scandalous accusation against the priest.

K1632.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 29 No. 50, Espinosa III Nos. 210f.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1632.p: A fox leads a donkey to a lion's den, but when the fox arrives the donkey kicks him so that he falls onto the lion's bed and is eaten.

K1633.p: A cock gives advice that causes trouble among the ox and the ass, but the master discovers the cause of the trouble and kills the cock.

K1635.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 99 No. 837, Keller.
K1635.p: Honesty and Fraud are partners and hire a housekeeper, agreeing to share her. Fraud falls in love with her and pays Honesty double his losses to give up his share, so the cheat loses.

K1636.r: Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 279), 116 (ST 262); Halm Aesop No. 10.
K1636.p: Maids kill the cock for waking them too early, but their mistress punishes them, so they must now get up even earlier.

K1637.r: He always answers his master’s remarks, “I have thought of the same thing too.” He falls into the trap when his master says, “I am going to sow salt.” Type 1574*.
K1637.p: A foreman who flatters his master is tricked in turn by that master.

K1641.r: *Penzer V 59 n. 2; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 69; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 247 No. 23.
K1641.p: A trickster lies in ambush for his intended victim, but the victim turns the trap around and kills the trickster.

K1641.1.p: A husband who plans to push his wife off a mountain is himself pushed over by her.

K1642.p: A trickster mole goes into his own tunnel to eat the common food, but a fox sees the molehill above it and kills him there.

K1643.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 281 No. 26; Chauvin II 88 No. 24.
K1643.p: An animal strangles its intended victim, then tries to eat it, and the victim's own trick ends with the animal caught in the trap.

K1645.r: (Cf. K551.4.3, K926, K1210.) U.S.: Baughman. Cf. Child Ballad No. 4.
K1645.p: A woman tells her lover to strip and turn his back, then he pushes her into the water or a pit instead.

K1651.p: A woman tries to set her own fierce watchdog on someone, but the dog turns on her and bites her.

K1652.p: A woman tries to push her husband into a river, but he steps aside and she falls in herself. She drowns because she has tied his hands so he cannot help her.

K1655.r: *Type 1585; *Prato RTP IX 537; *Dubsky RTP XXIII 427; Köhler-Bolte I 362; **Oliver JAFL XXII 395; *Bolte Wickram’s Rollwagenbüchlein 371 No. 36; Scala Celi 8a No. 51.—Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 139 No. 26; West Indies: Flowers 542.
K1655.p: On a lawyer's advice, a client pretends to be insane in court, and then keeps pretending when the lawyer asks to be paid.

K1655.1.p: The lawyer is refused his fee because, as the client argues, no argument is good without a witness, so the lawyer cannot prove his case for payment.

K1656.p: A trickster pretends to be dumb in court after a cart accident he caused, and the plaintiff's own complaints show he could speak, so the plaintiff is penalized.

K1657.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 847; Nouvelles de Sens. No. 1; Lithuanian: Balys Historical.
K1657.p: A dishonest official is outwitted by a peasant who picks a quarrel with him, which brings the ruler's attention to the official's abuses.

K1661.p: A courtier is ordered by the king in winter to deliver six loads of snow, and he waits until summer to present the order, then collects money instead.

K1663.r: The parent thinks the devil has got him and leaves the lovers in peace. von der Hagen III 36 No. 55; English: Child No. 281.
K1663.p: A lover is lowered into a girl's room in a basket at night, and a spying parent who stumbles into the basket is jolted about by the lover's helper.

K1664.p: A trickster sells his dog as mutton or opossum, then later eats the same dog, which the buyer had given to a friend of the trickster.

K1667.r: Penzer III 118ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 96a; *Chauvin IX 24 No. 13; Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 10 (Lee 266); *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 27; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 135 No. 1617*, Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman, *bin Gorion Born Judas II 131, 346, IV 132, 281; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1667.p: A dishonest banker is tricked into handing over the deposits he holds, because he expects even larger chests; the chests he receives are filled with stones.

K1667.1.p: A blind man gets back his stolen treasure by making the thief expect an even larger sum to invest.

K1667.1.1.p: A blind man recovers his stolen buried money by pretending he will bury even more. The greedy thief returns the original treasure, hoping to get the larger hoard, and the blind man keeps it.

K1667.1.2.p: The blind man asks the thief to invest a larger sum for him, and the greedy thief returns the stolen money in hope of getting more, so the blind man recovers his money.

K1672.p: A dwarf uses magic to make a girl fall in love with him, but he falls in love with her himself, and he loses her when he is forced to remove his magic.

K1673.p: A sage's advice is followed literally, and he is killed so that his blood can be mixed with a sacrifice.

K1674.p: A bear or tiger is put in a floating box in place of a woman, and it kills the villain who tries to steal her.

K1675.p: Swindlers are allowed to hide money, but the money they hide turns out to be a basket of stones.

K1676.p: A man pretending to be sick is roused to action by a beating.

K1676.1.p: A woman pretends to faint, and a magician beats her to bring her back to life, supposedly to drive out an evil spirit; she revives from the beating and the trick is exposed.

K1677.p: A magician boasts that he can turn black dogs gray and then back again, and a trickster challenges him to prove it by supplying a gray dog and making the magician do the transformation.

K1681.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 285 n. 52, (California): Gayton and Newman 59, 64; Africa: Werner African 162.
K1681.p: The culture hero who brings death into the world is the first to die from it: his own child dies, and he regrets his act too late.

K1681.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1681.1.p: The man who invents a death machine is the first person killed by it when he tries it out.

K1682.r: Disguise as ghost. Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 47 No. 326, Espinosa II Nos. 136—138.
K1682.p: A trickster disguises himself to frighten someone, but the intended victim beats him instead.

K1682.1.p: A man dresses in a sheet to scare someone, but his pet monkey copies him in a sheet; the frightened victim tells the 'big fear' to run, and the scarer, seeing the monkey, runs home in terror.

K1683.p: An old procuress is lured into a faithful wife's room, where the wife beats her and drives her out naked, so the tables are turned on the go-between.

K1684.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 301; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 63; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1684.p: A seller of pardons is robbed by a man whom he has already pardoned in advance, and the judge rules that this defence is valid.

K1685.r: *Type 763; Chaucer’s “Pardoner’s Tale”; *F. N. Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Boston, 1933) 834; *BP II 154; *Basset 1001 Contes III 181ff.; *Chauvin VIII 100 No. 73; *Wesselski Morlini 293 No. 42; *Bolte Montanus 564; *Basset RTP XIV 440; *Hart MPh IX 17; *Wells MPh XXV 163.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *bin Gorion Born Judas IV 41, 276; India: Cowell J[a]taka I 124, *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 386 No. 115; Eberhard FFC CXX 201f.; Korean: Zong in-Sob 186 No. 81.
K1685.p: Two or three men find treasure, and each tries to kill the others: one poisons another's wine, but the poisoned man kills him, drinks the wine, and dies too.

K1686.p: A servant takes revenge on his master by hiding a killed calf so that only its tail sticks out of the ground, which betrays the killing.

K1687.p: Two men swap jobs because each has been persuaded that the other's work is easier. Both end up worse off, as the deceiver's trick catches himself.

K1691.r: *Type 1029; Köhler-Bolte I 151; Wünsche 29, 33, 36ff., 47, 51ff., 61, 106; Fb “tjære” III 811a; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—7; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 115.
K1691.p: A bargain is made that anger must stop when the cuckoo calls; the ogre's wife climbs a tree and imitates the cuckoo, and she is shot down by a hunter.

K1691.1.r: A cruel master commands his serf to climb a tree and imitate the cry of the cuckoo; he shoots the “cuckoo.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3745.
K1691.1.p: A man is shot in the cuckoo's place, with the hunter mistaking him for the bird.

K1691.2.p: A servant who dislikes getting up early kills the devil's mother or grandmother, who has been crowing in place of the rooster.

K1692.p: A teacher instructs a pupil in the art of seduction, and the pupil, not knowing the woman is the teacher's own wife, seduces her and reports success to the teacher, who then fails in his attempts to catch them together.

K1693.p: A trickster tries to avoid paying tax by hiding eggs in his breeches, but the tax collectors make him sit down, and the eggs break into an omelet.

K1696.p: A trickster pretends to have found a purse, which he has filled with lead, and sells it to a merchant for ten crowns; he wins the lawsuit that follows.

K1700.p: A trickster fools someone by bluffing, pretending to be stronger or more dangerous than he is.

K1710.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 5; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 14 Nos. 3, 4; Africa (Wachaga): Gutmann 191f.; West Indies: Flowers 542.
K1710.p: A large animal, often an ogre, is frightened into submission by a bluff, typically by a small hero's trick.

K1711.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 245; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 359 No. 12.
K1711.p: A small hero makes an ogre believe he is much larger and stronger than he is, so the ogre is overawed and gives way.

K1711.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 90; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 53.
K1711.1.p: A tiger is made to believe that a porcupine's bristle is the hair of his enemy, and is overawed by the thought of such a formidable foe.

K1714.r: They have jumped on him from behind and he cannot see. He buys them off. India: Thompson-Balys.
K1714.p: Small boys bluff a tiger by threatening to harness it like a draft animal, and the tiger is cowed.

K1715.r: Types 126*, 1149; *BP I 160 n. 1; *Krappe Neophilologus XV 274ff.; Russian: Andrejev No. 126; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 249f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: *Dixon 191 nn. 15, 16, 192 n. 17; Africa: Weeks Jungle 394, Werner African 223, (Kaffir): Kidd 230 No. 2, (Vai): Ellis 191 No. 7, (Hottentot): Bleek 24; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 317, 320, 322; West Indies: Flowers 543; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 44 No. 9, 291 No. 49.
K1715.p: A weak creature convinces a larger, stronger one that it has eaten many of the big one's companions, and the big one is frightened into backing down.

K1715.1.r: (Usually hare and lion.) *Penzer V 49 n. 1; Chauvin II 88 No. 25; India: *Thompson-Balys; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 134 No. 18, (Virginia): Parsons JAFL XXXV 264 No. 12.
K1715.1.p: A weak creature shows a strong one its own reflection and frightens it by claiming that this is the enemy threatening to kill it.

K1715.1.1.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 282 No. 27; Indonesia, Malay, Hindu: Dixon 191 n. 16, *DeVries Volksverhalen I 362 No. 14.
K1715.1.1.p: A weak creature shows a strong one its own reflection and convinces it that the reflection is the head of the last animal the weak one killed.

K1715.1.2.p: A man shows a ghost its own reflection, and the ghost is frightened by it.

K1715.1.3.p: A man shows a demon its own reflection, and the demon is frightened by it.

K1715.2.r: *Type 1149; Aarne FFC XI 154; Dh IV 278; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 322.
K1715.2.p: A child or shepherd tells a tiger that its ten promised companions are only one tiger, and the tiger, thinking it lucky to escape alive, lets the small hero go.

K1715.3.r: *Type 125; BP I 237ff., 254; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 249f., 255f., 266; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Wakweli): Bender 54.
K1715.3.p: Sheep find a sack with a wolf's head in it and make a wolf believe they have killed a wolf, so he runs away in terror.

K1715.4.r: Chauvin V 23 No. 13 n. 1; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 255f., 266.
K1715.4.p: Enemies are scared off by being led to believe they will be eaten by the one they are attacking.

K1715.4.1.p: Spirits are scared away by being led to believe they will be eaten.

K1715.5.p: A leopard is frightened away when told that a lizard is nearby, since the lizard has bitten it before.

K1715.6.p: A trickster pretends to hunt a certain tree with which his ancestors killed tigers, and the tiger runs away.

K1715.7.p: A small, lame hero convinces a demon that he is a god, and threatens to eat the demon.

K1715.8.p: A hero tells his brother to take one of the enemies and that he can manage the rest, bluffing to make the enemies fear them.

K1715.9.p: A trickster claims to be a god's messenger sent to collect demon skins for his drum, and the demons bribe him with gifts instead of eating him.

K1715.10.p: A donkey claims to have killed a cow, and this boast frightens a tiger.

K1715.11.p: A lion is frightened away when someone stabs at it from inside an iron cage.

K1715.12.p: A smaller animal frightens a larger one by showing it a rope supposed to be its tail, curds supposed to be its spit, and winnowing fans supposed to be its ears.

K1715.13.p: A tiger is made to believe that its captor has eaten many crabs, so the tiger fears him and lets him go.

K1715.14.p: A fox overawes lion cubs with his boasting and then eats their food.

K1716.r: *Penzer V 101 n. 1; Chauvin II 96 No. 49; Panchatantra III 2 (tr Ryder 308); B[ö]dker Exempler 294 No. 54; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1716.p: A hare tricks a large animal, such as an elephant, by claiming to be the moon's envoy and saying the moon is angry, so the animal is frightened into submission.

K1717.p: A man makes giant shoes and leaves them outside his barn so that an ogre believes a giant lives there and stays away.

K1718.p: A hero scares off an ogre by boasting about his enormous relatives, so the ogre is awed and backs down.

K1718.1.p: The hero claims the thunder is the sound of his brother's wagon rolling, a bluff that impresses the ogre.

K1718.2.p: The hero claims the millstones are the pearls of his mother, a bluff meant to overawe an ogre.

K1718.3.p: The hero claims a huge cauldron of tar is his mother's kitchen pot, a bluff meant to overawe an ogre.

K1718.4.p: The hero claims a harrow is his mother's comb, a bluff meant to overawe an ogre.

K1718.5.p: The hero claims a plow is his mother's hoe, a bluff meant to overawe an ogre.

K1721.r: Dh III 142; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 301 n. 102; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 381 No. 7.
K1721.p: A hero proves he is a cannibal by a trick exchange of vomit, convincing an ogre or beast that he eats men.

K1721.1.p: A hero frightens a dog out of eating men by pretending to eat his own entrails.

K1721.2.r: S. A. Indian (Caingeng, Bacairi): Horton BBAE CXLIII (3) 294.
K1721.2.p: An ant-eater fools a jaguar by swapping excrement, so the jaguar believes the ant-eater eats the same things it does.

K1722.p: A monkey pretends that his house always answers him, so others think it is magical or that he has a strange companion.

K1723.r: Frightens wolf. American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 112 No. 14.
K1723.p: A goat pretends to be chewing rock, bluffing others into believing it has an unusually strong jaw or stomach.

K1725.r: The man says, “St. George’s dogs are coming!” The ogre flees. Type 1150; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 148; West Indies: Flowers 543f.
K1725.p: A trick in which wolves are called 'St. George's dogs,' so that other animals are frightened by a supposed powerful guardian pack.

K1725.1.p: An ox tells a jackal that dogs are chasing him, when the sound he hears is really water gurgling in the ox's stomach.

K1725.2.p: A tiger hears the sound of water dripping and thinks it is a dreadful monster, so it flees.

K1726.p: A giantess is afraid to leave her cave because of a statue of a hero standing in the entrance, which she mistakes for a real man.

K1727.p: A tiger is frightened by an unknown wind sound and runs away from it.

K1728.r: Ogre is overawed. *Type 1161; **Taylor MPh XVII 305ff.; **Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 33ff.; Christiansen “Kjætten paa D[ö]vre” Videnskapsselskapets Skrifter 2 kl. (1922) No. 6; *Fb “hund” I 678b; Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 434ff., (1928) 291—92; Scotland: Baughman.
K1728.p: A hero drives an ogre away with his bear; the next year the ogre asks whether the big cat is still alive, and the hero says it now has many kittens.

K1732.p: A boy gets rid of a troll by agreeing to take as wages as much as he can carry, then points out that the troll's load would be even larger, so the troll gives up.

K1733.p: A hero escapes from a room that is then burned, and when the ogre returns he finds the hero sitting calmly in the ashes, saying it was a bit hot. The ogre is convinced the hero has withstood fire and is frightened.

K1733.1.p: A giant is persuaded that the hero punched a hole through a wall with his bare hand, when in fact the hole had been bored beforehand.

K1735.p: A dog barks and pretends that he is only answering a dog who lives in the moon, so the listener is fooled into thinking his barking is something grander.

K1736.r: *Type 1165; Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, German, Finnish, Estonian, Livonian, Latvian, Lithuanian: *Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 137—161.
K1736.p: A troll is tricked into staying away from a christening: he is invited but told the other guests include the Virgin Mary and Thor the Thunderer. He stays away but sends the finest present.

K1741.p: The hero boasts that he can do a far bigger job than the one he was assigned, which frightens the ogre into giving in.

K1741.1.r: *Type 1049; *BP III 333; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—167; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1741.1.p: Told to bring in a tree, the hero asks why not the whole forest, and the ogre is frightened by the suggestion.

K1741.1.1.p: Told to bring home a tree, the hero plans to bring home six instead, bluffing about how much more he can carry.

K1741.2.p: Told to shoot one or two wild boars, the hero asks why not shoot a thousand with one shot, and the ogre is frightened.

K1741.2.1.p: Told to bring home one ox, the hero plans to bring home ten instead, bluffing about his strength.

K1741.3.r: Type 1049; *BP III 333; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 163—167.
K1741.3.p: Told to get water, the hero demands a bucket large enough to bring in the whole well, and the ogre is frightened.

K1741.3.1.p: Told to bring water in an ox skin, the hero plans to dig a canal instead, bluffing about the scale of his work.

K1741.4.p: A wrestler claims he could even carry away a mountain, boasting of strength far beyond the task at hand.

K1744.r: *Types 1045, 1650; Spanish: Espinosa Nos. 163—167; Missouri French: Carrière.
K1744.p: The hero threatens to pull a lake together with a rope, and the ogre is intimidated by the threat.

K1745.p: The hero threatens to haul away a warehouse with a rope, and the ogre is intimidated by the threat.

K1746.p: A trickster threatens to throw his weight into a cloud, and the ogre is intimidated by the boast.

K1755.r: He flees. *Type 1159; *BP II 530 n. 3. Cf. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1154*, 1164C*.
K1755.p: An ogre who was once caught in a vise is terrified when a man's wife stands on her head, and he mistakes her legs for a vise.

K1755.1.p: A man frightens a bear away by threatening to split its skull with his penis. A woman the bear meets shows it a scar from a similar injury, which is only partly healed.

K1756.p: To save the king's daughter from an ogre, an iron man is forged, and the ogre is terrified of it.

K1760.p: A category of other tricks in which a character bluffs to deceive someone, not covered by the more specific bluff types.

K1761.r: *Type 1612; N. A. Indian (Maliseet): Speck JAFL XXX 482 No. 7; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 190.
K1761.p: In a swimming contest from a ship, the hero straps a knapsack of provisions on his back, and his rival, frightened by this, gives up.

K1762.r: *Type 1611; N. A. Indian (Maliseet): Speck JAFL XXX 482 No. 7; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 190.
K1762.p: A trickster who cannot really climb a mast pretends to be an expert climber by challenging the sailors to do the same, and they accept him as skilled.

K1765.p: A poor man bluffs his way out of a court sentence by pretending to carry money: he keeps a stone in his purse to throw at the judge, and the judge, assuming he can bribe him, lets him go free.

K1766.p: A trickster frightens a stronger rival out of a contest simply by boasting about his own strength or deeds.

K1766.1.p: A trickster falsely claims he killed his foster-brother, and his men, impressed by such a fierce deed, follow him.

K1767.p: A goat sings a threatening song, and the threatened person buys it off with food and jewels instead of fighting.

K1771.p: A trickster makes a threat he does not intend to carry out, bluffing an opponent into backing down.

K1771.1.r: “I am glad, for I don’t like that kind of jesting.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 219 No. 450.
K1771.1.p: A man asks someone who has brushed against him whether he did it in earnest or in jest, and when the answer is "in earnest" the man's bluff of a challenge makes the other back down.

K1771.2.r: ... or. “Either you give me the road or I (will give it to you, or the like).” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 21ff. No. 450; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1564*.
K1771.2.p: A sham threat in which the bluffer offers the other person a choice between two outcomes, both of which are meant to frighten him.

K1771.3.r: Beggar says, “If you do not give me alms I shall have to do something I have never done before.” The alms are given and he is asked what he would have had to do. “Work.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 217 No. 450.
K1771.3.p: A bluffer threatens to do something he has never done before, to scare his opponent.

K1771.4.p: Two people who have challenged each other agree to stage a fake duel that looks dangerous but is not real.

K1771.5.p: A man threatens to break another's head, adding that only his status as a philosopher stops him, which is an empty threat.

K1771.6.p: A wife makes a sham threat to keep her jealous husband from going out or from noticing her, until her lover returns.

K1771.7.p: A sham threat of war is used to hold ships back, so that suddenly there are enough men left to crew the defending ship.

K1771.8.p: A man spreads a false dream prophesying that the ship will be wrecked, so people leave and make room for him to board.

K1771.9.p: A king is menaced into giving up his daughter by means of a fleet that is only borrowed, so that it looks like a real threat.

K1772.p: A trickster pretends to be angry in order to get his way.

K1774.p: A king leads his men along by pretending he will make peace with his brothers, when in fact he intends to fight them.

K1775.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 130; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 12 No. 1, (Benga): Nassau 153ff. No. 19, (Yoruba): Ellis 266, (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 88, 151, (Kaffir): Theal 165, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 384 No. 10, 395 No. 18; West Indies: Flowers 545. Cf. Chaucer Nun’s Priest’s Tale lines 343ff.
K1775.p: A trickster makes an insulting remark, but when asked to repeat it he changes the words to something harmless to turn aside anger.

K1776.p: A servant boasts that he has scolded his master, but he says it where the master cannot hear.

K1777.p: When someone looks at the hero too threateningly, the hero pretends he can no longer ride a horse, to avoid a challenge.

K1781.r: Type 804*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 811A*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 804*; Russian: Andrejev No. 804*.
K1781.p: A man threatens to build a church in hell, a bluff that gets him released from hell.

K1782.r: *Penzer V 186 n. 1; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 127 No. 110, Morlini 266 No. 4; Clouston Tales II 360ff.; *Herbert III 421 No. 82; Scala Celi 136b No. 762.
K1782.p: A courtier gains wealth by pretending to be close to the king, collecting bribes from people who think he has influence, though he has asked for nothing costly.

K1783.p: A shoemaker offers to trim the peasant's feet to fit the shoes he has made, and the peasant prefers to keep the ill-fitting shoes rather than lose his feet.

K1784.p: A herdsman bluffs that he will invade with huge herds, and is bought off with bribes from the neighboring peoples who want him to stay away.

K1784.1.p: A trickster falsely reports that his own people are about to invade, and receives money to buy them off.

K1784.2.p: On an otherworld island an adventurer sees great hornless oxen guarded by a giant and tries to frighten them; the giant mocks him and says the calves' mothers are on the other side of a mountain, so he leaves.

K1785.p: A bluffing miracle is said to require a man to be sacrificed first; no one volunteers, and the miracle is never performed.

K1786.p: A host serves many rare vintages and gains a reputation for a great wine cellar, but each vintage is only a small jug.

K1787.p: A man falsely claims he killed an elephant with his bare flat hand.

K1788.p: A fox threatens to catch a bird, and the bird appeases him by feeding him her young; the fox threatens to push down a tree or to fly.

K1791.p: A mock duel is staged so that the people involved will be recognized.

K1792.p: A person feigns not knowing who another is, so that he can speak his frank opinion of that person.

K1792.1.p: A person feigns ignorance of someone's identity so as not to reveal that the person is a king.

K1792.2.p: A person feigns ignorance of where the hero's weapons and horse are, in order to keep the hero in the monastery as a monk.

K1795.p: An illiterate man pretends to weep over a book he is reading, because he cannot get others to understand what it says.

K1796.p: A woman frightens a robber away by telling him that a parrot's cry is her husband's voice.

K1800.p: Deception carried out by disguise or by illusion.

K1810.p: Deception carried out by disguise, in which a character changes his appearance to pass as someone else.

K1810.1.p: A character disguises himself by putting on the clothes or carrying the equipment of a certain person.

K1810.1.1.p: A fool disguises himself by wearing the king's crown.

K1810.1.2.p: A lover disguises himself in the clothes of an enemy he has slain, so he can pass as that man.

K1810.1.3.p: A person takes a king's place by swapping clothes with him, so that the substitute is taken for the king.

K1810.2.p: A dog gets a disguise from a magician so that it can frighten a tiger.

K1810.3.p: A lover disguises himself as another knight so that he can get close to his sweetheart.

K1811.r: *Types 330A, 750A, 751, 752A, 753, 768, 785, 791; *BP II 210, III 198, 451; *Dh II 129; *Rohde Der Griechische Roman 451 n.; Fb “Sankt Peder” III 164a; United States (Mormon): **Lee, Hector, “The Three Nephites: the Substance and Significance of the Legend in Folklore” (Albuquerque, 1949), “The Three Nephites: a Disappearing Legend” Am. Notes and Queries II 35—38, Hand, “The Three Nephites” Am. Notes and Queries II 56—57, Fife, “The Legend of the Three Nephites among the Mormons” JAFL LIII 1—49; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 22, Beal XXI 307, *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 80, *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “Pierre”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 200, Grote I 36, 63, 88, 103, 160; Jewish: *Neuman, *bin Gorion Born Judas I 176f., 374; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Tawney I 370; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 19, 318, 473, 477, 648, 840, II 471, 504, 519, 572, 602, 1079, 1182, 1258, 1353, 1366; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 1f., 169; Japanese: Ikeda; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 69; S. A. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 316, (Chamacoso): Métraux MAFLS XL 28, (Huaroichiri): ibid. 158; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 177; West Indies: Flowers 545.
K1811.p: Gods or saints appear among people in disguise, visiting mortals while hiding who they really are.

K1811.0.1.p: A mortal gives hospitality to a god who is visiting in disguise, not knowing who the guest is.

K1811.0.2.p: A goddess or saint travels to earth disguised as a human and is captured by robbers, who release her after she promises to reveal the future of a newborn prince.

K1811.1.r: Test hospitality. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 770*, 930A*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1811.1.p: A god or spirit comes to people disguised as a beggar.

K1811.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 776; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1811.2.p: A deity visits mortals disguised as an old man or an old woman.

K1811.3.p: A god disguised as a doctor comes to cure a mortal.

K1811.4.p: A deity takes the form of a particular person in order to visit mortals.

K1811.4.1.p: Fate takes the form of a Brahmin's pupil to lure a man to the death that was prophesied for him.

K1811.4.2.p: An angel takes the form of a certain person.

K1811.5.p: A deity takes the form of an animal in order to visit mortals.

K1812.r: *Chauvin VI 45 No. 209; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 95.
K1812.p: A king travels or acts in disguise, hiding his royal identity from others.

K1812.0.1.p: A king who is in disguise is beaten by his own men, who do not recognize him.

K1812.1.r: Gives reward. Type 952; *BP III 450; Child V 67; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1812.1.p: A king travelling incognito is helped by a humble man.

K1812.1.1.p: An incognito king is asked for help by a humble man, who does not know who he is.

K1812.2.r: *Type 951; *BP III 393, 450; Penzer II 184f. n., VII 215ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: Boberg.
K1812.2.p: An incognito king joins a band of robbers.

K1812.2.1.p: An incognito king joins robbers and is told to take only six shillings, since the king has so many robbers already.

K1812.2.2.p: An incognito prince joins a band of gamblers, is beaten for showing courtesy, and returns home after realizing his folly.

K1812.3.p: A prince disguises himself as another prince in order to woo a princess.

K1812.4.p: A king travels in disguise and is taken in as a guest by a fisherman. Later the king reveals who he is and rewards his host with a city.

K1812.5.p: A king in disguise goes to the court of the man who defeated him, unrecognized, and is received there.

K1812.6.p: A ruler dresses up as a goblin or demon to scare a priest who is too fond of his wife.

K1812.7.p: A king disguises himself as an ordinary soldier and is killed in battle, which fulfills a prophecy that guarantees his side's victory.

K1812.8.p: A queen or princess travels incognito, hiding her royal identity.

K1812.8.1.p: A queen escapes her husband's persecution by disguising herself as a knight.

K1812.8.2.p: A princess travels disguised as a bishop or monk.

K1812.8.3.r: (Cf. H1187.) Köhler-Bolte II 647ff.; Liungman Två Folkminnesundersökningar 25 n. 1.
K1812.8.3.p: A queen visits her husband in disguise and bears a child by him as had been arranged.

K1812.9.p: A king in disguise rewards a farmer who has given him a gift.

K1812.10.p: A king escapes from a battle by disguising himself as a peasant.

K1812.11.p: A prince, or a king while still unrecognized, is sold into slavery while travelling incognito.

K1812.12.p: A king in disguise comes to help an enemy who earlier refused to speak ill of him.

K1812.13.p: A king travelling in disguise rewards strangers who treat him as an equal companion.

K1812.14.p: A lecherous prince disguises himself as a merchant in order to kill his grandchildren.

K1812.14.1.p: The prince disguised as a merchant is given hospitality by the enemy he intends to harm.

K1843.2.1.p: A wife takes her husband's mistress's place in his bed, and the husband then sends a message that she is dead.

K1843.2.2.p: A wife takes her husband's mistress's place in bed, but the husband has already tired of the mistress and had earlier put a servant there, so the wife is tricked in turn.

K1843.2.3.p: A wife takes her husband's mistress's place in his bed, and the husband, not knowing of the switch, invites his friends to share his good fortune.

K1843.2.4.p: A wife takes her place in bed with her husband, who is a sodomite, in order to satisfy him.

K1843.3.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1843.3.p: A wife puts an old woman in her place in her husband's bed.

K1843.4.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 35; B[ö]dker Exempler 280 No. 24; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1843.4.p: A wife has a maidservant pretend to be her while she secretly goes to meet her lover.

K1844.p: A husband tricks his wife by sending another person to sleep in her bed in his place.

K1844.1.p: A husband sends his strong servant to lie in his bed in his place, tricking his supernaturally strong wife, who is about to kill her husband.

K1844.1.1.r: Instructions are not followed. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1844.1.1.p: A husband has his servant take his place in bed, instructing him not to reveal the deception while the husband visits his mistress.

K1844.2.p: A substitute bridegroom takes the place of the husband on the wedding night to save him from a poison maiden.

K1844.3.p: A groom secretly swaps in a substitute in bed and hides himself so he can learn the secret his bride has promised to reveal.

K1844.4.p: A fairy takes the form of a queen's husband, visits her in bed, and fathers a son with her.

K1845.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 65 (Cuchulainn), *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; N. A. Indian (Mandan): Will JAFL XXIX 402; West Indies: Flowers 547.
K1845.p: A person is put in place of a warrior or leader in battle, so that the real one can avoid danger.

K1845.1.p: A warrior is tricked into attacking a stone pillar that has been dressed in the enemy's clothing and crown, mistaking it for the enemy.

K1845.2.r: Follower is killed. Irish myth: Cross.
K1845.2.p: A king who fears being killed by an enemy forces a follower to take his place on the throne.

K1846.p: A drunken husband wants to catch and beat a beggar, but his wife tricks him by substituting a calf for the beggar.

K1847.p: Children are secretly swapped with other children to deceive others about who the true heirs are.

K1847.1.p: Children are swapped so that a person can gain an inheritance by fraud.

K1847.1.1.p: A queen tells an anxious king that she will bear a son, but warns that harm will come to the child if the king looks upon him, so the birth can be faked.

K1848.p: A person secretly arranges for someone else to perform a required task or test in place of the one who was supposed to do it.

K1848.1.p: An impotent husband gets a substitute to pass the virility test, so his wife is deceived into thinking he is capable.

K1848.2.p: A ruler has a favorite perform the tasks required to win a bride, so that the ruler himself can win her.

K1848.3.p: A substitute is sent to carry out a quest in place of the person who was supposed to undertake it.

K1851.p: A letter is secretly changed on the way to its destination so that the message it carries is falsified.

K1851.1.p: A forged letter has the name of the god of death replaced by another name, altering the order it carries.

K1852.p: A sleeping potion is secretly swapped in for a poison, so the intended victim is only put to sleep.

K1853.p: A sacrifice is replaced by a substitute, so the intended victim is spared.

K1853.1.p: A trickster swaps an animal in for the human intended as a sacrifice, so the substitute animal is offered instead of the person.

K1853.2.p: Someone takes the place of a person who was to be sacrificed, so the intended victim is spared.

K1853.2.1.p: A hero takes the place of a princess who was to be given as a gift to a monster, so she is saved and he goes instead.

K1854.p: A servant pretends to be his dead master and makes a false will in the master's name.

K1854.1.p: A rascal lies in a dead man's place in bed and makes the dead man's will, passing himself off as the deceased.

K1855.p: A mother secretly substitutes her younger, favored son for the elder so that the father is deceived into giving him the blessing or inheritance.

K1858.p: A different specimen is substituted for the sample that is supposed to be tested in a laboratory, so the test result is false.

K1858.1.p: A substitute urine sample is handed in for the one to be analyzed, so the urinalysis gives a false result.

K1858.2.p: A substitute blood sample is given in place of the person's own for a blood test, so the result is false.

K1860.p: A person deceives others by pretending to be dead or asleep, lying still so that they appear lifeless.

K1861.r: India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 35; Africa (Bayaka): Johnson Grenfell 823.
K1861.p: A person pretends to be dead so that others will carry them somewhere they want to go.

K1861.1.r: Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 61; BP III 412 n. 1, IV 171; Basset Contes Berbères No. 13; Turkish: Giese Türkische Märchen 131; Africa (Swahili): Steere 351.
K1861.1.p: A hero sews himself into an animal hide and pretends to be dead, so a bird carries him up to a great height.

K1862.p: A person fakes their own death in order to meet their lover.

K1863.p: A person pretends to be dead in order to find out how soldiers are brought back to life.

K1864.p: A person spreads word of their own death so they can leave secretly without anyone noticing.

K1864.1.p: A person falsely reports another man's death in order to win that man's bride.

K1865.p: A person fakes a death to build up the reputation of a false relic.

K1866.p: A person pretends to be dead in order to get into the land of the dead.

K1867.p: A trickster pretends to be dead and then eats the food and offerings left on graves.

K1867.1.p: A trickster pretends to be dead and then eats the ripe fruit from a tree.

K1867.2.p: A trickster pretends to be dead and then eats the food left as offerings on a grave. The trick lets him feed while his victims think he is a corpse.

K1868.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 406; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 382.
K1868.p: A character deceives others by pretending to be asleep, so they let their guard down or reveal something.

K1870.p: A general heading for deceptions that create false appearances, such as tricks of the eye or fake scenes.

K1871.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 60, *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1871.p: A deception carried out by sleight of hand, quick tricks with the hands that make something seem to happen when it does not.

K1871.1.p: A trick in which someone appears to climb a silk thread thrown up into the air, which is really an illusion.

K1871.2.p: A fake healing in which the healer pretends to pull a foreign object out of the sick person's body, when in fact he has hidden it in his hand.

K1872.p: A general heading for disguising something so it is not seen for what it is, by hiding it or making it blend into its surroundings.

K1872.1.r: Surprises enemy. Each soldier carries branches. (Birnam wood comes to Dunsinane.) *Fb “skov” III 300a; Shakespeare’s Macbeth; Rohde Der griechische Roman 485; Grimm Kleinere Schriften V 43; Herrmann Saxo II 341, 498; Kurth Histoire poetique des Merovingiens 396ff.; Irish myth: *Cross.
K1872.1.p: An army is disguised so that from a distance it looks like a forest, hiding its real numbers and position.

K1872.2.p: Ships are hidden among reeds so that they look like an island from a distance.

K1872.3.p: A love letter is concealed inside an apple so that it is not noticed.

K1872.4.p: A wounded person hides his own wound by covering it with another wound, so that he will not be recognized.

K1872.5.p: The colorful banners of an army look like a flock of many-colored birds from a distance, hiding the soldiers.

K1872.5.1.p: Clods of earth kicked up by horses' hooves look like a flock of birds, disguising the riders' movement.

K1875.r: *Types 3, 1535, 1539; *BP II 1ff., 10ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 287; West Indies: Flowers 547.
K1875.p: A trickster makes a victim believe he is bleeding by stabbing a bag of blood, or by some other means, so that the victim thinks he is badly hurt.

K1881.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 246 s.v. “Doppelgänger”; Icelandic: FSS 38, Boberg; Irish: Plummer clxix, *Cross; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn VI (1900) 3ff.
K1881.p: A deception in which an absent person appears to be present, created by an illusion.

K1883.p: A general heading for illusions in which people see enemies that are not really there.

K1883.1.p: An attack is made on a phantom army that does not actually exist, created by illusion.

K1883.2.r: Irish: *Cross, Plummer clxix; Icelandic: *Krappe Études 131, *Boberg; Maori: Beckwith Myth 398. Cf. Sophocles’s Ajax, Cervantes’ Don Quixote.
K1883.2.p: Animals are attacked in the belief that they are men, because of an illusion.

K1883.3.p: Two soldiers, each thinking the other is a common enemy, kill each other.

K1883.4.p: Attackers are magically made to believe that a stone is their enemy, and they strike at it; in the note, they behead it.

K1883.5.p: A comrade is killed by mistake because the killer believes he is an enemy.

K1883.6.p: A man made invisible eats someone's bread, and the two people he is tricking end up quarreling, each believing the other ate it.

K1883.7.p: A trickster uses a mirror reflection to make his victim believe he is a captive of the trickster.

K1883.8.p: Images are arranged so that they look like guards keeping watch, fooling people into thinking a place is guarded.

K1883.9.p: A hero changes costumes so many times that people think many different men are present, believing he is an entire army.

K1884.p: Someone is made to seem dead when they are not, through a trick or illusion.

K1885.p: A dead person is made to appear alive again through a trick.

K1885.1.p: A lit sponge placed in a dead person's mouth produces smoke that makes it look as if the corpse is breathing.

K1886.p: Deceptive appearances in the natural landscape that mislead travelers.

K1886.1.p: A mirage: a false image of water or land seen in the distance, especially in deserts.

K1886.1.1.p: Someone follows a glowing tree in the desert that is an illusion and leads them astray.

K1886.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “brume”.
K1886.2.p: Mists or fogs that magically lead people astray and make them lose their way.

K1886.2.1.p: Magic makes enemies lose sight of each other while they are hunting, so they cannot find one another.

K1886.3.r: Is caught. Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV(1) 6 n. 1.
K1886.3.p: A false sunrise is created to deceive, and the agreed deadline is treated as passed; a wolf makes a fire to imitate dawn.

K1886.3.1.r: Marquesas: Handy 32, 109; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 516; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1146, T-G. 1/78); Tahiti: Henry 589; Tonga: Gifford 90, 144.
K1886.3.1.p: A person makes a rooster crow to imitate the cock crow of dawn, fooling others into thinking morning has come.

K1886.3.2.p: A victim is made to believe that a person's bare buttocks shown to them are the rising sun.

K1886.3.3.p: A false sunrise makes supernatural thieves drop their loot and run away.

K1886.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 411), 123 (ST 323); Halm Aesop No. 310.
K1886.4.p: Travelers mistake brushwood seen at a distance for a ship.

K1886.5.p: Companions are separated by an illusory city that appears to them, so they cannot find each other.

K1886.6.p: Illusory images of animals are made to appear on hilltops.

K1886.7.p: A hill or mountain that is only an illusion and does not really exist.

K1886.7.1.p: The Tuatha Dé Danann make an island look like a hog's back, a long ridge seen from afar, so it seems to be a hill rather than land. The island is an illusion created by supernatural beings.

K1887.p: Supernatural beings create sounds that are not really there, fooling listeners.

K1887.1.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 172; Greek: Pauly-Wissowa s.v. “Echo”; Chinese: Graham.
K1887.1.p: A voice repeats or answers a person as an echo, but the answer is actually a deception made by a supernatural being.

K1887.2.p: At night, spirits of the woods make noises that imitate trees falling and similar sounds, to frighten or mislead people.

K1887.3.p: Fairies make a sound seem to come from several directions at once, so a listener cannot tell where it is really coming from.

K1887.3.1.p: A saint's bell is heard ringing, but when people search for it, it is never found, because it is an illusion.

K1888.p: A light appears that is not real, a false or illusory glow created by supernatural means.

K1889.p: A miscellaneous group of other magical illusions and deceptions that do not fit the more specific categories.

K1889.1.p: A house appears to be on fire when it is not, an illusion meant to alarm or deceive people.

K1889.2.p: A man is told he can only be cured by his own child's blood. He is tricked into believing the child has been killed, and when he learns the child is alive, his overwhelming joy cures him.

K1889.3.p: Victims are given a drug and led into what they believe is Paradise, a false heaven. Afterward they are made to rob and kill to earn their way back in, and may die trying. The note links this to the Old Man of the Mountain.

K1889.4.p: Food or drink that is harmful tastes deceptively sweet, so people consume it without realizing the danger.

K1889.5.p: Night or darkness is created as an illusion, so it seems to be night when it is not.

K1889.6.p: A palace seems to float on water, but it is really made of glass, so the illusion fools the viewer.

K1890.p: Other deceptions made through disguise or illusion that are not covered by the more specific motifs above.

K1892.p: A trickster or other character deceives others by hiding, concealing themselves in a container or under something.

K1892.1.r: Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 34 No. 15, DeVries’s list No. 294.
K1892.1.p: A trickster hides inside a bag so that he can be carried by someone. His father copies the trick and is beaten for it.

K1892.1.1.r: Africa (Western Sudan): Frobenius Atlantis VIII 145ff. No. 81.
K1892.1.1.p: A trickster hides inside a box so that he can be carried by someone.

K1892.1.2.p: A trickster hides inside a basket and is carried away by someone.

K1892.2.p: A girl hides her lover under the clothing she is sitting on, concealing him from others.

K1894.p: A trickster fakes evidence of bad weather by dipping a cloak in water and showing it as proof that a storm has passed.

K1900.p: A general heading for tales of impostors who pretend to be someone they are not in order to deceive others.

K1910.p: A heading for tales in which someone poses as a spouse, taking a husband's or wife's place in marriage.

K1911.r: *Types 403, 408, 425, 450, 480, 510, 511, 533; Tegethoff 20; *BP I 79ff.; *Huet RTP XXII 1ff.; **Arfert Das Motiv von der unterschobenen Braut (Rostock, 1897); *M. Potanine Vostotchnye Motivy v srednevekom evropeiskom Epose (Moscow, 1899—see RTP XXII 8 n. 2); *Godden FL IV 142, 143 n. 1; *Hepding Hessische Blätter fur Volkskunde V 161; Cox 478, 501; *Cosquin Contes indiens 61ff.; Penzer VI 47 n. 1, 48, VIII 12ff., IX 55ff.; *Fb “brud” IV 64b.—French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 22, Sister Marie Ursule; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 61, 82 Nos. 445B*, 708A*; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Int., III No. 10, V No. 9; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham, Eberhard FFC CXX 47f.; Korean: Zong in-Sob 48 No. 28; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 177; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 350 nn. 262, 265; Africa: Werner African 230, (Zulu): Callaway 75, 85, (Kaffir): Theal 67, (Bushman): Bleek and Lloyd 85ff.
K1911.p: An impostor secretly takes the place of a wife without the husband knowing, and then sends the real wife away or kills or transforms her.

K1911.1.p: A heading for the different ways a false bride is substituted for the true one.

K1911.1.1.r: *Arfert Unterschobene Braut; *Type 533; **Liungman Två Folkminnesundersökningar 41ff.; Cosquin Contes indiens 69ff.; BP II 273; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 113; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 403D*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 403D*; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 178; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 118, 303, 313, (Kaffir): Theal 134, 145f., (Thonga): Junod 231, (Fjort): Dennett 128; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 266 No. 74.
K1911.1.1.p: On the way to the wedding, a false bride takes the place of the true bride.

K1911.1.2.r: *Types 403, 450, 480; *BP I 79ff., 99ff., II 284 n. 2; *Arfert Unterschobene Braut; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 383ff.
K1911.1.2.p: A false bride takes the true bride's place when the true bride gives birth to a child.

K1911.1.3.r: *Type 408; *Arfert Unterschobene Braut; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 120f., Espinosa Jr. Nos. 106—110; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1911.1.3.p: While the husband has left the true bride alone for a short time at a fountain, a false bride takes her place, and the impostor transforms her.

K1911.1.4.r: *Arfert Unterschobene Braut; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 446*; Russian: Andrejev No. 533B*; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 35, 43.
K1911.1.4.p: The true bride must complete a task to win her husband, and when she is exhausted she hands it to a servant, who then takes her place as the bride.

K1911.1.5.p: An old woman is put into the bridegroom's bed in place of the bride.

K1911.1.5.1.p: A man passes off his elder daughter as the younger one on the wedding night, so the groom receives the wrong bride.

K1911.1.6.p: A she-bear takes the place of the bride, and forces the true bride to swap places with her.

K1911.1.7.p: A ghost ogress pushes the bride into a hole in a tree and takes her place.

K1911.1.8.r: Africa (Hottentot): Karutz Des schwarzen Menschen Märchenweisheit (London, 1929) 140f. No. 27.
K1911.1.8.p: A false bride steals the true bride's clothes while she is bathing.

K1911.1.8.1.p: The false bride makes the child cry and demand its mother's clothes and ornaments, so that she can keep the mother's place.

K1911.1.9.p: A prince replaces the king's daughter, whom he was to bring to his father, with a peasant girl, because he has fallen in love with the princess himself.

K1911.1.10.p: An impostor kills a fairy, hides the body, and puts on the fairy's clothes to pass as her.

K1911.2.p: A heading for the ways the false bride treacherously gets rid of the true bride.

K1911.2.1.r: *Type 403, 450; *BP I 79ff., 99ff.; *Fb “and” IV 12b; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 120f., Espinosa Jr. Nos. 80, 106—110; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 383ff.; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 119.
K1911.2.1.p: The false bride transforms the true bride into something else.

K1911.2.2.p: The false bride pushes the true bride into water.

K1911.2.2.1.p: A false bride pushes the true bride into a river or lake, and she survives living inside a fish's belly.

K1911.2.2.2.p: A false bride pushes the true bride into a river, and she is found sitting at the bottom of the water spinning thread.

K1911.2.3.p: A false bride throws away the true bride's newborn children at birth, so the true bride is blamed or lost.

K1911.3.p: The true bride is restored to her rightful place as wife after the false bride has been exposed.

K1911.3.1.r: *Type 707; Köhler-Bolte I 277; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 67 No. 510, Espinosa II No. 113; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1911.3.1.p: An animal reveals that the bride who has taken the true wife's place is a substitute.

K1911.3.1.1.p: The true bride, who has been turned into an animal, shows her true identity in that animal form and reveals the substitution.

K1911.3.2.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 70, 74; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Int.; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1911.3.2.p: The true bride settles in a house near her husband, and so eventually gets his attention.

K1911.3.3.r: *Type 510; *Cox passim; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 22f.; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 122, 315, (Angola): Chatelain 43.
K1911.3.3.p: The husband tests the bride, for example by fitting her with a slipper or having her jump, and the false bride fails the test.

K1911.3.3.1.r: She is detected. *Type 510; *Cox 1—79, 87—121 passim; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 111f., Espinosa Jr. No. 119; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1911.3.3.1.p: To fit the shoe used in the husband's test, the false bride cuts off part of her own feet, which exposes her.

K1911.3.3.2.p: A magician tests the bride, and the false bride fails the test.

K1911.3.4.p: The true bride, reborn as a reed, reveals the truth about the false bride.

K1911.3.5.r: Africa (Hottentot): Karutz Des schwarzen Menschen Märchenweisheit (London, 1929) 140f. No. 27.
K1911.3.5.p: The true bride is restored by working as a mysterious housekeeper in her husband's home.

K1911.3.6.p: A snake takes in the true bride after she is thrown into a well, and cares for her.

K1911.4.p: A man dressed in women's clothing poses as a bride to be married to a beggar.

K1911.5.r: Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 120f.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1911.5.p: A bride with no money pretends to be wealthy.

K1912.p: A bride who is not a virgin uses various tricks to make others believe she is one.

K1914.p: A man who abducts a princess claims that her lover sent him to fetch her.

K1915.r: Penzer IX 55; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 329 n. 189; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 181ff.
K1915.p: A false bridegroom takes the place of the true bridegroom.

K1915.1.p: A monk becomes husband to a girl at night so that his friend can get the dowry.

K1915.2.p: Through a saint's power, a man is given his lover's form and sleeps with the princess; the lover had plotted the saint's death but was accidentally killed in the saint's place.

K1915.3.p: A handsome man secretly takes the place of an ugly intended bridegroom at the wedding and so wins the bride.

K1916.p: A robber poses as a fine gentleman to win a girl's hand in marriage.

K1917.p: A poor man pretends to be wealthy in order to win a bride.

K1917.1.r: She looks at the land; he points to the patch on his clothes. “That patch is mine.” *BP II 203.
K1917.1.p: A poor suitor claims to own a patch of land and, after the wedding, takes his bride to see it, dressed in shabby clothes.

K1917.2.p: A poor boy has an uncle lend him a coin and food to hold while the uncle woos for him, and the uncle tells the girl's father that the boy has money and plenty to eat.

K1917.3.p: A poor suitor's helpful animal reports to the girl that its master is wealthy, and so she agrees to marry him.

K1917.4.p: A poor wooer lies about his grand home, which he describes as having many lights and a goat pen; when a servant overhears and repeats it, the master marries his daughter to him, and the suitor explains the lights are stars shining through roof cracks and the single goat is tied to a tree.

K1917.5.p: A man wins a girl's love by pretending to be rich and noble, but the deception is discovered and he is banished.

K1917.6.r: Theft of gems. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1917.6.p: A suitor wins a girl by means of forged papers vouching for his wealth or standing.

K1917.7.p: A suitor strokes his whiskers and says all the land around them belongs to him, and the girl takes him to mean the fields and livestock they are passing.

K1917.8.p: A slave pretends to be a treasurer's son and carries a letter asking for a merchant's daughter's hand in marriage.

K1918.r: Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 273 No. 85; West Indies: Flowers 548.
K1918.p: A monster disguises itself and wins a girl by borrowing wedding garments one at a time, then returns them one by one and reveals its true monstrous form.

K1918.1.p: An ugly fish borrows the skin of a handsome fish to court and marry.

K1918.1.1.p: An ogre fools a widow by taking the form of her dead husband.

K1919.p: Miscellaneous tricks in which someone poses as a spouse to deceive a marriage partner.

K1919.1.p: A husband pretends to be his wife's brother in order to deceive others.

K1920.p: Children are secretly swapped for other children, so that each family raises someone else's child.

K1921.p: Parents secretly exchange their own children with one another.

K1921.1.p: The son of a king and the son of a smith are secretly exchanged, so each is raised in the other's household.

K1921.2.p: Two mothers swap their children, a boy and a girl, so each raises the other's child.

K1921.3.p: A queen swaps her own ugly twins for a slave's handsome son, so the slave's child is raised in her place. Later she recognizes the better character of the twins and switches them back.

K1922.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 46 n. 1.
K1922.p: A woman secretly replaces her own child with another baby and sells the child she was given. The two swap sleeping places to conceal the trick.

K1923.p: A person falsely presented as the rightful heir to a title, property, or throne, using a substituted child or other trick.

K1923.1.p: A nurse swaps children so that the child she favors will grow up rich and inherit wealth.

K1923.2.p: A man is tricked into believing his married daughter has given birth, when the child is actually a foundling. After the supposed mother dies, the father stands to lose the dowry when the child's real parents appear and claim him.

K1923.3.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 68; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 101.
K1923.3.p: A barren woman pretends to have given birth and passes off another woman's child as her own.

K1923.4.p: A woman falsely claims to be the mother of a child who has been chosen to become king.

K1923.5.p: A midwife takes a baby and substitutes it for the king's stillborn child, so the king has an heir.

K1923.6.p: A queen passes off a baby girl as a boy by having priests declare that the raja must not see his son for twelve years, so no one can check the child's sex.

K1924.p: A barren wife creates a child through magic and claims it as her own.

K1926.p: A false daughter is accepted as a child who has been restored to life after death, when she is really an impostor.

K1930.p: Impostors who betray and deceive their own companions, usually to take credit or position for themselves.

K1931.p: Impostors abandon or kill their companion and take his place, claiming his deeds or rewards.

K1931.1.r: *Type 506; **Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte; *BP III 490ff., 494; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 133—135; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 404ff.; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 284 No. 119.
K1931.1.p: Impostors throw the hero overboard into the sea.

K1931.1.1.p: An impostor tries to push his foster brother into the water, then cuts the rope so the brother drifts alone out to sea in a boat with no oars.

K1931.2.r: *Type 301; *BP II 301; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 53 No. 400B*; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1931.2.p: Impostors leave the hero stranded in the lower world, usually by letting go of the rope that was to haul him up.

K1931.3.p: Impostors kill the hero and take his place.

K1931.4.r: *Types 550, 551; *BP I 503ff., II 394ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 143.
K1931.4.p: Impostors throw the hero into a pit.

K1931.5.p: Impostors throw the hero into prison and take his place.

K1931.6.p: An impostor leaves the hero alone on an island and takes his place.

K1931.7.p: A treacherous impostor takes the hero's place and leaves him stranded on a high hill by pulling up the rope he was to be lowered down on. The impostor then claims the hero's place and rewards.

K1932.r: *Types 300, 301, 303, 506, 550, 551, 667*; *BP I 528ff., III 490ff.; *Ranke FFC CXIV 213f., 236; Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte; *Parsons FL XXXII 194ff.; *Tille FFC XXXIV 370; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 327 n. 183; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 278 Nos. 89, 90.
K1932.p: Impostors falsely claim the prize or reward that the hero actually earned.

K1933.r: *Types 300, 301, 533; *BP II 273ff., 284 n. 1; Icelandic: Göngu Hrólfs saga (FAS III) 274ff.; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 139, 151, 157.
K1933.p: An impostor makes the hero or heroine swear an oath never to reveal the deception.

K1934.p: An impostor forces the hero or heroine to swap places with him or her, taking their identity.

K1934.1.p: A magician or demon takes the king's place by swapping places with him, and is later exposed when the women of the harem recognize he is not the real king, so the true king is restored.

K1935.p: Impostors steal a princess who was rescued from danger, claiming the rescue for themselves.

K1935.1.p: The impostors who stole the rescued princess are exposed by a girl at the princess's wedding.

K1936.p: An impostor falsely claims to be the father of a princess's child.

K1937.p: An impostor pretends to be a dead count, taking on his identity.

K1938.p: A rascal pretends to be the heir of a dead man and collects money for it.

K1941.r: Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 185, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 624; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 351 n. 267; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 2 No. 1, 22 No. 2, 260 No. 38, (Kaffir): Theal 100.
K1941.p: An impostor disguises himself by wearing the skin of his victim, who he has flayed.

K1941.1.p: The disguised flayer tightens the stolen skin so that he looks beautiful.

K1942.p: Impostors are tricked into carrying the hero hidden in a box, because a woman makes them believe they will get her as a reward.

K1944.p: An impostor demands that a box be handed over in the king's name.

K1945.p: Someone fakes an illness to deceive and trick others.

K1945.1.p: A person claims that a sickness can be cured only by the death or humiliation of another person.

K1945.1.1.p: A mother-in-law has her head shaved and face blackened and is led around the city on a donkey, supposedly the only cure for her daughter-in-law's illness.

K1950.p: Pretending to have courage or fighting skill that one does not really possess.

K1951.p: A person falsely passes himself off as a brave warrior.

K1951.1.r: A tailor who has killed seven flies writes on a placard: “Seven at a blow.” He is received as a great warrior. *Type 1640; *BP I 148ff.; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 23; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 194f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 73 No. III; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 51; N. A Indian: *Thompson CColl II 430ff.
K1951.1.p: A boastful man who claims to have killed a fly with a single blow, saying he has killed seven at once.

K1951.1.1.p: A boastful man claims to have killed an elephant with a single blow. The trick works because the elephant has already been poisoned, so the claim is a sham.

K1951.2.r: *Type 1640; *BP I 148ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 430ff.
K1951.2.p: A fake warrior's horse bolts with him into battle. To save himself he grabs a cross from a graveyard and waves it around, and the enemy flees in fright.

K1951.2.1.p: The runaway fake cavalry hero, in his panic, tears the limbs off dead trees, which makes him look like a fierce fighter.

K1951.3.p: A boastful pretender terrifies soldiers merely by bragging about his strength and fighting ability.

K1951.3.1.p: A braggart who intimidates soldiers with his boasting is hired to serve at the palace.

K1951.3.2.p: A tiger is frightened away by the boasting of a sham warrior, who is taken for a brave man.

K1951.4.r: N. A. Indian (Cheyenne): Kroeber JAFL XIII 172. Cf. Falstaff in Shakespeare’s Henry IV part I.
K1951.4.p: A boastful coward is frightened by conspirators who plot against him, showing that his bold talk hides real cowardice.

K1951.5.p: An ordinary man gives himself a grand, impressive name and challenges the enemy chief to single combat. The enemy, believing him to be an exceptionally brave warrior, gives up his attack on the city.

K1952.p: A man pretends to be a prince or nobleman when he is not.

K1952.0.1.p: A Brahmin, a member of the priestly caste, takes on the appearance of a prince to deceive others.

K1952.0.2.p: A servant takes his master's prince's horse and clothes and passes himself off as the prince.

K1952.1.r: This is believed. *Types 545AB; BP I 325ff., III 487; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 4; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1952.1.p: A helpful cat tells a poor boy that he is really a dispossessed prince, and the boy then acts on this claim.

K1952.1.1.r: Type 545; *BP III 487f.; India: Thompson-Balys; East Africa: Rochemonteix Quelques Contes Nubiens (Cairo, 1888) 55ff. No. 5, (Swahili): Steere 13ff.
K1952.1.1.p: A helpful animal tells a poor boy that he is a dispossessed prince. The real person in question is a wealthy man who lost his clothes while swimming after a shipwreck.

K1952.2.p: A poor boy posing as a prince at the king's court always claims that he has better things waiting for him at home.

K1952.3.p: Brothers pose as princes, believing that their real parentage is not good enough for their merit.

K1952.4.p: An impostor claims to be the son of an earl who has been exiled.

K1952.4.1.p: An adventurer poses as the son of a dead king to gain status.

K1952.5.p: A messenger sent to woo a princess poses as the king and suitor himself, but the princess refuses him.

K1952.6.p: An impostor arrives carrying a letter that authorizes him to be placed on the throne.

K1952.7.p: Thieves set up a poor weaver as a prince so that they can collect the tribute and gifts meant for him.

K1953.p: A cowardly man pretends to be brave and daring, fooling others into thinking he is a fearless hero.

K1953.1.p: A coward brags that he has scared off a bear, when in fact his wife killed the bear and he ran away.

K1954.p: A poor man pretends to be wealthy, creating an appearance of riches he does not have.

K1954.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 70 No. 545C*; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1954.1.p: A clever cat secretly borrows a measure of money for its master, so the master seems to be rich and gains a reputation for wealth.

K1954.2.p: A drunken man pretends he wants to buy an elephant, and by doing so convinces the king that he must be rich.

K1955.r: Chauvin II 93 No. 39; BP III 369ff.; B[ö]dker Exempler 289 No. 42; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 126; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 271a; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 17.
K1955.p: A person pretends to be a physician or doctor without real medical skill, fooling patients and collecting fees.

K1955.1.r: *Bédier Fabliaux 476; *Basset 1001 Contes I 382; *Crane Vitry 241 No. 254; Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXVI 89 n. 1; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1955.1.p: A fake doctor cures his patients by threatening them with death, frightening them into recovering. The trick is a sham healing done through intimidation.

K1955.1.1.p: A man promises to cure a fat abbot of a stomach ailment by starving him, until the abbot admits he can eat anything.

K1955.1.2.p: A fake doctor frightens his patients out of their illness by treating them harshly and threatening them with death. The cure comes from the fear, not from real medicine.

K1955.2.r: *Chauvin VIII 106 No. 81; Pierre Faifeu No. 20; Nouvelles Récréations No. 59; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles Nos. 20, 21.
K1955.2.p: A sham physician claims to diagnose a patient's illness entirely from examining urine, when he actually relies on observation and reasoning from small clues.

K1955.2.1.p: A sham doctor uses pepper as a remedy for every illness, and by chance it happens to cure a patient.

K1955.3.p: A sham physician claims to predict whether an unborn child will be a boy or a girl, saying it looks like a boy from one side and a girl from the other. The woman bears twins and the husband pays the doctor.

K1955.4.r: Pierre Faifeu No. 18; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 133 No. 1550A*; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K1955.4.p: A sham physician supposedly treats an ailment by catching a flea, opening its mouth, and placing flea powder inside it.

K1955.5.r: She has grown. Clouston Noodles 102; *Penzer V 91 n. 1.
K1955.5.p: A fake doctor tells a king that his daughter can be made to grow up quickly, claims he must send for medicine, and meanwhile keeps her shut away; after several years she is shown to the king as grown.

K1955.6.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 51 No. 340*; India: *Thompson-Balys; Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 193 n. 1.
K1955.6.p: A fake doctor makes a secret deal with the devil: the devil enters a girl, and the doctor earns a reward for driving him out.

K1955.6.1.p: A cheating demon kills people so that his pupil can revive them and collect the reward for the cure.

K1955.7.p: A sham physician refuses to take the same medicine he prescribes to others, and is found out as a fraud.

K1955.8.p: A sham physician gives a relative a medical degree, making an unqualified person appear to be a real doctor.

K1955.8.1.p: An ignorant young man buys a medical degree and so becomes a doctor without any real learning.

K1955.9.p: An ignorant doctor decides his prescriptions by drawing lots, choosing whichever remedy comes up.

K1955.9.1.p: A sham physician hands out prescriptions at random, without any regard for what the patient actually needs.

K1956.p: A person pretends to be a wise man, faking learning or wisdom to impress and fool others.

K1956.1.r: *Type 1641; BP II 401ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 791; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 79; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1956.1.p: A fake wise man, who is really a charlatan, cures someone with purgative pills and helps find a lost horse, but the pills are what actually get the credit.

K1956.1.1.p: A fake wise man claims he can find stolen goods through magic words or an incantation, when he has really forced the thieves to reveal where the goods are.

K1956.2.r: *Type 1641; BP II 401ff., 413; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 302; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 284 No. 117.
K1956.2.p: A fake wise man hides something himself and then is paid a reward for finding it again.

K1956.2.1.p: A fake wise man secretly sees where a jewel has been hidden and then pretends to find it by magic, collecting a reward.

K1956.3.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 134 No. 1550B*, Espinosa II No. 55; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1956.3.p: A fake wise man announces, as if by supernatural knowledge, that the thieves were robbers.

K1956.4.r: Unmasked. Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 484), 137 (ST 427); Halm Aesop No. 286.
K1956.4.p: A fake wise man, supposedly all-knowing, cannot even find his own house.

K1956.5.p: A fake wise man shuts himself away alone, pretending to study hard, when he is really just killing flies.

K1956.6.p: A fake wise man, working with a girl, pretends to interpret a dream she has claimed to have had, and insists she be allowed to marry the man of her own choice.

K1956.7.p: A fake wise man claims to know something from a dream, when he has really overheard the conversation that gave him the information.

K1956.8.p: A fake wise man burns down the house where he claimed to keep his marvelous books, so that he is never called on again.

K1956.9.p: A fake wise man makes a weather prediction that turns out to be right, purely by accident.

K1956.10.p: A boy pretending to be a magician makes a supposedly all-knowing pig's head shake and move in front of his enemies, so that it seems to identify them as dishonest men.

K1958.r: It is a tax receipt. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 282 No. 332.
K1958.p: A fake teacher pretends to read a document brought to him as if it were a letter.

K1961.p: A fake churchman pretends to be a member of the clergy without really being one.

K1961.1.p: A fake parson or priest, who is not really ordained, poses as a genuine clergyman.

K1961.1.1.p: A peasant disguised as a priest preaches a sermon about the troubles and hardships of ordinary laymen.

K1961.1.2.p: A fake parson gets through his church duties by repeating the same phrase over and over or by saying just a few words of Latin.

K1961.1.2.1.r: *BP III 116; Fb “messe” II 582a; Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 182; Boccaccio Decameron VI No. 10 (Lee 179); *Wesselski Arlotto I 174ff. No. 3; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1835*; Prussian: Plenzat 77; Italian Novella: Rotunda; West Indies: Flowers 549.
K1961.1.2.1.p: A parody sermon: a mock sermon that imitates and ridicules a real one.

K1961.1.3.p: A fake parson secretly saws through the pulpit almost all the way, then predicts a miracle; when he preaches, the pulpit collapses.

K1961.1.4.p: A fake priest convinces a man that he can help him discover buried treasure, and takes his money in the process.

K1961.1.5.p: A fake holy man: a trickster who pretends to be a pious religious figure, such as a parson or priest, in order to deceive others.

K1961.1.5.1.p: A jackal disguises itself as a saint or holy man to fool people and gain something from them.

K1961.2.p: Someone pretends to be the pope, the head of the church, without being entitled to the office.

K1961.2.1.r: (Pope Joan.) *J. J. I. von Döllinger Die Papst-Fabeln des Mittelalters@2 (Stuttgart, 1890) 1—53; same translated by A. Plummer (London, 1871) 273—9; *M. le Comte d’I*** (= Jules Gay) Bibliographie des ouvrages relatif’s à l’amour@3 (Nice and London, 1872) V 419—23; Alphabet No. 601.
K1961.2.1.p: A woman disguises herself as a man and gets herself elected or accepted as pope.

K1961.3.p: The devil takes the form of a monk to deceive people.

K1961.4.p: Someone falsely poses as a bishop, a senior church official, to deceive others.

K1961.5.p: Someone falsely poses as an abbot, the head of a monastery, to deceive others.

K1962.r: *Chauvin V 233 No. 132; Jewish: *Gaster Exempla 191 No. 28, *Neuman; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K1962.p: A person claims to speak for God or receive divine messages without genuine authority, deceiving people with a false prophecy or revelation.

K1962.1.p: Mohammed places seed in his ears so that trained doves come to feed there; he then tells people the birds bring messages from God.

K1963.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 329 n. 189.
K1963.p: A person falsely claims to have magical powers and uses tricks to deceive others into believing in them.

K1963.1.r: *BP III 202; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 51 No. 99; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 137 No. 103.
K1963.1.p: A fake magician is shown to be a fraud by a clever girl who sees through his tricks.

K1963.2.p: A fake magician promises to make someone fall in love using magic; the victim is then frightened, robbed, or otherwise thrown into confusion by the magician or an accomplice.

K1963.3.p: A master pretends to be a magician and plays tricks on his servant to frighten or fool him.

K1963.4.p: A fake magician breathes out fire to frighten the people he is cheating.

K1963.5.p: A trickster pretends to be a necromancer, a sorcerer who raises the dead, in order to seduce the necromancer's wife.

K1963.6.p: A fake magician convinces his wife or her husband that demons can carry them through the air or to other places by magic.

K1964.r: *Wesselski Gonnella 106 No. 9; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
K1964.p: A person falsely poses as an astrologer, claiming to predict the future from the stars, in order to deceive others.

K1965.p: A person falsely poses as a crystal-gazer, claiming to see the future or hidden things in a crystal ball, to deceive others.

K1966.p: A person poses as an alchemist, someone who claims to turn base metals into gold or silver, in order to cheat others.

K1966.1.p: A fake alchemist steals money from a corpse and then claims he has made the silver himself.

K1966.2.p: An alchemist, who claims to have a secret process for making gold, gets paid in advance for revealing it.

K1967.p: A juggler promises to fly from one house to another in front of a crowd, then keeps them waiting until dusk and slips away.

K1968.p: A person falsely pretends to be a great hunter or fisher to impress others.

K1968.1.p: A person buys game or fish and passes it off as his own catch to prove his skill as a hunter or fisher.

K1969.p: Miscellaneous tricks in which a person falsely displays some kind of prowess or power.
