K1969.1.p: A person falsely boasts of having made a long voyage and so receives canoes, which he then takes for himself.

K1969.2.p: A warrior buries oversized armor so that later people will believe soldiers were giants.

K1969.3.p: A servant pretends to be his master, taking on the master's identity.

K1969.3.1.p: A servant hides inside the corpse of his dead master and takes the master's place, so he can pass as the master.

K1969.4.p: A person pretends to be a god or deity.

K1969.4.1.p: A weaver pretends to be a god.

K1970.p: Tricks in which fake miracles are staged to deceive people.

K1971.r: *Type 1380; von der Hagen II 141f. No. 29; Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIX 215; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 239; *Taylor MPh XV 227 n. 1; *BP III 120ff.; *Chauvin II 91 No. 34.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 659; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 272, Coster-Wijsman 25 Nos. 3, 4, 5; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 431, 437; West Indies: Flowers 549—552.
K1971.p: A man hides behind a statue or tree, speaks in its voice, and pretends to be God or a spirit.

K1971.1.r: *Type 1380; *Taylor MPh XV 227 n. 1; Stiefel Zs. f. Vksk. VIII 74ff.; Panchatantra III 18, (tr. Ryder) 370; Russian: Andrejev No. 1380; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1971.1.p: A wife asks her hidden husband, who is speaking from behind a statue, how to fool him; he advises her to feed him well.

K1971.1.1.p: A trickster hides in a hollow tree and eats the food his wife has been persuaded to bring for a bird.

K1971.2.r: Type 1575*; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 203 No. 403; Russian: Andrejev No. 1575*.
K1971.2.p: A man hides behind a tree and threatens his debtor in a divine voice; the debtor, believing God is calling, pays the debt.

K1971.3.p: A boy hides behind a tree and tells a woman, in a divine voice, about the poor food he receives; she believes God is speaking and gives him better food.

K1971.3.1.p: A maid speaks from behind a statue of the Virgin and advises her mistress to give the servants better food.

K1971.4.p: A husband, speaking from behind a saint's statue, advises his wife to spin.

K1971.4.1.r: *Type 1405; BP III 44; *Hdwb. d. Märchens II 148a nn. 381-391.
K1971.4.1.p: A wife, speaking from behind a tree, advises her husband not to make his wife work.

K1971.5.r: Type 1380*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1380A*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1380*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1380*; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 272.
K1971.5.p: A hidden man, speaking from behind a tree or statue as if he were God, forces a wife to confess that she has committed adultery.

K1971.5.1.p: A man hidden behind a tree, pretending to be God, forces a girl to admit she has an illegitimate child. In a variant, he claims to have prophesied that he is the father so that he can marry her.

K1971.6.p: A girl hidden behind a tree, speaking as if she were an angel, gives advice to a suitor who does not want to marry her, and he marries her because he believes the advice comes from heaven.

K1971.6.1.r: Von der Hagen II xv No. 29.
K1971.6.1.p: A wife hidden behind a tree gives her husband advice about his marital duties, speaking as if from a divine source.

K1971.7.p: A man hidden behind a crucifix greets a drunk man with "Good Evening," and the drunk man, believing Christ is speaking to him, takes it as a divine message.

K1971.8.p: A man hidden behind an image gives a suppliant an unwelcome answer, and the image is blamed for it.

K1971.8.1.p: A sexton hidden behind a crucifix tells an old maid she will never have a husband. She answers that the Christ Child knows nothing about it and that she is praying to his mother instead.

K1971.9.p: A sexton hidden behind a statue tells an old maid who is praying for a husband to raise her foot to her neck, which is a mocking answer.

K1971.10.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: *Dixon 202 n. 39.
K1971.10.p: A trickster hidden in a sacred tree announces that he is destined to marry the princess.

K1971.11.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 391 No. 16.
K1971.11.p: A trickster hidden in a tree, speaking as a divine voice, declares that the tree and its fruit belong to him. Others who hear the voice think God is speaking and leave.

K1971.12.r: *Penzer V 59 n. 2; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 61, 277; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K1971.12.p: An impostor pretending to be God from inside a tree is discovered, and the tree is burned.

K1971.13.p: A supposed idol promises a teacher a fixed payment for his book once it is finished. The dupe overhears that the promise is really from a hidden man and pays him a bargain price now for what he would later have received.

K1971.14.p: A man hidden behind an idol in a temple tells robbers that they will have good loot but must leave half of it in the temple.

K1972.p: Oracular images are said to be inhabited by spirits or priests who secretly give the answers to those who consult them.

K1972.1.p: A statue is made to raise its arm. In the example, a woman who wants to go on pilgrimage to meet her lover pretends that a saint's statue has raised its arm in answer to her prayer.

K1972.2.p: A priest fakes a miracle by making the congregation believe that a painting of the Virgin is weeping real tears.

K1973.p: A jackal hides inside the carcass of a bullock and makes the people think that its voice is the voice of God.

K1974.p: A living man lies at a grave and pretends to be the dead man speaking from the grave.

K1975.p: Tricksters who have not mowed the grass tell their angry master, "May the grass grow up again!" When he looks, the grass has grown to full height, as if the curse had worked.

K1975.1.p: Tricksters put a wasp nest into a wallet or bee-hive and give it to their master with the curse, "May it turn to wasps!" The wallet turns out to contain wasps, as if the curse had worked.

K1975.2.p: A trickster claims that rupees he has been paid will turn to ashes if a tired woman rides the horse carrying them, then collects payment when ashes appear under the saddle.

K1975.3.p: A trickster claims that food will turn raw, a sham miracle used to excuse a lazy wife who brings her husband uncooked food in the field.

K1976.p: A fake holy relic is presented as having miraculous powers.

K1976.1.r: Feigned resurrection. Tricksters enriched as a result. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K1976.1.p: Two friars take a dead man's arm and claim it is a relic that works miracles; one of them challenges its powers in public and pretends to be struck dead.

K1980.r: K2165. Sham blind man throws suspicion on real blind.
K1980.p: Miscellaneous other kinds of fraud and pretense that do not fit the more specific categories.

K1981.p: A person pretends to be deaf and mute in order to deceive others.

K1981.1.p: A trickster pretends to be deaf and mute so that a stingy man takes him in and gives him hospitality.

K1982.r: Herbert III 282; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 210f.
K1982.p: A beggar in disguise gets charity from the same person three times by appearing to be a different person each time.

K1983.p: A trickster pretends to be a helper and secretly eats the food women have stored away.

K1984.r: Type 1459**; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 702; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1984.p: Girls put on a false show to make suitors think they are more desirable than they really are.

K1984.1.r: *Type 1457; *BP III 237; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. III 58, VII 320; Japanese: Ikeda.
K1984.1.p: Sisters who have been warned not to speak forget and talk, and are found out to be the women they are pretending not to be (sisters pretending to be lisping).

K1984.2.p: A girl pretends to eat very little, but the suitor sees her baking and discovers she eats a lot.

K1984.2.1.p: A girl claims she has overeaten on a nightingale's thigh, a tall excuse for having a small appetite.

K1984.3.p: A girl with an ugly name is given a new, prettier one by her mother, but she does not recognize it and her mother has to call her by the old name.

K1984.4.p: Ugly women complain of flowers falling on them, and a king who overhears them thinks they must be delicate and beautiful.

K1984.5.p: A blind fiancée gives herself away by mistaking one object for another.

K1985.p: A deceiver raises a large-headed, large-eyed bird that is actually an owl. When he learns the bird's age, he kills it, and the imposture is exposed.

K1986.p: The devil disguises himself as a candidate for confirmation in the church.

K1987.r: Dh. I 175; Nouvelles de Sens No. 5.
K1987.p: The devil disguises himself as a man and goes to church.

K1988.p: A brother or sister obtains a religious blessing that was meant for someone else.

K1988.1.p: One sister borrows another's clothes and receives a religious blessing in her place.

K1991.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 380 No. 5, (Kaffir): Theal 188; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 353 No. 62; Antigua, West Indies: Johnson JAFL XXXIV 59; Bahamas: *Parsons MAFLS XIII 104; West Indies: Flowers 552—554.
K1991.p: A hare or jackal makes horns of wax and pretends to be a horned animal, but the horns melt by the fire.

K1992.r: Disappears when man demands to see the wounds on his hands and feet. Type 797*.
K1992.p: The devil disguises himself as Jesus to deceive people. In Thompson's note, a man is forbidden to cut wood on Sunday, which a deceiver of this kind would use as a pretext.

K1994.p: A wise man is sent by a king to a rival king and gives him advice that seems helpful but actually serves the sender's own interests.

K2000.p: A general heading for tales about people who pretend to be good or friendly while secretly intending harm.

K2010.p: A person pretends to be a friend but then secretly attacks the one he has pretended to be friends with.

K2010.1.r: **A. H. Krappe The Legend of Roderick, the last of the Visigothic Kings and the Ermanarich Cycle (Heidelberg, 1923); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K2010.1.p: A man pretends to be a friend of the king but then attacks him, to avenge the king's violation of the man's wife.

K2010.2.p: A person feigns friendship in order to take revenge for a murder.

K2010.3.p: Wolves make a false truce with sheep; once the sheepdogs have been sent away, the wolves attack and eat the sheep.

K2011.r: (Red Riding Hood.) *Type 333; BP I 37, *42, 234; *Saintyves Perrault 215, 222; Missouri French: Carrière; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 83.
K2011.p: A wolf disguises itself as a grandmother in order to get into the house and kill a child.

K2011.1.p: A wolf disguises itself as the child's mother in order to get in and kill the child.

K2011.1.1.r: Africa (Rundi): Zuure L’Ame du Murundi (Paris, 1932) 340ff. No. E5, 345f. No. E7, (Luba): DeClerq ZsKS IV 213ff. No. 13.
K2011.1.1.p: An ogre who is the child's father disguises himself as the mother in order to kill the child.

K2011.1.2.r: Africa (Kenya): Browne Vanishing Tribes of Kenya (London, 1926) 211ff.
K2011.1.2.p: A bogey or monster imitates the child's mother in order to kill the child.

K2011.1.3.p: A hyena disguises itself as the child's father in order to kill the child.

K2011.1.4.p: A leopard disguises itself as the child's brother in order to kill the child.

K2011.2.p: A tiger-ogress pretends to be the girls' mother and explains away her tail as a boil, so that she can deceive them.

K2012.p: A false friend persuades a man to throw his wife out of the house, and then he seduces her.

K2013.p: An enemy is invited to a wedding with a relative of the host, and is attacked there instead of being welcomed.

K2013.1.p: An enemy is invited to a meeting and then attacked.

K2014.p: Women pretend to weep over a warrior's wounds, but in fact try to make the wounds worse or inflame them.

K2014.1.p: A king has a wounded ally treated by leeches, but bribes them to put beetles, barley awns and similar things into the wounds.

K2015.p: A rich man adopts a child, but really wants to get rid of him.

K2021.p: A hypocrite shows friendship to someone and then turns on them with an attack.

K2021.1.p: A man, paid a debt, is allowed by a woman to kiss her, but he bites her cheek and leaves a lasting scar.

K2021.2.p: A man pretends to kiss a relative in greeting but bites him instead.

K2021.3.p: A man embraces another man to find out whether he is hiding gold in his belt.

K2022.p: A rejected suitor makes friends with a married woman's husband and then kills him while they are out hunting.

K2023.p: Badgers are treacherously killed even though a prince had promised them safety.

K2026.p: A crow accepts an owl's hospitality and then burns the owls to death.

K2027.p: A fox gets a rooster to confess and then eats him.

K2030.p: Double dealers: characters who appear friendly while secretly working against others.

K2031.r: Wienert FFC LVI *51 (ET 104), 96 (ST 88); Halm Aesop No. 229.
K2031.p: A dog keeps switching between biting hares and fawning over them, so it is unclear whether he is their friend or enemy.

K2031.1.p: A dog acts friendly toward a guest while sitting at his master's table, but on the street he barks at the same man, a double-dealing trick that tricks the guest.

K2032.p: A magpie leads other magpies into his master's net by promising that the master will teach them to talk.

K2033.p: A trickster makes a basket for his partner the tiger to carry meat in, but leaves the bamboo attached to its roots, so the tiger is left behind.

K2034.p: One reward is promised to several helpers at once, so each expects to get it.

K2034.1.p: A king's daughter is secretly promised in marriage to several men in order to get each one to help.

K2035.p: Supernatural beings appear in dreams to two opposing kings and tell each how he can defeat the other.

K2036.p: A helper steals the prize that the hero obtained at the end of a quest.

K2037.p: A jackal persuades a deer to steal from a farmer, then tells the farmer, who catches the deer.

K2041.p: A physician who deceives those who employ him.

K2041.1.p: A physician is hired to poison an enemy, but he is secretly working for that enemy and so is also hired to poison his own master who sent him.

K2042.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 293 No. 52; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2042.p: A crow tricks owls by pretending to have been cast out by the crows, then uses the secret hiding places he learned from the owls to lead the crows to victory.

K2043.p: A wolf pretends to slander a tiger, and the fox agrees with him. Later the fox tells the tiger that he was only testing the wolf's malice.

K2050.p: A person pretends to be virtuous or good in order to deceive others.

K2051.p: An adulterous wife pretends to be extremely delicate and easily upset, so no one suspects her of wrongdoing.

K2051.1.p: An adulterous wife pretends to be ashamed before a male statue, a mirror, or a male fish, as a show of modesty.

K2051.2.p: An adulterous wife pretends to faint when her husband strikes her with a rose. She has in fact let her lover abuse her, so the faint is a cover.

K2051.3.p: An adulterous wife pretends great disdain for men and will look at none except her husband and her lover.

K2051.4.p: Women dress their heads modestly and look respectable, though they are immoral underneath.

K2052.p: A bride pretends to be far more sensitive and modest than she really is.

K2052.1.r: Wears gloves, etc. to bed. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K2052.1.p: A bride or wife pretends to be modest when she is not.

K2052.2.p: A girl who is frightened by love becomes insatiable once she gives in to it.

K2052.3.p: An oversensitive bride pleads a headache or some other excuse to avoid intimacy. When she changes her mind, the groom gives her the same excuse in return.

K2052.4.p: A widow who pretends to be oversensitive or hypocritically virtuous about sex and remarriage.

K2052.4.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 21; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K2052.4.1.p: A doctor prescribes sexual intimacy as a cure for a widow's ailments. She first claims she would rather die, but changes her mind when her daughters beg her to accept the treatment. The daughters then adopt the same treatment as a preventive.

K2052.4.2.p: A widow who claims to hate intimacy rejects a eunuch who offers good business skills to manage her estate, though she herself wants a husband for that purpose.

K2052.4.3.p: A man consoles his daughter, whose husband is dying, by telling her he has already chosen another husband for her. She is insulted by this, but as soon as her husband dies she asks her father for details about the new man.

K2054.p: A trickster pretends to be honest in order to swindle a victim. He claims to have found a bag of gold, and a confederate claims it upon a correct description. The onlooker is thus tricked into trusting the trickster with a large sum of money.

K2054.1.p: A boy pretends to make a long journey to pay back a debt of a single penny. This wins the man's trust, and then the boy robs him.

K2055.p: A fox confesses his sins, but right after the confession he is ready to steal again.

K2055.1.r: After wringing the gander’s neck, excuses self saying: “He should not have hissed at the saint.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 165*.
K2055.1.p: A wolf joins the company of saints and promises to stop killing animals, though he has no intention of keeping that promise.

K2056.p: A hypocritical stepmother weeps as her husband leaves, promising to take good care of his children even though they beat her. In fact she beats them instead.

K2057.p: A hypocrite pretends to refuse gifts with his mouth, yet secretly stretches out his hands to take them.

K2058.p: A person pretends to be pious and virtuous in order to deceive others.

K2058.1.p: A man who appears to be a holy ascetic (sadhu) is secretly a thief.

K2058.2.p: A false ascetic teams up with a tiger and shares the prey the tiger catches, though he has deceived the tiger about his virtue.

K2060.p: Someone's hypocrisy is discovered and exposed.

K2061.p: An animal with a treacherous plan pretends to be harmless or helpful, but its scheme is noticed and stopped.

K2061.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 36), 68 (ET 326), 97 (ST 110); Halm Aesop No. 283.
K2061.1.p: A wolf offers to take over as shepherd guarding the sheep, but its real plan to eat them is recognized.

K2061.1.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 138), 96 (ST 99); Halm Aesop No. 269; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2061.1.1.p: The wolf, posing as a shepherd, suggests getting rid of the sheep's guard dogs, and this proposal reveals his plan.

K2061.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 125), 96 (ST 96); Halm Aesop No. 38.
K2061.2.p: A fox pretends to be playing with the sheep, but a dog sees through this and chases him away.

K2061.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 373), 96 (ST 104); Halm Aesop No. 372.
K2061.3.p: A dog licks and fawns over a sick sheep, but the shepherd realizes the dog is hoping the sheep will die.

K2061.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI *53 (ET 137), 96 (ST 90); Halm Aesop No. 270; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 216.
K2061.4.p: A wolf tries to coax a goat down from a high place so it can be caught, but the plan is detected.

K2061.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 136), 96 (ST 91); Halm Aesop No. 284; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 216.
K2061.5.p: A starving wolf asks a sheep to fetch it water, but the sheep recognizes the trick and the plan fails.

K2061.6.r: *Crane Vitry 202 No. 166; Herbert III 15; Wienert FFC LVI 46 (ET 41), 53 (ET 135), 96 (ST 86).
K2061.6.p: A wolf offers to help a sow give birth as a midwife, but its real intent to eat the piglets is discovered.

K2061.7.r: Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 30), 53 (ET 127), 96 (ST 87); Halm Aesop No. 16.
K2061.7.p: A cat offers to act as doctor for a cock and hen, but its real intent to eat them is discovered.

K2061.8.p: A crocodile tells a dog to drink in the river without fear, but the dog realizes the crocodile means to eat it and the plan is detected.

K2061.9.r: Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 128), 96 (ST 97); Halm Aesop No. 15.
K2061.9.p: A cat hangs on a wall pretending to be dead, but the mice detect the trick and avoid it.

K2061.10.r: Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 126), 96 (ST 94, 222); Halm Aesop No. 400.
K2061.10.p: A fox's scheme is detected by crickets, who find cricket wings in the fox's excrement, revealing that he had eaten them.

K2061.11.p: A jackal hired as nurse for leopard cubs eats their food instead of caring for them.

K2062.r: Wienert FFC LVI 69 (ET 330), 96 (ST 103); Halm Aesop No. 164; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2062.p: A thief tries to feed a watchdog to quiet it, but the dog sees the plan and does not fall for it.

K2063.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1450A; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K2063.p: A woman who appears chaste and virtuous is caught committing adultery.

K2064.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 533.
K2064.p: A man posing as a holy hermit is caught in a secret love affair, exposing him as a hypocrite.

K2065.p: A hypocrite's false piety is revealed when Death appears and the true feelings of the person are shown.

K2065.1.p: A wife who claims she would gladly let Death take her in her sick husband's place is exposed when Death comes, because she points to her husband as the one to take.

K2090.p: A general heading for other tales in which someone's false or two-faced behavior is exposed.

K2090.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 323), 102 (ST 151); Halm Aesop No. 99.
K2090.1.p: A peasant speaks kindly to crows but then chases them away from his planted seed, showing his hypocrisy.

K2091.p: Someone pretends to be sick in order to find out a secret.

K2091.1.p: Someone pretends to be sick in order to get better food.

K2093.p: A guardian who was supposed to protect a pair of fleeing lovers betrays where they are hiding.

K2094.p: A person pretends to return love in order to help a suitor win the beloved's heart.

K2095.p: A general heading for tales in which a person pretends to be innocent or honest about stolen goods.

K2095.1.p: A man announces that he has found a lost jewel but says it so softly that no one can hear, so he can keep it while claiming an honest conscience.

K2095.2.p: A hypocrite refuses to share in a stolen chicken but still takes some of the gravy.

K2096.p: A general heading for tales in which someone pretends to be generous or charitable but is not.

K2096.1.p: A hypocrite vows to give coins to charity but breaks the vow, and when he tries to hand over the coins they turn out to be underweight.

K2096.2.p: A thief robs a miserly man of his hoard, then gives a tenth of it to the poor as a banquet, which is a kind of mock charity.

K2097.p: A miser attends mass to appear pious before going on to commit usury, lending money at interest.

K2098.p: A king sends his regrets over the death of a man he has himself ordered executed.

K2100.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; West Indies: Flowers 555.
K2100.p: A general heading for tales in which someone is wrongly accused of a crime or offense.

K2101.r: *Marc “Die Achikarsage” Studien zur vgl. Literaturgeschichte II 393ff.; *DeVries FFC LXXIII 365ff.; 374ff.; Jewish: *Neuman.
K2101.p: A minister who has been falsely accused wins back his position through his own cleverness.

K2102.p: A hero who has been falsely accused is sent on a dangerous mission as punishment.

K2104.p: A valuable jewel is given to a king, and the giver is then falsely accused of stealing it. The accusation is used to ruin the innocent person.

K2110.p: Someone spreads lies to damage another person's reputation. This heading covers slander in general.

K2110.1.r: *Types 451, 706, 707, 712, 883A, 892; BP I 20, 79ff., *86, 99ff., 295ff., II 121ff., 273, 380ff., *392, III 85ff., 488; **Arfert Das Märchen von der unterschobenen Braut; Hibbard 21ff., 35; **Schlauch Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 12ff.; *Kittredge Arthur 241 n. 1; *Cox 478, 501;—Irish myth *Cross; Jewish: *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 257; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 107 No. 891*; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 526, 536; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 385ff.; Africa (Wakweli): Bender 96.
K2110.1.p: A wife is falsely slandered and defamed by someone who wants to ruin her.

K2110.1.1.p: A man's lover falsely tells him that his wife has leprosy, so that the wife is slandered and cast out.

K2111.r: *Reinhard PMLA XXXVIII 456 n. 102; **Bloomfield Trans. Am. Philos. Assoc. LIV 141; *Penzer II 120, IV 104, 107, V 176; *Dickson 178 n. 44; Boje 76; *Faverty Harvard Studies and Notes in Phil and Lit. XIII 81ff.; Heptameron No. 70; Saintyves Saints Successeurs 213ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 68, 128 Nos. 515*, 1516*, Espinosa III No. 146, Keller; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 6, *Rotunda; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 151 n. 2, II 63 n. 4, 74 n. 2, 106 n. 3, Fox 104; Jewish: *Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 336; India: Cowell J[a]taka I 265, IV 117, *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 264, 529; Chinese: Werner 192; Chinese-Persian: *Coyajee JPASB XXIV 191; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 326 n. 178.
K2111.p: A woman makes advances to a man, is rejected, and then accuses him of trying to force himself on her. This is the Potiphar's wife story.

K2111.0.1.p: A man tells a story to distract a woman who is pressing him for an affair, to calm her desire.

K2111.1.p: A stepmother makes advances to her stepson, and when he refuses she tries to poison him. Her own son drinks the poison by accident and seems to die, so she accuses the stepson of murder. A doctor later reveals that the drink was a sleeping potion, not poison, which exposes the plot.

K2111.2.p: A woman whose advances were refused accuses a man of stealing from her.

K2111.3.p: A friar sleeps with a woman, then refuses to keep his promise to her, and she accuses him of rape.

K2111.4.p: An adulterous wife tricks her husband into killing a man she claims was pressing her for sex, when he was really her lover.

K2111.5.p: A mother falsely claims that her son has committed incest with her.

K2111.6.p: A girl makes a false accusation against a bishop.

K2112.r: (Usually by unsuccessful suitor.) (Crescentia, Genoveva, Susanna.) *Types 712, 883A; **Wallensköld Le conte de la femme chaste convoitée par son beaufrère (Acta Societatis Fennicae XXXIV, Helsingfors, 1907); *Köhler-Bolte I 392, 582; *BP I 18, 305 n. 1, Chauvin VI 159 No. 323, *167 No. 327; Ward II 680; Herbert III 342; *Dickson 72, 166 n. 12; *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 361f.; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 136 No. 116; Alphabet Nos. 147, 672; **J. Kentenich Die Genovefalegende (Trier, 1927); Oesterley No. 249; Scala Celi 27b, 32a Nos. 179, 183; Hilka Neue Beiträge z. Erzählungslit. des Mittelalters 13 No. 11; *Graber Festschrift für Eugen Mogk (1924) 525ff.; *Revue des Langues romanes LII 163ff.; Archiv f. Literaturgeschichte XII 132ff.; *von der Hagen I c—civ; Hibbard 12, 21, 29ff., 35; *Puckett MPh XIII 609.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 660; Chinese: Graham; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 152.
K2112.p: A woman is falsely slandered as an adulteress or prostitute.

K2112.1.r: *Types 882, 892; *Köhler-Bolte I 211f.; bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 257; *Grünbaum Jüdischdeutsch Chrestomathie 421ff.; *Paris Romania XXXII 481ff.; *Hilka Neuphilologische Mitteilungen (1913) 16ff.; Dunlop-Wilson II 73f.; Chauvin VII 159.—Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 311.
K2112.1.p: False signs are produced to make it look as if a woman has been unfaithful. Her tokens are stolen, or her hidden marks are secretly seen by someone's treachery.

K2112.1.1.p: A man is shown a finger as proof of his wife's unfaithfulness. A maid was substituted for the wife, and her finger was cut off by the lover.

K2112.2.r: *Fb “seng” III 187b; *Child II 39ff.; Hibbard 35, 285 n. 5; *Dickson 166 n. 14; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 138 No. 63.
K2112.2.p: A leper or beggar is secretly put into a queen's bed so that she will be found guilty of adultery.

K2112.2.1.p: A man places a donkey's foal under a princess's bed-covers and then accuses her of lying with it.

K2112.2.2.p: A page is tricked into hiding behind a woman's bed curtain, where he can be found and used to incriminate her.

K2112.2.3.p: A maidservant's accomplice pretends to be leaving the woman's bedroom, so that it looks as if he has been with her.

K2112.2.4.p: A false fetus or miscarriage is put into an innocent woman's bed, so that she appears to have had an illegitimate abortion.

K2112.3.p: A man hides in a woman's house to escape pursuers, and his presence there leads to her being falsely accused of adultery or sexual misconduct.

K2112.4.p: A villain threatens to bring a naked servant to a woman's house and make it look like she has been sexually involved, so she submits to him out of fear of the accusation.

K2112.5.p: Other ways of framing an innocent woman so that she appears to be an adulteress or prostitute.

K2112.5.1.p: A handkerchief is deliberately left in a woman's room so that she will be accused of wrongdoing.

K2112.5.2.p: Someone gives food to a madman, which causes a woman to be falsely accused as a result.

K2113.p: A princess disguised as a man is falsely accused of having an improper relationship with the queen.

K2113.1.p: A girl disguised as a man is falsely accused of being unfaithful.

K2113.2.p: A wealthy woman makes advances to an ascetic who turns out to be a girl in men's clothing; when rejected, she accuses him of adulterous assault.

K2114.p: A man is falsely accused of being unfaithful to his wife or lover.

K2115.r: *Types 707, 710; *BP I 13ff., 20, II 380ff.; *Schlauch, Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 21; *Huet Revue d’Ethnographie et de Sociologie II 200; *Chauvin VII 97 No. 375 n. 1; *Dickson 39ff. nn. 39, 40, 45; Fb “kattekilling” II 111; *Cox 486.—Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Wells 130 (Emare); Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 2, *Rotunda; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 137, Espinosa II Nos. 99—104; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 383; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 116; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 190 No. 28, (Benga): Nassau No. 22.
K2115.p: A woman is falsely accused of giving birth to animals; her real children are removed and animals are substituted for them.

K2115.0.1.p: Jealous queens tell a queen who is about to give birth to put her head into a hole at the bottom of a grain bin, so that she cannot see what she delivers.

K2115.1.p: A malicious story claims that a man is the son of an animal.

K2115.2.p: A malicious story claims that a woman has given birth to objects instead of a child.

K2115.2.1.p: Stones are secretly swapped in place of newborn babies.

K2115.2.2.p: A woman is slandered by a story that she gave birth to a log instead of a child.

K2115.3.p: A prophecy says a pregnant woman's child will be an ogre, so that she will be killed.

K2116.p: An innocent person is accused of murder.

K2116.1.r: Dickson 72, 225; *Hibbard 26ff.; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 385 n. 4; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2116.1.p: An innocent woman is accused of murder.

K2116.1.1.r: *Type 451; BP I 70ff.; *Dickson 43, 73 n. 26; *Schlauch, Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 12; *Hibbard 26ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 94f.; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 311 No. 56; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 89, 99—103; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 321. See also references to K2116.1.1.1.
K2116.1.1.p: An innocent woman is accused of killing her newborn children.

K2116.1.1.1.r: *Types 652, 706, 710, 712; *BP I 13ff., 18 n. 1, 20, II 121ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 392, 582; Chauvin VI 159 No. 323; *Dickson 38ff. nn. 34, 42, 45, 48, 49; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2116.1.1.1.p: An innocent woman is accused of eating her newborn children.

K2116.1.1.1.1.p: A wife is falsely shown to have eaten her newborn child, because puppy bones are passed off as the child's remains as evidence against her.

K2116.1.2.p: A queen is wrongly accused of poisoning her husband the king, because ignorant doctors cannot find the true cause of his illness; she is burned at the stake.

K2116.1.3.p: A girl is wrongly accused of murdering her lover, and the investigation finds that the poisonous breath of a toad was actually the cause of death.

K2116.1.4.p: A queen in disguise is wrongly accused of killing a child who was left in her care.

K2116.2.p: A man is wrongly accused of murder.

K2116.2.1.p: A religious hermit (anchorite) is wrongly accused of murder.

K2116.2.2.p: A man is accused of having starved a woman to death and stealing her treasure, though he is innocent.

K2116.3.p: A person wounds himself or herself and then falsely accuses another person of attempting murder.

K2116.4.p: A murderer raises a loud outcry so that an innocent person is blamed and accused of the killing.

K2116.5.p: A warrior is falsely accused of having killed his sleeping enemy, the accusation being that he could not have done it had the enemy been awake.

K2117.r: (Cf. K2115, K2116.) *Type 706; *BP I 295ff.; Hibbard 26ff.; *Schlauch, Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 12ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 119; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 2, Rotunda.
K2117.p: A wrongly accused wife is slandered because a letter announcing the birth of her children is switched on the way to the king, so the king receives a false message against her.

K2117.1.p: A husband's letter ordering that his wife be treated well is secretly altered into an order for her execution.

K2121.p: A man is slandered by being falsely said to have seduced or deflowered a princess.

K2121.1.r: S. A. Indian (Amuesha): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 149.
K2121.1.p: A brother is falsely accused of being the father of his sister's child, though she became pregnant by supernatural means.

K2121.2.r: Icelandic: Þiðriks saga II 164—9, Boberg; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 393.
K2121.2.p: A king's loyal servant is falsely accused of having an improper relationship with the queen.

K2123.r: Sham sickness. India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 427.
K2123.p: An innocent woman is falsely accused of practicing witchcraft.

K2124.p: A woman is slandered by being falsely described as an ogress, a monstrous man-eating female giant.

K2125.p: A woman is slandered by being falsely said to be possessed by demons.

K2125.1.p: A girl is falsely reported to be possessed by a demon, so that her suitors are frightened away.

K2126.p: A knight is falsely accused of sedition, that is, of plotting rebellion against his lord or king.

K2126.1.p: A king's advisor is falsely charged with treason. The accusers are later exposed and punished.

K2126.2.p: A man loyal to the king is falsely accused of secretly serving another king as a spy.

K2127.p: Someone is falsely accused of stealing.

K2127.1.p: A man who wants a woman that a group of men are quarreling over accuses those men of having kidnapped his wife.

K2127.2.p: A false queen hides horsemeat in the bed of a pregnant woman so she will be exposed as a thief who eats horses.

K2128.p: A prince is slandered by being called a bastard, meaning he was born illegitimately.

K2129.p: Miscellaneous slanders, in which people are falsely accused of various faults.

K2129.1.p: A jealous monk falsely tells others that a novice is lazy.

K2129.2.p: A sick crew is falsely called magicians, so that no one wants to deal with them.

K2129.3.p: Stepsisters scatter sugar in a girl's litter so flies gather on her. A would-be bridegroom, disgusted, orders the bearers to abandon her in the jungle.

K2129.4.p: A family is falsely accused of stinginess by people they have hosted and fed.

K2130.p: Characters who stir up trouble and quarrels between others.

K2131.r: BP II 129; Irish myth: *Cross (cf. K2130); India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1028; Africa (Wakweli): Bender 40.
K2131.p: A trickster makes two friends each suspect the other of plotting against him.

K2131.1.r: Cat tells eagle that sow is trying to root down the tree: eagle is frightened and dares not leave tree. Cat tells sow that eagle plans to carry off pigs: sow dares not leave. They starve and fall victims to the cat. Wienert FFC LVI 54 (ET 143), 99 (ST 130, 421).
K2131.1.p: A cat sows suspicion between an eagle and a sow, who live in the same tree, so that they become enemies. In the note, all three are happy until the cat intervenes.

K2131.2.r: Chauvin II 86 No. 18; Penzer V 42-63, 130 n. 1; B[ö]dker Exempler 277 No. 17; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2131.2.p: A jackal, out of envy, convinces a lion that his friend the bull is plotting against him, so the lion turns on the bull and kills him.

K2131.3.p: A woman ruins two men's friendship by pretending to whisper secrets to one of them.

K2131.4.p: A trickster fills a supposed treasure chest with trash. The joint owners then each accuse the other of stealing from it.

K2131.5.p: A treasure-producing animal is placed in a family's herd to cause quarrels and hatred among them.

K2132.p: A troublemaker carries a false message of love between a hero and a maiden.

K2134.p: A servant places the skin of a dead dog in the bed of his mistress and master, to make trouble between them.

K2135.r: Penzer II 113; *Chauvin VIII 144 No. 145 B; *Zs. f. Vksk. IX 188ff., 311ff.; *Oesterley No. 283; Herbert III 198; *Cosquin Études 82, 116; *Paris Romania V 454ff.; Hertz Deutsche Sage im Elsass (1872) 283ff.; Dunlop-Wilson II 49; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2135.p: A steward advises a courtier to turn his head away when serving the king, claiming the king dislikes his bad breath. He then tells the king that the courtier turns away to avoid the king's bad breath, so the courtier falls into trouble with the king.

K2136.p: Officers are praised in a backwards way, so that their real merit brings trouble on them and on their master.

K2137.r: *Type 1741; *BP II 129; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 364; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 245 No. 543; Chauvin VI 179 No. 341; *Fb “[ö]re” III 1181a; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2137.p: A servant who has eaten the chickens blames the priest's guest, telling him to flee and telling the priest the guest stole chickens, so the priest chases the innocent guest.

K2138.r: Beehive in bed. Bees sting family and cause father to kill son. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1878*.
K2138.p: A troublemaker arrives at a house riding a wolf and asks for shelter, and the wolf then kills the sheep.

K2141.p: Jealous courtiers turn the lion king against his wise adviser, the jackal, by falsely claiming the jackal stole the lion's food.

K2142.p: Two people are each separately told that the other has died.

K2150.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 303 No. 74; Spanish Exempla: Keller; West Indies: Flowers 555.
K2150.p: An innocent person is framed so that he seems guilty of a crime.

K2151.r: *Types 1536C, 1537; *Taylor MPh XV 221ff., 226 n. 1; **Suchier Der Schwank von der viermal getöteten Leiche (Halle a. S., 1922); *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 598; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 214 No. 438; Köhler-Bolte I 190; Bédier Fabliaux 469; BP II 10; Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 73 n. 3.—Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 176, 189, *Espinosa JAFL XLIX 181—193; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K2151.p: A corpse is passed from person to person so that each is accused of murder. The trickster is paid to keep quiet, and the note describes the thrice-killed corpse.

K2151.1.p: A living man is mistaken for someone bringing back a corpse and begs the trickster to spare his life.

K2152.r: Most references to K2151 apply to this motif as well. *Cox 501; Christiansen Norske Eventyr No. 1536; *Clouston Tales II 242; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 176, 189; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 197 No. 96; N. A. Indian (Micmac): Rand No. 57, (Zuñi): Cushing 255, (Ojibwa): Schoolcraft Hiawatha 246.
K2152.p: A corpse is arranged so that a dupe speaks to it and, getting no reply, knocks it over, and he is then accused of murder.

K2152.1.p: A dead dog is set up so that a woman knocks it over, making her seem to have killed or hurt someone.

K2152.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1537A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1537 I*.
K2152.2.p: A corpse's legs lead to a false accusation of murder against an innocent person.

K2153.p: A trickster wounds himself and then accuses others of having hurt him.

K2153.1.r: Africa (Kaffir): Alexander and Mohl Mitteilungen des Seminars für orientalische Sprachen VIII (3) 24ff., (Vandau): Boas and Simango JAFL XXXV 170ff. No. 7, (Thonga): Junod 232ff. No. 2, (Lamba): Doke MAFLS XX (1927) 71 No. 31.
K2153.1.p: An animal nurse wounds herself so that the blame for the eaten young falls on another animal.

K2155.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 26, 44, Beal XXI 307, 316; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 555.
K2155.p: Evidence of a crime is left in a place so that an innocent dupe is blamed for it.

K2155.1.r: *Types 652, 712; *BF I 18 n. 1; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 89, India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 369 No. 20. See also all references to K2116.1.1. West Indies: Flowers 536.
K2155.1.p: Blood is smeared on an innocent person, leading to an accusation of murder.

K2155.1.1.r: See references to K2155.1. Dickson 74, 225; Hibbard 25 n. 5.
K2155.1.1.p: A bloody knife is hidden in an innocent person's bed, leading to an accusation of murder.

K2155.2.p: Slanderers kill a woman and leave her body near Buddha's cell so that suspicion falls on the monk.

K2156.p: An innocent man is forced to write a letter of treason, which leads to his death sentence.

K2165.p: A fake blind man causes suspicion to fall on a real blind man, then confesses his own deception so the real blind man is punished.

K2171.p: A cat steals a sausage from the table, but the dog is beaten by the mistress for it.

K2172.p: Rats cause cats to be blamed and killed for damage the rats themselves do, since the rats' raids rise and fall with the number of cats.

K2175.p: A grandmother secretly ruins the family's cooking by putting dirt and hair into the pot and sand into the water they fetch, so the innocent grandchildren are blamed and whipped.

K2200.p: A general heading for stories about wicked villains and traitors who betray others.

K2210.r: Distinction between treacherous relatives and cruel relatives (S0-S99) is frequently impossible to make. Relatives whose treachery seems to be uppermost have been listed here; those usually possessing power over their charges and exercising their power in a cruel fashion have been listed under cruel relatives. India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2210.p: A general heading for betrayals carried out by a person's own relatives.

K2211.r: *Types 301, 502, 506, 550, 551; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “jalousie”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 49 No. 328*A, Espinosa II Nos. 120f., III Nos. 141f., Espinosa Jr. Nos. 81, 202—204; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 323; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham, Eberhard FFC CXX 125; Marquesas: Handy 86; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/615); Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 170; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 68.
K2211.p: A brother secretly betrays another brother, usually the elder one, to harm or cheat him.

K2211.0.1.p: An elder brother or elder brothers act treacherously against a younger sibling.

K2211.0.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: *Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 43; Mono: Wheeler No. 22.
K2211.0.2.p: A younger brother or younger brothers act treacherously against an older sibling.

K2211.1.r: *Types 315, 712; Dickson 178, Schlauch Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 108; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 139, 151, 157.
K2211.1.p: A man's brother-in-law, his sister's or wife's brother, betrays him.

K2211.2.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K2211.2.p: A foster brother betrays the hero by falsely accusing him of theft.

K2212.r: *Types 300, 315, 425, 706, 709, 780; *BP I 551, III 2; Dickson 29 n. 3; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 138-141; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 125; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 382ff., 391; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 297.
K2212.p: A sister secretly betrays a brother, usually the elder sister.

K2212.0.1.p: A treacherous sister tries to poison her brother.

K2212.0.2.p: A sister who has become the mistress of a robber or giant plots against her brother.

K2212.0.3.p: A treacherous queen has her own brother killed.

K2212.1.p: Stepsisters act treacherously against the hero.

K2212.2.r: *Type 706; BP I 295ff.; *bin Gorion Born Judas I 364; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 315C*; India: Thompson-Balys.

K2213.r: *Types 560, 561, 566, 612, 670, 1350, 1510; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 315B*, 894*; Russian: Andrejev No. 315B*, 894*; Prussian: Plenzat 25; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 315B*; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman, *bin Gorion Born Judas III 90ff., 95; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 93, 884, 998, II 491, 510, 516, 1014; Japanese: Ikeda; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 381, 385; Africa (Fang): Trilles 277, Tessman 113f.
K2213.p: A wife secretly betrays her husband.

K2213.1.r: *Type 1510; **Grisebach Die Wanderung der Novelle von der treulosen Witwe durch die Weltliteratur (Berlin, 1889); *Crane Vitry 228 No. 232; *Chauvin VIII 210 No. 254; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 752; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 93; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas III 240ff.; *315.
K2213.1.p: A widow who swears undying grief at her husband's grave is unfaithful: she offers her love to a knight guarding a hanged man and hangs her own husband's corpse in place of the stolen body so the knight can escape.

K2213.2.p: A faithless wife and her lover throw the hero overboard into the sea.

K2213.2.1.p: A queen in love with a fakir pushes her husband into a well because the fakir tells her to.

K2213.3.r: (Cf. K2213.5.) Malone PMLA XLIII 413, 419, 432; Boje 62; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 103; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2213.3.p: A wife conspires with her lover to kill her husband.

K2213.3.1.p: A faithless wife arranges the deaths of her husband and their children so she can be free to be with her lover.

K2213.3.2.p: A faithless wife poisons her husband so she can be with her lover, but the lover, fearing he would meet the same fate, refuses to come to her.

K2213.3.2.1.p: After the wife has poisoned her husband, her lover demands that she bring him her husband's head as proof.

K2213.3.2.2.p: A wife plots to kill her husband, but her lover replies that he could never touch a woman who is a murderer.

K2213.3.3.p: A faithless wife tricks her husband while she goes out secretly to look for her lover.

K2213.3.4.p: A queen who is in love with her own brother has her husband, the king, killed.

K2213.4.r: *Oertel JAOS XXVIII 96; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2213.4.p: A wife reveals a secret that her husband has entrusted to her, betraying him.

K2213.4.1.r: Huet 134; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 97, *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 302; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Cameroon): Ittman 77.
K2213.4.1.p: A hero's wife reveals the secret of his weak spot, which is how he can be harmed or defeated.

K2213.4.2.p: The devil persuades his wife to get him drunk and then find out what he is secretly doing, which is building the ark, so the secret is betrayed to others.

K2213.5.r: (Cf. K2213.2.) *Type 612; *BP I 126ff.; *Wesselski Märchen 188; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 226. Cf. Paris Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 4.
K2213.5.p: A husband, at great cost to himself, brings his dead wife back to life, but she immediately abandons him and plots with a lover to kill him.

K2213.6.p: A faithless wife uses magic or trickery to turn her husband into something else.

K2213.7.p: A faithless wife betrays her husband by telling her father about him.

K2213.8.p: A faithless queen helps her lover take the throne by driving the king from his kingdom.

K2213.9.p: A faithless wife urges her sons to make war on their own father.

K2213.10.p: A faithless wife tricks her husband into freeing her lover, who has been imprisoned or bound.

K2213.11.p: A treacherous queen tricks the king into giving the kingdom to her son.

K2213.12.p: A young queen murders her old husband, the king, so she can take a new, younger husband.

K2213.13.p: A queen kills her husband to avenge his earlier killing of her father and brother.

K2213.14.p: A queen deceives her husband to avenge his killing of her lover and her brother, as in the tale of Helgi.

K2213.15.p: A treacherous queen lures her husband into a chest and hands him over to a hostile king. He is hung up between two fires, but his second wife cuts the cords so he falls, kills his enemy, and wins back his kingdom.

K2213.16.p: A wife betrays her husband out of revenge because he once took a second wife.

K2214.p: Children who betray their own parents or family, acting as villains against those who raised them.

K2214.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 117 n. 3; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2214.1.p: A daughter who betrays her family or does harm to those close to her.

K2214.1.1.p: A daughter has her aged father burned on the same funeral pyre as her dead husband, supposedly to honor the husband.

K2214.2.p: A daughter-in-law who betrays or plots harm against her own family by marriage.

K2214.2.1.p: A daughter-in-law secretly schemes to harm her husband's mother.

K2214.3.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 286.
K2214.3.p: A son who leads a rebellion against his father, even though the father gave him everything he has.

K2214.3.1.p: A foster son who betrays and rebels against the man who raised him.

K2217.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2217.p: An uncle who betrays or harms his relatives.

K2217.1.p: A nephew murders his kindly uncle in order to inherit his money.

K2218.p: Treacherous in-laws, meaning relatives gained through marriage who betray the family.

K2218.1.p: A mother-in-law falsely accuses her innocent daughter-in-law of wrongdoing.

K2218.2.p: A father-in-law who betrays or harms his son-in-law or daughter-in-law.

K2220.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
K2220.p: Rivals who act treacherously against one another out of jealousy or competition.

K2220.0.1.p: Jealous rivals persuade someone to break a taboo, or sacred prohibition, to bring about their downfall.

K2221.r: (Cf. K2230.) *Type 560, 561; Malone PMLA XLIII 417; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/10).
K2221.p: A rival in love, such as a wife's lover or a competitor for affection, who acts treacherously.

K2221.1.p: A woman poisons another woman who has succeeded in winning her rival's place or love.

K2222.r: Type 450; Dickson 29 n. 3, 41 n. 41; Irish myth: Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 2; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 526; Africa: Werner 203, (Basuto): Jacottet 246 No. 36, (Fjort): Dennett 47 No. 7, (Ekoi): Talbot 312.
K2222.p: A co-wife, or fellow concubine, who schemes against another wife or concubine of the same husband.

K2230.p: Lovers who betray one another or betray a third party.

K2231.p: A mistress, or lover outside marriage, who acts treacherously toward her partner or others.

K2231.1.p: A adulterous wife or mistress arranges for her lover to be murdered. She betrays the man she is involved with to death, often to get rid of him or to protect her affair.

K2232.r: English and Scottish: Child Ballads Nos. 4; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2232.p: A male lover who betrays the woman who loves him. This is the heading for the treacherous male lover type.

K2232.1.p: A man pretends to love a woman, takes advantage of her affection, and then abandons her. He leaves her after betraying her trust.

K2240.p: A heading for tales in which officials and tradesmen act treacherously. They are villains who betray those they serve or deal with.

K2241.p: An innkeeper who betrays or cheats his guests, often by robbing or harming them.

K2242.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 437; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2242.p: A steward, the manager of a household or estate, who betrays his master.

K2243.r: Dickson 74 n. 31; *Boje 62; Schlauch Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 98.
K2243.p: A seneschal, a senior household official, who betrays the person he serves.

K2244.p: A gatekeeper or doorkeeper who betrays those he is supposed to guard, for example by letting enemies in.

K2245.p: A marshal, an officer in charge of arranging or commanding, who betrays his lord.

K2246.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 7; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2246.p: A prince who acts treacherously toward others, betraying or deceiving them.

K2246.0.1.p: A princess or queen who acts treacherously, betraying or deceiving others.

K2246.1.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (Z-G. 13/420).
K2246.1.p: A king who acts treacherously, betraying or deceiving his subjects or others.

K2246.1.1.p: A king secretly sends out spies so that he can find excuses to fine people and collect money from them.

K2247.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 8; Icelandic: Boberg.
K2247.p: A lord, a noble or landowner, who acts treacherously toward those under him or those who trust him.

K2248.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 9; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 715; Jewish: Neuman.
K2248.p: A minister, an adviser or government official, who betrays the ruler he serves.

K2248.1.p: The son of a treacherous minister, who also acts treacherously.

K2249.p: A heading for treacherous officials and tradesmen not covered by the more specific types above.

K2249.1.p: A potter, a maker of clay pots, who acts treacherously and betrays others.

K2249.2.p: A treasurer, the official in charge of money, who betrays his master by stealing or deceiving.

K2249.3.p: A goldsmith, a maker of gold objects, who acts treacherously and betrays those who trust him.

K2249.4.p: A merchant or tradesman who betrays the person he deals with or works for, cheating or harming them through deceit.

K2249.4.1.p: A butcher who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2250.r: Types 450, 652; Dickson 236 n. 37; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 12; Malone PMLA XLIII 417 n. 9; Icelandic: FFC LXXXIII xxxvi—vii, *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “jalousie”. P365. Faithless servants.
K2250.p: A general heading for servants and workers who betray their masters or employers through deceit or treachery.

K2250.1.p: A servant who betrays his master through deceit or treachery.

K2251.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 19; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Icelandic: *Boberg.
K2251.p: A slave who betrays his master through deceit or treachery.

K2251.1.r: *Penzer VI 47 n. 1; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 61 No. *445B, Espinosa Jr. No. 114.
K2251.1.p: A slave-girl who betrays her master or mistress through deceit or treachery.

K2252.r: *Types 408, 553; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K2252.p: A maidservant who betrays her master or mistress through deceit or treachery.

K2253.p: A barber who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2254.p: A cook who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2255.p: A general heading for herdsmen who betray those they serve through deceit or treachery.

K2255.1.p: A swineherd who betrays the person he serves through deceit or treachery.

K2255.2.p: An ox-herd who betrays the person he serves through deceit or treachery.

K2256.p: A stable-groom who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2257.p: A gardener who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2258.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 16; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
K2258.p: A peasant who betrays the person he serves or works for, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2259.p: A general heading for other servants and workmen who betray those they serve through deceit or treachery.

K2259.1.p: A woodsman who betrays the person he serves or works for, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2259.2.p: A lamplighter who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2259.3.p: A potter who betrays the person he serves or works for, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2259.4.p: A sailor who betrays the person he serves, deceiving or harming them through treachery.

K2260.p: Villains are often people who are dark-skinned, dark-haired, or unusually colored, and such characters are frequently traitors in folk tales.

K2260.1.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 417 n. 9; Icelandic: Boberg.
K2260.1.p: A dark-skinned man turns out to be a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2260.2.p: A dark-skinned woman turns out to be a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2261.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 408—432 passim; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 56, 60 Nos. 408A*, 435*, Espinosa II Nos. 120f., Espinosa Jr. Nos. 106—110; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Int., I No. 2, V No. 5.
K2261.p: A Black or Moorish character is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2261.1.p: A Romani (gypsy) character is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2262.r: *Type 300; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 241b n. 14; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 68.
K2262.p: A charcoal-burner, a dark-skinned worker, is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2265.p: A red knight is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2270.p: Villains are often characters with physical deformities or disabilities, which marks them as wicked in folk tales.

K2271.r: *Cosquin Lorraine I 46 No. 3; Malone PMLA XLIII 417 n. 9; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.

K2272.p: A villain is crippled or lame.

K2273.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 477a; BP I 83 (Grimm No. 11); India: Thompson-Balys.
K2273.p: A villain has only one eye.

K2273.1.p: A villain is blind, as well as one-eyed in the sense of having lost sight in an eye, here meaning a fully blind villain.

K2276.p: A leper is cast as a villain.

K2277.r: Schlauch Chaucer’s Constance and Accused Queens (New York, 1927) 104.
K2277.p: A dwarf is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2280.p: Churchmen are often portrayed as treacherous villains who betray others in folk tales.

K2281.p: A bishop is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2282.p: A cardinal is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2282.1.p: Boniface VIII, while still a cardinal, poses as an angel and tricks Pope Clement V into giving up his office.

K2284.p: A priest is cast as a treacherous villain who betrays others.

K2284.1.p: A chaplain or religious adviser secretly betrays the person he serves.

K2284.2.p: A brahmin, a Hindu priest, secretly betrays the person he serves.

K2285.r: **M. Bloomfield “On False Ascetics and Nuns in Hindu Fiction” JAOS XLIV 202ff.; *Penzer III 211 n. 1, V 102 n. 2, VI 12 n. 1, IX 23 n. 2; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
K2285.p: A villain pretends to be a holy ascetic or a nun in order to deceive others.

K2285.1.p: A holy ascetic who turns out to be the villain of the story.

K2285.2.p: An anchorite, a hermit who has withdrawn from the world, acts as a treacherous villain.

K2286.p: A wise man or sage turns out to be the villain of the story.

K2290.p: A general heading for other kinds of villains and traitors not listed under more specific headings.

K2291.p: A beggar secretly acts as a treacherous villain against others.

K2292.p: A physician secretly betrays or harms the person he is treating.

K2293.p: An old woman acts as a treacherous villain against others.

K2294.p: A host who welcomes guests secretly betrays or harms them.

K2295.p: Animals act as treacherous villains against others.

K2295.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 51 (ET 111), *65 (ET 290), 139 (ST 448); Halm Aesop No. 356.
K2295.1.p: A partridge acts as a treacherous betrayer.

K2295.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI *51, 59 (ET 108, 200), 135, 139 (ST 404, 446); Halm Aesop No. 5.
K2295.2.p: An eagle acts as a treacherous betrayer.

K2295.3.p: A cock or rooster acts as a treacherous betrayer.

K2295.4.p: A lizard acts as a treacherous betrayer.

K2295.5.p: A camel acts as a treacherous betrayer.

K2296.p: A partner in a shared venture secretly betrays the others.

K2296.1.p: A partner who is a robber secretly betrays his companions in a robbery.

K2297.p: A friend secretly betrays or deceives the person who trusts him.

K2297.1.p: A man leaves his sweetheart in the care of a friend, and the friend tries to force his attentions on her; when she resists or it comes out, he claims the whole thing was only a test of her fidelity.

K2297.2.p: While a friend is away, a man takes the friend's mistress for himself.

K2298.p: A counselor or advisor who secretly works against the person he serves, betraying them.

K2299.p: A miscellaneous category of villains and traitors that do not fit the more specific types listed in this group.

K2299.1.p: An astrologer who betrays the person he serves, typically by deceiving them with false predictions or readings.

K2299.2.p: Whole peoples or tribes who act treacherously toward others.

K2300.p: A general heading for tricks and deceptions in folk literature that do not fall under the more specific categories.

K2310.p: Deception achieved through equivocation, meaning using words with double or misleading meanings so that the literal truth misleads the hearer.

K2311.p: A person is allowed only one cake during Lent, so the peasants make a single cake as huge as a cart wheel.

K2312.p: Someone obeys an oath or command to the letter while defeating its evident purpose, using literal interpretation to deceive.

K2312.1.p: A woman who has been sworn to secrecy about something talks to her unchristened child, since that does not count as telling a Christian.

K2312.2.p: A saint, forbidden from coming before his monastery's face after vowing it, returns by walking backwards so he never faces it.

K2313.p: Bad news about a death is broken gently through a series of false explanations that prepare the listener before the truth is told.

K2314.p: A saint wins a remission of tribute for a day and a night, which is in effect forever, since there is only one day and one night in time.

K2314.1.p: Something is borrowed for a day and a night, and the borrower then keeps it, arguing that the loan period is literally the whole of time.

K2314.2.p: A king is persuaded by a saint to remit tribute until Luan, a word that means both Monday and Doomsday, so the remission lasts forever.

K2314.2.1.p: A water-monster lets a saint set a cauldron over its head until Luan, meaning the cauldron stays there forever.

K2315.r: **Krohn Mann und Fuchs 61ff.; Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 324), 102 (ST 150); Halm Aesop No. 35; *Köhler-Bolte I l; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 35 No. *161, Espinosa Jr. No. 24.
K2315.p: A peasant has hidden a fox and promised not to reveal it, but when hunters ask, he says the fox went over the hill while pointing at the basket where it is hidden.

K2316.p: Thieves dig up a field and drain a tank after a miser says his gold is hidden there, hoping to find the treasure.

K2319.p: A miscellaneous category of deception by equivocation, covering cases not listed under the more specific motifs.

K2319.1.p: A man carries soil from Ireland and Scotland with him so that, wherever he stands, he can claim to have one foot in each country, which tricks people about where he really is.

K2319.2.p: A warrior challenges an opponent to single combat, then fights using his sons and grandsons, who he argues still count as himself because they belong to him.

K2319.3.p: A saint hides a fugitive from a king by giving an answer that is technically true, so the king leaves satisfied; later a suspicious trickster finds and arrests the fugitive anyway.

K2320.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 5; West Indies: Flowers 536.
K2320.p: A trick in which someone is deceived by being frightened, by a scare or fake danger set up to make them flee or give way.

K2321.r: *Type 1536; *Taylor MPh XV 225 n. 1; Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 73, 360; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2321.p: A corpse is propped up or displayed to scare people, so they believe a dead body is there or flee from it.

K2321.1.p: A man who killed his own mother uses her corpse, posed as if alive or as a scare, to extract gifts from people who are frightened of it.

K2321.2.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 69.
K2321.2.p: A dummy made to look like a corpse is set up to frighten people.

K2322.r: *Type 1536B; *BP III 485; **Pillet Das Fablaiu von les trois bossus menestrals (1901); *Taylor MPh XV 223 n. 3; *Chauvin VIII 72; *Herbert III 203; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 31f.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
K2322.p: A woman accidentally kills three hunchbacked brothers and gets a drunkard to throw them into a river; he keeps seeing them come back to life and, in his terror, drowns her hunchbacked husband.

K2323.r: *Type 104; *BP I 425; Dh IV 209; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 246—248.
K2323.p: In a war between wild and tame animals, the cat raises her tail, which the wild animals take for a gun, so they run away in fear.

K2323.1.p: Before a battle between birds and four-legged animals, the fox's raised tail is to signal the attack; gnats sting the fox under the tail, he drops it, and the animals flee.

K2323.2.r: Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 246—248; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 89.
K2323.2.p: A he-goat bleats and frightens animals that had gathered for a fight, so they all run off.

K2323.3.p: An old woman and a tiger each meet the other and both flee in terror.

K2324.p: A trickster hides from a strange animal by frightening it away, so the frightened bear falls from the tree and hurts itself.

K2324.1.p: A dangerous wild animal is frightened away when an ass brays.

K2325.p: A devil is frightened off by the threat that someone will bring his mother-in-law to him.

K2327.p: A wolf who has captured a ram is frightened by the ram playing a fiddle, and the ram escapes.

K2335.p: A parson is tricked into giving up his room by being told that a snake is in it.

K2336.p: A tiger is frightened away from a man who has taken refuge in a tree, by the man's stick and rope.

K2338.p: To drive away a parasitic priest, a wife tells him her husband has gone to get drunk and will kill him with a rice mortar when he returns, so the priest leaves in haste.

K2345.p: An ogre is frightened by a rustling sound, and a man frightens him by setting juniper on fire.

K2345.1.p: A tiger, hearing the clash of knives, believes it is a leak in the house of the being he fears, and flees.

K2345.2.p: A bear is scared away when a wife's sneezing sounds to it like something frightening, so the trickster escapes. The deceiver uses fear of a sudden noise to drive off an ogre.

K2346.p: A carved wooden figure is set up to look like a guard or warrior, and it scares invaders away. The deceiver tricks attackers into fleeing from a fake figure.

K2350.p: A general category of clever tricks and plans used to outwit an enemy in war.

K2351.p: Animals are used as helpers to win a battle, by being sent or made to attack or confuse the enemy.

K2351.1.r: **Krappe MPh XXIII 7ff.; **DeVries Arkiv för Nordisk Filologi XLVII 66ff.; Stender-Petersen Edda Nordisk Tidsskrift f. Litteraturforskning 1929, 145—64; Herrmann Saxo II 93; *Liebrecht 109f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
K2351.1.p: Birds are sent to fly into a besieged city carrying fire, which sets the city ablaze. The tale is set in Cirencester.

K2351.1.1.p: Foxes have burning material tied to their tails and are let loose to run through enemy cities and fields, burning them down.

K2351.2.r: *Fb “bi” IV 36b; Deutschbein I 256; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1249; *Liebrecht 75; India: *Thompson-Balys.
K2351.2.p: Bees are thrown into a fortified enclosure so they sting and drive out the enemies inside.

K2351.2.1.p: Bees are carried in a drum, and when the drum is struck or opened they swarm out and defeat the attacking army.

K2351.2.2.p: Ashes are magically changed into bees, wasps, scorpions and snakes, which drive the invading army away to help a hero.

K2351.3.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 528; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 246—248; Jewish: Neuman.
K2351.3.p: Mice and hogs are released among enemy war elephants and cavalry, causing them to panic and flee.

K2351.4.p: An elephant made drunk on palm toddy is sent to charge at the enemy.

K2351.5.p: Horses are frightened by the noise or sight of war instruments and are driven backward into the enemy's ranks.

K2351.5.1.p: Birds are used to frighten the enemy's horses so that the riders are thrown to the ground.

K2351.6.p: Wild horses have bags of stones tied to their tails and are driven into the enemy camp, causing a stampede.

K2351.6.1.p: A horse carrying a basket of powdered peppers is sent into the hostile camp, and the enemy is overcome.

K2351.6.1.1.p: Hot pepper mixed with flour is supplied to the enemy camp, and the enemy, thinking they have been poisoned, retreat.

K2351.7.p: A saint sends a wild fawn into the enemy army; all the soldiers follow it, and the enemy leader, who opposed the saint, is killed.

K2351.8.p: A huge rat is used as a strategy to get into an enemy city, by making a burrow through the walls.

K2352.p: Women spread shawls on the path of the enemy so that they become tangled in them, and the enemy is easily defeated.

K2352.1.p: Fresh animal hides are spread on the ground so the enemy slips and falls.

K2353.p: A defender drops treasure down from the walls onto the besiegers below, and the falling load crushes them. The enemy is lured into a deadly trap by greed.

K2354.p: Priests who secretly work for the enemy drag out a religious service so the city's defenders stay busy and distracted, letting the enemy destroy the city.

K2356.p: Women defending a place throw ashes into the eyes of attacking soldiers, blinding them so they are beaten.

K2356.1.p: A man is blinded when dust is thrown into his eyes, and while he cannot see, a thief robs him.

K2357.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Panchatantra III 5 (tr. Ryder 328ff.).
K2357.p: A character gets into an enemy's camp or castle by pretending to be someone harmless, so they can spy, attack, or take it from inside.

K2357.0.1.p: A character disguises themselves in order to spy on the enemy.

K2357.0.2.p: The rightful owner of a castle is let back in while disguised as a monk, but the conqueror has taken it in his absence. The conqueror had been told the owner was dead, and the owner uses this disguise to get inside and retake or seize it.

K2357.1.r: Herrmann Saxo II 210; Irish myth: Cross; Collingwood Sagabook of the Viking Society X (1) 134.
K2357.1.p: A character disguises themselves as a musician to get into an enemy camp.

K2357.2.p: A character disguises themselves as a pilgrim to get into an enemy camp or castle.

K2357.3.p: A character disguises themselves as an old man to get into an enemy camp.

K2357.4.p: A rabbi pretends to be dead so that he is carried out of the besieged city, then gets close to the enemy once outside.

K2357.5.p: Weapons are hidden in a disguise, such as in a cart or bundle, so that they can be carried past enemy guards into the enemy camp.

K2357.6.p: A woman disguises herself as a man to get into an enemy camp, and while inside she kills the enemy king.

K2357.7.p: A character wears the clothes of an enemy they have killed to get into the enemy's castle.

K2357.8.p: A character disguises themselves as a woman to get into an enemy camp or castle.

K2357.9.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Grote I 276.
K2357.9.p: A character disguises themselves as a beggar or poor person to get into an enemy camp or castle, or to spy.

K2357.10.r: (Cf. K1817.4.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
K2357.10.p: A character disguises themselves as a merchant to get into an enemy castle.

K2357.11.p: A character disguises themselves as a leper to get into an enemy camp.

K2357.12.p: A character disguises themselves as a carpenter or other tradesman to get into an enemy camp.

K2357.13.p: A character disguises themselves as a juggler or performer to get into an enemy camp.

K2357.14.p: A person disguises himself as a common peasant (churl) in order to get into the enemy's hall or stronghold unnoticed.

K2357.15.p: Warriors hide inside baskets strapped to oxen, and the oxen are driven into the enemy camp pretending to carry food; the warriors then jump out and capture the camp.

K2358.p: A man disguised as an animal is sent among the enemy, and the trick is arranged so that the other side is the first to shed blood.

K2361.p: A woman avoids being harmed by soldiers by greeting them cheerfully instead of showing fear.

K2362.r: *DeVries Arkiv f. Nordisk Filologi XLVII 56ff., 67ff.; Wilken Geschichte der Kreuzzüge II 321ff.; Herrmann Saxo II 126; Icelandic: Boberg.
K2362.p: A castle is taken when an attacker pretends to be dead and is then carried or let inside, where he can open the way for his men.

K2363.p: Spies falsely report that the enemy is weak, so the commander launches an attack too early and is defeated.

K2364.r: English: Malory X 32; Greek: Iliad XVI 84.
K2364.p: A fireship (a burning vessel sent among them) sets the enemy's ships on fire.

K2364.1.p: The enemy is defeated when the forest where they are hiding is set on fire.

K2365.p: The enemy is tricked or forced into abandoning a siege and going away.

K2365.1.r: Grimm Deutsche Sagen 460, 470, 504; Von der Leyen Sagenbuch III 1 No. 75, 2 No. 278; Lübbing Friesische Sagen 65; Laport FFC LXXXIV 182; Herodotus I ch. 22; Ovid Fasti VI 349ff.; Japanese: Ikeda.
K2365.1.p: The besiegers are made to lift the siege by pretending that the besieged city has plenty of food and does not need to surrender.

K2365.2.p: The attackers show off their wealth by shooting golden apples over the walls, which persuades the city to surrender.

K2365.3.p: Enemy soldiers are won over and desert to the other side because the king displays great wealth and generosity.

K2366.p: A trickster falsely promises to surrender a city to the enemy; when the enemy enters, they are attacked and defeated.

K2366.1.p: A trickster pretends to admit defeat and invites the enemy and their friends to the fort for a ceremony, then attacks them there.

K2367.p: An attacker scatters beads inside a protective hedge so that the defenders tear the hedge apart looking for them, letting the attacker in.

K2368.p: The enemy is tricked into overestimating their opponents' strength and so retreats.

K2368.1.p: The sound of artillery is faked to frighten the enemy.

K2368.1.1.p: People run a wagon back and forth over a corduroy (log) bridge so that it sounds like artillery firing.

K2368.2.p: Sounds of a staged mock battle frighten away the attacking force.

K2368.2.1.p: Sounds of battle coming from a playhouse frighten away the attacking soldiers.

K2368.3.p: A fake doctor gives medicine to a king's army, which makes the soldiers appear sick and carried off on litters. The invading enemy, seeing this, flees in the belief that a plague has struck.

K2368.4.p: Besiegers are tricked into lifting their siege by making them believe the people inside the city have received reinforcements.

K2369.p: A general heading for miscellaneous war tricks and military strategies that deceive an enemy, not covered by the more specific categories.

K2369.1.p: A raider pretends to be a poor beggar so that the king will underestimate his real strength.

K2369.2.p: A group of warriors is hidden in a pit on the battlefield and comes out only during the fighting, surprising the enemy.

K2369.2.1.p: The largest part of the fleet stays hidden and does not come out until late in the battle, when it can turn the outcome.

K2369.2.2.p: A treacherous king takes part in the battle only after he sees which side is likely to win, then joins the winners.

K2369.3.p: The treacherous ruler of a besieged city sends his own sons to hand the city over to the enemy.

K2369.4.p: A person asks for payment to be postponed in order to gain time to gather reinforcements.

K2369.5.p: Besieging enemies are drowned when the river is diverted to flood their position.

K2369.6.p: A city is captured by turning a river away from its course through the city, so the riverbed becomes empty and the enemy soldiers march through it into the city.

K2369.7.p: A pretended wish to discuss peace is used as cover while secretly gathering reinforcements.

K2369.8.p: A cauldron holding a lit torch is brought into the enemy camp, supposedly to serve food. When the torch is uncovered, it signals the attack.

K2369.9.p: Fairy mist is mistaken by the enemy for smoke from their own burning ships.

K2369.11.p: A hero creates confusion in the enemy camp at night, so the soldiers attack one another, believing enemies have infiltrated their camp.

K2369.12.p: Poisoned food is sent to the enemy camp to kill those who eat it.

K2369.12.1.p: Enemy leaders are invited to a banquet and then poisoned.

K2369.13.p: Thorny brambles are piled in a river crossing (ford) to stop enemies from crossing.

K2370.p: A catch-all heading for deceptions that do not fit the more specific categories.

K2371.p: Deceiving God, the saints, the gods, or fate themselves.

K2371.1.r: *Type 330; *BP I 343, II 189, III 303; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 210; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 164, 349; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2371.1.p: A trickster gets into heaven by deceiving its gatekeepers or guardians.

K2371.1.1.p: The trickster asks Saint Peter for permission to pick up a cap or leather apron that he has thrown just inside the gate, and so gets in.

K2371.1.2.p: The trickster demands back a gift he once gave to Saint Peter as charity, then sits on it inside heaven as if it were his own property.

K2371.1.3.p: The trickster throws a magic wishing sack through the gate and wishes himself inside it, so he is carried into heaven.

K2371.1.4.p: The trickster slips into heaven by sitting in Saint Peter's chair.

K2371.1.5.p: The trickster sneaks into heaven by slipping in right behind a holy person who is allowed through.

K2371.1.6.p: The trickster gets an angel drunk, and the angel, while intoxicated, tells a woman how to get into heaven.

K2371.2.p: A person tricks the gods or God into helping him avoid a fate or destiny that was prophesied for him.

K2371.3.p: A person words a request to God so cleverly that one wish grants wealth, descendants, and restored sight together: he wants to see his great-grandsons playing in the street and eating cakes from golden dishes from the top floor of his mansion.

K2371.4.p: A dog is sent ahead so that its owner does not have to see his husband transformed into something else.

K2373.p: Two enemies are reconciled through gifts, but the son of one secretly tells the other that the gifts were sent by the one who receives them, so the trick reveals the truth.

K2376.r: Anderson FFC XLII 360; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 924B*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1637*.
K2376.p: At a meal, each guest gives his neighbor a slap on the ears, and a soldier passes the slap on to the king only to hand it back to the courtier who gave it to him.

K2377.p: Someone gets into a walled garden by swimming up a stream that flows in from outside.

K2378.p: A combatant pretends to give way for a time, gaining an advantage over the enemy.

K2378.1.p: A player is allowed to win the first game on purpose, so that he will be willing to play for bigger stakes.

K2378.2.p: A warrior agrees to flee in order to win later in the fight.

K2378.3.p: Enemies are fooled by a pretended flight, drawn into a position where they can be beaten.

K2378.4.p: A fighter holds back his own ammunition until the enemy has used up all of his.

K2378.5.p: A hero sleeps through the first part of a battle and only joins in later.

K2381.p: A ruler starts a war to distract his people from the bad way he is governing.

K2382.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 281 No. 25; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
K2382.p: One animal harms another through a trick or false pretense.

K2382.1.p: A bird tricks another bird into letting it pull out its feathers.

K2382.2.p: A dwarf deer glues another animal's eyes shut with paste, then pretends hunters are approaching so the animal panics or is harmed.

K2383.p: A cat is tied to the tail of a stubborn horse so that the cat's clawing and fright force the horse to move.

K2384.p: A man is tricked into becoming someone's sworn brother so that he will help that person against the person's own mother.

K2385.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 193ff., 352f.; India: Thompson-Balys.
K2385.p: A demon possesses a person and will not leave until its wishes are granted.

K2388.p: Someone tries to kill another by throwing a knife at them.
